title: Quantifying Regulatory Bottlenecks in South Korea’s Clinical Trial Approval Process Through an Analytic Hierarchy Process Framework
abstract: Purpose: Drug lag is a critical issue limiting South Korea’s pharmaceutical competitiveness and patient access, and it has been linked to delays in the Investigational New Drug (IND) review process. This study aimed to identify key barriers affecting IND review efficiency in South Korea by analyzing real-world industry experience and to propose concrete strategic actions to mitigate drug lag. Methods: We employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. First, we used grounded theory to identify problematic factors within the IND process through semi-structured interviews. We then applied the Analytic Hierarchy Process to evaluate these factors, followed by a quadrant analysis of importance and urgency to identify top-priority tasks. Results: Three core categories (rationality and patient-centricity, professional review, and operational efficiency), were identified as key domains for enhancing IND efficiency. Rationality and patient-centricity emerged as the most important and urgent criterion, followed closely by professional review. Within rationality and patient-centricity, four sub-criteria placed in the first quadrant (highly important and highly urgent): integration of patient needs into evaluation, global regulatory harmonization, acceptance of scientific evidence for new modalities, and adoption of overseas regulatory standards. Two sub-criteria within professional review (expert team review and standardized review guidelines) were also pinpointed in the first quadrant. Although operational efficiency ranked lowest, simplified Korean translation requirements stood out as the most critical factor within this category. Conclusion: Transitioning from focusing on procedural speed toward embracing regulatory flexibility to enhance scientific rationality and patient access is a viable pathway for mitigating drug lag in South Korea. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Negotiation impasses as meaningful outcomes: How AI is changing the cost structure of walking away
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often expected to improve negotiation by strengthening information processing and analytical consistency. We argue that its effects on impasses are more selective. Extending the impasse cause, type, and resolution (ICTR) model, we distinguish two pathways. The first pathway is analytical augmentation: AI can reduce unwanted impasses caused by misunderstanding, poor option generation, and coordination failure. The second pathway runs through behavioral flexibility: Humans sometimes reach mutually acceptable agreements through aspiration adjustment, face-saving, and relational repair. Systems configured to apply stable decision thresholds and optimize focal-party outcomes without relational objectives reduce this flexibility and can thereby increase forced impasses. Which pathway dominates depends on AI's role as advisor or counterpart; its objective, training, and prompt; and whether agreement primarily requires analytical problem solving or interpersonal flexibility. These predictions concern system behavior, not whether AI experiences fatigue or social pressure: systems can be designed to respond to relational cues without experiencing them. Wanted impasses depend on both parties' underlying preferences, which AI does not change; AI instead helps negotiators recognize incompatibility sooner and justify walking away more openly. AI therefore changes the composition and meaning of impasses rather than uniformly increasing or decreasing agreement. Remaining impasses may reveal genuine incompatibility, but they may also reflect misspecified objectives or failures to encode principals' relational and economic costs. © 2026 The Authors

title: When AI wears a face: How AI appearance shapes intentionality attributions in service success and failure
abstract: Customer-facing AI agents are becoming frontline service interfaces, yet firms still face a consequential design question: should these agents look human-like or robot-like? This research examines how AI agent appearance shapes consumers' intentionality attributions in AI-mediated service encounters and how these inferences translate into satisfaction and future AI use intention. Drawing on attribution theory and anthropomorphism research, we propose that human-like and robot-like appearances do not have uniformly positive or negative effects; rather, their effects depend on consumers’ evaluations of service outcomes and their familiarity with AI. A 2 (AI agent appearance: human-like vs. robot-like) × 2 (service outcome: success vs. failure) between-subjects experiment was conducted with 350 U.S. participants in an airline customer-service chatbot context. Results reveal a reversal across outcome evaluations. When consumers experienced service success, robot-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than human-like AI, particularly among those with lower AI familiarity. When consumers experienced service failure, human-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than robot-like AI, although this effect weakened and reversed among consumers with higher AI familiarity. Perceived intentionality, in turn, increased satisfaction and future AI use intention, supporting a moderated mediation process. These findings reframe AI appearance as an attributional cue rather than a simple humanization strategy and demonstrate that consumers interpret the same AI appearance differently depending on how they evaluate the service encounter. Managerially, the results suggest that firms should not assume that increasing human likeness will universally improve customer responses. Instead, marketers should consider how different customer segments, particularly those varying in AI familiarity, are likely to interpret and respond to AI appearance cues across diverse service experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Towards a datafication framework for higher education institutions student success: A systematic review
abstract: Customer success is key to customer retention. Seemingly, this is equally true in the higher education space, as students are customers of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) and, therefore, the primary reason for HEIs' existence. In view of this, it is important to understand and improve student success, which is dependent on different data indicators. Being guided by student success data indicators in HEI administration is necessary as it’s beneficial to both HEIs and their students, as through it, students can complete their qualification on time, and HEIs generate revenue. In the South African context, with its high unemployment rate and high dropout rates, understanding HEI student success is vital. However, HEIs are accustomed to collecting data rather than utilizing it for transformational activities, there has been an increase in research/publications on student success datafication frameworks in higher education in South Africa. However, these studies in isolation do not give the complete picture. This paper aims to systematically review the South African-based HEI student success data-related frameworks, including their underlying principles, trends, challenges, gaps, and future opportunities for improvement. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses method was used. Based on a clearly outlined search strategy, 508 publication abstracts were considered for review. Of these abstracts, 40 were selected for further review based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and thereafter, 16 publications were included in the final review. The systematic review findings indicated that mostly data point indicators exist as compared to datafication frameworks. Furthermore, limited studies have been conducted on private higher education institutions in South Africa. Additionally, public sector studies have focused on first-year students; therefore, no segmentation. The implication of this study is that it sets the tone for future work within datafication, student success, and higher education, potentially enabling HEIs to approach transformational data. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: When and why are negotiators overly pessimistic? The psychology of under-trust innegotiation
abstract: Research on negotiation has devoted considerable attention to the risks of misplaced trust, particularly the possibility that negotiators may be exploited by deceptive counterparts. Less attention has been given to the opposite form of trust miscalibration: under-trust, and particularly, unwarranted pessimism regarding counterparts' honesty. This review focuses on such undue distrust and proposes a misperceived motivations account to explain its emergence. According to this account, negotiators' excessive distrust stems from an asymmetry between the motives that negotiators attribute to their counterparts and the motives that actually guide those counterparts’ behavior. When deciding whether to behave honestly, negotiators are driven not only by self-interest but also by concerns about moral self-image and anticipated moral emotions, which constrain dishonesty. However, when deciding whether counterparts are honest, negotiators assume that their counterparts are primarily motivated by self-interest and fail to foresee the constraining moral-identity concerns. We integrate evidence from the literature on negotiation, trust, and moral psychology to explain why pessimism is especially likely to emerge and persist in competitive bargaining contexts, highlight circumstances that may attenuate or amplify it, and identify implications for theory and research, alongside practical inferences for fostering truthful disclosure and credible honesty in negotiation. © 2026 The Authors

title: Do users trade performance for eco-visibility? Digital pollution awareness and stated preferences for social media platform configurations
abstract: Digital platforms face growing pressure to demonstrate environmental responsibility, yet users’ preferences for eco-visible features remain underexplored relative to functional attributes. Using a full-factorial rating-based within-subject conjoint survey with a UK sample (N = 345) recruited to match national census distributions of age, sex, and ethnicity, combined with hierarchical linear modelling, this study decomposes willingness to use social media platforms across four attributes: media quality, loading speed, eco-visibility, and advertising frequency. Results show that technical attributes — media quality (relative importance = 34.9%) and loading speed (34.5%) — jointly dominate eco-visibility (8.1%), revealing a persistent performance-over-sustainability hierarchy in elicited trade-off preferences. A full 4 × 4 cross-level moderation analysis incorporating all 16 attribute-by-moderator interactions with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction identifies advertising receptivity — rather than green self-identity or environmental awareness — as the strongest individual-difference moderator, showing a dual pattern: it simultaneously attenuates the reduced-ads utility and amplifies the loading-speed premium. Green self-identity attenuates the media-quality premium but does not amplify eco-visibility utility; none of the eco-visibility moderations — by green self-identity, social comparison orientation, or digital environmental attitude — is confirmed. Exploratory benefit segmentation identifies three preference profiles — Technical Optimizers, Eco-Aware Pragmatists, and Ad-Averse Minimalists — revealing a sign reversal in eco-visibility utility across profiles. Theoretical and practical implications for sustainable platform design, multiple-comparison practices in conjoint moderation research, and green digital marketing are discussed. © 2026 The Authors

title: Why they come (back): Motive clusters of seasonal employees and their multiple workplace commitments
abstract: This study develops seasonal employee typologies for the Alpine tourism and hospitality sector by connecting motives for seasonal work with varying levels of different workplace commitments and return intention. Conceptualizing the destination as an analytical lens rather than merely context, this study examines how employees’ social, economic, and leisure motives affect their commitment to the organization, coworkers, job, and destination. Drawing on survey data from 381 hospitality employees in an Alpine destination in Austria, cluster analysis, analysis of variance, and post hoc tests were applied. The analysis identified four employee clusters (lifestyle seekers, dedicated professionals, practical earners, and social contributors) that significantly differ in their motivational profiles, commitment patterns, and demographic characteristics. The findings demonstrate that commitment among seasonal employees extends beyond the organization and differs across motive-based segments. These differences may shape guest interactions and service delivery, ultimately impacting service quality, visitor satisfaction, and overall destination performance. By integrating a motive-based segmentation with a multi-target commitment perspective, this study advances research on seasonal tourism employment and underscores how destination-specific contexts impact employee attitudes and behaviors. The results offer insights for adapting recruitment and retention strategies to distinct employee profiles in seasonal hospitality settings. © 2026 The Authors

title: Documentor mindsets: Considerations when contributing learning resources for software development technologies
abstract: Many volunteers contribute learning resources for software development technologies online. We interviewed 26 volunteer contributors, i.e. documentors, to understand why and how they design, create, and contribute software documentation. From a qualitative analysis of our interviews, we identified sixteen considerations that documentors have during the contribution process, along three dimensions, namely motivations, topic selection techniques, and styling objectives. We grouped conceptually related considerations to elicit five mindsets that documentors have during the creation of software documentation. We contribute a framework for describing documentor mindsets, and their associated considerations across the three dimensions. This framework provides a structure and vocabulary for reasoning about the documentation contribution process. Based on the framework, we surface the need to reconsider existing perspectives of the documentation creation process, including the role of the documentor and metrics to measure documentation quality. Our insights can inform software documentation creation tools and future research on user generated learning resources. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Not alone: How group photos enhance audience responses to virtual influencers
abstract: Although marketers increasingly use virtual influencers to engage consumers, concerns about authenticity continue to limit their effectiveness. This research examines whether group photos can make virtual influencers appear more socially connected and authentic, thereby improving audience responses. We propose that, compared with no-person images or solo photos, group photos provide visual social cues that place virtual influencers in recognizable interpersonal contexts and make them appear more socially connected in shared experiences. Across one large-scale field study and two experiments, we test this proposition. Study 1 draws on a large-scale Instagram dataset of 17,878 posts from 109 virtual influencers collected between 2023 and 2026, with the main analyses based on 8558 non-video posts and finds that group photos receive higher post engagement than no-person images and solo photos. Study 2 provides controlled experimental evidence consistent with this effect and suggests that perceived social connectedness and perceived authenticity sequentially account for the relationship between group photos and favorable post evaluations. Study 3 identifies virtual influencer type as an important boundary condition: group photos are more effective for human-like virtual influencers, whereas this advantage weakens for cartoon-like virtual influencers. These findings contribute to research on virtual influencer humanization and authenticity by showing that visual social connectedness can make virtual influencers appear more socially embedded, more authentic, and more favorably evaluated. title: Understanding grey sheep users in recommender systems: A systematic and critical review of detection, modeling, and evaluation
abstract: Grey sheep users (GSUs), characterized by weak or unstable alignment with the broader user population, remain a challenge in collaborative filtering-based recommender systems. Despite extensive efforts devoted to their detection and treatment, a clear and consistent understanding of GSUs is still lacking. Existing studies typically adopt model-dependent definitions and often assume that GSUs necessarily reduce recommendation quality. This paper presents a systematic and critical review of GSUs, covering their definition, detection strategies, modeling paradigms, and evaluation practices. We revisit the classical similarity-based interpretation and show that the effect of GSUs depends on model design rather than being inherently harmful. Based on this observation, we introduce a refined conceptual perspective that describes GSUs as users with consistently misaligned preference patterns, and further propose a dynamic view that distinguishes between short-term irregular behavior and stable preference differences. We then provide a comprehensive taxonomy of existing approaches, including detection-dependent methods and detection-free strategies, and analyze their underlying assumptions and limitations. We further show that the form in which a detection result is expressed constrains which handling strategies are available, and that this correspondence is rarely exploited in practice. A key finding of this study is that current research is limited by weak evaluation practices. In particular, the absence of ground truth, inconsistent definitions, and dependence on aggregate performance metrics lead to circular reasoning and unreliable conclusions. Finally, we outline future research directions toward more robust modeling frameworks and user-centered evaluation protocols, with the aim of establishing a clearer conceptual foundation and guiding the development of more reliable and inclusive recommender systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Understanding event tourism competitiveness: From stakeholder-constructed attributes to visitor valuation
abstract: This study examines event tourism competitiveness by integrating stakeholder-constructed competitiveness attributes with visitor valuation. Using Hong Kong as the primary empirical context and London as a validation context, the study combines thematic analysis, confirmatory composite analysis (CCA), and a discrete choice experiment (DCE). The thematic analysis identifies six competitiveness dimensions, including Resource Synergies, a novel dimension capturing cross-sector and cross-boundary integration. The DCE results show that Resource Synergies functions as a direct destination selection criterion for MICE participants, whereas its direct effect is not significant among leisure-event visitors. Professionalism and Facilities emerges as a universal competitiveness driver for both groups, while leisure-event visitors prioritise experiential distinctiveness and international content. These findings advance event tourism competitiveness research by explaining how competitiveness attributes are constructed by stakeholders and differentially valued in the event tourism context. title: AI-driven cultural and creative packaging design and user purchase intention: AI-disclosure perspective based on SEM-ANN hybrid analysis
abstract: Generative AI has introduced new possibilities for cultural and creative packaging design. This study examines how cultural symbol compatibility, design innovation, and aesthetic experience are associated with purchase intention through functional value, emotional value, social value, and epistemic value. Perceived factual disclosure and perceived narrative disclosure are further incorporated as moderators. A combined SEM-ANN approach is used to examine the linear relationships and nonlinear predictive importance of the study variables. The results indicate that the three perceived design attributes are indirectly associated with user purchase intention through multiple consumption-value pathways, although statistical support varies across the specific indirect effects. The principal theoretical contribution is to identify AI disclosure as a differentiated boundary condition in the conversion of consumption value into purchase intention. Perceived factual disclosure does not significantly moderate the relationships involving functional value or social value. Perceived narrative disclosure is associated with a weaker relationship between emotional value and purchase intention and a stronger relationship between epistemic value and purchase intention. The study extends research on AI-assisted cultural packaging and provides practical implications for AI disclosure in high-end product contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When culture meets citizenship: The moderating role of instructional leadership
abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of organizational culture and instructional leadership in shaping the organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) of high school teachers, as well as to explain the social mechanisms underlying this relationship. Specifically, this study answers questions regarding the extent to which organizational culture influences teachers' OCB, the role of instructional leadership in this relationship, and why statistically significant patterns emerge in the context of school organizations. The study uses a sequential explanatory mixed methods design, with the quantitative stage conducted through a survey of 285 public and private high school teachers in Gresik Regency, analyzed using AMOS-based Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The qualitative stage was carried out through semi structured interviews to deepen and explain the quantitative findings. The results show that organizational culture has a significant effect on teachers' OCB, while instructional leadership has no significant direct or moderating effect. This indicates that cultural factors play a more dominant role than formal leadership practices in influencing teachers’ discretionary behaviors.Qualitative findings explain that teachers' OCB develops as a result of the internalization of collective values, trust, and peer relationships that are deeply rooted in school culture, while instructional leadership is perceived more as an administrative practice than an empowering pedagogical relationship. This study makes a theoretical contribution by repositioning organizational culture as the main mechanism of social exchange in the formation of teachers' OCB, as well as emphasizing the contextual and contingent nature of instructional leadership in educational organizations. In addition, the study highlights the importance of strengthening value-based school culture to sustain teachers’ professional commitment and collaboration. These findings enrich the study of OCB and instructional leadership through the epistemological integration of quantitative and qualitative approaches. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: What drives versus what is required: Sufficient and necessary conditions for consumer intention in an unfamiliar wellness service
abstract: Despite the growing importance of wellness and health tourism, little is known about how individuals who have never experienced thermal spa treatments form intentions toward such services. This study addresses this gap by mobilizing an extended Theory of Planned Behavior framework enriched with subjective knowledge and expected health benefits. Based on a large-scale survey of French non-users, we combine Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling and Necessary Condition Analysis to examine both enabling and constraining mechanisms of intention formation. The results show that all predictors contribute positively to intention, with subjective norm emerging as the most influential factor. However, the necessity analysis reveals a markedly different causal structure: only subjective norm, expected health benefits, and perceived behavioral control establish threshold conditions that must be satisfied for higher levels of intention to occur. In contrast, subjective knowledge and attitude, although significant, do not operate as indispensable conditions. These findings reveal an asymmetry between the factors that raise intention and those that set the threshold for it. They suggest that, in this context, intention depends on socially mediated validation, not on individual evaluation alone. For managers, the priority is the conditions that must be met for intention to form - social legitimacy, credible health benefits, and feasibility - rather than interventions, such as information or persuasion, that intensify intention only once those conditions are in place. © 2026 The Authors

title: How does empowering leadership shape employee service innovation behavior? The roles of employee adaptability and job crafting
abstract: Based on conservation of resources theory, this paper examines how empowering leadership (EL) predicts service innovation behavior (SIB) through employee adaptability. The present paper also investigates job crafting (JCR) as a moderator between EL and employee adaptability. The proposed moderated mediation model was tested with multiple sources of data in the hotel industry. The results based on partial least squares structural equation modeling suggest that EL boosts employee adaptability that in turn engenders heightened SIB. The positive effect of EL on adaptability is stronger among employees high on JCR. More importantly, the positive indirect impact of EL on SIB via employee adaptability is stronger among employees who craft their jobs and optimize the work environment. The originality of this study is evident in its focus on employee adaptability and JCR as critical factors that shape the relationship between EL and SIB. Furthermore, it offers significant theoretical and practical implications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Self-awareness and negotiations
abstract: How does directing attention toward oneself, or self-awareness, affect one's performance in a negotiation? This article reviews recent research on self-awareness and discusses the implications of these findings for a negotiator's actions before, during, and after a negotiation. Before a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's choice to negotiate in the first place, one's planned strategy, and one's preparedness to manage difficulties. During a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's ability to adapt one's tactics and make ethical choices, and outward expressions of self-awareness may affect one's counterpart's perceptions of oneself. After a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's self-reflection and ability to improve. Altogether, these findings shed light on a variety of possible effects of self-awareness on negotiations, and point to directions for future research. © 2026 The Author

title: When does inconsistency help? The nonlinear effect of AI summary-rating inconsistency on consumer purchase intention
abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in e-commerce platforms, AI-generated review summaries have emerged as an important information source for consumers. A growing concern is AI summary-rating inconsistency, defined as the degree to which the evaluative valence conveyed by an AI-generated review summary diverges from the aggregate product rating displayed on the same product page. However, prior research has paid limited attention to this specific form of cross-format evaluative cue conflict. This research investigates the nonlinear relationship between AI summary-rating inconsistency and consumer purchase intention and the psychological processes underlying this relationship. Using a mixed-method design, Study 1 analyzes 2654 product observations from Newegg and provides association-based marketplace evidence using nonlinear regression. Study 2 employs a 3 (AI summary-rating inconsistency: low vs. medium vs. high) × 2 (RIR feedback cue: high approval vs. high disapproval) between-subjects experiment to examine perceived trust in AI and cognitive load, as well as the moderating role of RIR. The findings show an inverted U-shaped pattern: moderate inconsistency is more persuasive than either low or high inconsistency. Perceived trust in AI and cognitive load operate as two parallel psychological processes, with trust transmitting a positive pathway and cognitive load transmitting a negative pathway. In addition, RIR serves as an important boundary condition by strengthening the trust pathway and weakening the cognitive-load pathway when summary-level user feedback is favorable. These findings contribute to research on AI-mediated review information, trust in AI, and consumer decision making, and offer practical implications for optimizing AI-generated review summaries in online retail. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Clouds and crowds: A meta-analysis of air pollution and tourism demand-experience dynamics
abstract: Empirical evidence on how air quality shapes tourist responses remains inconsistent. Drawing on a meta-analytical framework and cognitive-relational theory, this study synthesizes the effects of air pollution on demand- and experience-related outcomes across the travel process. The analysis pools 974 estimates from 58 demand studies and 92 estimates from 8 experience studies on destination-side pollution, as well as 483 estimates from 17 demand studies on origin-side pollution. After correcting for publication bias, air pollution has a mild, partly remediable adverse effect on tourism demand, while evidence for tourist experience is less consistent. The demand effect remains robust across destination-only and origin-destination settings, whereas origin-side air pollution has a negligible, statistically insignificant positive effect. Meta-regression results indicate that between-study heterogeneity is mainly driven by international tourism contexts, online word-of-mouth measures, PM2.5 or air quality index measures, and long-run effects. This meta-analysis provides actionable implications for scenario-based planning, forecasting and econometric practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Home economics and sustainable futures: A systematic literature review
abstract: This study aims to systematically examine the development, thematic structure, and research trends in Home Economics from 2015 to 2024, with an emphasis on its contribution to a sustainable future. Through the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach with Scopus indexed article data sources, a total of 22 articles were analyzed using a combination of thematic synthesis methods and bibliometric visualization through the VOSviewer tool to identify developing research patterns, relationships, and clusters. The results of the analysis show that Home Economics research has shifted its focus from traditional discussions of household skills to a multidisciplinary approach that emphasizes sustainable education, family economic literacy, health, and social responsibility. The keyword mapping process uncovered to have five major clusters—education, sustainability, health, students, and digital literacy—that intersect to have within the broader framework of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). Quantitatively, publication trends show a significant increase over the past three years (2021–2024), reflecting to have the increasing global interest in issues concerning welfare and sustainability in the field of education. The main findings also suggest that Home Economics is increasingly being positioned as a transformative discipline that integrates economic literacy, environmental awareness and social responsibility. Theoretically, the results of this study expand the framework of Home Economics as a humanistic and ecological science, while practically, the implications confirm the need for contextual, collaborative, and project-based curriculum and pedagogy innovations to address the challenges of the 21st century. These implications are important for curriculum developers, educators, and policymakers in integrating sustainability values into the education system. In conclusion, this study confirms that Home Economics has a strategic role in shaping a sustainable future through education. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: AI for guilt, human for encouragement? The interaction effects of creator type and emotional appeal on green purchase intention
abstract: Green advertising inherently embeds emotional appeal to drive consumer responses. The proliferation of generative AI has shifted the creator from solely human-dominated to a hybrid landscape where AI-generated and human-generated coexist. Drawing on schema theory and attribution theory, this study investigates the interaction effects between creator type (AI-generated vs. human-generated) and emotional appeal (guilt vs. encouragement) in green advertising on consumers' green purchase intention. Three experiments, including two scenario-based lab experiments (one with a Chinese sample and one with an international English-speaking online sample) and a field experiment with actual purchase data from a live-streaming retailer, provide consistent support for our hypotheses. The results reveal that AI-generated guilt appeal elicits higher consumers’ green purchase intention than the human-generated one, mediated by reduced green moral pressure (a burden-alleviating pathway); conversely, human-generated encouragement appeal elicits higher purchase intention than the AI-generated one, mediated by green self-efficacy (a capacity-enhancing pathway). Furthermore, attribution focus moderates these interaction effects: behavioral attribution strengthens the advantage of AI-generated guilt appeal, whereas personal attribution strengthens the advantage of human-generated encouragement appeal. These findings move beyond the adversarial AI versus human comparison by demonstrating an interaction between disclosed creator type and emotional appeal in green advertising. The framework contributes to green advertising literature by integrating creator type and emotional appeal through an interaction logic, advancing schema theory and attribution theory in the green marketing context. The findings also provide actionable guidance for retailers on strategically collaborating AI and human in green advertising creation to maximize persuasive effectiveness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: A longitudinal study of supervisor support as a moderator in maintaining work engagement during working from home: A moderated moderated-mediation model
abstract: Maintaining employee work engagement during extended periods of work from home (WFH) is essential for sustaining productivity. Although prior research highlights the detrimental effects of job stress and imbalanced work demands on burnout and engagement, few studies explore how supervisor support mitigates these effects over time. This study examines such relationships as WFH progresses. Panel data from 145 participants, collected at multiple time points over a 10-month period, reveal that as the WFH period extends, supervisor support becomes increasingly effective in alleviating the negative impact of job demands and perceived stress on burnout. This reduction in burnout subsequently contributes to the sustained work engagement of employees. These findings offer valuable insights into the role of supervisor support during extended WFH periods and provide recommendations for managing burnout and maintaining engagement in remote work environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The impact of AI-based information system integration embedded with ESG considerations on perceived overall organizational performance
abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-based information system integration, conceptualized as a perceived integration capability embedded in organizational workflows, is associated with perceived overall organizational performance. It focuses on the mediating roles of dynamic capability activities, employee AI action readiness, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices, defined as routinized monitoring, disclosure, and governance activities. Using survey data from 496 employees in firms with AI systems, the proposed framework is tested through structural equation modeling and supplemented by machine-learning-based predictive analysis. The results indicate that AI-based information system integration is associated with perceived overall organizational performance mainly through indirect pathways. It is positively associated with employees’ awareness of AI-supported sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring activities and with their readiness concerning the practical applicability of AI-supported information in daily work, both of which are associated with stronger ESG practices and higher perceived overall organizational performance. Its direct association with ESG practices is positive but weaker than the indirect pathways through dynamic capability activities and employee AI action readiness. Bootstrapped analyses support parallel and sequential indirect effects, while multi-group analyses show that the overall relationship pattern is stable across small and medium-sized enterprises and large enterprises. This study contributes by shifting attention from AI adoption to the perceived integration of AI into organizational workflows and by identifying dynamic capability activities, employee AI action readiness, and ESG practices as complementary pathways linking AI integration to perceived overall organizational performance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Engaging consumers with varying budgets for battery electric vehicles in the post-subsidy era
abstract: China's BEV market must now engage the early majority to sustain broader penetration in the post-subsidy era. However, existing research inadequately explores how manufacturer-led strategies and psychological factors differentially shape the adoption decisions of this emerging consumer segment, particularly across varying budget levels. To address this gap, this study develops an integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) model to jointly examine the effects of psychological determinants and multiple manufacturer-led strategies on BEV adoption. The analysis draws on 1200 stated-preference responses from prospective BEV buyers in Beijing and Shenzhen. Findings indicate that budget level significantly drives consumer heterogeneity in psychological drivers, while the relative effectiveness of manufacturer-led strategies remains consistent across groups: bundled insurance packages yield the largest marginal effects, followed by advanced intelligent driving services and lottery-based discounts, with price discounts being the least effective. title: When more becomes less: Cumulative eWOM volume and automobile sales
abstract: Consumers increasingly rely on electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) when purchasing high-involvement products, yet whether an expanding stock of accumulated reviews continues to benefit product performance remains unclear. This study investigates the relationship between cumulative eWOM volume and automobile sales using a panel dataset from the Chinese automobile market covering 2013 to 2025. Contrary to the conventional view that more reviews are always beneficial, we find that cumulative eWOM volume is negatively associated with subsequent automobile sales. A 1% increase in cumulative eWOM volume is associated with approximately a 0.206% decrease in automobile sales. This negative association is stronger when accumulated ratings exhibit greater heterogeneity, measured by both cumulative rating variance and entropy, providing evidence consistent with an information overload explanation. In addition, greater cumulative eWOM volume is associated with fewer newly generated reviews, which partially mediates its negative association with automobile sales. The negative association is weaker when cumulative eWOM ratings are higher, when a larger proportion of cumulative reviews is recent, and for higher-priced automobiles. Additional analyses show that the association persists when recent reviews are excluded from the cumulative measure, across automobile age groups and sample periods, and is stronger for domestic and conventional vehicles. These findings extend the eWOM research by showing that the value of accumulated reviews depends not only on their availability but also on their composition and processing demands. The findings also suggest that manufacturers and platforms should encourage recent reviews and emphasize recent evaluations and aggregate ratings in review presentation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Post-negotiation behavior and attitudes: We have a deal, now what?
abstract: Negotiators often equate “winning” with securing favorable agreement terms, yet the agreement is only one outcome of the negotiation process—and may not be the most important, particularly when interactions continue after the deal. This review broadens the lens to encompass post-negotiation outcomes, including emotions, satisfaction, relational perceptions, contract implementation, and subsequent behaviors. Considering a wider range of outcomes deepens understanding of the costs and benefits of negotiation, and can shed light on negotiation initiation and strategy. Integrating post-negotiation behavior also reveals when and why economic and relational motives collide. By treating agreements as the beginning, rather than the endpoint of negotiation, individuals can better align economic and relational objectives and ultimately maximize value beyond the bargaining table. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Whose story do we live? Experiential authorship threat in AI-mediated hospitality journeys and its consequences for meaning, memory, and engagement
abstract: AI now functions as hospitality's concierge, curating itineraries, wellness plans, and trip narratives at scale. While such systems boost efficiency and personalisation, they raise a symbolic concern central to hospitality: when algorithms pre-write the journey, do guests still feel like the authors of their own experiences? This research introduces and validates Experiential Authorship Threat (EAT), defined as the perceived loss of agency, ownership, and self-authored meaning when AI curation displaces the guest's narrative role. Across six studies (scenario-based, embedded-field, and interface experiments; total n = 2073), AI (vs. human) curation elevates EAT, especially under rigid itineraries (Study 1), and EAT, rather than adjacent constructs, drives symbolic and behavioural disengagement through diminished psychological ownership, particularly among guests high in narrative identity (Study 2). Framing AI as a co-creator rather than a curator, and offering editable rather than pre-filled itineraries, restores autonomy and authorship and improves engagement and satisfaction (Studies 3 and 4). The cost of EAT is greatest for symbolic, identity-relevant trips and high-identity-salience guests (Study 5) and persists in impoverished post-trip memory (Study 6). Theoretically, the research integrates self-determination, narrative identity, and meaning-maintenance perspectives to position EAT as a distinct psychological mechanism in hospitality. For managers, preserving guest authorship through framing, interface design, and symbolic sensitivity emerges as a design priority alongside accuracy and speed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The complex role of perspective taking in negotiations
abstract: To reach an agreement, successful negotiators typically need to understand two things: what they themselves are willing to accept, and what the other side is willing to accept. Understanding the other party's threshold requires perspective taking. In negotiations over goods or services, these judgments shape perceptions of the bargaining zone: the range of outcomes both parties would prefer to walking away without an agreement. The present paper examines how negotiators form perceptions of the bargaining zone. These perceptions have important downstream consequences, influencing everything from the offers negotiators make to the agreements they reach. We review work on how negotiators form perceptions of what their counterpart is willing to accept. Perspective taking can help negotiators estimate the lowest price a seller would accept or the highest price a buyer would pay. However, it can also lead negotiators to erroneously internalize the other party's perspective as if it is relevant to their own valuation. As an example, we demonstrate that buyers are willing to pay more for the same good when the seller gives up an entire endowment rather than only part of it, although the seller's end state should not affect buyer's willingness to pay for the good. These findings show how taking the other party's perspective can shape valuations, fairness judgments and negotiations outcomes. We conclude by discussing implications for multi-issue bargaining and strategic framing, highlighting how psychological heuristics and social context interact to shape outcomes in complex real-world situations, such as salary negotiations and real estate transactions. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Selecting a project-delivery structure for Indonesia's first nuclear power plant: an expert AHP-weighted anchored-rating analysis of the bankability–strategic-control trade-off
abstract: Indonesia's energy policy and supply plan include nuclear generation, shifting attention from adoption to delivery. This study evaluates five case-anchored delivery configurations against 14 criteria covering ownership, contractual risk allocation, strategic national value, and financing feasibility, using a hybrid AHP-weighted anchored-rating model: 19 purposively selected Indonesian experts derived criterion weights by pairwise comparison and rated each configuration on an anchored nine-point scale; each respondent's weights and ratings were combined before aggregation. All 95 pairwise matrices met CR ≤ 0.10 under software-enforced consistency requirements, whereas agreement on dimension priorities was weak (Kendall's W = 0.187). Within this panel and under the administered profiles, a host-majority public–vendor joint venture scored highest (0.710), ahead of a state-utility configuration (0.638); its margin arose from perceived bankability, construction-risk allocation, and funding access, not from strategic national value, the largest-weighted dimension (34.4%). Priority heterogeneity alone reversed the group choice for no respondent; assessment heterogeneity reversed it for five. A1 led in over 98% of resampling and weight-variation draws, but the lead reversed when its seven contracting and financing ratings were lowered together by more than about 1.2 points. Newcomer delivery choices should weigh the risk bearer's control rights, exposure, and loss-absorption capacity, not nominal allocation alone. title: How Sociodemographic Factors Shape Community Well-Being in Sustainable Tourism Destinations
abstract: Tourism significantly contributes to the livelihoods of host communities, influencing their social, environmental, and economic development. However, residents’ diverse demographics and attitudes often shape their perceptions of tourism, affecting the level of support or opposition within these communities. Such demographic factors may influence how individuals perceive tourism’s benefits and drawbacks, leading to regional variations in engagement. This study examined the relationship between sociodemographic factors, New Silk Road (NSR) infrastructure, community well-being, and tourism sustainability in destination areas. Specifically, it analysed correlations among NSR infrastructure, demographic variables, tourism impact (TI), quality of life (QOL), place image (PI), and support for tourism development (STD). Data were collected during the NSR infrastructure project in Turkistan, Kazakhstan. The findings indicated that 24 of 28 relationships between variables were statistically significant, demonstrating strong associations. Additionally, post-hoc analysis revealed significant differences in satisfaction with non-material aspects of life—affected by respondents’ income, occupation, and parental status—providing valuable insights for policymakers to develop targeted strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Too much of a good thing? The curvilinear effects of job clarity on career satisfaction and creativity among hospitality employees
abstract: This study challenges the assumption that greater job clarity always benefits service employees. Drawing on self-determination theory and the Too-Much-of-a-Good-Thing framework, we test a moderated curvilinear mediation model linking job clarity, career satisfaction, and creativity, with career calling as a boundary condition. Using three-wave, multi-source data from 164 supervisor–employee dyads in Chinese hotels, results reveal inverted U-shaped relationships between job clarity and both career satisfaction and supervisor-rated creativity. Career satisfaction mediates this curvilinear effect. Moreover, career calling amplifies the curvature—employees high in calling gain greater motivational and creative benefits as clarity increases but experience sharper losses at very high clarity levels. These findings position job clarity as a dynamic and context-dependent resource, offering theoretical and managerial insights for fostering creativity and well-being among hospitality employees. © 2026 The Authors

title: Hierarchical DEMATEL-based key risk identification for urban public safety within grid management
abstract: With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The increasing sensory richness of digitally-mediated experience
abstract: Digital interfaces were once sensorially sparse. Contemporary technologies have changed this dramatically, expanding the sensory richness of digital interfaces across visual, auditory, haptic, olfactory, and even gustatory modalities, collectively narrowing the perceptual gap between digital and physical worlds. We present findings from a growing, multidisciplinary body of evidence examining how these evolving sensory affordances shape individuals' perceptions, judgments, and behaviors. We conclude by offering a selection of future research directions with particular attention to those whose implications extend beyond any single sensory channel into more fundamental questions about human experience. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Forecast-guided multi-task scheduling for autonomous electric ride-hailing fleets under charging and maintenance constraints
abstract: Autonomous electric ride-hailing fleets require real-time coordination among passenger dispatching, proactive repositioning, charging, and maintenance. This paper proposes a forecast-guided rolling framework that combines an attention-based spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ASTGCN) with Enhanced Kuhn-Munkres (EKM) multi-task assignment. ASTGCN predicts grid-level demand, while a virtual-node (VN) mechanism converts forecasted regional shortages into bounded point-level relocation tasks at feasible points of interest (POIs). Passenger orders, VN-based repositioning, charging, and maintenance are then coordinated in a common vehicle-task graph after infeasible vehicle-task pairs are filtered according to battery, health, time-window, charging-capacity, and maintenance-capacity constraints. A residual-based search mechanism reduces the computational burden introduced by graph expansion. Experiments using real-world ride-hailing data show that the proposed framework achieves a system matching rate of 79.76%, which is 5.52 percentage points higher than the classical Kuhn-Munkres matching baseline. It reduces average passenger waiting time to 6.68 min, corresponding to a 14.41% reduction compared with the non-predictive scheduling variant. It also improves spatial supply-demand balance, reducing the normalized demand-supply difference to 0.128, and completes each rolling scheduling decision within 1.42 s on average. The incremental ablation study further shows that virtual-node-based forecast conversion mainly improves service quality and spatial balance, while the residual-based search mechanism reduces computation time from 22.45 s to 1.42 s without observed degradation. These results indicate that the main value of the proposed framework lies in converting demand forecasts into executable multi-task assignments for real-time autonomous electric fleet operation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: More alike than unalike: Contextually aligned authority arguments amplify sustainable choices across cultures
abstract: Most research is conducted in Western societies, with few studies from Latin America. This oversight has led to a narrow understanding of the effectiveness that various sustainability-oriented interventions have in countries with different cultural values. As consumers play a vital role in mitigating climate change issues, this behavioral field experiment investigates whether reliance on the authority and commitment-consistency principles from social influence increases individuals' inclination to choose sustainably, and whether the effectiveness of these principles is culturally contingent. Participants from Ecuador and Norway (N = 346) were randomized to one of three conditions (control vs. authority vs. commitment-consistency), with the latter two conditions containing a message tailored to its associated social influence principle. After replying to some survey items, participants made a choice between a more (vs. less) sustainable option. A chi-square test revealed that both social influence conditions jointly boosted choice likelihood of the more sustainable option relative to the control condition, supporting our initial preregistered hypothesis. However, contrary to our second preregistered hypothesis, a regression-based simple moderation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 1) showed no country moderation in the effectiveness of these social influence principles; instead, the results were largely attributable to the authority condition alone, which was considerably more effective than both other conditions across countries, regardless of participants' trust in authorities and their need for consistency. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of contextually aligned authority arguments as a viable way to foster pro-environmental behaviors. © 2026 The Authors

title: When regulatory-focus language matches the product category: A within-person computational analysis of reviews from an online retail platform
abstract: Online review platforms use helpfulness votes and related signals to rank and solicit reviews. This study tests whether regulatory-focus-related language is associated with helpfulness in a category-sensitive manner. We analyze 391,047 Amazon reviews from eight product categories classified a priori as promotion-oriented or prevention-oriented. Promotion language concerns gains, aspirations, and enjoyment. Prevention language concerns safety, reliability, and problem avoidance. Category assignments and language measures were benchmarked against human ratings of 800 products and 1136 reviews, respectively. The primary analyses compare within-reviewer deviations in 153,655 reviews from 20,787 reviewers represented in both category types, thereby accounting for additive time-invariant reviewer differences under the specified model. The same reviewers used a higher density of promotion language in promotion-oriented categories and a higher density of prevention language in prevention-oriented categories, with paired Cohen's d values of. 20 and. 14, respectively. Within reviewers, matched-language count was positively associated with log(1 + helpful votes), and its coefficient exceeded the mismatched-language coefficient, p <. 001. Category-specific count estimates were positive in all eight categories, although their magnitudes varied. The median count-based double/debiased machine-learning point estimate across five seeds was also positive. The association was small. A one-standard-deviation within-reviewer difference in matched-language count corresponded to a 2.39% difference in the model-implied geometric mean of 1 + helpful votes. Adding promotion and prevention density terms and their category interactions increased internal five-fold cross-validated R2 by ΔR2 =. 0002. The hypothesized response-surface pattern did not characterize the central data region. The findings are associational and do not distinguish regulatory fit from informational attribute relevance. They warrant prospective tests of whether category-congruent language measures improve review ranking or solicitation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Exploring Technology Probe applications in software engineering practice
abstract: Background: The development of software systems relies on user feedback, which can be captured with Validation Sessions (VS); however, VS are often conducted in an ad hoc manner. Technology Probe (TP) offers a participatory design method for capturing user perception; however, its application in software engineering lacks structure. Aim: This study consolidates evidence on TP applications in software engineering and identifies practices that support the systematic use of TP. Methods: A Literature Study, inspired by Rapid Reviews, was conducted in Scopus using backward and forward snowballing, screening 530 studies and selecting 53 primary works across the trials that support the results. Thematic analysis was employed to extract motivations, outcomes, and challenges associated with the use of TP in software engineering. Results: Through thematic analysis and open coding, 11 evidence-based characteristics were identified describing the use of TP in software engineering. These characteristics formed the foundation of an evidence-based checklist developed to assess and guide the development of TP techniques. Conclusion: It was found that TP has been applied across a variety of domains, with diverse techniques being crafted. Therefore, the checklist developed in this research aims to assist future researchers in crafting their techniques and supporting their decisions. © 2026 The Authors

title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. This suggests that achieving DEI goals in AI-integrated workplaces requires attention not only to the properties and behavior of AI, but also to employees’ beliefs about AI itself. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Emotional Factors in Quality Negligence: A Study of Residential Real Estate Construction Professionals
abstract: Quality negligence in the construction industry, a significant originator of legal crises, is predominantly attributed to technical and procedural failures. However, the pivotal role of construction professionals' emotions as a precipitating factor remains a critically unexamined research area. This study addresses this gap by investigating the influence of specific emotions on quality negligence and its subsequent escalation into legal crises for construction firms. The research employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. Initially, a comprehensive literature review and unstructured interviews with industry experts identified seven prominent emotions (anxiety, guilt, pride, shame, elevation, injustice, and gratitude). Subsequently, a quantitative phase involved distributing a self-administered questionnaire to 162 Indian construction professionals within the Indian residential construction sector to assess their emotional states and quality negligence levels. Data analysis using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) indicated a statistically significant positive relationship between quality negligence and five emotions. The effects, in descending order of magnitude, were elevation (β=0.406, p<0.001), shame (β=0.405, p<0.001), gratitude (β=0.321, p<0.001), pride (β=0.261, p=0.009), and anxiety (β=0.179, p=0.047). In the final phase, consultations and brainstorming sessions with industry experts were used to identify the resulting legal crises and to establish a novel emotion-quality negligence-crises framework. This framework models the pathway from emotional antecedent to quality negligence and its culmination in a legal crisis. The study provides a critical diagnostic tool for practitioners in the real estate sector to mitigate risk and offers a new theoretical model for academics analyzing this psycho-legal connection. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: Trust begins at home: The role of psychological distance in trust transfer for emerging technology
abstract: The widespread adoption of emerging technologies holds substantial potential to benefit societal development. However, fostering public trust and acceptance of emerging technologies, which involve complex underlying principles and are in pre-commercialization stages, remains a critical multifaceted challenge. To address this issue, this study draws on trust transfer theory to identify an effective mechanism for enhancing people's trust in emerging technologies. Specifically, we propose and test that trust in emerging technologies can be transferred from that in familiar institutions of the public by reducing psychological distance to such technologies. Analyzing quota-sampling data, we find that greater consumption of news about local brain–computer interface (BCI) achievements was associated with greater trust in local technology institutions. Institutional process and purpose trust were, in turn, associated with lower psychological distance to BCI, which was associated with greater general trust in BCI and, subsequently, stronger BCI use intention. The corresponding pathway was not supported for performance trust. These findings extend trust transfer theory by introducing psychological distance as a vital mechanism. Practically, this study demonstrates a route through which practitioners can promote public acceptance of unfamiliar and emerging technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Evolution and lifecycle mapping of research methods based on the Boston Matrix in library and information science from 1995 to 2025
abstract: Developing an evolution framework for research methods is essential for advancing Library and Information Science (LIS), but existing research method schemas remain fragmented and limited. This study proposes an automated framework combining AI-driven methods to mine, classify, and a temporal analysis based on the Boston Matrix to map the lifecycles of research methods. Using a comprehensive dataset of 31,913 articles from 21 LIS journals (1995–2025) as a validation corpus, the framework integrates semantic clustering for bottom-up entity extraction with generative top-down ontology mapping. This approach dynamically maps methods into a four-stage lifecycle schema: mainstream, emerging, marginalized, and mature, revealing distinct evolutionary trajectories and the broader computational turn within LIS. Validated through quantitative threshold testing and qualitative evaluation, the proposed framework significantly reduces manual coding subjectivity and enhances replicability. By empirically comparing the subfields of librarianship and information science, this study accounts for inherent thematic variations and uncovers their distinct paces of methodological adoption. Ultimately, this study offers a robust automated framework for longitudinal methodological tracking, theoretically demonstrating how diverse AI-driven and traditional methods synergistically coevolve and assume distinct scholarly roles within the emerging AI4Science paradigm. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Who gets to negotiate? Tracing gender gaps in structural empowerment with people analytics
abstract: Gender differences in compensation and career advancement are often examined through the lens of negotiation behavior, initiation, outcomes, and stereotyping. We shift attention to the organizational structures that precede and shape formal negotiations. Drawing on organizational gender research, we use structural empowerment as an organizing framework to review and synthesize the literature on organizational structures that may shape who gains access to negotiations and the negotiation power employees bring to them. Existing research documents gender differences in access to opportunities, information, support, and resources, yet their implications for negotiation access and power remain underexamined. We explain how people analytics can help scholars and practitioners trace these dispersed and longitudinal processes and outline directions for future research. We conclude with methodological, ethical, and theoretical considerations associated with using people analytics to examine these questions. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Crowding and green choice: Understanding a U-shaped relationship in China's organic food market
abstract: Organic food represents a product category in which safety-and-health attributes and environmental attributes are both salient, making it an appropriate context for examining how retail situations shape sustainable consumption. This study investigates the nonlinear effect of shopping crowding on organic food purchase behavior and purchase intention, and further examines whether different crowding levels activate different organic food attribute cues. First, transaction records from a large supermarket chain in China provide associational evidence of a statistically supported U-shaped relationship between shopping crowding and organic food purchase behavior, with the turning point located in the upper portion of the observed crowding distribution and modest changes in predicted purchase probability. Second, a randomized scenario experiment provides causal evidence for the low–moderate–high nonmonotonic pattern in organic food purchase intention and identifies distinct indirect-effect structures involving positive emotion and perceived loss of control. Third, a 2×2 experiment compares the two crowding endpoints and shows that environmental-responsibility cues are relatively more effective under low crowding, whereas safety-and-health cues are relatively more effective under high crowding. Taken together, the findings extend crowding research and sustainable consumption research by identifying a nonlinear crowding effect, integrating compensatory control theory with consumer emotion theory, and showing how the match between retail situations and product attribute cues shapes organic food choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Emotion-aware retailing: Using biometrics to decode consumer experience in physical–digital environments
abstract: The physical retail space, when blended with digital touchpoints, has created a multi-sensory consumer experience that cannot be fully measured in real time using legacy survey-based approaches. The work examines the opportunities offered by biometric technologies, such as electrodermal activity (EDA), facial action coding, eye-tracking, and heart-rate variability (HRV), to decode shoppers' affective experiences in a phygital retail space. The study is based on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework and affective computing theory, and has a mixed-methods experimental design that involved 312 study participants, who were offered four types of retail formats: department store, grocery hypermarket, experiential flagship store, and click-and-collect hub. All participants were given biometric sensors to wear and were monitored across three consecutive stages: browsing, assessment, and purchase decision. Behavioral and transactional data were used in real time and fused with multimodal biometric responses to create emotion maps for spatial retail areas. The findings show statistically significant positive relationships among high EDA arousal, positive facial affect, and conversion rates at digital interface points. Quantitatively, an optimal engagement window was identified at moderate stimulation levels (EDA = 2.10 μS), yielding a peak conversion rate of 41.2%. In contrast, HRV suppression was associated with decision paralysis at higher stimulation levels. Demographic cohorts and segmentation analysis showed that younger consumers reacted with much more emotion to augmented reality features and individualized digital signs. Eye-tracking and facial action coding confirmed that younger shoppers (<35) sustained an 8.42-s fixation duration with high positive affect (0.74) in flagship zones, whereas older cohorts (≥35) exhibited severe sensory avoidance. The article contributes to the theoretical understanding of emotion-behavior relationships in the store setting and offers practical guidance for store designers, digital experience architects, and consumer psychologists. Embargoes on biometric retail analytics that protect privacy are also discussed. Keywords: biometric sensing, emotion-aware retailing, phygital retail, electrodermal activity, consumer experience, affective computing, eye-tracking, heart-rate variability. The updated structural framework successfully bridges the gap between environmental retail inputs and transactional behavioral choices through intermediate biometric telemetry. Phygital spaces with heavy digital footprints create pronounced shifts in physiological processing, where elevated electrodermal activity predicts transaction completion up to an threshold point, beyond which severe heart-rate variability suppression signals choice paralysis. © 2026

title: Algorithmic fairness as a human–technology interaction problem
abstract: Algorithms shape high-stakes decisions across society. While promising efficiency, algorithms also raise fairness concerns. This article proposes that algorithmic fairness is best understood as a human–technology interaction problem rather than a purely technical challenge. Algorithms can reproduce human biases, amplify them through feedback loops, or create new forms of unfairness through objectives, proxies, and seemingly neutral variables. Yet they can make decision processes more explicit, disparities more visible, and actively mitigate discrimination. Fairness depends not only on statistical properties but also on how algorithms are designed, used and experienced by those affected by their decisions. This article therefore offers an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates insights from social justice, psychology, computer science, judgment and decision-making, and management. © 2026 The Author

title: When do hedonic appeals backfire? Credibility, scepticism and the disconnect between emotional engagement and pro-environmental intention
abstract: This study examines why emotional engagement with hedonic sustainability communication does not always translate into pro-environmental behavioural intention. Drawing on the Persuasion Knowledge Model and Truth-Default Theory, it investigates consumer responses to pleasure- and comfort-based hotel food-waste messages. A sequential mixed-method design combined a laboratory experiment, projective interviews, and a follow-up online experiment testing green scepticism. Findings show no robust statistically significant physiological differentiation across message types, but substantial differences in perceived credibility, sincerity and emotional meaning. Pleasure-based appeals were interpreted as enjoyable but superficial and less trustworthy; comfort-based appeals were warmer and more relational, yet both hedonic appeals produced lower behavioural intention than the control message. Green scepticism strengthened this negative effect, particularly for comfort-based appeals. The findings suggest that hedonic sustainability communication operates less through heightened physiological arousal than through interpretive credibility evaluation, particularly among sceptical consumers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The role of psychological factors on the mathematics achievement among alternative learning students in the Philippine context
abstract: This study examined the role of key psychological factors such as self-efficacy, self-regulation, and time management in explaining the mathematics achievement among students enrolled in an alternative learning system (ALS) at selected public high schools in the school districts of Cebu, Philippines. Grounded in educational psychology, a descriptive-correlational research design was employed to specifically investigate the factors relating to mathematics achievement in nonformal learning environments. Data were collected from 180 ALS students through validated survey questionnaires and a mathematics achievement test. The respondents were identified through a convenience sampling technique. The data gathered were treated via descriptive statistics to determine the levels of prychological factors and inferential statistics to examine their predictive influence on mathematics achievement by multiple regression analysis. The results revealed that the students demonstrated high self-efficacy, while self-regulation and time management were rated at moderate levels. Multiple regression analysis revealed that all three psychological factors significantly predicted mathematics achievement, with self-efficacy emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by self-regulation and time management. These findings indicate that students’ belief in their capabilities and their ability to regulate learning behaviors contribute meaningfully to mathematics achievement, even within flexible and nontraditional learning environments. The study contributes empirical evidence on the psychological factors of mathematics achievement among ALS students which remains underrepresented in the literature. Findings underscore the importance of strengthening learners’ psychological competencies to support academic achievement in alternative education settings. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating mastery-based tasks, strategy instruction, and time management support within ALS programs to strengthen students’ psychological competencies, enhance achievement in mathematics, and promote more effective learning outcomes. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Reframing artificial intelligence as an observable market signal: Extending Signaling Theory in luxury fashion retail
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming luxury fashion retail; however, existing research primarily views AI as an operational technology that enhances efficiency and personalization. Less attention has been given to how consumers interpret AI-enabled marketing applications as signals of luxury brand meaning. Drawing on Signaling Theory, this study conceptualizes AI-enabled marketing applications as market signals through which consumers infer luxury brand attributes. Using a multi-method design comprising survey-based structural equation modeling (n = 362), exploratory consumer segmentation (n = 101), and sentiment analysis of 193 online reviews, the study examines how AI shapes perceptions of exclusivity, authenticity, innovation, and responsiveness and how these perceptions influence luxury brand performance. The findings reveal that AI-enabled marketing applications do not show a statistically significant direct effect on brand performance; instead, their effects operate through these four signaling dimensions. The exploratory segmentation identifies three consumer profiles with different signaling perceptions, while sentiment analysis reveals generally positive evaluations alongside concerns about excessive automation and diminished human interaction. The study extends Signaling Theory by positioning AI-enabled marketing applications as market signals through which technological capabilities acquire symbolic brand value. Managerially, the findings suggest that luxury brands should deploy AI strategically to reinforce symbolic value while preserving exclusivity and authenticity. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
