title: Psychological vulnerability in conversational AI: How incentive and urgency manipulations alter trust formation and privacy behaviour across healthcare, financial, commercial, and security contexts
abstract: Users increasingly interact with conversational AI systems in sensitive domains, yet little is known about how psychological manipulation techniques systematically alter privacy decision-making and trust formation across different contexts. We examined how two manipulation mechanisms, incentive-based (Need & Greed) and urgency-based (Time), influence user behaviour in healthcare, financial, commercial, and home security interactions.In a within-subjects experimental study (N=30[jls-end-space/]) using an interactive, scenario-based methodology, we investigated how context shapes vulnerability to manipulation. Participants engaged with control, Need & Greed, and Time conditions across four domains whilst we measured trust, comfort levels, willingness to disclose information, and perception of privacy and security.Both manipulation techniques significantly reduced comfort (p<0.001[jls-end-space/]) and increased information disclosure (p<0.05[jls-end-space/]), but context moderated these effects substantially. Time pressure increased trust in healthcare contexts whilst decreasing it in financial domains, revealing domain-specific vulnerability patterns. Qualitative analysis identified psychological mechanisms underlying these effects: prior digital experiences, agent characteristics, urgency sensitivity, and context-dependent risk assessment.These findings demonstrate that psychological vulnerability to manipulation operates through context-specific pathways, challenging one-size-fits-all protection approaches. The research provides empirical evidence for developing domain-aware security frameworks that address psychological dimensions alongside technical protections, advancing both human-computer interaction theory and practical system design. © 2026 The Author(s). title: From smart cities to smart villages: Evolution, domains, and policy implications for smart rural development
abstract: Smart villages have evolved from early parallels with urban smart city models into a comprehensive, multidimensional framework that integrates digital infrastructure, agriculture, local enterprises, tourism, and sustainability. This expanded framework recognizes the unique characteristics and potentials of rural areas, moving beyond the urban-centric logic of technology adoption. This review aims to examine the conceptual evolution of smart village research, track emerging methodological trends, and analyze global implementation trajectories. In the early stages, many studies concentrated on definitional debates and approaches that were primarily centered on technology. However, more recent perspectives have begun to emphasize the importance of integrating technological innovation with social innovation, community empowerment, participatory governance, and environmental stewardship. Methodological approaches have also advanced significantly, shifting from conceptual reflections and single-case studies toward more diverse methods including comparative studies, bibliometric mapping, and participatory action research. These evolving methods enable a deeper and more nuanced understanding of smart village dynamics. Regional approaches demonstrate distinct emphases: European initiatives focus on service revitalization and smart specialization; Asian and African strategies prioritize connectivity, renewable energy access, and digital inclusion; while Latin American programs increasingly integrate climate-smart agricultural practices. Despite regional differences, common challenges remain, including the persistent rural digital divide, fragmented coordination among multiple stakeholders, issues of financial sustainability, and the emergence of new forms of inequality. Policy directions increasingly stress the importance of place-based strategies, building local capacities, establishing supportive governance structures, and fostering inclusive participation. The review concludes by identifying critical areas for future research, such as the creation of unified evaluation metrics, conducting longitudinal impact assessments, and embedding smart village initiatives within broader rural development and climate resilience agendas. Overall, smart villages represent dynamic and promising pathways for driving innovation-led, inclusive, and sustainable rural transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: From design attributes to social life: Modelling conviviality in urban underground spaces
abstract: From being infrastructure utilities, urban underground spaces (UUS) have developed into multipurpose public spaces that combine commercial, cultural, and transit functions. While their technical and spatial contributions to compact urbanism are evident, their capacity to foster conviviality, the experiential quality of inclusiveness, sociability, and shared belonging, is less understood. This study develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework that operationalizes conviviality in UUS by linking seven spatial-perceptual dimensions (safety and security, identity and meaning, accessibility, functionality, environmental comfort, aesthetics, and structure and form) to behavioral mediators of willingness to use and social interaction, culminating in perceived conviviality. Using the Theatre-Shahr underground complex in Tehran as a case study, data were collected through structured surveys and analyzed via Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that although environmental factors generally have a positive indirect effect on perceived conviviality, social interaction emerges as the primary mechanism shaping conviviality in urban underground spaces, while willingness to use plays only a complementary and limited mediating role in this process. Among the environmental factors, accessibility, environmental comfort, and safety and security show the strongest effects. In contrast, some variables, particularly identity and meaning and structure and form, do not demonstrate statistically significant effects in certain pathways. These findings suggest that planning and design strategies for urban underground spaces should prioritize environmental qualities that support social interaction, to enhance perceived conviviality. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. The findings of this study will help academics and policy makers to design institutional arrangements which are fit-for-purpose for bringing accountability for nature. © 2026 The Authors. title: Identification of subgroup causal effects in randomized trials under nonignorable missingness of covariates and outcome variables simultaneously
abstract: Randomized experiments are widely regarded as the gold standard for causal inference. However, identifying subgroup causal effects becomes particularly challenging when pretreatment covariates and outcome are subject to simultaneous nonignorable missingness. The study investigates the identifiability of subgroup causal effects under five increasingly complex missing data mechanisms, ranging from an ignorable mechanism to nonignorable mechanisms in which missingness depends on different combinations of treatment, covariates, and outcome. Identification is established under several nonignorable mechanisms without imposing restrictive parametric assumptions. For the most challenging mechanism, identification is established under a parametric model with specific assumptions on the outcome distribution and the missingness mechanism. For estimation and inference, a fractional-imputation Expectation-Maximization algorithm is developed to maximize the observed-data likelihood. Simulation studies compare the proposed estimator with complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, and a full-data oracle estimator, demonstrating satisfactory finite-sample performance across the considered missingness mechanisms. The practical utility of the proposed method is further illustrated using data from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Workplace responses to perpetration of family and domestic violence: a global scoping review
abstract: Introduction Family and domestic violence (FDV), which includes intimate partner and family violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace interventions addressing the issue of FDV have predominantly concentrated on providing support to victim-survivors, while there is limited research regarding employer responses to employees who perpetrate such violence. Method A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources, and 28 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Practical applications Effective workplace responses to perpetration of FDV should consider work design factors, referral pathways and confidentiality protections which are guided by graduated accountability models and regulatory frameworks. © 2026 The Authors.

title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and fear of missing out: Evidence from network analysis and a daily diary study
abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and fear of missing out (FoMO) are common psychological vulnerabilities during emerging adulthood, yet their item-level organization and daily temporal associations remain underexplored. Study 1 ( N = 875) used item-level network analysis in an undergraduate sample to examine the conditional association structure of IU and FoMO. Study 2 ( N = 235) used a 14-day diary design and dynamic structural equation modeling to examine their within-person temporal associations at the construct level. In Study 1, IU and FoMO formed two communities with stronger within-community than cross-community connections. In Study 2, both constructs showed autoregressive continuity and positive bidirectional cross-lagged associations. Higher daily IU was associated with higher next-day FoMO, while higher daily FoMO was associated with higher next-day IU. Together, the findings describe complementary aspects of the IU-FoMO relationship: Study 1 identifies candidate item-level interface domains, whereas Study 2 independently shows temporal coupling between daily IU and daily FoMO at the construct level. These findings may inform future research and the development of interventions for uncertainty-related distress and socially specific missing-out concerns among college students. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Audit fees under accounting and auditing standards: A communicative action perspective
abstract: This study investigates audit fee determination under accounting and auditing standards by moving beyond dominant economic and agency-based explanations toward a critical, normative perspective. The study conceptualizes audit fees as a social construct shaped by the interaction between professional judgment, regulatory systems, and market forces by using Theory of Communicative Action developed by Jürgen Habermas. Using a semisystematic literature review (SsLR), this research synthesizes empirical audit fee studies published between 2010 and 2024 and analyzes them through a Habermasian lens to explore the tension between the auditors’ professional lifeworld and the systemic logic embedded in accounting and auditing standards. A comprehensive search of the Scopus database resulted in a final sample of 33 empirical studies. These studies were then used as the basis for an analysis examining how accounting and auditing regulations contribute to the colonisation of audit fee-setting practices. The findings indicate that standards such as IFRS, auditing standards, and regulatory oversight regimes function as steering mechanisms. These standards orient audit fee determination toward instrumental rationality, compliance, and risk mitigation. While these standards enhance transparency and comparability, they also increase audit complexity, documentation requirements, and litigation risk. The limitation of this study is that it depends on empirical literature with quantitative data. Nevertheless, this study contributes by expanding audit fee research into a normative-communicative framework, highlighting audit fees as a guiding medium in modern audit systems. This study offers a novel critical perspective by positioning audit fees as outcomes of communicative and power relations rather than purely economic transactions. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: “The Right to Repair”: A systematic literature review and research agenda for an emerging interdisciplinary field
abstract: The Right to Repair (R2R) is an important arena in which restrictive repair practices, including limits on access to spare parts, manuals, software, and specialised tools, as well as product designs that inhibit repair, are being contested. Although scholarly interest in R2R is growing rapidly, research remains fragmented across disciplinary and empirical domains, limiting the development of a coherent understanding of its implications for technology-society relations. In response, this paper presents a systematic literature review that maps and synthesises existing research on R2R. Specifically, it (1) consolidates empirical evidence on the implications of R2R; (2) examines how the concept has been theorised across disciplines; and (3) identifies key conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. By organising this literature into coherent thematic domains and tracing the relationships between them, the review argues that the effective realisation of R2R depends on a socio-technical capacity: the practically exercisable ability to repair produced through the interaction between legal entitlements, technological architectures, economic arrangements, and social capabilities. It also reveals disciplinary and geographical imbalances and identifies four tensions structuring future research: formal ownership versus effective control, legal entitlement versus practical repair capacity, universal frameworks versus situated repair practices, and systemic transformation versus continuity. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Dependent development at the energy transition: placing lithium imaginaries in Neoliberal and Contentious Peru
abstract: We examine lithium and development imaginaries in mining-dependent Peru, asking: What are these imaginaries? What narratives underpin them? Who articulates and shares them, and from where? What forms of state (in)action are envisioned in relation to them? The case study elucidates how alternative “imagined futures” coexist within a natural resource–dependent economy. The ruling national elites in Lima have a neoliberal imagination, treating lithium like any other mineral resource in the country. In contrast, professional elites in the mineral-rich but peripheral region of Puno adopt a resource nationalist view, advocating for direct state involvement in lithium industrialization and the transformation of the domestic energy system, shaped by beliefs on Bolivia's developmental pathway. Among rural community leaders as well as political and social leaders in the districts near lithium and uranium deposits, however, the prevailing idea is that of a social license. In this view, each community has the capacity to negotiate development terms with mining companies independently. In the broader imagination at the resource periphery of a peripheral national economy, the state is perceived primarily as a minimalist governmental actor, necessary only to oversee and ensure the enforcement of mine-community agreements and to provide basic infrastructure. Thus, elites at the political center and communities near expected resource developments converge in their immediate pursuit of rents promised by resource commodification. In the dominant discourses, environmental concerns are often subordinated to economic development goals. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The Olympic effect revisited: 1950–2019
abstract: Rose and Spiegel (2011) identified a positive trade-promoting effect of hosting the Olympic Games, yet they did not account for multilateral resistance terms in their analysis, which are emphasized in the structural gravity model by Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). This paper revisits the trade effects of the Olympics using a nonparametric matching method developed by Chang and Lee (2011), analyzing a comprehensive gravity dataset encompassing 187 economies from 1950 to 2019. Our findings suggest that hosting the Olympics is positively associated with bilateral trade. For pairs in which both countries have hosted, the matching estimate corresponds to a long-run trade difference with an implied increase of approximately 15 times relative to matched nonhost pairs. Under an assumed trade elasticity of 4, this estimate corresponds to an illustrative trade-cost equivalent of approximately 50%. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: What impacts can intertemporal trading have on carbon markets across different development stages? An economy-wide analysis
abstract: Carbon markets have encountered challenges such as limited flexibility and substantial price volatility. Intertemporal trading mechanisms, as one of the important ways of green finance, have been proposed as a potential solution to improve market efficiency. However, existing studies frequently overlook whether the intricate internal mechanisms of carbon markets are suitable for introducing intertemporal trading. To comprehensively analyze the effect of intertemporal trading, this study employs a computable general equilibrium model incorporating an intertemporal dynamic mechanism and a carbon market module. This study designs scenarios focusing on total quotas, sectoral coverage, quota allocation, and intertemporal trading to simulate and compare their macroeconomic impacts. The results suggest that intertemporal trading is particularly beneficial in carbon markets that prioritize later-stage reduction, experience rapid sectoral coverage, or have a high auction rate. Under these conditions, introducing intertemporal trading can help reduce long-term carbon prices while promoting the development of cumulative GDP and household welfare. It is noted that the output of sectors covered by the carbon market undergoes an initial contraction in the early stage, followed by a gradual increase in the later stage. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: A socio-technical maturity framework for design firms to enable the transition to design-out-waste in Indonesia's construction sector
abstract: The construction sector remains a major driver of resource depletion and solid waste generation, with a substantial share traceable to early design-stage decisions. Design-out-Waste (DoW) strategies, including waste-efficient documentation, modern construction methods, and prefabrication, represent a proactive approach to enhancing lifecycle resource efficiency. However, their implementation remains fragmented, particularly in developing-country contexts, partly due to the lack of a structured framework for assessing organisational maturity. This study addresses this gap by developing an empirically grounded socio-technical maturity framework for DoW implementation in building design firms. The framework integrates five socio-technical dimensions into a single operational model encompassing processes & procedures, people & culture, industry structures, technology, and goals & incentives. Using data from 116 construction professionals, Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to validate the measurement and structural relationships, while Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) provided empirical importance values for weighting the maturity dimensions and attributes. These weights were subsequently integrated with a five-level maturity scoring scheme to operationalise the assessment framework. The results reveal an interdependent socio-technical structure, with Industry Structure emerging as the most influential dimension and an important upstream driver of other organisational capabilities. The resulting framework provides an empirically weighted basis for assessing organisational readiness, identifying capability priorities, and guiding DoW implementation towards circular construction. It also provides a structured basis for informing environmental assessment, project appraisal, and policy interventions aimed at improving resource efficiency and waste prevention. © 2026

title: GenAI-enabled human–AI collaboration: An integrative review of local augmentation, hidden work, and governable synergy
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming part of everyday knowledge work, where it can accelerate drafting, coding, summarization, ideation, customer communication, and other language-intensive tasks. Yet the organizational problem is conversion: local GenAI gains create organizational value only when they survive the full work system, including verification, coordination, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability. Drawing on 251 academic and practice-facing sources across information systems (IS), management, human–computer interaction, human factors, organizational theory, and responsible AI, this article synthesizes why GenAI-enabled work often produces local augmentation but less often yields governable organizational synergy. The review develops three findings. First, GenAI shifts the relevant unit of collaboration from a one-step task interaction to a recurrent production-and-revision workflow in which human framing, prompting, verification, correction, and reuse become part of the value-producing system. Second, the augmentation-to-synergy boundary is net work-system value: visible task gains and reallocation benefits must exceed work displaced across roles and time into verification, rework, coordination, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability. Third, durable synergy requires behavioral embedding and multi-outcome governance: prompts, memory, feedback traces, review routines, and escalation rules must improve local fit while keeping reliance, learning, ownership, risk, and accountability observable. The article contributes a work-system conversion account that distinguishes substitution, augmentation, and synergy as different organizational states; a trace-centered behavioral-embedding view of how recurring GenAI use becomes a persistent, history-dependent workflow state within established sociotechnical IS theory; and a governance-instrumentation account that evaluates visible gains together with hidden labor, learning, ownership, risk, reviewability, and accountability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Artificial intelligence is not enough to enhance organizational performance
abstract: This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI), supply chain visibility, supplier integration, and organizational performance through the lens of Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT). Drawing on empirical data from UK-based organizations that have adopted AI technologies, we employ structural equation modeling along with mediation and moderation analyses to test our hypotheses. The findings indicate that AI does not have a significant direct effect on performance; instead, its impact is fully mediated through supply chain visibility and supplier integration. This supports the view that AI-driven supply chain visibility acts as an information-processing mechanism that enhances firms' ability to coordinate, collaborate, and integrate with supply chain partners, thereby improving organizational performance. Furthermore, supply uncertainty positively moderates the relationship between supplier integration and performance, amplifying the benefits under conditions of higher uncertainty. This study contributes to the literature by clarifying AI's indirect role in driving performance and highlighting the importance of embedding AI within broader organizational capabilities. It also offers practical insights for managers seeking to leverage AI to enhance supply chain integration and organizational effectiveness. © 2026

title: Events under fire: Developing an urgent anthropology for events during armed conflicts
abstract: This conceptual and methodological research note addresses event industry dynamics during armed conflicts, proposing an urgent anthropology approach to document transformations in real time. Using Ukraine as an example, we illustrate how event organizations have adapted to existential threats since the 2022 Russian invasion, demonstrating resilience through cultural initiatives, charitable events, and creative repurposing of resources. We argue that these practices have the potential to sustain cultural identity and to contribute to economic development, social cohesion and morale in conflict settings. To overcome the methodological and ethical challenges of traditional ethnography in war zones, we propose a novel citizen science framework within the urgent anthropology paradigm, leveraging digital technologies, social media, and participatory methods. This approach can decentralize knowledge production, mitigate researcher risk, and create longitudinal archives of industry adaptations. Our proposal supports SDG 16 by suggesting ways to link events and tourism research to peace, justice, and institutional resilience. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Your recommendation and my choice: The impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion
abstract: Personalized recommendation features launched by integrated online shopping platforms with multi-brand competition trap consumers in the dilemma of product choice constrained by algorithmic recommendation convergence, and induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. Against this backdrop, this article systematically examines the existence, antecedents, and boundaries of consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. The results show that algorithmic recommendation convergence significantly triggers consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion and suppresses their purchase intentions. Specifically, in addition to perceived lack of self-control affecting algorithmic recommendation aversion, consumers' state of choice overload caused by homogeneous recommendation convergence is the key reason for perceived lack of self-control and the emergence of algorithmic recommendation aversion. Meanwhile, the results further demonstrate that in multi-brand markets with multi-oligopolistic brand coexistence, brand agglomeration further narrows consumers' brand and product choice scope, making it more likely to induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. In contrast, in a single-brand-dominated market structure, the core brand effect can leverage its dominant market position and market recognition to mitigate the impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. These findings expand the research perspective on consumer algorithmic bias, emphasize the importance of brand strategies, and provide timely and critical insights for understanding and alleviating consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Phygital pop-up stores: Measuring immersion, novelty, and post-visit purchase behavior using eye-tracking and biometrics
abstract: Phygital pop-up stores hybrid retail environments fusing physical spaces with digital layers represent an accelerating frontier in contemporary retailing. However, the precise cognitive mechanisms through which these sensor-driven environments translate immediate sensory engagement into durable long-term consumer choices remain under-theorized. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model, Expectation Confirmation Theory, and Trust Theory, this study develops an integrated model positioning consumer trust as a critical mediator between phygital experiential antecedents and downstream purchasing commitments. Primary data were collected from 612 adult consumers across the United Kingdom and Australia via a stratified intercept sampling protocol. Objective measures of consumer immersion were captured using eye-tracking metrics and galvanic skin response indices embedded within a structured self-report survey. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) reveals that while immersive experiences, novelty, interactivity, and enjoyment associate positively with retrospective post-visit purchase behavior within a 30-day window (R2 = 0.482), consumer trust functions as the dominant direct predictor (β = 0.274, p < 0.001) and an essential gatekeeper mediating the immersion–purchase pathway. Multi-group analysis indicates that tech experience significantly moderates immersion and interactivity tracks, whereas gender exhibits structural invariance. This biometrically validated framework offers strategic resource-allocation priorities for experiential retail developers. © 2026

title: The effects of adolescents' digital and environmental literacy on parents’ green consumption: A reverse intergenerational socialization perspective
abstract: Drawing on reverse socialization theory, this study examines how adolescents' digital and environmental literacy influence parents' green consumption behavior (GCB). Using matched adolescent–parent survey data, we employ PLS-SEM to test net and mediating effects and fsQCA to identify configurational pathways leading to high levels of parents' GCB. The results show that adolescents' digital literacy and environmental literacy are both positively associated with parents' GCB. Parents' decision-making confidence mediates the relationship between adolescents' digital literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a capability empowerment pathway, whereas parents' personal norms mediate the relationship between adolescents' environmental literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a norm activation pathway. The fsQCA results further identify nine configurational pathways, indicating that parents’ GCB is characterized by equifinality and conditional substitution. This study extends reverse socialization theory to the context of family green consumption and offers practical implications for promoting green consumption within families. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Carbon trading in community-based forest management: A bibliometric mapping of scientific publications from 2000 to 2025
abstract: Carbon trading in community-based forest management (CBFM) has emerged as a promising mechanism for simultaneously addressing climate change mitigation and improving the welfare of rural communities. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 203 scientific publications obtained from Scopus, covering the period 2000 to 2025, with an analytical focus on the period 2010-2024. Using VOSviewer v.1.6.20 and Scopus's built-in analysis, this study analyzes publication trends, author participation patterns, geographic distribution, journal sources, and thematic structure through author collaboration, co-occurrence of keywords, and bibliographic linking networks. Results show a sharp acceleration in publication growth following key climate policy milestones, including the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (2013), the Paris Agreement (2015), and COP26 (2021), with a record 21 articles published in 2024. Nepal and Indonesia emerged as dominant knowledge producers, collectively contributing 42.4% of total publications. Thematic mapping identified three main research clusters: carbon governance in CBFM, carbon measurement and quantification, and multifunctional forest landscape ecology. A critical knowledge gap was identified: while the supply side of carbon measurement of forest carbon stocks and biomass has been well documented, the demand side of how communities access, negotiate, and fairly obtain benefits from carbon markets remains largely unexplored. These findings underscore the urgent need for interdisciplinary research that links technical carbon measurement with institutional, economic, and social dimensions of equity to promote fair and scalable carbon trading within the framework of community forest governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: “Crossing the river by feeling the stones”: Sub-national agency in China's highway maintenance marketisation
abstract: Marketisation reforms in China are often described as an extension of Western New Public Management (NPM), yet their meanings and effects vary substantially across regions and remain poorly understood from the perspective of policymakers themselves. Drawing on document review and interviews with sub-national officials and practitioners involved in highway maintenance in two underdeveloped provinces, this study examines how marketisation is interpreted, justified, and enacted through a "learning by doing" process shaped by administrative legacies, political incentives, and constrained market environments. The analysis shows that NPM-related principles, such as competition and performance management, are selectively adapted rather than directly transplanted, producing hybrid arrangements that combine bureaucratic control with quasi-market practices dominated by state-owned enterprises. The study identifies four narrative frames through which policymakers explain and evaluate reforms, as well as the recurring strategy of deliberate inaction, which emerges as a pragmatic response to tensions between central expectations and local socio-economic realities. It also considers the broader implications of marketisation for highway service performance, public satisfaction, fiscal sustainability, and technical capacity, pointing to uneven outcomes and persistent governance tensions. By foregrounding sub-national agency and context-sensitive adaptation, the article contributes to understanding policy transfer, the institutional logics shaping China's state-led market reforms, and the prospects for more sustainable infrastructure governance in less developed regions. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Negotiation and relationships: Insights from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature
abstract: Negotiations often unfold within ongoing relationships, making relationships integral to negotiation processes and outcomes. Yet, despite repeated calls for greater attention to relational dynamics, behavioral negotiation research has largely relied on paradigms that minimize the role of relationships. We review research from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature (e.g., on close relationships, marketing, strategy, and operations) that conceptualize negotiation as embedded within ongoing relationships. We show that negotiations in relationships unfold under distinct starting conditions that shape negotiators’ interpretations, judgments of appropriateness and risk, and the interplay between negotiation processes, outcomes, and the longer-term relationship. As a result, negotiations in relationships often involve managing both objective and relational interests simultaneously, producing beliefs, behaviors, and outcomes that differ from dominant findings in behavioral negotiation research. We conclude by encouraging more dynamic, relationally embedded perspectives and methods that capture how negotiation unfolds across ongoing relationships and repeated interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The impact of omni-channel strategies on consumer behavior in sport product purchases
abstract: This study addresses the gap in understanding sports consumers' behavior regarding omni-channel strategies, with a focus on the moderating roles of customer experience and brand trust. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and commitment-trust theory, a quasi-experimental omnichannel retail setting was utilized with a sample of 166 sports product consumers. The results indicate that consumer outcomes differ significantly across strategies for repurchase intention, customer satisfaction, and brand loyalty (p < .001, partial η2 ranging from 0.454 to 0.521). Specifically, following the logical progression of the consumer journey, Webrooming emerged as the primary driver for repurchase intention (M = 4.94), whereas the Online-to-Offline configuration was most effective in enhancing customer satisfaction (M = 4.96) and brand loyalty (M = 4.96). Scheffé's post-hoc tests revealed several significant pairwise differences, confirming that channel advantages are outcome-specific: digital research excels in driving intent, while integrated physical touchpoints are essential for securing relational outcomes. Customer experience and brand trust both significantly moderated the effects of omni-channel strategies on all three outcomes. In both cases, differences between strategies were more pronounced among consumers with lower experience and trust.This study elucidates the differential impacts of omni-channel strategies on sports product consumers and highlights the importance of methodological rigor, specifically post-stratification weighting as a robustness check, in enhancing the generalizability of retailing research. The substantive conclusions remained unchanged when the same models were re-estimated on the raked, weighted sample, confirming the stability of the findings under post-stratification adjustment. © 2026 The Authors

title: One count, three processes: Rethinking administrative stability in Korea's fuel-cell and renewable licensing pipeline
abstract: Administrative amendment counts conflate recurrent filings, schedule revisions, and changes in project ownership or specification. This article develops a Frequency-Magnitude-Type framework for interpreting incomplete development records and identifying the additional information needed for monitoring. Applied to Korea's RPS-era generation-licensing pipeline, it combines action-specific filing counts, planned-deadline displacement, and filing types over common project-age windows. Rebuilding the April 2001-June 2026 ledger yields 4804 records and a dated panel of 1813 projects; principal comparisons use 1018 projects with closed three-year windows. Fuel cells and onshore wind show no statistically detectable difference in extension incidence or intensity, whereas onshore wind has 1.44 times the adjusted deadline displacement among projects with positive movement. Project-level joint analysis adds distinctions that separate technology comparisons conceal. Twenty projects record positive deadline movement without a preparation-period extension, and projects with exactly one extension exhibit different displacement distributions. Ownership-transfer tags further distinguish administrative histories within the same frequency groups. Missing deadlines are retained as missing information rather than unchanged schedules. The resulting profiles describe administrative activity, not commissioning, and direct attention to the records needed to investigate it. The historical case thus provides a recording and interpretation framework for monitoring emerging development regimes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Registered Report - Stage II: Do good, feel luckier: How cause-related marketing in unpredictable tourism products boosts tourists’ purchase intention?
abstract: Marketing unpredictable tourism experiences like aurora or wildlife viewing poses distinct challenges due to their inherent uncertainty, yet research on effective strategies remains limited. In Stage I of this Registered Report, we proposed that cause-related marketing (CRM) would boost purchase intention for unpredictable tourism products more effectively than traditional discounts by activating a karmic investment mechanism (i.e., self-luck expectancy), especially under consumer-focused framing. Through an eye-tracking experiment, a quasi-experimental field study, and three scenario-based experiments, we found no conclusive evidence that CRM outperforms discounts in increasing purchase intention, nor support for the mediating role of self-luck expectancy. Although a moderating influence of protagonist focus was observed, its effect contradicted our hypothesis. However, an unexpected finding emerged: luck primes significantly elevate self-luck expectancy and enhance purchase intention. These results suggest that practitioners should either exercise caution in deploying standard CRM from a cost-benefit perspective or enhance its utility by fostering deeper consumer moral engagement. © 2026 The Authors.

title: From expectations to experience: How tasting plant-based fermented foods shapes consumption intentions
abstract: Increasing consumption of plant-based fermented foods (PBFF) is beneficial for both public health and environment, yet intake among Western meat-eaters remains low. This study examined how sensory exposure to PBFF (sourdough bread, plant-based fermented dairy and meat alternatives), the timing of sensory exposure, and expected and actual liking influence intentions to increase PBFF consumption, and whether food neophobia moderates these effects. Data were collected over three weeks via an online pre-survey (n = 143), a laboratory experiment (n = 143), and an online post survey (n = 127). In the laboratory, participants were randomly assigned to either report their consumption intentions before tasting PBFF (n = 70) or after tasting PBFF (n = 73). Results showed that tasting PBFF attenuated the negative association between food neophobia and intention to increase consumption of PBFF. Patterns in the data suggested that intentions shifted at the first measurement following sensory exposure: participants who tasted before reporting intentions, changed intentions in the laboratory, whereas for those who reported intentions prior to tasting, changed intentions at follow-up. Product-specific patterns were observed: tasting increased intentions for the well-liked sourdough bread, but decreased intentions for the lesser-liked plant-based fermented meat. Sensory liking of the specific PBFF product was the strongest predictor of intentions for sourdough bread and plant-based fermented dairy, beyond expectations, whereas effects for plant-based fermented meat were weaker and less consistent. These findings highlight the importance of positive sensory experiences in shaping intentions to increase consumption of plant-based fermented foods, particularly among more food-neophobic meat-eaters. © 2026 The Authors

title: Shared but feared: A vulnerability-sensitive account of consumer responses to post-crisis service environments
abstract: Shared service environments are typically designed to facilitate comfort, efficiency, and positive consumer experiences. In post-crisis contexts, however, these environments may also be appraised through concerns about exposure, controllability, and personal vulnerability. Building on a context-specific refinement of the organismic component within the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this research examines how residual infection-related fear is associated with consumer responses to shared service environments in a post-pandemic context. A two-study design was implemented within a single French-language survey (N = 425). Study 1 tested whether residual infection-related fear was associated with avoidance of public service environments through differentiated forms of health anxiety. Structural equation modeling showed that residual infection-related fear was positively associated with both personal and interpersonal health anxiety, but only personal health anxiety was associated with avoidance, yielding a significant indirect effect through the self-focused pathway. Study 2 experimentally manipulated store density (high vs. low) and sanitary signals (present vs. absent) to examine how servicescape cues influenced perceived crowding and shopping satisfaction. Results showed that higher density reduced satisfaction, but this negative effect was attenuated when sanitary signals were present. Perceived crowding did not mediate the density–satisfaction relationship. A separate exploratory analysis indicated that the overall association between sanitary signals and satisfaction was more positive among individuals reporting higher residual infection-related fear. Taken together, the findings suggest that post-crisis responses to shared service environments may reflect the interplay between situational cues and heterogeneous vulnerability orientations, consistent with a vulnerability-sensitive appraisal system. The research offers a context-specific contribution to servicescape theory by suggesting that, under residual health-threat salience, organismic processes may require a more differentiated specification in contexts marked by residual threat, and by highlighting how visible safety-related cues may improve evaluations of dense service environments. Exploratory evidence further suggests that the overall association between such cues and satisfaction is more positive among consumers who remain more sensitive to infection-related risk. © 2026 The Authors

title: When perception meets reality: explaining measured food waste through consumer behavior in a university dining hall
abstract: Food waste (FW) in university dining halls generates significant environmental and economic impacts, yet most studies rely on self-reported measures and rarely combine behavioral perceptions with objective waste data. This study investigates the determinants of consumer FW by integrating individual plate-waste measurements with behavioral and dining-related factors in a university dining hall setting. Data were collected from 422 diners using a 31-item questionnaire, along with individual measurements of avoidable plate waste after meals. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied to examine behavioral relationships and differences across demographic and meal-related groups. Average plate waste reached 51.5 g per person, with higher waste levels observed during lunch and among female diners. Self-perceived waste behavior, intention to reduce FW, and sensory satisfaction were directly associated with the measured amount of discarded food. In contrast, consumer knowledge, portion size perception, and available eating time influenced only perceived waste behavior, revealing a disconnect between awareness and objectively measured PW. The findings highlight the importance of dining context and meal satisfaction in shaping consumer FW and demonstrate the value of integrating subjective perceptions with objective waste measurements. By combining behavioral evidence with direct waste quantification, this study advances methodological approaches to consumer FW research and provides insights for designing more effective waste reduction strategies in institutional food services. © 2026 The Authors

title: Using emojis to uplift emotion: Effects on mental health chatbots’ performance
abstract: As AI-based chatbots increasingly expand access to mental health support, understanding how text-based systems convey emotional attentiveness without face-to-face nonverbal cues is important. Emojis may serve as lightweight paralinguistic cues, yet their effects in mental health support remain unclear. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and psychological ownership theory, this study examines associations between emoji use and users’ emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Two scenario-based online experiments were conducted in China using random sampling through Credamo, yielding 459 valid responses (59 in the pretest and 400 in the main study). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and the PROCESS macro. Across the experiments, emoji use was associated with more favorable emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Mediation analyses supported an indirect pathway through perceived warmth and psychological ownership, whereas the corresponding competence-based pathway was not supported. AI literacy strengthened the perceived warmth–psychological ownership association but, contrary to predictions, weakened the perceived competence–psychological ownership association. Moderated mediation analyses provided preliminary support for AI literacy strengthening the warmth-based indirect effects of emoji use on emotional well-being and continuance usage intention. The corresponding effect on satisfaction was not supported. These findings extend research on AI-mediated mental health support by identifying a warmth–psychological ownership pathway and the differentiated role of AI literacy. The study also offers preliminary, context-bounded guidance for the strategic and context-sensitive use of emojis in supportive, non-clinical chatbot interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees
abstract: Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings. © 2026

title: Tourism's temporal pathways: A deceleration framework
abstract: This research introduces Tourism Deceleration as a theoretically grounded framework for understanding temporal recalibration in tourism. Building on social acceleration theory and consumer deceleration framework, we conceptualize tourism deceleration as a situated temporal negotiation through which travelers recalibrate pace, attention, mobility, digital connectivity, and presence. Using hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis supported by LLM-assisted coding and human validation, we analyze 367 unique Reddit posts and 21,554 comments related to slow travel and long-term travel. The findings show that decelerated travel is often negotiated through practical, social, and personal constraints rather than simply chosen as a preferred travel style. Episodic deceleration remains the most explicit form of decelerated travel, while extended duration often intersects with embodied practices, reduced mobility pressure, and selective negotiation of digital technologies. The research note contributes by distinguishing tourism deceleration from slow tourism and explaining how travelers manage time under conditions of choice, context, and constraint. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The evolving science of negotiation alternatives: New contexts, new perspectives
abstract: We review the past decade (2016 – present) of empirical research on negotiation alternatives across multiple disciplines, including dyadic bargaining, international trade, and civil conflict interventions. Three themes emerged in our analysis: First, research has focused on how the effects of a negotiator's BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) are not person-invariant but are instead moderated by the characteristics of the party who “holds” the BATNA. Second, studies are establishing the conditions under which negotiation alternatives can backfire and hurt a negotiator's performance. Third, an emerging stream of research challenges our conventional understanding of BATNA by highlighting its perceptual nature and the possibility that it may exist on multiple levels within a given negotiation. We close by outlining future directions for each of these emerging themes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Exploring the evolution of public cognition toward generative AI through sentiment-topic mining and community detection in social graphs
abstract: The swift advancement of Generative AI(GAI) improves content production efficiency and generates commercial value, yet it presents complex governance issues, including misinformation and technological misuse. To investigate the cognitive evolution of the public and the characteristics of the online opinion ecosystem regarding GAI, this study collected 105,384 GAI-related posts and comments from Sina Weibo between 2023 and 2026. A semantic-topological social graph(ST-Graph) was constructed from textual semantics, engagement feedback, and user profile features, and a Contrastive Learning-based Graph Neural Network(ConGNN) was employed for node representation learning and community detection. Additionally, StructBERT-based sentiment classification was combined with DeepSeek-based key attribute and trigger-word extraction to analyze emotional orientations and cognitive focuses across communities. Experimental findings indicate that ConGNN achieved the highest Silhouette, ARI, and NMI values among the compared methods, while the yearly community partitions yielded Silhouette coefficients ranging from 0.4002 to 0.4476. These results indicate relatively clear separation in the learned representation space and consistent clustering under the evaluated settings, supporting the effectiveness of ConGNN for the constructed ST-Graph. Sentiment analysis shows that public attitudes toward GAI are generally positive, but vary across publishing entities. Public figures garner the greatest number of remarks, with positive feedback from Enterprises constituting the predominant share(49.3%). Government mainly garner neutral feedback(70.9%), however Media and Organizations/Institutions observe a greater share of negative remarks(38.9% and 41.2%). Aspect-level analysis further indicates that public cognition is shifting from early technological expectations and substitution anxiety toward institutional concerns, especially demands for anti-counterfeiting, content credibility, and digital governance mechanisms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Nodding of virtual humans does not necessarily increase customer trust: a temporal analysis
abstract: Virtual humans can potentially facilitate engaging customer interactions, but remain rarely used in customer service. Their embodiment enables virtual humans to use non-verbal listening cues like nodding. Nodding is theorized to increase trust in virtual humans, but literature on this effect is scarce, inconsistent, and only uses measurements after interactions. This study therefore aims to research how nodding of virtual humans influences customer trust, by (1) studying the following hypothesized mediation: nodding (social cue) triggers perceived responsiveness (social signal), which subsequently increases trust (social response); and (2) studying temporal trust dynamics within a customer interaction using exploratory analyses. An online experiment (N = 429) was performed, using a between-subjects design with two conditions: a virtual human either nodded during listening or did not. To isolate nodding optimally, participants watched a video of a customer interaction: a virtual human advised a customer on a wardrobe. While watching, participants used a slider scale to keep updating their temporal trust in the virtual human. Afterwards, participants answered questionnaires on trust and perceived responsiveness. Results showed that nodding did not increase trust or perceived responsiveness, nor did nodding build temporal trust. Temporal trust was built throughout the customer interaction, mostly when the virtual human was speaking. Exploratory analysis found that nodding increased anthropomorphism. Possibly, nodding did not influence trust because other social cues already caused trust-building. Virtual human developers should therefore be aware that nodding does not necessarily build customer trust. The temporal trust scale was useful for visualizing trust-building throughout customer interaction videos. © 2026 The Authors

title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy
abstract: Influencer marketing has become an integral part of retail branding strategies. As the creator economy continues to expand, influencer collaborations are now viewed as strategic partnerships rather than promotional activities. Despite this transition, sustaining authentic and long-term brand-influencer partnerships remains a significant yet underexplored challenge. Combining Social Exchange Theory (SET) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT) into a unified motivational-exchange framework, this research focuses on how brand practices operate simultaneously as relational exchange resources and as psychological need-satisfying inputs within influencer–brand partnerships. With a mixed-methods two-phase approach, this study exmains how brand ethical–purpose alignment, autonomy support, and AI co-creation are linked to influencers' sense of ownership and thriving, as well as citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity. In Study 1, 22 semi-structured interviews were conducted with professional influencers across four regions, intended to understand their lived partnership experiences. In Study 2, responses from 422 influencers were analysed using structural equation modelling and moderation analysis. The study also examines serial indirect pathways through which brand practices are associated with voluntary citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity via Collaboration Ownership and Influencer Thriving. The findings suggest that autonomy support, purpose alignment, and AI co-creation enablement are positively associated with influencers' ownership and thriving. These again are associated with higher levels of voluntary advocacy and intentions to continue partnerships. Therefore, the research positions influencer collaboration as relational rather than transactional and highlights the significance of autonomy, ethical-purpose congruence, and relational fairness in understanding sustainable relationships between influencers and brands. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Why skilled migrants stay or leave host countries: A belongingness theory perspective
abstract: While skilled migrants have a high propensity to quit their jobs and leave host countries, little is known about why some skilled migrants leave while others stay. This paper draws on belongingness theory to examine the mediated effects of work and non-work sense of belonging between skilled migrants’ local language proficiency and host country exit, and the moderated effects of work and non-work social support from locals between local language proficiency and both belonging types. Regression analyses of time-lagged, multisource data collected from 159 foreign academics in Japan suggest that local language proficiency was positively related to work sense of belonging, which was subsequently negatively related to host country exit. Furthermore, the positive relationship between local language proficiency and work sense of belonging was stronger when work and non-work social support were high. This paper contributes to the literature by providing a novel perspective on skilled migrants’ host country experiences, shifting the focus from withdrawal cognitions to belongingness and host country exit, and integrating language proficiency into the theory of belongingness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The impact of consumer culture positioning on multinational brand premium: The moderating role of global identity
abstract: Multinational brands often charge higher prices in emerging markets than in their home markets. Although such multinational brand premiums can improve profitability, they may also invite consumers to compare prices across countries and evaluate the premium as unfair. This research examines how consumer culture positioning (CCP) shapes consumers' willingness to pay a multinational brand premium through price fairness perceptions, operationalized as perceived price unfairness, and how this process depends on consumers' global identity. Across a pretest and three experiments in China, we compare Global Consumer Culture Positioning (GCCP) with Local Consumer Culture Positioning (LCCP) in a multinational restaurant-brand context. Experiment 1 establishes the main effect of CCP and the mediating role of perceived price unfairness. Experiment 2 replicates this pathway and examines chronic global identity as a boundary condition. Experiment 3 further tests the moderation through situationally activated global versus local identity. The results generally show that GCCP, relative to LCCP, reduces perceived price unfairness and increases willingness to pay a premium. The fairness-based indirect effect becomes stronger as chronic global identity increases and when global identity is situationally activated. The findings integrate global branding and pricing research by showing when cultural positioning can make a higher price appear more acceptable rather than merely enhance brand image. The study also provides managerial implications for multinational and local brands operating in emerging retail and service markets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How local–global identity shapes physical-digital preferences through convenience preference
abstract: Despite the functional advantages of digital products, consumers’ preferences between digital and physical formats remain highly heterogeneous in a marketplace where globalization and renewed localism coexist. Drawing on identity-based motivation theory, this research examines how local versus global identity influences consumers' preferences for physical versus digital products through convenience preference. Across three studies (five sub-studies), we demonstrate that a relatively stronger local-over-global identity is associated with greater preference for physical over digital consumption formats. Further analyses reveal an asymmetric effect that local identity drives stronger preferences for physical products, whereas global identity does not produce a corresponding increase in preference for digital formats. We further identify convenience preference as the underlying mechanism, showing that stronger local identity reduces convenience preference, thereby increasing preference for physical products. These findings reconceptualize physical versus digital preferences as identity-consistent choices rather than purely functional evaluations. By identifying convenience as an identity-contingent motivational preference, this research advances identity-based motivation theory and provides timely insights into how identity orientations shape consumer preferences amid ongoing digital transformation and heightened societal attention to globalization–localism dynamics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Geopolitical risk and tourism firm resilience: Global evidence
abstract: This paper analyzes how geopolitical risk affects the performance of tourism firms and identifies the conditions under which its adverse effects are mitigated. Using a global panel of 1438 firms across 39 countries from 2007 to 2021, we find that heightened geopolitical risk significantly reduces firms’ market valuations. Drawing on risk perception theory, network theory, and institutional theory, we show that this effect is conditional rather than uniform. Specifically, firms located in countries with stronger international tourism network embeddedness experience weaker negative effects, as network connectivity facilitates demand diversification and adaptive responses. Similarly, higher institutional quality reduces the adverse impact of geopolitical risk by enhancing stability and policy credibility. These findings are robust to alternative measures and estimation methods. The paper provides new evidence on the transmission of geopolitical risk and highlights the role of structural and institutional factors in shaping resilience in the global tourism sector. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Imperfection in motion: Implied motion reduces negative associations of imperfect produce
abstract: Food waste remains a major sustainability challenge, with imperfect fruits and vegetables often rejected due to their appearance. Prior studies suggest that food choices are mostly automatic, implicit, and habitual, rather than made through deliberated choice. Such insights suggest why explicit messaging to increase consumers' imperfect food purchasing has shown limited effectiveness and highlight opportunities for behaviour change via less mindful means. This study investigates the extent to which negative implicit associations for “imperfect” (vs. “perfect”) exist, and whether implied motion (e.g., fruit splashing into water) can mitigate these evaluations. In a pre-registered study, participants (N = 145) completed an in-person multi-dimensional Implicit Association Test (IAT) to examine their implicit attitudes in static and motion contexts. Results showed that participants' implicit associations were positive for perfect produce and negative for imperfect produce, suggesting an “Ugly = Bad” association. However, exposure to implied motion imagery significantly reduced this negativity effect toward imperfect fresh produce, while having no significant effect on perfect produce. Our findings link implicit attitudes to sustainable food acceptance and demonstrate the potential of visually-based interventions, such as implied motion, to reduce negative aesthetic biases and support behaviour change aimed at increasing acceptance of imperfect produce and reducing food waste. © 2026 The Authors

title: Examining the layered veil of pay transparency: Implications for perceived ambiguity, sensemaking, and negotiation
abstract: In the last decade, pay transparency—making pay information more accessible and understandable—has become a defining workplace reform. We examine the common assumption that pay transparency reduces pay disparities by improving negotiation outcomes. Our cross-disciplinary review suggests that pay transparency's effects on negotiation hinge on three factors: (1) how transparency is operationalized (i.e., what type of pay information is shared); (2) how people interpret the information provided; and (3) whether transparency alone can motivate and equip individuals to leverage that information to negotiate effectively. We distinguish three interrelated negotiation-relevant layers of pay transparency—job offer, peer, and market—and then assess how these reduce ambiguity, shape negotiator sensemaking, and influence negotiation processes and outcomes. We conclude by outlining implications for future negotiation research and practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Predicting the future of retail services: Trends, technologies, and strategic imperatives for 2025–2035
abstract: The rapid convergence of digital platforms and shifting consumer behaviors is driving an unprecedented structural transformation across the global retail landscape. This paper examines the systemic evolution of retail channel revenue distributions and operational capabilities, establishing the critical strategic imperatives required to navigate market disruption over the 2025–2035 horizons. The primary objective of this study is to empirically model the longitudinal shifts between traditional physical retail, e-commerce, and physical channels, while concurrently diagnosing the capability gaps across diverse corporate scales. Methodologically, this research deploys a mixed-methods empirical framework, integrating a quantitative survey of 418 retail industry professionals with qualitative interviews from 32 senior executives across six countries, analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA. The empirical findings reveal a definitive market polarization: traditional physical retail is projected to contract significantly from 54.3% to 30.8%, while e-commerce expands to claim a dominant 52.7% revenue share by 2035. Our multi-method analysis validates that digital-physical integration and AI-driven personalization (β = 0.38, p < .001) directly resolve post-pandemic operational vulnerabilities, emerging as the primary drivers of future performance outcomes. Longitudinal analysis confirms a steady decline in traditional commodity metrics, while scenario simulations warn that small and medium-sized enterprises face a severe (66.5%) market share loss under unmitigated polarization. To address this structural market polarization, this study provides a rigorous, data-driven defense by establishing the Retail Evolution Framework (REF) to explain how systemic retail survival requires aligning operational tools with shifting institutional norms. The study bridges the dynamic capabilities gap under the Resource-Based View while offering actionable strategies for ethical data governance. Practically, these insights provide an actionable investment roadmap for corporate managers to redirect capital allocations from physical footprint expansion into automated data ecosystems and cloud-based logistics architectures to maintain long-term competitive viability. © 2026

title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered. © 2026 The Author(s).

title: Disclosing AI without losing consumers: When and how AI disclosure works in advertising
abstract: Extant research on AI disclosure examines its negative impact across various domains, but limited attention has been paid to why these effects occur and how they can be mitigated in advertising. To address this gap, we examine why consumers react negatively to AI disclosures in advertising, identify the boundary of this effect, and propose strategies to mitigate it. Across three studies, we show that AI disclosure reduces consumers’ attitudes toward the advertisement and purchase intentions through decreased perceived creativity. More importantly, we find that product type serves as a boundary condition for this effect, and that the negative influence of AI disclosure (vs. human designer disclosure) is attenuated when AI is identified as an employee. Implications for both theories and practices are discussed. © 2026

title: Survival of Contractor Consortiums in the Road Construction Industry during Economic Crisis
abstract: Road construction industries worldwide are periodically exposed to economic crises, which are cyclical in nature and often characterized by high inflation, currency depreciation, resource shortages, and institutional inefficiencies. In such conditions, traditional procurement methods frequently struggle to maintain project continuity, prompting the emergence of local contractor consortiums as a more resilient alternative. This study examines how contractor consortiums in the road construction sector adapted to recent economic crises and sustained operations amid unprecedented challenges. A qualitative research approach was adopted, involving 14 semistructured interviews with industry experts. Manual content analysis identified key adaptive measures, including financial pooling, shared equipment and labor, agile internal coordination, and proactive engagement with public authorities. These mechanisms enabled many consortiums to continue project delivery despite severe economic and operational constraints. However, the effectiveness of these measures was constrained by rigid legal and contractual frameworks, limited digital integration, fragmented stakeholder collaboration, and delayed institutional responses. To enhance future resilience, the study recommends modernizing contractual systems, strengthening digital adoption, and improving public-private coordination. The findings contribute to construction management research in crisis contexts by demonstrating the viability of consortium-based procurement and providing practical guidance to support the long-term sustainability of local contractor consortiums in the road construction sector. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: Institutional resilience and land-acquisition governance: Participation and conflict-management mechanisms in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project
abstract: This study examines governance performance during infrastructure land acquisition and the role of institutional resilience in supporting implementation. Using survey data from 108 public-sector implementers involved in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project in Indonesia, the relationships among institutional resilience capacities, participatory governance, conflict-management mechanisms, and governance performance were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Learning capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to participatory governance, while buffering capacity was positively related to conflict-management mechanisms. Participatory governance showed no direct relationship with governance performance but its indirect relationship through conflict-management mechanisms was statistically significant. Buffering capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to governance performance, while learning capacity showed no significant relationship. The findings reveal differentiated governance roles across resilience capacities and distinguish direct capacity–performance relationships from process-based relationships involving stakeholder participation and conflict-management mechanisms. In conflict-prone land acquisition, conflict-management mechanisms emerged as an important governance process linking stakeholder participation with governance performance. The study shows how different resilience capacities support different governance functions during land-acquisition implementation. © 2026
