title: Perceived control and stress reactivity in algorithm-supported hiring decisions
abstract: Algorithms increasingly determine who gets interviewed, flagged, or passed over in hiring, often without explanation, consistency, or any mechanism for response. Yet the psychological mechanisms through which algorithm-supported decision-making shapes stress responses remain insufficiently specified. This article develops a theoretically grounded framework linking diminished perceived control to stress reactivity in algorithm-mediated decision-making contexts. Drawing on self-determination theory, decision-making process frameworks, and psychological safety, the manuscript integrates empirical evidence from research on AI hiring practices, including findings on Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) individuals navigating applicant tracking systems. The framework identifies three primary mechanisms through which AI-supported decision-making may influence stress reactivity: limited transparency, inconsistent decision processes, and constrained opportunities for feedback. This work offers a foundation for empirical work on how technologically mediated environments shape cognitive appraisal, perceived control, and stress. These dynamics extend beyond hiring to any structured assessment context in applied behavioral and clinical settings. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. title: Models for risk management in the procurement process within organizational contexts: A systematic literature review
abstract: Over the past decade, supply chain management has faced extreme volatility, culminating in the unprecedented disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, resilience in procurement has transitioned from a secondary attribute to an indispensable requirement for operational continuity. This study classifies the state of the art in procurement risk management within the post-pandemic landscape (2021–2025). It analyzes the transition from reactive approaches toward predictive and prescriptive perspectives to address supply chain volatility. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Based on a structured search in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, an initial pool of 1,109 records was screened. This resulted in a final sample of 107 high-impact peer-reviewed articles. These studies were evaluated using thematic content analysis and classified into ten technical categories based on their functional orientation. The evidence reveals a fragmented methodological ecosystem where Hybrid Models (21.5%) and Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM, 16.8%) techniques predominate. A shift is observed from static approaches toward the integration of robust optimization, tail risk metrics like Conditional Value at Risk, and Machine Learning. However, a gap is identified between algorithmic complexity and corporate adoption. The study establishes that Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Blockchain are indispensable governance requirements to overcome the black box problem in strategic decision-making. This research contributes a functional classification of tools based on their diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive orientation. Furthermore, it provides managers with a tiered roadmap to achieve analytical maturity. This guides organizations from foundational visibility using synthetic indices, through fuzzy multi-criteria evaluations, toward the responsible implementation of stochastic programming and AI. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: The persuasive power of video in hospitality: How guest-generated video reviews influence customer engagement
abstract: Guest-generated video reviews are increasingly prevalent on online travel platforms, yet their effects and mechanisms remain underexplored. Drawing on media richness theory, this study is among the first to examine whether and how such reviews enhance customer engagement, measured by subsequent review volume. We adopt a multimethod approach that combines econometric analysis with a controlled experiment to establish causal inference and uncover underlying mechanisms. Using a 24-month panel of 4471 hotels on Ctrip.com, difference-in-differences results show that guest-generated video reviews significantly increase customer engagement, with stronger effects for higher-tier or large hotels. Experimental evidence further demonstrates that these effects operate through increased information diagnosticity and social presence. Additional video content analysis reveals that human presence, higher informational richness, better visual quality, and longer duration further amplify the positive effects. These findings extend media richness theory to consumer-generated video reviews and offer insights into how richer review media stimulate engagement in hospitality settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How to move you? The persuasive effects of influencer narrative styles in recommending tourism activities
abstract: Influencers exert significant promotional effects in tourism marketing; however, few empirical studies have examined how different types of tourism activities can strategically leverage these effects through influencer narrative style. To address this gap, this study draws on Heuristic-Analytic Theory to investigate how personal and professional narrative styles align with relaxing and challenging tourism activities to maximize influencers’ persuasiveness. The study analyzes secondary data from 1187 social media posts and conducts three scenario-based experiments with 1438 participants. Results show that personal narrative style is more persuasive for relaxing activities, whereas professional narrative style works better for challenging activities. Moreover, experience resonance and knowledge acquisition are identified as key underlying mechanisms. Notably, the study introduces temporal distance in travel decision as a moderator, highlighting the importance of dynamic temporal cues in influencer recommendations. The findings provide valuable theoretical contributions and practical implications for optimizing influencer marketing strategies in the tourism context. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The road to hell is paved with good intentions: How does the construction of low-carbon cities affect corporate low-carbon technological innovation in manufacturing?
abstract: Low-carbon technological innovation (LCTI) is crucial for decarbonization and global climate change mitigation. Taking China's Low-carbon City Pilot (LCCP)—a pioneering exploration for low-carbon development through policy innovation—as an exogenous policy shock, this study utilizes a staggered difference-in-difference-in-differences model and the data of China's manufacturing firms to examine the causality between the voluntary carbon regulation and LCTI. For the first time, the results indicate that the LCCP enactment significantly hinders corporate LCTI, contradicting the predictions of the Porter hypothesis. Mechanism analysis reveals that under the LCCP framework, local governments are authorized to design innovative policies tailored to their specific conditions and are responsible for their own assessment. Using a two-stage LLM-based approach to construct a climate policy uncertainty perception index, we confirm that this “bottom-up” approach introduces significant policy uncertainty faced by firms and weakens their motivation for LCTI involvement. Furthermore, the compliance costs associated with the policy crowd out the funds for LCTI, further hindering firms from engaging in LCTI. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the adverse impact is more evident among firms exhibiting high risk aversion, ones with high artificial intelligence (AI) technology exposure, ones situated in non-resource-based cities, and state-owned ones, and that the adverse impact is significant for emission reduction technologies and zero-carbon technologies, but not for negative-carbon technologies. Additionally, all three pilot batches negatively impact corporate LCTI, suggesting that institutional modifications have not led to intended positive outcomes. This empirical research offers novel evidence regarding the efficacy of the LCCP and yields valuable policy insights—stable policy expectations and robust supervision mechanisms are crucial for achieving policy goals. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Not naive, just gullible: psycho-cognitive vulnerability and fraud victimization in Italy
abstract: Fraud represents a growing and complex threat in contemporary societies, with consequences that extend beyond economic losses. Despite increasing international evidence, limited research has examined the psychological and cognitive factors associated with fraud victimization in the Italian context, particularly in relation to online scams. This study examines individual differences and fraud experiences among 600 Italian adults through an online survey assessing sociodemographic characteristics, fraud experiences, personality traits, gullibility, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy. Results revealed that more than half of the sample (n = 416) reported exposure to scam attempts, most of which occurred through remote channels (either exclusively online or in combination with offline channels). A smaller subset (n = 115) reported actual fraud victimization. A binomial logistic regression was conducted to identify individual factors associated with fraud victimization among exposed individuals. Gullibility emerged as the only statistically significant predictor, indicating that higher gullibility was associated with a greater likelihood of victimization, whereas sociodemographic characteristics, personality traits, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy were not significantly associated with victimization. These findings highlight that fraud prevention strategies may benefit from considering psycho-cognitive vulnerability factors alongside traditional financial and digital literacy initiatives. © 2026

title: Anger regulation scale for adolescents (ARS-A): Psychometric properties of the Portuguese version and its associations with emotion regulation, depression, and anxiety
abstract: Adolescence is marked by difficulties in anger regulation, which are linked to internalising and externalising problems. Despite this, the instruments currently available to measure anger regulation in adolescents have a limited evidence base and require further investigation. The present study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the Anger Regulation Scale for Adolescents (ARS-A) in the Portuguese context. A sample of 432 adolescents aged 11 to 18 (M = 13.73, SD = 1.61) from different regions of Portugal participated in this study. The factor structure and model fit were assessed through Principal Component Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis, using the Solomon method for equivalent sample splitting. All subscales demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and fit indices, confirming the original three-dimensional structure after two items were removed. Pearson correlations with other measures of behavioural and cognitive emotion regulation were consistent with theoretical expectations, although not all associations were as expected. Correlations between anger regulation, depression and anxiety corroborated the relationship between dysfunctional anger regulation and emotional distress. The ARS-A is a reliable and valid measure of anger regulation for adolescents. © 2026 The Authors.

title: When health labels increase indulgent food purchase intention
abstract: Health labels are widely used in front-of-package communication and are generally expected to facilitate healthier decisions. We examine whether such labels can also increase consumers' indulgent food purchase intention. Across six studies, health labels attached to indulgent products were associated with greater attentional or motivational salience (Study 1a), higher digital-ad click-through rates (CTRs) (Study 1b), a higher likelihood of selecting an indulgent product in an incentive-compatible raffle (Study 1c), and stronger purchase intentions (Studies 1d–3). Study 2 provides statistical support for a serial indirect effect involving justification for purchase and perceived guilt, whereas perceived healthfulness did not mediate purchase intention in the models tested. Study 3 identifies brand equity as a boundary condition of the claim effect on purchase intention. The observed pattern raises concerns that health labels on indulgent foods may unintentionally lower consumers' psychological restraint, potentially increasing overall favorable responses to indulgent foods in real-world settings. Practically, the results suggest that health labels should be evaluated in relation to products' overall nutritional profiles and brand contexts. © 2026

title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions
abstract: The dialectic relationship between the production of post-growth knowledge and ongoing construction of social reality is a complex one, but one that warrants attention. In this scoping review, we respond to the emergent interest in post-growth politics and theories of change. We aim to complement existing reviews of post-growth policy proposals and recommendations with an analysis of peer-reviewed studies on interventions – deliberate attempts by one state, market or civil society actor to influence another. Drawing on a socio-ecological systems leverage points perspective embedded within a political economy inspired mapping of social forces, we develop a conceptual framework for explaining strategic trade-offs made by actors to achieve various forms of depth.Our findings point to asymmetrical relationships between actors-executor pairs and a pattern of neoliberal subjectification in both intervention design and analytical focus. We also find that whilst post-growth interventions can readily achieve discursive depth, it is often accompanied by institutional shallowness and temporal fragility. We conclude with reflections on strategic implications for post-growth researchers and movements. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

title: Empowering leadership in educational contexts: A bibliometric analysis to guide management in the framework of SDG 4
abstract: Empowering leadership (EL) has emerged as a critical leadership approach in educational contexts, particularly in response to increasing demands for innovation, teacher autonomy, and sustainable institutional development. However, despite the rapid growth of studies in this field, the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, thematic evolution, and contribution to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) remain fragmented and insufficiently synthesized. Therefore, this study aims to provide a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of EL research in educational settings indexed in the Scopus database from 1999 to 2026. A total of 84 publications were analyzed using bibliometric performance indicators and science mapping techniques, including co-authorship analysis, keyword co-occurrence, three-field plot visualization, citation analysis, and thematic clustering, supported by Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. The results reveal a strong upward publication trend with a coefficient of determination of R² = 77.54%, particularly accelerating after 2018 and reaching the highest output in 2025. Citation influence remains concentrated in foundational studies published in high-impact journals such as Journal of Applied Psychology, Journal of Knowledge Management, and Leadership Quarterly. China and Indonesia emerge as major international collaboration hubs, while Indonesia shows the strongest author–keyword linkage. Keyword analysis identifies dominant themes related to psychological empowerment, teacher autonomy, innovative work behavior, job satisfaction, and distributed leadership. Notably, 74 out of 84 publications (88.1%) are aligned with SDG 4, highlighting the strong integration of EL research with global educational sustainability agendas. This study offers the first structured intellectual map of EL in education, identifies influential contributors and emerging research directions, and provides evidence-based guidance for educational leadership development aligned with quality education and sustainable transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Modality effects in human–technology interaction
abstract: This paper reviews emerging research on how different interaction modalities influence information processing and behavior when using new technological devices. A conceptual framework of modality effects is proposed which argues that different input (vocal, haptic) and output modalities (audial, visual) can trigger both cognitive and affective processes that alter users' downstream behaviors. For example, information consumed audially from voice technology rather than visually on a screen can enhance both cognitive load (i.e., cognitive process) and one's sense of social presence (i.e., affective process), which ultimately shape the types of choices made through the technology. The work concludes with a discussion of future research directions in this domain. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life. title: Hero products and the value of position in live streaming commerce evidence from Douyin
abstract: Every livestream sales session has one product that sells best, and the minutes in which it is shown are when the broadcast's audience peaks. This paper asks what that moment is worth to the products around it: can the items that follow the hero, or those shown just before it, turn the traffic it attracts into sales of their own? Using 260,252 product–session observations from 8123 Douyin sessions and an event-study design with session fixed effects, we find conversion highest in the slot immediately after the hero, exceeding products more than five positions away by 0.0177. The advantage is not borrowed traffic. It appears before the hero as much as after it, and only the adjacent slot breaks that symmetry; when the same product is compared with itself across sessions in which it sat at different distances, most of the advantage disappears except beside the hero. The running order therefore reveals mainly which products a streamer places near the featured item, and we report a positional association rather than an attention spillover. What survives is conditional. Scoring each product's own listing title with a large language model, we find that credibility signals attenuate the advantage while informativeness moves it in both directions, and the advantage exists only where the hero appears in the first third of the running order, vanishing when it is held until the end. For managers, the slots flanking an early-placed hero are worth allocating deliberately; positions further down the lineup are not. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The dual impact of cap-and-trade policies on innovations and the moderating role of accumulated resources
abstract: While the cap-and-trade policy is a widely adopted mechanism for addressing climate change, its impact on firms' innovation portfolio remains underexplored. To balance regulatory compliance with profitability, firms must strategically allocate limited resources across different technology innovations based on their existing resource endowments. This study examines how the cap-and-trade policy alters firms' innovation resource allocation across different types of technologies with a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical validation. Our theoretical model suggests that while the policy encourages firms to invest more in green technology, it may crowd out resources from more profitable conventional innovation. This effect is less pronounced for firms with substantial stocks of green innovation resources, but stronger for those with extensive conventional innovation stocks. Using a difference-in-differences approach and firm-level patent data covering enterprises affected by China's regional cap-and-trade pilots, we find that the policy reduces the share of conventional patents by 5.951 percentage points on average, confirming the crowding-out effect. Our moderating analysis further reveals that each additional accumulated green patent mitigates this negative impact by 0.018 percentage points, whereas each additional accumulated conventional patent amplifies it by 0.002 percentage points. Additional significant heterogeneity is also observed, conditional on industry characteristics (pollution intensity, competition intensity, and SOE dominance) and firm-level attributes (R&D intensity, profitability, and governance structure). These findings underscore the importance of guiding highly regulation-sensitive firms toward a balanced innovation transition while encouraging less regulation-sensitive firms to engage more actively via well-targeted and supportive policies that foster both green and conventional innovation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Negotiation across the social sciences: An interdisciplinary review
abstract: Psychological investigations have generated numerous insights into how two parties bargain. To build on this literature, we review recent research across multiple disciplines, focusing on aspects of negotiation that have received relatively little attention, namely individual differences, multiparty negotiations, and contextual factors. Insights into individual differences are observed in the developmental psychology, artificial intelligence, and social psychology literature. Investigations in these domains show that young children can think strategically about exchange, that individual differences shape the information negotiators obtain and how they utilize information, and that situational factors can constrain or facilitate the expression of individual differences. Insights into multiparty negotiations emerge from the social networks and political science literature. Investigations in these domains explore novel multiparty dynamics, highlighting the importance of structural position in bargaining, and demonstrating that relationship history can shape coalition formation. Insights into contextual factors emerge from the economic and public health literature. Investigations in these domains challenge assumptions about core negotiation concepts such as power and alternatives. Overall, an interdisciplinary perspective on negotiation complements and enriches psychological understanding, and provides implications for interventions, future theoretical development, and empirical research. © 2026 The Authors

title: Folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy: A bibliometric study and systematic literature review
abstract: The forces of globalization and digital transformation have intensified attention toward the need to strengthen cultural identity through education, including the use of folklore as a meaningful learning resource. However, existing studies on folklore in learning remain fragmented. While much of the literature focuses on either cultural preservation or specific educational applications, the gap lies in a systematic exploration of folklore's pedagogical role across different contexts and educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the development of research on folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy through a bibliometric approach combined with a systematic literature review. For the bibliometric analysis, metadata records of articles published between 2015 and 2025 were processed from the Google Scholar database. Data for the systematic literature review were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and the article selection process followed PRISMA procedures. A total of 41 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer, while article identification and screening were supported by Publish or Perish. The bibliometric findings indicate a significant increase in publications over the past decade, accompanied by a thematic shift from cultural heritage preservation toward the integration of cultural values within educational contexts. The SLR findings show that the research is predominantly qualitative in nature, with folktales and legends as the most frequently used forms of folklore, and books and e-modules as the main learning media employed to strengthen cultural literacy. The findings suggest that folklore-based learning fosters students’ cultural awareness, internalizes values, strengthens identity formation, and deepens the understanding of local culture. This study contributes by providing a more integrated understanding of folklore as a pedagogical tool for cultural literacy, emphasizing its role in curriculum design. Future research should focus on expanding methodological diversity and exploring broader applications of folklore-based learning across various educational contexts. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Brand stereotypes, information processing, and consumer acceptance of Chinese automobiles: The moderating roles of perceived brand globalness and brand credibility in an emerging market
abstract: Stereotypes about Chinese products persist in many developing economies, even as Chinese manufacturers have substantially upgraded their technological capabilities and product quality. However, the cognitive pathways linking systematic and heuristic information processing to consumers’ stereotype-based perceptions of brand warmth and competence remain underexplored in the evaluation of high-involvement foreign products. Drawing on the heuristic-systematic model, stereotype content model, and signaling theory, this study develops and tests a process-based framework explaining how information processing routes shape stereotype-based brand perceptions, which in turn influence product evaluations and purchase intentions toward Chinese automobiles in Vietnam. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed. A qualitative phase with 20 in-depth interviews was conducted to explore consumers' cognitive processes and refine the theoretical framework. Subsequently, survey data from 638 Vietnamese consumers were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings demonstrate that systematic information processing strengthens perceived brand competence and warmth, whereas heuristic processing weakens both dimensions, thereby reinforcing brand stereotypes. Perceived brand competence and warmth enhance product receptivity, judgment, and quality, which collectively drive purchase intention. Perceived brand globalness weakens the negative effects of heuristic information processing and amplifies the positive effects of systematic information processing on stereotype-related perceptions. Brand credibility strengthens the conversion of product-level evaluations into purchase intention. Theoretically, this study integrates HSM, SCM, and ST to clarify the sequential relationships linking information processing, stereotype-based brand perception, product evaluation, and purchase intention. Practically, the findings offer actionable guidance for Chinese automobile brands seeking to attenuate legacy stereotypes and build consumer acceptance in culturally resistant emerging markets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Beyond data disclosure: A health system transparency framework informed by evidence and Iranian insights
abstract: Objectives: Although transparency is widely recognized as a cornerstone of good health governance, existing studies have often addressed individual dimensions of transparency, with limited integration of these dimensions into a comprehensive conceptual framework for health systems. This study aimed to develop a conceptual framework for health system transparency by integrating evidence from Iran. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in six sequential phases between 2021 and 2024. Three systematic scoping reviews synthesized existing transparency frameworks, implementation principles, and the applications, benefits, risks, barriers, and opportunities of transparency in health systems. Findings were complemented by in-depth interviews with 35 Iranian experts, refined through three expert panels involving 16 participants, and finalized using a three-round modified Delphi study with 23 participants in the final round. Results: The resulting framework conceptualizes transparency as a multi-level governance system comprising strategic contexts and infrastructures, stakeholder interactions, implementation drivers and constraints, transparency application domains, and tactical and technical implementation principles. Rather than viewing transparency as information disclosure alone, the framework emphasizes dynamic interactions between governance conditions, data users, feedback mechanisms, and potential contributions to organizational learning and system improvement. Conclusion: The proposed framework provides an integrated conceptual foundation for designing, implementing, and evaluating transparency reforms in health systems. Although informed by evidence from Iran, its governance-oriented architecture may be transferable to other health systems, provided that context-dependent components are adapted to local institutional, political, legal, and socio-cultural conditions. Public interest summary: Health system transparency is more than making information publicly available. This study developed a framework showing how transparency can become part of everyday health system governance. It identifies the political, administrative, economic, and social conditions needed to support transparency, the role of citizens, researchers, media, and other data users in creating demand for information, and the factors that can either support or hinder implementation. The framework also identifies key areas where transparency is needed, including governance, finances, medicines, workforce, research, and healthcare services, and provides practical and technical principles for implementation. Although developed using evidence from Iran, the framework addresses transparency challenges that may also arise in other health systems and may help policymakers design more coordinated and sustainable transparency reforms. Its broader structure may also be relevant to other public sectors, although contextual adaptation would be required. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

title: How certification credibility and benefit framing shape heterogeneous consumer responses to sustainable products in e-commerce
abstract: On e-commerce platforms, sustainable products succeed or fail on a compressed product page where certification logos, benefit descriptions, and platform trust cues compete for attention. Retailers treat these cues as interchangeable signals, yet they address two different questions: can the product be trusted, and is it right for me? Signalling theory answers the first through costly, verifiable certification; goal-framing theory answers the second through benefit claims activating competing motivations. Whether they operate as one mechanism or two remains unresolved in retailing research. Using a discrete choice experiment with 477 Chinese consumers analysed through aggregate conditional logit, latent class analysis, and trust-stratified models, we show they are separable strategic levers. The certification credibility hierarchy (dual and international premiums above the domestic schemes) holds broadly across all three motivational segments, whereas benefit-framing valuation differs sharply between them, and this segment-level dissociation is the evidence for their separability. Platform trust does not significantly moderate certification premiums. Latent class analysis reveals a dual-motivated majority (53.5 per cent) that stated self-classification systematically understates, making choice-derived rather than self-reported segmentation essential for targeting. Extending goal-framing theory, the study's central contribution shows certification quality as a novel external cue: superior certification shifts dual-motivated consumers' default health preference toward environmental framing, narrowing it to near-parity, with a ¥16.68 break-even threshold at which the two framings reach indifference. These findings show heterogeneous consumer response is structured by the interaction between signal architecture and motivational composition, with implications for certification investment, benefit communication, and segmentation in sustainable retailing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: A fairness-aware TabTransformer framework for credit scoring with high-cardinality regional bias
abstract: This study examines whether fairness constraints must come at the expense of performance in credit risk models. We introduce a deep learning framework rooted in the TabTransformer architecture, integrating a Normalized Covariance Penalty into the loss function to mitigate regional bias over a high-cardinality sensitive attribute, the 27 Brazilian states. A real-world mortgage dataset of 1,529,211 contracts, under a strict unawareness-at-inference protocol and calibrated using Platt scaling, is benchmarked against industry standards and against fairness-aware alternatives from the pre-, in-, and post-processing families. The fairness-constrained model achieved an AUC of 0.751, above its unconstrained counterpart (0.745; DeLong p < .001) and Random Forest (0.735), while reducing the maximum True Positive Rate (TPR) gap across states to 0.445, against 0.499 for XGBoost, and reaching the lowest Demographic Parity difference among all evaluated models. XGBoost retains a statistically significant advantage in raw discrimination (ΔAUC (Formula presented)); among models that keep inference blind to the regional attribute, however, the proposed framework offers the most favorable fairness–performance profile and dominates the equity-constrained region of the empirical Pareto frontier. A decomposition across the 27 states shows that the penalty compresses the regional TPR distribution in both directions, raising the mean TPR of the three worst-served states, and a leakage audit confirms a measurable reduction in the regional information carried by the scores. Sensitivity analyses over the penalty weight and training seeds, module ablations, and replications on public credit datasets support the robustness of these findings. © 2026 The Authors. title: Urban economic resilience and low-altitude logistics industrial agglomeration: Implications for reliable deployment
abstract: Low-altitude logistics (LAL) is a complex urban cyber-physical freight system comprising uncrewed aerial vehicles, eVTOL aircraft, airspace management, and ground infrastructure. Reliable deployment requires technical validation, regulatory compliance, and commercially sustainable operations, while urban socioeconomic conditions may provide supporting resources. This paper develops an interpretable causal learning framework to evaluate how urban economic resilience influences LAL industrial agglomeration, measured by the log-transformed stock of registered LAL-related enterprises. Utilizing panel data from 296 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2010–2024, we quantify urban economic resilience via an improved entropy-weighted TOPSIS model and integrate panel fixed-effects, double machine learning, causal forests, and SHAP attribution to estimate average effects under identifying assumptions and examine spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear predictive contributions. The results indicate that urban economic resilience significantly fosters LAL enterprise concentration, yet reveals a distinct resilience saturation pattern: mid-resilience cities exhibit the largest estimated effects on LAL industrial agglomeration, whereas marginal returns diminish in highly resilient metropolitan centers. SHAP decomposition reveals that household wealth accumulation, income levels, and fixed-asset investment are primary contributors to industrial presence. These findings identify urban economic conditions associated with LAL industrial agglomeration and offer implications for the economic foundations supporting reliable deployment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: How social media content shapes enrollment intention: Distinguishing firm-generated and user-generated effects through TPB and self-identity
abstract: The increasing reliance on social media has transformed how prospective students gather and evaluate information when selecting universities. This study examines how firm-generated content (FGC) and user-generated content (UGC) influence students' behavioral intention to enroll in private universities through psychological mechanisms grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and self-identity. Specifically, the study investigates both direct and indirect effects of FGC and UGC on behavioral intention, mediated by attitude toward behavior, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and self-identity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed, with data collected from 295 final-year high school students in Banten, Indonesia. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that FGC has a significant direct and indirect effect on behavioral intention, whereas UGC does not have a significant direct effect but appears to operate primarily through indirect pathways. Among the mediators, subjective norms emerge as the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude toward behavior and self-identity. In contrast, perceived behavioral control does not significantly influence behavioral intention. The findings suggest that FGC and UGC function through distinct mechanisms. While institutional content can directly shape behavioral intention, user-generated content primarily influences intention through social and psychological processes. These results highlight that the effectiveness of social media communication depends not only on information exposure but also on how information is cognitively evaluated, socially validated, and integrated into individuals' self-concept. This study contributes to the literature by distinguishing between different types of social media content and extending the TPB framework with self-identity in the context of higher education decision-making. The findings provide insights for understanding how digital communication influences complex behavioral decisions in contemporary educational environments. © 2027 Malque Publishing, .

title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: THE POWER OF FACIAL EXPRESSIONS IN SALES AVATARS: ELEVATING CONSUMER INTERACTION IN METAVERSE COMMERCE
abstract: Metaverse commerce is reshaping e-commerce by offering immersive and interactive shopping experiences. Sales avatars, defined as digital representations of firm frontline employees in metaverse commerce, play critical roles in delivering real-time and interactive experiences. Drawing on the theory of affordances and the needs-affordances-features framework, this study investigates how the facial expressions of sales avatars (smiling vs. crying) influence consumer avatars’ interaction outcomes and the underlying mechanisms through subcultural appeal. Further, we test when the mechanism by which sales avatars’ facial expression leads to consumer interaction outcomes via subcultural appeal is amplified or weakened depending on sales avatar’s anthropomorphism. We conducted four experiments in which consumers were exposed to virtual commerce contexts that we built on the VRChat metaverse platform. The results reveal that unlike real-world interactions, crying sales avatars compared to smiling sales avatars elicit higher intentions to interact with the sales avatar, purchase a virtual item from the sales avatar, and spread positive WOM about the experience. This counterintuitive effect is driven by consumers’ heightened perceptions of subcultural appeal in the crying sales avatar context. However, when sales avatars exhibited high anthropomorphism (human-like vs. cartoon-like), the positive effect of the crying expression weakened. These findings provide actionable insights into how to strategically leverage sales avatars’ facial expressions in highly immersive metaverse commerce, where consumers’ desire for subcultural values is relatively high. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: Green by association? Restaurant presence on food-waste reduction platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal for brand equity
abstract: Food-waste reduction platforms allow restaurants to redistribute surplus food, but their branding implications remain unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we conceptualize restaurant presence on these platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal that embeds sustainability and commercial meanings within the same marketplace cue. Across three experiments, we examine whether this hybrid signal enhances restaurant brand equity through green brand image and whether consumer residence and restaurant type condition its effects. Study 1 shows that platform presence enhances brand equity, partially through green brand image. Study 2 replicates the main effect and provides directional evidence that the premium of platform presence may be stronger among urban than rural consumers. Study 3 shows that this effect depends jointly on consumer residence and restaurant type, and that mediation through green brand image is evident primarily for full-service restaurants. These findings identify platform presence as a hybrid, context-dependent sustainability signal with branding implications. © 2026 The Authors

title: Optimising construction health and safety training: the role of training design and firm size
abstract: Background The construction industry is one of the most hazardous sectors globally, responsible for a disproportionate share of work-related injuries and fatalities. Construction health and safety (H&S) training is widely recognised as a critical component for improving workers’ H&S competence and reducing accident rates. Despite extensive investment in training programmes, research indicates that learning effectiveness varies across construction firms and may be associated with differences in training design and organisational context. However, empirical understanding of whether firm size moderates the relationship between specific training design dimensions and learning effectiveness is limited. Objective This study investigated the relationships between training design dimensions (training content relevance, facilitator competence, opportunity for practice, and learning environment) and learning effectiveness in construction H&S training while assessing the moderating role of firm size. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 80 construction professionals from medium- and large-scale firms. Data were collected using 5-point Likert scales to measure training design dimensions and learning effectiveness. Correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and moderation analysis using PROCESS were performed to test the hypothesised relationships. Results Multiple regression showed that the four training design dimensions jointly explained 64% of the variance in learning effectiveness ( R2 = 0.64, adjusted R2 = 0.62), with all four dimensions showing significant positive associations. Moderation analysis showed that firm size significantly moderated the relationship between training design quality and learning effectiveness (interaction B = 0.19, p = 0.033), with a stronger conditional effect among large firms ( b = 0.62) than medium-sized firms ( B = 0.43). Conclusions This study extends the training effectiveness literature by showing that the relationship between training design quality and learning effectiveness varies according to organisational context, with firm size representing a potential boundary condition. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Choice set expansion and dual-domain loss aversion in food delivery platforms: Evidence from price-time trade-offs
abstract: This study examines how delivery-tier expansion shapes online food delivery choices when price-time trade-offs are held constant. Drawing on context-dependent choice theory and prospect theory, we conducted a between-subjects discrete-choice experiment with 438 South Korean consumers assigned to either a two-tier menu (Free and Economy) or a three-tier menu (Free, Economy, and Single-order). Paid options offered the same price per minute saved, isolating choice-set structure from economic efficiency. Adding single-order delivery significantly reduced free delivery selection and captured 30.49% of choices. Economy delivery's incumbent-relative share increased slightly but not significantly, indicating no reliable canonical compromise effect. Across logit and cross-nested logit models, price loss aversion was associated with free delivery selection, whereas time loss aversion was associated with faster paid tiers, especially single-order delivery. The findings position delivery portfolios as behavioral segmentation devices in platform-mediated hospitality services. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Organisational capability for digital health transformation in long-term care: development of a conceptual framework
abstract: Background: Digital health transformation in long-term care (LTC) involves more than the adoption of digital technologies. Organisations must coordinate leadership, workforce capability, infrastructure, governance and implementation processes to sustain digital systems within continuing care environments. Existing implementation and digital maturity approaches address important aspects of digital transformation but provide less explanation of how organisational capabilities interact as a system within LTC. Objective: This study develops an evidence-informed organisational capability framework for digital health transformation in LTC and proposes relationships among capabilities potentially relevant to sustained digital system use. Methods: An evidence-informed framework development approach was used. Published evidence from digital health, healthcare management, implementation and organisational research was examined to identify recurring organisational mechanisms associated with digital transformation. Related mechanisms were grouped into capability domains, and proposed relationships among the domains were conceptualised. The resulting domains were integrated into the Long-Term Care Digital Capability and Alignment (LTC-DCA) framework. Results: LTC-DCA comprises seven interdependent organisational capability domains: strategic digital leadership, organisational readiness, workforce development systems, technology and data infrastructure alignment, governance and ethical oversight, implementation and integration mechanisms, and performance and learning systems. The framework conceptualises these domains as a connected capability system in which changes in one domain may influence others. Performance and organisational learning are proposed as feedback mechanisms that may support continued adjustment and alignment. Conclusions: LTC-DCA shifts attention from technology adoption towards the organisational capabilities potentially involved in integrating, sustaining and adapting digital systems within long-term care. The framework is evidence-informed and conceptually specified rather than empirically validated. Future research could examine its domains, proposed relationships and indicators across different LTC settings and investigate whether they are associated with sustained digital system use and organisational performance. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

title: The paradox of withdrawal: How managerial turnover intention and attitudes shape performance appraisal quality in high-contact service
abstract: Purpose: Performance appraisal quality depends on the discretionary effort of the rater. This study examines rater-side psychological antecedents of appraisal rigor among hospitality managers, focusing on how managers’ positive attitudes toward the job and the organization drive appraisal quality and whether that relationship is disrupted by the managers’ own turnover intention. Design/methodology/approach: Data were collected from 318 U.S. hospitality managers through a multi-stage screening protocol on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Because job satisfaction and organizational commitment were empirically indistinguishable in the sample (r = .976), a higher-order Managerial Attitudes factor was specified to test the two attitudinal hypotheses jointly. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to estimate direct and moderating effects. Common method variance was addressed procedurally and through a marker-variable technique combined with an unmeasured latent method construct. Findings: Managerial Attitudes had a strong positive relationship with self-reported appraisal quality (β =.71 in the method-adjusted model). Contrary to the “withdrawal–negligence” prediction of Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, turnover intention showed a small but significant positive direct association with appraisal rigor, and its interaction with attitudes was not statistically significant. The pattern is consistent with a “Lame Duck Objectivity” account in which anticipated exit releases managers from certain political constraints on evaluative candor, but reverse causality, statistical power, and measurement limitations remain plausible alternatives that the design cannot rule out. Originality/value: The study reframes managerial withdrawal as a scope condition of COR rather than a uniform trigger of task disengagement, and it demonstrates the utility of a higher-order attitudinal factor for handling discriminant-validity breakdown in hospitality data. Boundary conditions on generalizability — including racial and gender homogeneity of the sample, single-source measurement, and cross-sectional design — are discussed in detail, and a program of multi-source, longitudinal, and gender- and race-balanced replications is proposed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Exploring the role of green human resource management in enhancing employee well-being and job satisfaction in the it sector
abstract: Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) has received a growing academic interest with organizations starting to incorporate the sustainability of the environment into their strategic human resource management. The present paper offers a synthesis and systematic review of the existing body of literature to identify the impacts of GHRM practices on employee well being, job satisfaction as well as environmental performance, especially in the IT industry. A systematic literature review was conducted. The sources of records were Google Scholar (n = 317) and Scopus (n = 312), which returned 629 preliminary studies. After applying inclusion criteria based on peer-review, relevance and timeframe criteria, 156 articles were selected for detailed analysis. Literature was grouped based on the Ability-Motivation-Opportunity (AMO) framework to assess the performance of GHRM practices in the main HR functions. The results show that green training and development (80% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) and reward management (85% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) have the greatest correlation with the employee engagement and sustainability outcomes. The other contribution made towards the development of a psychological green climate and the encouragement of organizational citizenship behaviour towards the environment (OCBE) is recruitment, job design, and performance appraisal. Nevertheless, there are gaps of measurement structures and multi-level empirical validation of sectors. The research finds out that holistic integration of GHRM between HR functions boosts employee motivation, job satisfaction, and performance on organizational sustainability. Organizations can attain long-term competitive advantage by integrating environmental values into the HR systems, especially those operating in the knowledge-intensive sectors like the IT sector, in addition to promoting the sustainability of the larger society. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Leaning into risk: How slanted typeface logos increase perceived risk of efficacious products
abstract: Marketing practice commonly uses slanted typeface logos on product packaging to convey movement and vitality, yet existing research has paid limited attention to the potential conflict between this low-level visual feature and the core claims of specific products. Drawing on the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), this research examines when and why slanted typeface logos on packaging increase consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products, revealing the underlying mechanism and boundary condition. Across three controlled experiments and one incentive-compatible experiment, this research manipulates the form of typeface logos on packaging and evaluates its effects and subsequent behavioral responses. Study 1 shows that, compared with an upright typeface logo, a slanted typeface logo increases consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products. Study 2 supports the mediating role of design instability: a slanted typeface logo triggers a visually perceived sense of imbalance, which further induces consumers’ risk inferences about the product; meanwhile, arousal, perceived movement, and perceptual fluency do not emerge as significant mediating mechanisms. Study 3 identifies the moderating role of cognitive load, showing that high cognitive load amplifies the effect of a slanted typeface logo on perceived risk. Study 4 further provides behavioral evidence through an incentive-compatible experiment, showing that consumers are less likely to choose the product in the slanted typeface logo condition. Overall, this research reveals a boundary of the visual marketing principle that “slanting implies vitality” in the context of efficacious products. These findings enrich theoretical understanding of the boundary conditions under which peripheral visual cues operate within the ELM framework and offer practical implications for the context-specific management of brand visual identity systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Transforming hospitality and tourism services through artificial intelligence: The influence of experiential dimensions on user satisfaction, continuance intentions, and word-of-mouth
abstract: This study investigated how five key experiential dimensions (i.e., embodiment, human-oriented perception, feeling of security, emotions, and co-experience) shaped user satisfaction with AI-enabled services in hospitality and tourism settings and how satisfaction subsequently influenced continuance intention and word-of-mouth. Data was collected through an online survey of 380 participants who had previously used AI-enabled hospitality or tourism services, and structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed hypotheses. The results revealed that embodiment, human-oriented perception, feeling of security, and emotions had a significant impact on user satisfaction. In addition, satisfaction was positively associated with continuance intentions and positive word-of-mouth, underscoring the importance of experiential dimensions in sustaining user engagement. The findings extend theoretical understanding by identifying user experience as a determinant of post-adoption behavior in AI-enabled service contexts. The study further provided practical insights for designing emotionally attuned, secure, and human-oriented AI systems that foster satisfaction and customer loyalty. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Hard-work orientation as an individual difference: Passion and subjective vitality as sequential mechanisms of student engagement
abstract: Effort has a well-documented dark side: excessive work has been linked to burnout, and persistence after failure to hopelessness. Effort is also an individual difference, in that people vary in how strongly they believe effort is valuable and necessary for achievement. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study asks why an effort-oriented disposition might generate psychological resources rather than deplete them. Passion and subjective vitality were tested as a sequential motivational and energetic process linking hard-work orientation to student engagement, using three-wave time-lagged data from 524 students in northern India. Hard-work orientation was positively associated with passion, subjective vitality, and engagement. Both mediators carried significant indirect associations, and the serial indirect pathway through passion and subjective vitality was also significant. The findings locate the bright side of effort in how effort is regulated rather than in how much of it is expended. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Environmental qualities in green and natural spaces: Fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature as pathways to perceived visit-related health benefits
abstract: Rising levels of stress and mental ill-health have intensified interest in nature-based public health approaches, including green social prescribing and nature as medicine. However, it remains unclear whether different environmental qualities are associated with different aspects of visit experience, and how these experiences relate to perceived visit-related health benefits. This study examined direct associations of biodiversity, safety, accessibility and cleanliness problems with perceived visit-related health benefits, and indirect associations involving fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature. Cross-sectional data from 19,814 adults in England who reported a recent visit to a green or natural space in the People and Nature Survey (PaNS) were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In the direct-effects model, biodiversity, safety and accessibility were positively associated with perceived visit-related health benefits, whereas cleanliness problems showed a negative association. Most of these direct associations were substantially attenuated when the two visit experiences were included, and both experiences were positively associated with perceived benefits. The pathway model also revealed differentiated associations across experiences, with safety most closely associated with fresh air / peace and tranquillity, biodiversity with feeling closer to nature, and cleanliness problems showing a negative indirect association through fresh air / peace and tranquillity. By considering qualities of the setting alongside experiences during the visit, the findings highlight the value of a quality-experience-benefit perspective in which different environmental qualities may show different patterns of association with perceived visit-related health benefits through particular visit experiences. This perspective may help inform the selection and management of natural settings used in nature-based public-health approaches, particularly where specific visit experiences are intended to be supported. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: THE VALUE OF RECOMMENDATIONS FROM SOCIAL MEDIA ANALYSTS IN ONLINE INVESTMENT COMMUNITIES
abstract: This study examines the informational value of stock recommendations issued by social media analysts through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using comprehensive data from Seeking Alpha, we demonstrate that these recommendations significantly predict abnormal stock returns over a two-month horizon, with no subsequent reversal, suggesting that they convey incremental information not captured by sell-side analysts or textual sentiment. Guided by SDT, we further show that predictive accuracy varies systematically with analysts’ motivational contexts. Recommendations are more informative when issued by analysts identified as traders, whose direct financial stakes deepen the internalization of extrinsic incentives, and by analysts with high comment-section engagement, where interactive feedback supports needs for competence and relatedness. Conversely, predictive ability declines with longer platform tenure, consistent with motivational saturation as psychological needs become satisfied, and with higher posting frequency, where cognitive overload undermines need satisfaction. Finally, we find that both editorial selection and user-driven engagement effectively identify recommendations with greater ex-post informativeness. In an era of information abundance in online investment communities, our SDT-grounded analysis offers investors guidance for signal extraction and provides platform designers with principled insights for fostering higher-quality content ecosystems. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior
abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. While existing GenAI literature has largely focused on the scale, frequency, and operational patterns of its application, it has largely overlooked the inherent imbalances within these P-R cycles. Building on control theory, this study investigates how and when GenAI usage is related to employees’ corner-cutting behavior (CCB). Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. By conceptualizing GenAI usage through the dual lenses of expectation induction and cognitive friction operating within P-R cycles, our findings extend and refine traditional perspectives on human-AI interaction in the workplace. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. Therefore, this study constructs a multi-source heterogeneous hypergraph with higher-order semantics, spanning the “Science-Technology-Industry” dimensions. By mapping the structural phase transitions of weak signals across an “Outlier-Mutation-Key Node” trajectory, we devise a quantifiable indicator system to shift the analytical paradigm from static retrospective detection to dynamic evolutionary tracking. Using a dataset of 145,316 papers, 79,050 patents, and 5941 project records from the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) fuel cell domain (2015–2024), we identify 226 candidate nodes exhibiting this trajectory. A two-round Delphi expert evaluation confirms 193 of these nodes as expert-confirmed weak signals, establishing Delphi-validated reference labels for subsequent model evaluation. We then employ Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Dynamic Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN), and Large Language Models (ZS-LLM and ICL-LLM) to prospectively predict weak signals with disruptive potential. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). This synergy between higher-order topology and semantic intelligence effectively filters stochastic noise and enables meaningful predictive capability of emerging technologies, providing an exploratory decision-support framework for technology foresight. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Where AI enters the product development process: Task orientation, human identity threat, and purchase intention
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Across three studies with U.S. consumers in fashion-related contexts, this research examines how the task AI performs and how its role is framed shape consumer responses to products developed with AI involvement. Study 1 maps consumers’ perceptions of fashion-related tasks along a logic–intuition continuum and identifies trend forecasting as a logic-oriented task and design as an intuition-oriented task. Study 2 compares AI involvement in these two contrasting product-development tasks and finds lower purchase intention when AI is involved in design rather than trend forecasting, with heightened human identity threat accounting for part of this difference. Study 3 focuses on the intuition-oriented design context and shows that framing AI as complementing rather than replacing human designers is associated with lower identity threat and higher purchase intention. Together, the findings suggest that consumer responses depend not only on whether AI participates in product development, but also on where AI is positioned within the process and how its contribution relative to human creativity is framed. This research advances understanding of task-dependent responses to AI by identifying human identity threat as a mediator linking AI involvement to purchase intention and by showing how role framing can shape purchase intention when AI participates in creative work. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Smart and green solutions in the catering and hospitality: A review of the existing literature
abstract: The integration of digital technologies and sustainability practices is reshaping the catering and hospitality industry, yet research on smart and green solutions remains fragmented. This study maps the intellectual and thematic development of this field through a bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed publications using VOSviewer, Biblioshiny, and Microsoft Excel. The findings reveal substantial growth in research interest and increasing interdisciplinary contributions across countries, institutions, and authors. Keyword analysis identifies artificial intelligence, sustainability, digital transformation, and social media as dominant themes, while circular economy, Internet of Things (IoT), and customer behavior represent emerging areas. The analysis also highlights a relatively underexplored intersection of AI, IoT, and circular economy, suggesting important opportunities for future research. By consolidating the intellectual structure and emerging themes, this study provides a research agenda for advancing smart and sustainable solutions that enhance operational efficiency, customer experience, environmental performance, and competitiveness in the hospitality sector. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use. © 2026 The Authors

title: Corporate strategy for the green transition: Are executive incentives effective?
abstract: This paper examines whether green incentives embedded in executive compensation schemes are associated with a reorientation of firms' innovative activities toward environmentally sustainable technologies. Drawing on agency theory and the attention-based view of the firm, we conceptualize green incentives as governance and management-control devices that can mitigate managerial short-termism and channel executive attention toward long-horizon environmental objectives, thereby redirecting firms' technological search. Using a panel of publicly listed U.S. and European firms that participate in the Carbon Disclosure Project over the period 2010–2020, we analyse green innovation as a multi-stage process comprising the reorientation of technological search (the distance of firms' patent portfolios from green domains), knowledge recombination (the citation of green prior art in non-green patents), and realized green innovation output (green patent counts and shares). Firms adopting green incentives exhibit higher green innovation output, a significant repositioning of their knowledge portfolios toward green technological domains, and a greater integration of green knowledge into non-green technologies. These associations are weaker among firms experiencing a recent deterioration in carbon performance, and are strongest among continental European firms. Overall, the findings suggest that executive green incentives are associated with the direction, and not merely the volume, of firms' innovative activities, highlighting the role of internal governance mechanisms in sustainability transitions while recognising the limits of causal inference in observational data. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Policy-driven electrification in rural areas: Integrating carbon pricing and activity-based costing in strategic decision models
abstract: Rural electrification is essential for sustainable development; however, balancing upfront infrastructure investment, carbon reduction, and long-term economic performance remains a significant decision problem. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework that combines Activity-Based Costing (ABC), carbon taxation, and optimization modeling to compare Progressive Replacement, Hybrid Carbon Market Electrification, and One-Time Replacement. The analysis uses a 10-year planning horizon, a 5% benchmark discount rate, and a USD 30/tCO2 carbon tax in a normalized planning-scale scenario. Recalculation from the annual scenario tables gives cumulative direct operational emissions of 41,800 tCO2 for Progressive Replacement, 28,100 tCO2 for the Hybrid Carbon Market strategy, and 10,000 tCO2 for One-Time Replacement. Using the 5% benchmark discount rate, corresponding total-system NPVs are approximately USD 2.863 million, USD 1.527 million, and USD 1.313 million, respectively. Sensitivity analysis further indicates that One-Time Replacement remains the lower-cost strategy across the reported carbon-tax and discount-rate scenarios. The framework clarifies how electrification timing, activity-level costs, and carbon-price exposure jointly shape rural electrification decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
