title: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE COIN: CLICKBAIT’S INFLUENCE ON CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION IN SOCIAL MEDIA
abstract: As social media increasingly operates within algorithm-driven attention economies, clickbait has become a pervasive engagement tactic. However, prior research has not fully explained the psychological mechanisms linking clickbait to downstream consumer behavior. Existing studies have also largely treated clickbait as an isolated persuasive cue, overlooking its dynamic interactions with other elements in social media ecosystems. Drawing on psychological reactance theory (PRT) and uses-and-gratifications theory (UGT), this study develops an integrated framework to examine when clickbait harms versus facilitates consumer responses. Across four experiments, we test a sequential mediation model in which perceived intrusiveness and advertising avoidance transmit the effects of clickbait on purchase intention. We further introduce message appeal congruence as a key boundary condition. The results indicate that clickbait does not uniformly produce negative outcomes. When headline-induced motivations align with the gratifications delivered by the content, perceived intrusiveness and reactance are attenuated. When they are misaligned, advertising avoidance increases and purchase intention declines. This research advances the clickbait literature by shifting attention from static credibility judgments to dynamic goal-directed processing and by identifying gratification fulfillment as an upstream regulator of psychological reactance in social media contexts. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: Institutional co-development cues in retail food choice: Reducing perceived risk in alternative protein acceptance
abstract: Alternative proteins are increasingly available to consumers through retail and online food channels, yet their unfamiliarity often heightens perceived risk at the point of product evaluation. This research examines whether identifying an alternative-protein product as co-developed with an official agricultural research institute (OARI) functions as a retail-facing institutional cue. Across four experiments with Chinese consumers, an OARI co-development cue generally increased acceptance of plant-based, cultured-meat, and insect-based products. Study 2 showed that the cue increased acceptance by reducing perceived risk. Study 3 showed that this risk-reduction pathway was stronger among consumers with greater food neophobia. Study 4 demonstrated that the cue reduced risk and increased acceptance when trust in the named institution was high, but not when it was low. The findings contribute to consumer retailing research by showing how institutional co-development cues can reassure consumers evaluating unfamiliar food innovations, and why such reassurance depends on both consumers' need for risk reduction and trust in the named institution. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Macroprudential policies and dollarization: implications for the financial system and a cross-exchange rate regime analysis
abstract: Macroprudential policy has gained prominence in promoting financial stability. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of macroprudential measures in curbing credit growth over a 22-year period across 129 countries. It further examines how macroprudential policy interacts with dollarization and other exchange rate regimes. Our findings indicate that tightening macroprudential measures are associated with lower credit growth within one quarter following implementation. The estimated associations are similar across the system and difference GMM specifications. Additionally, macroprudential policies are associated with significantly lower non-performing loan rates in dollarized economies compared to most other exchange rate regimes. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Unpacking the pathways from green intellectual capital to green recovery performance: The power of employee voice and intrinsic motivation
abstract: Our paper proposes and tests a moderated mediation model that examines how green intellectual capital relates to green recovery performance, highlighting green promotive and prohibitive voice behaviors as mediators and intrinsic motivation to share knowledge as a moderator. Results based on time-lagged data gathered from FLEs in environmentally certified Spanish hotels revealed that the association between green intellectual capital and green recovery performance operated through green voice behaviors. Both green promotive and green prohibitive voice behaviors mediated the green intellectual capital-green recovery performance link. However, intrinsic motivation to share knowledge strengthened only the promotive pathway. This finding underscores an asymmetry in how motivational states condition the translation of intangible resources into recovery behaviors. Our research positions voice behavior as a proximal mechanism through which green intellectual capital translates into sustainable outcomes and shows that the amplifying role of intrinsic motivation depends on the form of voice at stake. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When service environments signal ideology: Customer responses to ideological cues
abstract: Service environments increasingly contain visible cues that communicate political engagement, religious identities, LGBTQ + affiliation, environmental advocacy, and other collective values. Although servicescape research has traditionally emphasized atmospheric, aesthetic, and functional cues, less is known about how customers interpret ideological cues embedded within routine service encounters. Drawing on servicescape research and social identity theory, this research examines how ideological servicescape cues are associated with customer discomfort, avoidance intentions, and stated store-choice decisions. Three preregistered, scenario-based experiments in a coffee shop context examine ideological cues displayed through employees and the physical service environment. Study 1 shows that political cues generate greater discomfort than environmental and lifestyle cues, although they do not differ significantly from religious or LGBTQ + cues. Study 2 shows that matching political cues displayed across employee and environmental touchpoints generate greater discomfort than political cues displayed through a single source, while perceived authenticity does not account for this association. Study 3 shows that political cues are associated with lower stated store choice than environmental cues, particularly when matching political cues appear across employee and environmental touchpoints. Across studies, customer discomfort statistically accounts for part of the association between ideological cue conditions and avoidance intentions or stated store-choice decisions. The findings extend servicescape scholarship by showing that politically charged symbolism may shape customer responses through both cue content and cue-source configuration. Because the studies rely on scenario-based experiments and stated responses, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of observed marketplace behavior or realized financial outcomes. © 2026 The Authors

title: Employee-led disclosure of anthropomorphism in tourism GAI failure recovery: A mind perception model from tourists and employees
abstract: Generative AI (GAI) is increasingly mediating tourism service encounters, reshaping GAI failure recovery within a broader tourist–employee–GAI service configuration, in which GAI serves as the failure source, employees act as recovery agents, and tourists are the end recipients. Drawing on Mind Perception Theory, we theorize and test a post-failure recovery tactic in which employees intentionally foreground anthropomorphic aspects of the failing GAI during recovery interactions. Across six scenario-based experiments and two on-site simulation studies ( N = 2061), results provide convergent evidence that employee-led disclosure of GAI anthropomorphism (vs. control) improves recovery outcomes for both tourists and employees through mirrored mechanisms. Specifically, it increases tourist forgiveness by elevating perceived GAI experience and increases state employee satisfaction by elevating perceived GAI agency. These benefits weaken under high tourist anger or employees' perceptions of tourist anger and are further contingent on tourists' AI expertise and employees’ competitive versus collaborative mindset. The findings advance tourism research by offering parallel dyadic evidence on GAI failure recovery beyond a tourist-centric lens, extending Mind Perception Theory through stakeholder-contingent effects of perceived experience and perceived agency, and repositioning anthropomorphism in recovery as a co-produced mechanism jointly enacted through employee framing and available GAI interface affordances. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Invisible data infrastructure and cross-domain digital innovation: Evidence from data groups in China
abstract: This study examines whether and how formalized data governance reshapes firms’ digital innovation by exploiting the staggered establishment of municipal data groups in China. Using a difference-in-differences design and Chinese A-share listed firms from 2008 to 2024, we find that municipal data group establishment significantly expands firms’ cross-domain digital innovation. This effect is stronger among state-owned enterprises, regulated industries, firms in cities with lower technological complexity, and regions with more developed market and factor environments. Additional analyses provide evidence consistent with several potential pathways: municipal data groups are associated with changes in R&D uncertainty, managerial innovation expectations, interregional collaboration, and innovation activities. Further analysis reveals a quantity–quality divergence: data group establishment increases patent output but is associated with lower average measured patent quality, particularly among firms receiving stronger innovation incentives. This pattern is consistent with multiple explanations, including incentive responses and innovation composition changes. By conceptualizing municipal data groups as Invisible Data Infrastructure, this study advances research on digital governance and corporate innovation by showing how institutionalized data access and coordination mechanisms expand firms’ innovation boundaries. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Market-driven or state strategic-driven? A hybrid driving paradigm and evolution of mission-oriented innovation ecosystems in aerospace engineering
abstract: How national strategies and market forces jointly organize innovation for complex and uncertain space missions, such as deep space exploration, and why distinct driving logics retain their differences while incorporating governance mechanisms from one another remain important questions for research on mission-oriented innovation ecosystems. This study develops the Drive–Organization–Adaptation–Value (DOAV) analytical framework and conducts a longitudinal comparison of SpaceX's deep space exploration program and the China Manned Space Program, tracing stage-specific mission demands, local task gaps, mechanism entry, and coupling at task interfaces. The findings reveal a sequence of conditional relationships. First, mission mandates and resource conditions shape initial driving relations and produce distinct configurations of organization, adaptation, and value. Second, when stage-specific demands reach the configuration performance boundary, the leading actor can address local task gaps through internal adjustment or admit heterogeneous mechanisms when complementary capabilities and executable interfaces are available. Third, coupling at task interfaces links organization, adaptation, and value, encouraging convergence in governance mechanisms while leadership relations retain identifiable continuity at the defined long-term mission level. On this basis, the study distinguishes instrumental hybridization, asymmetric structural hybridization, and mission co-shaping according to mechanism embedding depth and the reach of governance feedback. Mission co-shaping is retained as a conditional theoretical extension within the process explanation of the DOAV dynamic adaptation mechanism. The findings inform the coordination of public objectives and firm innovation capabilities in major scientific and technological missions, including space exploration, and the design of collaborative rights, responsibilities, and verification arrangements in response to stage-specific tasks. © 2026 IAA. title: How should conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products? Matching recommendation set granularity with time pressure
abstract: With the widespread application of conversational recommendation agents (CRA) on e-commerce platforms, an increasing number of consumers use a CRA to support product choices. Existing research has mainly focused on the accuracy of CRA recommendations, with limited attention paid to how candidate products should be organized and whether this organization should be adapted to consumers' current decision contexts. Drawing on the product set granularity perspective and the heuristic–systematic model, this study examines the matching effect between recommendation set granularity (coarse vs. fine) and time pressure (high vs. low) on consumers' intention to adopt CRA recommendations and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms. The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure. The two matching effects operate through perceived fluency and perceived attractiveness, respectively. Furthermore, consumer knowledge affects the relative effectiveness of the two matching strategies: the match between coarse recommendation set granularity and high time pressure is more effective for consumers with low product knowledge, whereas the match between fine recommendation set granularity and low time pressure is more effective for consumers with high product knowledge. These findings extend CRA research from recommendation content to the organization of candidate products and provide guidance for retail platforms to adjust recommendation set granularity according to consumers’ time pressure and product knowledge. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The automation paradox: Efficiency gains vs. workforce concerns in human-AI collaboration
abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security. © 2026

title: Good listening as a wise negotiation tactic
abstract: Listening is a foundational interpersonal skill. Effective listening is central to managing the dual demands of negotiation: competing over limited resources while sustaining cooperation and trust. Nevertheless, limited research has shed light on how to listen effectively in negotiation. Integrating research from psychology, communication, and negotiation, we identify three common listening traps that undermine negotiation effectiveness: negotiators tend to focus too much on: (1) the self (and too little on others); (2) resolving disagreement (and too little on exploring it); and (3) what is said (and too little on what remains unspoken). We propose three approaches for effective listening in negotiations: (1) listening to understand rather than persuade; (2) listening for movement and change; and (3) making listening observable through concrete verbal and nonverbal behaviors. We argue that high-quality listening improves both informational and relational outcomes by facilitating deeper information exchange, increasing trust, and supporting integrative agreements. By highlighting high-quality listening as a wise negotiation tactic, this article illustrates how negotiators can better navigate the tension between cooperation and competition in mixed-motive interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Unveiling the effects of multidimensional urban shrinkage on urban flood resilience: A case study of the Yangtze River Basin, China
abstract: Climate change poses growing flood-management challenges for cities undergoing economic, demographic, and spatial decline. Using 1921 city-year observations for 113 prefecture-level cities in China’s Yangtze River Basin (YRB) from 2007 to 2023, this study develops a six-subsystem urban flood resilience (UFR) framework encompassing socioeconomic conditions, ecological environment, infrastructure, institutional support, spatial structure, and climate stress. The analysis integrates CRITIC-TOPSIS, coupling coordination analysis, GeoShapley, mechanism tests, and probabilistic scenario simulation. The results reveal four main findings. (1) Both UFR and subsystem coordination improved significantly, with Sen slopes of 0.0023 and 0.0059 per year, respectively. (2) Drainage infrastructure, economic activity, and fiscal capacity made the largest predictive contributions, whereas the associations of population and spatial shrinkage were smaller, more heterogeneous, and more dependent on local context. (3) The mechanism tests further indicate partial pathways through population density and impervious surface. (4) The expansion scenario produces the highest projected coordination level, followed closely by SSP1, whereas SSP3 yields the lowest trajectory. Economic shrinkage remains below the baseline, whereas population- and spatial-shrinkage trajectories are not clearly separated from it in several comparisons. These findings identify robust associations and scenario-dependent pathways rather than causal effects. The analysis is subject to data constraints relating to event-level inundation, damage, and infrastructure condition, suggesting that future research should incorporate finer-scale hazard and asset-condition information and extend validation to other river basins. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Capability, opportunity, and motivation for healthy eating: Exploring gender-specific pathways
abstract: Women generally consume a healthier diet than men; however, both fall short of dietary guidelines. Health behaviour theories are often applied in a gender-neutral manner, implicitly assuming that explanatory models operate similarly across groups. This conceptual replication tested the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model for dietary behaviour, originally evaluated in a female-dominant sample, in a male-dominant sample (N = 1358; 67% male). Using the same measurement battery and a closely aligned analytic approach, structural equation modelling indicated acceptable overall fit, with the COM-B model explaining 22% of the variance in diet quality. As in the original study, capability and opportunity were associated with behaviour indirectly through motivation, which was the strongest predictor of diet quality. At the indicator level, the male-dominant model retained action control and habits (capability), descriptive norms and the home food environment (opportunity), and self-efficacy, intentions, affective attitudes and perceived behavioural control (motivation), whereas identity, decision-making barriers, instrumental attitudes and the shopping environment indicator were not retained during trimming. These differences, relative to the female-dominant model, suggest potential variation in how COM-B constructs are operationalised across gender-dominant samples and should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Discriminant validity concerns (habits–action control; self-efficacy–intention) further indicated overlap between conceptually distinct constructs in the male-dominant sample. Overall, findings support the stability of the higher-order COM-B pathway while highlighting potential group differences in indicator contributions, with implications for measurement and population-sensitive intervention design. © 2026 The Authors. title: What makes human service distinctly human in the AI era? Conceptualizing and measuring authentic relational service competency
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Addressing this gap, we introduce Authentic Relational Service (ARS) as a distinct form of service through which frontline employees create genuine, contextually responsive, and relationship-centered customer interactions. We further conceptualize authenticity as a competency-based capability and develop a measure of Authentic Relational Service Competency (ARSC), which enables frontline employees to enact ARS. Using established scale-development procedures, this study identifies and validates four dimensions of ARSC: perspective-taking, patience, creativity, and agility. By conceptualizing and operationalizing Authentic Relational Service as a distinct human service capability, this research advances theory on human-AI service differentiation and provides a foundation for understanding uniquely human value creation in service contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Affordances and paradoxical engagement in virtual immersive learning platforms: A configurational analysis across demographic groups
abstract: Virtual immersive learning platforms (VILPs), integrating immersive technologies, gamified design, and learning tools, enable meaningful engagement in learning while also creating possibilities for compulsive engagement. Drawing on a sociotechnical affordance perspective, this study examines how configurations of affordances are associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and how these pathways vary across demographic conditions. Using a mixed-methods design, we first uncover the core affordances of VILPs and organize them within a sociotechnical perspective. We then employ a two-stage fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine affordance configurations associated with different engagement outcomes and the role of demographic conditions. The findings show that meaningful and compulsive engagement are associated with distinct combinations of affordances and these configurational patterns vary across demographic conditions. These findings advance understanding of VILP engagement by revealing the configurational pathways associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and offering practical insights into designing more inclusive and responsible learning platforms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Synergy or backfire? Adding virtual influencers to advertisements featuring human influencers: The roles of sensory cues and temporal framing
abstract: In recent years, virtual influencers (VIs) have emerged as a salient presence in brand communication. Firms are increasingly featuring them alongside human influencers (HIs) in advertising campaigns. Yet whether such HI–VI co-endorsement creates synergy or instead backfires remains unclear. Drawing on cue utilization theory and the elaboration likelihood model, this research examines how endorsement format, defined as advertisements featuring only HI(s) versus HI–VI co-endorsement, and advertising sensory cue type (distal vs. proximal) jointly shape consumers’ purchase intentions, and how this relationship varies across temporal frames (past vs. future). Results from four experiments (total N = 1293) show that advertisements featuring both an HI and a VI are more effective than advertisements featuring only HIs when distal sensory cues are emphasized, but less effective when proximal sensory cues are highlighted. These effects operate through two distinct mechanisms: perceived novelty explains the synergy associated with HI–VI co-endorsement under distal sensory cues, whereas perceived authenticity explains the advantage of advertisements featuring only HIs under proximal sensory cues. Moreover, future-oriented framing strengthens the novelty-based effectiveness of HI–VI co-endorsement, whereas past-oriented framing favors advertisements featuring only HIs through authenticity-based evaluations, particularly when proximal sensory cues are emphasized. By identifying when HI–VI co-endorsement succeeds or fails, this research extends endorsement theory from a source-substitution perspective to a hybrid co-endorsement perspective and provides practical implications for advertising strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Developing instrument to measure the glass ceiling phenomenon among female academics in Indonesia
abstract: The persistence of the glass ceiling phenomenon in academia indicates the necessity of developing a contextually valid and reliable measurement instrument, particularly within Indonesian higher education institutions. Instruments developed in different cultural settings are often unable to fully capture the structural and sociocultural dynamics influencing female academics' career advancement in Indonesia. This study aims to develop and validate a comprehensive measurement instrument that reflects these contextual specificities and improves measurement accuracy in assessing career advancement barriers. A quantitative research design was employed using a survey approach. Instrument development was conducted through the integration of two established questionnaires originating from India and Europe, followed by contextual adaptation. Data were collected from female lecturers employed at Catholic universities in Indonesia. The two preliminary questionnaires were administered to the same initial group of female academics. For the final validation, the integrated instrument was administered to the initial respondents together with additional participants, resulting in a larger validation sample. The measurement model was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with SmartPLS. Reliability and validity were assessed through composite reliability, Cronbach's alpha, average variance extracted, and discriminant validity criteria. The findings indicate that the newly developed instrument demonstrates strong reliability and validity across all dimensions, with acceptable thresholds achieved for composite reliability and convergent validity. Compared to the adapted international instruments, the final instrument exhibits higher cultural relevance and improved measurement precision. Several dimensions were more accurately captured, particularly those related to organizational culture, informal networks, and discriminatory promotion practices, indicating a stronger alignment with the Indonesian academic environment. The study contributes to the refinement of measurement approaches in gender-related research by providing a robust and context-sensitive instrument. The instrument is expected to support future empirical studies and institutional policy evaluations aimed at reducing gender disparities in academic career advancement and leadership positions in Indonesia, while also enabling more accurate diagnosis of structural and cultural barriers. title: ST-AHM: a soft-threshold sparse-attention hypergraph model with contrastive learning for session-based recommendation
abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next interaction from anonymous, short-lived behavioral sequences. A central challenge is to capture higher-order dependencies within sessions and collaborative information across related sessions while limiting weak contextual relations. We propose ST-AHM, a dual-channel model that jointly represents within-session and cross-session information. In the within-session channel, hypergraph convolution captures higher-order item dependencies. Hypergraph-specific sparse attention (HSPA) then averages scaled compatibility scores across attention heads before applying Sparsemax. This operation creates a consensus-based sparse support while retaining head-specific value projections, thereby reducing the propagation of weakly supported relations. An identity-free blank node summarizes the enhanced sequence and produces a context-dependent session-intent representation without relying directly on the last item. In the cross-session channel, Jaccard similarity between session item sets defines a relational graph. Relational graph convolution propagates collaborative information, and the blank-node representation acts as a blank-node-derived query for aggregating relevant cross-session context. A contrastive objective aligns valid interaction representations with the blank-node-augmented view of the same session and distinguishes them from shuffled representations. Across Tmall, Diginetica, and 30Music, ST-AHM outperformed the evaluated baselines, including DCL-BPM, DiffSBR, and MSGAT. Its average improvements were 19.23% for HR@10, 12.71% for HR@20, 23.19% for MRR@10, and 24.28% for MRR@20. These results support the joint modeling of within-session and cross-session information while reducing the influence of weak relations. title: Circular economy approaches to sustainable food waste management in the hospitality and food services sector
abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) as a model has become a widespread approach to promoting sustainability through the restoration and regeneration of products and materials within production and consumption. Despite the plethora of work done, research on the application of CE principles for food waste management in the hospitality and food services (HaFS) sector remains scarce. This study adopts a conceptual review approach and follows the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to address this gap through exploring the role of CE in reducing and managing food waste in the HaFS sector through a review of papers between 2015 and 2026. The findings indicate that collective efforts of both actor-internal (hospitality managers and staff) and actor-external (customers, local authorities and government) stakeholders are essential to achieve sustainable and circular practices. Additionally, a framework that supports managerial decision-making by aligning with external stakeholders to enable circular food waste management is proposed for adoption in the HaFS sector. This research also calls for further research on CE implementation in the HaFS sector, both in terms of policy and practical approaches. © 2026 The Authors

title: Why (not) subscribe? Drivers and barriers of grocery replenishment subscriptions
abstract: Subscription models are gaining importance across retail sectors, yet a picture of consumers’ evaluations of replenishment subscriptions for regularly needed products, particularly groceries, is still lacking. Drawing on perceived value theory and technology acceptance research, this study proposes a value-risk framework for replenishment subscription adoption. It contrasts four value-related drivers (time efficiency, supply reliability, cognitive relief, and cost efficiency) with four corresponding risk-related barriers (time concerns, supply mismatch concerns, lock-in concerns, and financial concerns) and examines their effects on perceived usefulness, attitude, and ultimately usage intention. Two structural models, a ‘drivers model’ and a ‘barriers model’, were estimated using quota-representative surveys in Germany (N = 493) and the UK (N = 339), complemented by multigroup analysis. The results show that subscription evaluations are inherently ambivalent: positive and negative evaluations coexist, but drivers account for considerably more variance in perceived usefulness and attitude than barriers, while financial and supply mismatch concerns still exert strong negative effects. Convenience proves multidimensional: while cognitive relief outweighs time efficiency as a driver of perceived usefulness, distinct barrier facets also show different relevance. The cross-country comparison reveals common patterns alongside differences. Retailers are advised to communicate the benefits of subscriptions more concretely rather than through generic convenience claims. However, relying just on benefit communication is insufficient: adoption also hinges on actively mitigating perceived risks, with messaging tailored to a market's maturity and familiarity. © 2026 The Authors

title: When products speak: The effects of product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication on consumer responses to carted products
abstract: Shopping cart abandonment is a pervasive challenge in e-commerce, with more than 70% of online shopping carts failing to convert into purchases. In this context, this research examines whether and how anthropomorphic communication directed at carted products influences consumers' responses to shopping cart reminders. Across five experiments, we find converging evidence that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication enhances consumers' purchase-related responses to carted products. Study 1 shows that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication generates stronger responses than both non-anthropomorphic and brand-as-subject anthropomorphic communication, while Study 2 demonstrates that these effects are robust across different levels of pity conveyed in the message. Study 3 identifies state empathy and perceived interestingness as parallel mediators. Study 4 further demonstrates that these indirect effects are stronger among consumers with an emotional (vs. rational) decision-making style. Finally, Study 5 extends the findings to behavioral responses, showing that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication increases behavioral cart re-engagement and reduces consumers’ reported likelihood of cart abandonment. This research advances understanding of anthropomorphic communication in shopping cart contexts and offers actionable guidance for the design of shopping cart reminders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens
abstract: Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice. © 2026 The Author(s).

title: Organizational responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI versus human failures in government services
abstract: Existing research provides only limited insights into whether, compared to traditional human service failures, artificial intelligence (AI) failures in government services lead the public to attribute more responsibility to the service organization, and whether outsourcing necessarily alleviates organizational responsibility attribution. To advance this debate, this study conducted three pre-registered survey experiments. Study 1 (N = 1112) reveals that citizens attributed more responsibility to the service organization for AI service failures than to human service agents. The effect was mediated by the perceived service provider's controllability, rather than by counterfactual thinking. Study 2 proposed and tested two distinct pathways, namely the responsibility-transfer and controllability-transfer pathways. The objective was to explain how diminished controllability perceived at the individual service provider level increases the attribution of responsibility to the organization. Empirical evidence (N = 1084) supports the responsibility-transfer pathway. When citizens perceive that AI agents have less control over services than humans, they assign less responsibility to the AI agent and transfer more responsibility to the service organization. Study 3 (N = 1007) examines whether disclosing that the AI agent was externally developed mitigates the attribution of organizational responsibility. Compared to in-house AI systems, outsourcing to either a state-owned enterprise or a private enterprise, rather than to other government organizations, reduced organizational responsibility. In this study, this reduction was substantial enough to eliminate the disparity between AI and human service failures. This study advances theories of responsibility attribution in the digital era, highlighting the nuanced role of outsourcing transparency and the responsibility-transfer mechanism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms
abstract: Amidst the crowded media environment and growing consumer disconnection from nature, leveraging biophilia - the innate human tendency to connect with nature - offers a compelling way for service firms to attract and engage consumers. Although biophilia in service environments has been studied, its comprehensive application in service-firm promotions - both direct and indirect - remains underexplored. This research advances service literature by examining the effects of direct and indirect biophilia in service advertising using schema congruity theory. Across two studies, we show that indirect biophilia led to more favorable ad evaluations compared to direct biophilia and no biophilia (control). Although direct biophilia is known for restorative effects, we show that indirect biophilia in service advertising (i.e., abstract depictions of natural scenes, nature-like materials, and color schemes) outperforms direct biophilia by eliciting perceived novelty and mystery, which in turn enhance ad evaluations and behavioral intentions. Furthermore, our findings indicate biophilia yields the greatest benefits when the service is conceptually aligned with nature. Overall, this research supports using biophilia in service ads to boost consumer engagement. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Comparing applicants’ self-presentation in artificial intelligence versus human interviews: The role of opportunity to perform and contingency-based interactivity
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in employment interviews. Although AI interviewers may enhance the efficiency and standardization of personnel selection, their effects on applicants’ authentic and inauthentic self-presentation remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on impression management theory, this study examines how AI interviewers, relative to human interviewers, shape applicants’ self-presentation and why differences arise. Across four studies, we find that applicants facing AI interviewers perceive fewer opportunities to perform than those facing human interviewers. This reduced opportunity to perform, in turn, weakens not only exaggerated self-enhancement but also authentic self-presentation and authentic self-enhancement. These findings indicate that AI interviewers do not constrain deceptive impression management. They also dampen the expression of genuine strengths and self-relevant information. The results also show that contingency-based interactivity can mitigate this disadvantage by enhancing applicants’ perceived opportunity to perform and narrowing the gap between AI and human interviewers. By identifying both the constraining effects of AI interviewers and the design conditions that can reduce them, this study advances the research on AI interviews and offers practical implications for the design of more effective AI-enabled interview systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How retailers build authenticity over time: A longitudinal study of transparency, frontline brand enactment, customer-company identification, and sales growth
abstract: Retailer authenticity is treated as a commercial asset, yet its relevance may depend on identity conversion. This longitudinal study separates retailer-controlled evidence from customers' higher-order authenticity judgments and from the self-definitional response that follows. Retailer transparency supplies informational evidence concerning disclosure, clarity, accuracy, and candor, whereas frontline brand enactment supplies behavioral evidence that employees embody the retailer's professed identity. Three waves of matched survey data from 10,214 loyalty customers nested in 208 stores in China are linked to a 12-month archival comparable-sales-growth window beginning during the closing month of Time 3. Multilevel longitudinal structural equation modeling indicates temporally ordered positive associations from Time 1 transparency and frontline brand enactment to Time 2 authenticity, from Time 2 authenticity to Time 3 customer-company identification, and from store-level identification to follow-up sales growth. The direct authenticity-growth association is not reliable after identification is modeled. The authenticity-identification association is stronger at higher prestige, recorded frontline interaction frequency, and brand familiarity, consistent with proposed conditions of cue diagnosticity and identity relevance. The study's central contribution is an evidence-judgment-identity-performance account: the observed pattern links authenticity with commercial performance through identification, without establishing that this is its only pathway or that a direct premium is absent. The field design establishes temporal order and covariation, not random assignment or causal identification. © 2026

title: Nuclear ship Mutsu and the 1974 radiation leak Incident: Technical background and management lessons
abstract: During its experimental voyage in September 1974, Japan’s first nuclear-powered ship, Mutsu, experienced abnormal radiation during a low-power reactor test conducted approximately 800 km east of Cape Shiriya in Aomori Prefecture. The immediate technical mechanism involved fast-neutron streaming and secondary gamma-ray generation caused by an inadequate shielding configuration. Although the event did not involve major fuel damage or a large release of radioactive material, it developed into a serious operational and political problem, leading to resistance to the ship’s return and to a government investigation. This paper reconstructs the incident and reviews the technical and organizational conditions that shaped its occurrence and subsequent handling. Drawing on official reports, technical records, and prior studies, it examines how inadequate project integration, limited design review, contractual separation, and communication failures complicated what began as a shielding-design problem. Using action system theory of management as a heuristic framework, we organize key task-level findings and relate them to recurrent patterns in major public technology projects. The case indicates that, in prototype nuclear systems, technical adequacy alone is insufficient: integrated review, clear responsibility, and effective communication are also essential to safe development and testing. title: Using reusable ceramic vs. disposable cellulose-pulp plates in a wine tasting service in Italy: Findings from a life cycle assessment application experience
abstract: Wine tourism, including winery visits, tastings, and cultural events, boosts sustainable development but generates environmental impacts ranging from food and wine production to tasting services. This study applies Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), focused on Carbon Footprint (CF), to compare the use of reusable ceramic vs. disposable cellulose-pulp plates in a tasting service in an Apulian winery. A cradle-to-grave analysis reveals that, in baseline scenario, reusable plates showed a slightly higher CF than single-use plates (0.0668 vs. 0.0635 kgCO₂eq/person served, respectively). Based on the results obtained, process optimisation solutions were identified: it was found that using photovoltaic-powered energy-efficient dishwasher may reduce the CF of reusable plates by 67%, reducing the impact to 0.0179 kgCO₂eq/person served in the best-performing scenario. Five service configurations were then tested over a total of 2500 customers served in six months, assuming a constant optimal dishwasher loading efficiency (i.e., operating exclusively at full capacity). Whilst the absolute reuse rate of the plate stock inherently scales with customer volume (averaging approximately 73 uses per plate in the baseline period), the results showed that, without technological improvements, the lowest-impact option was to serve 500 people with reusable plates and 2000 with disposable plates. Overall, this study extends the application of Life Cycle Assessment from conventional production systems to experiential tourism services. The findings demonstrate that the environmental performance of tableware is not solely dictated by intrinsic material properties, but is fundamentally driven by the systemic operational configuration, including dishwashing efficiency, service volumes, and the carbon intensity of the electricity mix. Consequently, this study provides a novel, scalable methodological framework to support wineries and tourism operators in designing scientifically grounded, lower-impact tasting services. © 2026

title: River tourism based on community participation and regional linkages for sustainable livelihoods: The case of Can Tho City, Vietnam
abstract: This study examines the role of community-based river tourism and regional linkages in supporting sustainable livelihoods in Can Tho City, Vietnam. A convergent mixed-methods approach was employed, combining surveys of 385 tourists, 47 local households, and 18 tourism officials and community representatives with 36 semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), cluster analysis, and multiple regression, while qualitative data were integrated through thematic coding, triangulation, and SWOT analysis. The findings indicate that community-based river tourism contributes to livelihood diversification, income generation, skill development, and social capital formation. Participating households reported relatively high livelihood stability (mean = 3.87) and moderate government support (mean = 3.59), whereas regional linkage participation remained low (mean = 1.79). EFA results revealed a common factor linking government support, regional cooperation, and livelihood outcomes, with factor loadings ranging from -0.64 to -0.51. For tourism officials and community representatives, EFA identified two governance dimensions—regional coordination and community-enterprise synergy—which explained 84.83 of the total variance. Tourists reported high overall satisfaction (mean = 4.35), strong community interaction (mean = 4.61), positive perceptions of cultural preservation (mean = 3.71), and willingness to pay for tourism services (mean = 3.98). Regression analysis showed that cultural preservation perception was the only statistically significant predictor of tourist satisfaction ( β = 0.146, p = 0.004 ). Open-ended responses highlighted key development priorities, including reducing crowding ( 29.6 ), increasing the availability of tour guides ( 26.8 ), enhancing cultural activities ( 23.9 ), and extending tour duration ( 19.7 ). Overall, sustainable livelihood outcomes depend not only on community participation but also on effective governance, cultural preservation, and stronger regional integration. The findings provide empirical evidence and practical implications for sustainable tourism planning in riverine destinations of the Mekong Delta. Copyright (c) 2026 The Authors. title: Toward a relational typology: Mapping social entrepreneur-resident interactions in community-led tourism social entrepreneurship
abstract: Research on tourism social entrepreneurship has focused on exogenous models while overlooking host communities' agency. The aim of this study was to examine interactions between social entrepreneurs and residents in the context of community-led tourism social entrepreneurship. The exploratory qualitative study design involved three fieldwork phases. We used two dimensions—the initiator's primary motivation and the embeddedness forms in the responder's actions—to identify four relationship types: traditional bonding ties, instrumental ties, patron–client ties, and value-congruent alliances. The social action and embeddedness theories guided our examination of relational formation. Findings further reveal a model of power shift and relationship dynamics. This model suggests that a power shift involves three principal stages centered around dependence. In summary, we provide here a typological framework for analyzing social entrepreneur–resident interactions and offer practical insights into sustainable community development. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Escaping the AI cage: construction workers’ perceived risk with AI gives rise to unsafe behaviors
abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The psychology of AI-mediated communication across languages
abstract: Communication across languages is increasingly mediated by artificial intelligence (AI). This creates opportunities for people with different language backgrounds to communicate in their respective native languages. AI-mediated communication can therefore reduce cognitive effort, disfluency, and social stigma associated with speaking a non-native language. At the same time, non-native language use influences cognitive, emotional, and social processes that go beyond the accurate transmission of meaning. By affecting these processes and introducing new cues, AI-mediated communication could also have unintended effects on communication effectiveness and social evaluations between interlocutors. We examine the conditions under which these effects may help or hinder cross-linguistic interactions and identify directions for research on the psychology of cross-linguistic communication as AI language tools become prevalent. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Beyond Technology Readiness Levels: Developing and Evaluating an Industry 5.0 Innovation Readiness Framework for Regulated Life Sciences Manufacturing
abstract: Purpose: Regulated life sciences manufacturing organisations face increasing pressure to adopt Industry 5.0 (I5.0) innovations while maintaining patient safety, product quality, data integrity, and regulatory compliance. Existing assessment models provide useful perspectives on technical maturity, expectation dynamics, and organisational innovation capability, but do not fully assess whether an innovation is ready to progress responsibly in a regulated, multi-stakeholder environment. This paper develops an I5.0 Innovation Readiness Framework and presents a preliminary practitioner-informed evaluation of its use in regulated life sciences manufacturing. Methods: This paper uses design science research structured through the Double Diamond process. The framework was developed through literature review, advisory feedback, subject matter expert input, practitioner workshops, case-based application, surveys, and thematic analysis. Evaluation was conducted with a small, purposively selected cohort of 16 practitioners from a single educational-industry programme. Results: The framework comprises three linked tools: the Innovation Maturity Assessment, Innovation Maturity Rubric, and Innovation Readiness Levels. Across two exploratory workshops involving 16 experienced practitioners, participants reported that the framework supported clearer discussion of readiness and improved visibility of adoption risks. In Workshop 2, descriptive feedback indicated that 91% of respondents viewed Innovation Readiness Levels as clearer than Technology Readiness Levels, 82% found the framework useful for comparing innovation timelines, and 75% would recommend it. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary practitioner feedback rather than sector-wide validation. Conclusion: The findings support the conceptual distinction between innovation readiness and technology readiness and indicate the need to assess technical, regulatory, organisational, stakeholder, and societal dimensions together when evaluating I5.0 innovation in regulated manufacturing. Further evaluation with broader industry cohorts, quality and regulatory professionals, and regulatory stakeholders is required. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Contextualizing negotiation research: The unique dynamics of buyer–supplier negotiations
abstract: Effective buyer–supplier negotiations are important for organizations to attain their goals and for wider society to have a reliable supply of goods and services. These negotiations also have distinctive characteristics that differentiate them from other negotiation settings, such as personal buyer–seller negotiations, which have attracted much of the attention in the negotiation literature. Given the differences between professional buyer–supplier and personal buyer–seller negotiations, some findings from personal negotiations may have limited applicability in supply chain settings, while others hold across contexts. These findings have important implications for both negotiation research and education, calling for careful contextualization based on the type of negotiation. By reviewing recent studies in the supply chain management literature, this article highlights several common dynamics of buyer–supplier negotiations and how they affect negotiation outcomes. These dynamics are broadly categorized into the non-exhaustive themes of power in ongoing buyer–supplier relationships, other relational factors (supply network complexity, cross-cultural relations, and AI adoption), and negotiation strategies in buyer–supplier relationships (distributive, integrative, and mixed strategies), providing scholars with an overview of selected recent research on buyer–supplier negotiations. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: LLMs’ reshaping of people, processes, products, and society in software development: a qualitative exploration with early adopters
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping software development, but their impact across the full software development lifecycle is underexplored. Existing work tends to focus on isolated activities such as code generation or testing, leaving open questions about how LLMs affect developers, processes, products, and the broader software ecosystem. We address this gap through semi-structured interviews with sixteen early-adopter software professionals who integrated LLM-based tools into their day-to-day work in early to mid-2023. We treat these interviews as early empirical evidence and compare participants’ accounts with recent work on LLMs in software engineering, noting which early patterns persist or shift. Using thematic analysis, we organize our findings around four dimensions: people, process, product, and society. Developers reported substantial productivity gains from reducing mundane tasks, streamlining search, and accelerating debugging, but also described a productivity-quality paradox: they frequently discarded generated code and shifted effort from writing code to critically evaluating and integrating it. LLM use was highly phase-dependent, with strong uptake in implementation and debugging but limited influence on requirements gathering and collaborative work. Participants developed new competencies to use LLMs effectively, including prompt engineering strategies, multi-layered verification, and security-conscious integration to protect proprietary data. They also anticipated changes in hiring expectations, team practices, and computing education, while emphasizing that human judgment and foundational software engineering skills remain essential. Our findings, consistent with evidence from large-scale studies, offer actionable implications for developers, organizations, educators, and tool designers seeking to integrate LLMs responsibly into professional software practice. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: When stigmatized workers become consumers
abstract: Existing research on occupational stigma has focused primarily on workplace consequences, with less attention to how stigmatized service workers respond to service failures as consumers. Guided by cognitive appraisal theory, this sequential mixed-methods study integrates 20 interviews with a survey of 429 frontline workers in China. Qualitative findings show that perceived occupational stigma heightens sensitivity to disrespect and identity threat, whereas perceived work dirtiness shapes whether failures are attributed to situational constraints or preventable neglect. Quantitative results indicate that both constructs are positively associated with customer aggression and tolerance. Aggression may function as confrontational problem-focused coping, whereas tolerance reflects emotion-focused coping, and both are positively related to service recovery satisfaction. Service recovery performance strengthens these relationships. The study applies cognitive appraisal theory to an underexplored dual-role context and shows how distinct occupational perceptions shape appraisal, coping, and recovery evaluations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Examining perceptual spillover effects in social media influencer marketing effectiveness: A PLS-SEM and fsQCA approach
abstract: Social media influencers (SMIs) play a pertinent role in shaping brand evaluations, yet how influencer-level perceptions translate into brand-level evaluations and SMI marketing effectiveness remains unclear. Drawing on spillover effects as a theoretical lens, a two-stage quantitative approach was adopted. Results from the Stage 1 serial mediation model suggest that SMI social attractiveness is directly associated with purchase intention and indirectly associated with purchase intention through brand attitude. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, perceived SMI authenticity does not mediate the relationship between social attractiveness and purchase intention. Consistent with a spillover interpretation, perceived SMI authenticity serves as an evaluative facilitator associated with brand-level evaluations rather than directly with purchase intention. In a separate Stage 2, fsQCA was used to explore configurations associated with SMI marketing effectiveness, which, in this study, encompasses both transactional and non-transactional dimensions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When passion breeds silence: How coworkers’ work passion elicits envy and employee silence in hospitality workplaces
abstract: While work passion is well-studied as an intrapersonal motivational construct, its interpersonal consequences for coworkers remain underexplored. Drawing primarily on the Social Functional Theory of Emotions, we examine how employees' observed work passion functions as a social signal that elicits coworker envy and, in turn, shapes silence behaviors. Across four studies (three experiments and a multi-source dyadic field study with hotel employees), we find a robust asymmetric pattern: harmonious passion primarily elicits benign envy, which is associated with prosocial silence, whereas obsessive passion primarily elicits malicious envy, which is associated with deviant silence. Cross-path effects were weaker and less consistent across studies. An exploratory field-study finding suggests that obsessive passion may occasionally relate to benign envy, although this association did not emerge in the experiments and warrants replication. This research extends passion theory by highlighting its interpersonal signaling effects and reframes silence as a strategic emotion-regulation response. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Investigations of the cascading effect of hotel entrepreneur's optimism on employees’ work behaviors and customers evaluations in small and medium hospitality enterprises
abstract: Given the significant proportion of small and medium hospitality enterprises (SMHEs) in the hospitality and tourism industry, this study focuses on the influential role and the power of entrepreneurs. Integrating optimism theory and social learning theory, we delineate how the entrepreneur's attributes and leadership exert a cascading effect across hierarchical levels, impacting both employees and customers. A multisource field study (248 entrepreneurs, 681 employees, and 1179 customers) shows that an entrepreneur's optimism drives adaptation to new leadership styles, i.e., e-leadership and green leadership, crucial for achieving the organization's goals regarding digital transformation and sustainability. An entrepreneur's e-leadership positively affects employees’ creative performance, while green leadership has a crossover effect on employees’ green behaviors, ultimately increasing customer satisfaction and ratings. We discuss new implications for understanding both the emergence and the profound effects of new leadership styles, especially in the context of SMHEs in the hospitality and tourism industry. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Leveraging big data analytics for sustainable competitive advantage: A model of operational performance
abstract: Big Data Analytics (BDA) has become an important organizational capability for strengthening firm performance and sustaining competitive advantage. This study examines how Big Data Acceptance, Big Data Assimilation, and Big Data Routinization contribute to Organizational Performance with Big Data Analysis (OPBDA), and how the resulting organizational benefits, such as smarter management decisions, increased innovation and agility, and improved organizational efficiency, relate to sustainable competitive advantage. Survey data collected from 414 respondents in China were analyzed using IBM SPSS 23.0 and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings show that acceptance, assimilation, and routinization of big data positively and significantly influence OPBDA. OPBDA, in turn, significantly improves management's decision-making and organizational efficiency, while its relationship with Increased Innovation and Agility is not statistically significant. The study highlights the importance of effectively assimilating and routinizing BDA within organizational processes to strengthen managerial decision-making, operational efficiency, and sustained competitive positioning. © 2026

title: Consumers and local short food supply chains: Critical purchasing factors
abstract: Short food supply chains (SFSCs) are considered an effective way to promote greater sustainability in agri-food production. In this regard, there is increasing interest from consumers in short supply chain initiatives, as well as from academia and society in general. Despite their importance, limited research on consumers and SFSCs is available in emerging countries. This study, conducted in Colombia, aimed to identify factors influencing consumers' food purchases through local SFSCs (L-SFSCs). For this purpose, a quantitative analysis was performed based on a logistic regression model, comparing frequent L-SFSCs consumers with a control group of non-consumers. It was found that socio-economic characteristics of the consumers, such as age range, level of education and income level, are factors that determine the purchase of food through L-SFSCs. Also, geographical proximity had a significant effect on the purchase of food through L-SFSCs. In addition, positive attitudes towards L-SFSCs also condition the purchase of food through this alternative distribution format. Recommendations are provided, both for the adoption and promotion of L-SFSCs, as well as for the competitive improvement of existing L-SFSCs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Operational constraints in professional kitchens: A theory of constraints perspective on food waste reduction
abstract: Professional kitchens, where core foodservice operations occur, generate up to two-thirds of total food waste. Although recent research has increasingly acknowledged the managerial and operational dimensions of food waste, limited attention has been devoted to explaining how these constraints interact within an integrated operational system. Addressing this gap, this study applies the Theory of Constraints (TOC) and qualitative triangulation through structured observations and in-depth interviews with kitchen staff to identify and analyze waste reduction constraints across kitchen workflows. Four interrelated constraint dimensions were identified, and workflow-tracing analysis revealed a sequential constraint chain in which policy and market constraints appear to influence resource conditions that are reflected in behavioral constraints, where throughput constraints become most visible. Applying Goldratt's Five Focusing Steps across this chain generates prioritized interventions. The study reframes waste as a systemic outcome of upstream pressures and offers a structured diagnostic framework for effective intervention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The dark side of AI customer service: How service failures damage consumer-brand relationships
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) customer service is increasingly used as a frontline interface, yet its failures may create relational damage that extends beyond a single service encounter. Drawing on service failure theory and consumer-brand relationship literature, this research examines how AI service failures are formed and how they influence negative consumer-brand relationships. Study 1 collected 3208 online complaint records from a major Chinese consumer complaint platform. After data cleaning, 2824 valid complaints were analyzed using Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling, which identified ten complaint topics and further synthesized them into five AI service failure dimensions: functional failure, informational failure, systemic failure, interactional failure, and service recovery failure. Study 2 used survey data from 965 Chinese consumers and applied PLS-SEM, Artificial Neural Network (ANN), fsQCA, and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). The results show that all five failure dimensions positively influence negative consumer-brand relationships. Informational failure and systemic failure emerge as particularly influential across linear, predictive, and configurational analyses. The findings advance AI service failure research by developing a data-driven typology of failures and demonstrating that AI-mediated service breakdowns are not merely technical problems but relational threats that undermine consumer trust, satisfaction, and engagement with brands. However, because this research focuses on Chinese consumers and complaint data from a single national platform, future studies should examine whether the proposed failure typology and relational effects can be generalized across different countries, cultures, platforms, and regulatory environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Lost in the narrative: How embedded content reduces sales on short video commerce platforms
abstract: Embedded content on short video commerce platforms, which integrates product-focused content with creators' self-focused content, has been widely adopted as a strategy to enhance viewer engagement and drive product sales. Despite its prevalent application, the effect of embedded content on product sales remains unclear. While self-focused content may reduce advertising avoidance, it risks distracting attention from the product, thereby making its effect on subsequent product sales unclear. To explore the sales effect of embedded content and its underlying mechanisms, we employ a mixed-methods approach, combining an observational study with a randomized experiment. Our empirical analysis reveals that a higher ratio of self-focused content decreases product sales. Heterogeneity analyses further uncover several measures to mitigate the negative impact: optimizing commercial embedment timing, increasing creator positive facial expressions, and enhancing product visual salience. Finally, we conduct a randomized experiment to validate the dual-path mechanism, which shows that self-focused content indeed reduces ad avoidance but also reduces ad attention, thereby affecting viewers’ purchase intentions through two opposing pathways. Our findings advance theoretical understanding of embedded content through a dual theoretical perspective and offer practical insights for practitioners on short video commerce platforms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Paying for the future? Cross-season pre-sale product launch strategy in hotels
abstract: Traditional hotels face persistent seasonal demand imbalance, with weak off-peak demand and constrained peak-season capacity. Drawing on Contingency Theory, this study examines cross-season pre-sale as a context-dependent hotel revenue management configuration and investigates how different configurations (i.e., no pre-sale, self-run pre-sale, and platform-based pre-sale) fit varying operating conditions. Results show that cross-season pre-sale does not universally outperform conventional practices; its value depends on the balance among incremental demand, impacts on existing demand, and implementation costs. Moreover, neither self-run nor platform-based pre-sale always dominates, as their relative effectiveness depends on the trade-off between platform-enabled market reach and channel costs. The study identifies boundary conditions for effective cross-season demand coordination and offers practical guidance for configuration choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Driving impact? How imperfect displacement shapes heterogeneous rebound in carsharing
abstract: Green technologies, products, and services, such as carsharing, are commonly promoted as pathways to lower environmental impacts by increasing efficiency. Yet rebound effects, behavioral and economic responses to improved efficiency, may erode these environmental impact reductions. Many rebound studies assume perfect displacement, where a new technology or mode of service provision fully replaces an existing service on a one-to-one basis. While analytically convenient, this assumption overlooks real-world complexity and consumer heterogeneity. Using survey data from nearly 4500 Belgian carsharing users, we compare rebound estimates under perfect displacement with those based on reported shifts in mobility. Under the perfect displacement assumption, we find a 53% rebound effect. When accounting for imperfect displacement, however, rebound effects vary widely across users. While median effects remain positive (20%–46%), at the individual level rebound effects range from substantial net benefits to strong rebound (5th–95th percentile: −331% to 147%). A cluster analysis further reveals distinct user groups with systematically different impacts, underscoring that displacement patterns vary not only in scale but also in direction. These findings suggest that carsharing's environmental impact is highly user-dependent, and that relying on a single aggregate estimate may mask critical behavioral variations. As this case study demonstrates, accounting for imperfect displacement in rebound analysis is critical for advancing theory and for tailoring more effective policy interventions. © 2026 The Authors. title: Factors influencing language choice of the Chơ Ro ethnic minority in Southern Vietnam: A socio-structural analysis
abstract: This study examines the structural and socio-psychological factors shaping the language choice of the Chơ Ro— an indigenous community of fewer than 30,000 members in Southeast Vietnam—to identify the determinants of linguistic persistence amidst rapid industrial expansion. In the context of industrialization in Vietnam, ethnic minority communities navigate significant challenges related to language maintenance. This paper argues that Chơ Ro language choice reflects a phenomenon of language persistence, in which internal cultural motivations and communal networks function as determinants against the pressures of language shift. Utilizing a convergent mixed-methods design, the study analyzed quantitative data from 472 bilingual participants in Dong Nai, triangulated with qualitative data from 30 semi-structured interviews conducted with village elders and cultural custodians. The regression model yielded an adjusted R2 of.862, indicating that the independent variables account for 86.2% of the variance in language choice. Results indicate a predictive hierarchy: Cultural motivation (CM) emerged as a determinant predictor (β = 0.271, p < 0.001), followed by Endogamous social networks (ESN) (β = 0.225, p < 0.001) and Domain functional expansion (DFE) (β = 0.195, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that the Chơ Ro language remains a functional medium in domestic and communal domains, supported by Intergenerational Transmission Strength (ITS) (β = 0.171) and Institutional Support (IS) (β = 0.166). Qualitative themes reinforce these results, identifying a gendered buffering mechanism where domestic socialization counteracts external industrial pressures. This research provides an empirical framework for policy interventions aimed at addressing ethnolinguistic vitality through the reinforcement of community-based linguistic assets. By documenting the resilience of a small-scale minority, the study contributes to a comparative theory of bilingualism in urbanizing contexts, emphasizing that internal conviction and communal structures are necessary to mitigate linguistic attrition in high-density economic zones. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .
