title: DCET: Multi-scale decomposition and channel clustering enhanced multivariate time series forecasting
abstract: Existing multivariate time series forecasting methods address multi-scale structures and channel heterogeneity by either enhancing model expressiveness with deeper and wider network architectures or by preprocessing sequences to attenuate certain frequency components. However, these approaches often lead to increased training costs, instability from over-reliance on model capacity, difficulty in handling multiple scales, and failure to consider differing structural relationships between channels. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel framework called DCET (Decomposition and channel Clustering Enhanced multivariate Time series Forecasting), which integrates a cascading two-stage decomposition process, channel clustering, and a ChebyKAN residual head within a single unified model. The main contribution of DCET lies in its ability to directly address multi-scale and channel heterogeneity in a more efficient manner by simplifying the model structure while preserving its expressiveness. Specifically, DCET introduces an unsupervised learning-based module for parameter sharing among similar variates, and applies the two-stage decomposition to capture multi-scale features. Nonlinear models are used to represent complex fluctuations, while linear models capture long-term trends. Moreover, a multi-objective training approach minimizes both the overall prediction error and the errors of decomposed components. We validate DCET through experiments on eight public datasets, demonstrating improved prediction accuracy, robustness, and flexibility in handling high-dimensional, heterogeneous time series with manageable model complexity. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: XAI in the human-agent-environment loop: how do task, explanation strategy, and AI literacy shape user engagement?
abstract: This study explored how tasks, explanation strategies, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy levels collectively influenced human interaction with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in a single-target prediction task. Using a within-subjects experiment with 70 participants, the study examined combinations of four AI-assisted prediction tasks—varying in prediction target (human-related vs. human-unrelated) and stakes (high vs. low)—and six explanation strategies (model-based, comparison-based, input influence-based, sensitivity-based, demographic-based, and case-based), across participants with varying AI literacy (AIL). Results showed that explanation strategies had the most significant impact on human-XAI interaction in most aspects, especially on prediction change with XAI assistance. Additionally, explanation strategies significantly affected all perception and experience indicators, except for curiosity. Compared to the scope of explanations, the content provided by strategies had a greater influence on user predictions. Strategies with trends and ratios, such as case-based (CA) and demographic-based (DE), were more effective. Conversely, strategies lacking trends and ratios, such as model-based (MO) and comparison-based (CO), were generally the least effective. For users, AI literacy influenced all performance metrics, especially re-prediction time. Higher AI literacy was significantly associated with longer re-prediction time. Tasks had moderate impacts on the XAI interaction process, especially experience measures. In the human-related tasks (recidivism and shipwreck survival prediction), participants reported lower subjective experience ratings among the tasks examined, particularly regarding perceived justice. In the high-stakes, human-unrelated task (wine quality prediction), participants gave the most favorable experiential ratings among the tasks in the study. Furthermore, second-order effects related to explanation strategies had significant impacts on various metrics. On the one hand, the interaction between explanation strategies and task characteristics influenced prediction changes. Global explanations, such as the input-influence-based (IN) and MO strategies, performed better on human-related tasks than on human-unrelated tasks. In contrast, local explanations, such as the sensitivity-based (SE) and CO strategies, showed the opposite pattern. On the other hand, the impact of explanation strategies on user perception and experience was moderated by AI literacy. Users with lower literacy tended to prefer local explanations, while users with higher literacy preferred global explanations. The content of the XAI explanation significantly affected the quality, while the scope had subtle interactive effects with different tasks and users. These effects with XAI, majorly interpreted through the Elaboration Likelihood model (ELM), provide evidence supporting adaptive XAI within the human-agent-environment loop. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Cross cultural patterns of linguistic aggression and aggressive combat content enjoyment: A computational study of PUBG reviews across six continents
abstract: This study explores global patterns of linguistic aggression and appreciation for aggressive combat content as expressed in reviews of PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds (PUBG), analyzing over 18.7 million Google Play Store English language reviews from over 80 countries. Grounded in the General Aggression Model (GAM), it integrates media psychology, cross cultural communication, and computational social science to assess emotional expression in user generated content. Two indices, Aggression Score and Appreciation of Aggressive Content (AAC), were constructed using NLP, sentiment analysis, and lexicon-based tagging to capture hostile sentiment (anger) and positive reinforcement (joy, ratings, likes) in aggression-related reviews. Results reveal a significant increase in the average intensity of both scores over time, with reviews grouped under South America exhibiting higher average aggression and AAC scores within the dataset, while reviews grouped under Australia show comparatively lower levels of these measures. The study uses GAM as a conceptual lens to interpret large-scale, naturalistic expressions of aggression and enjoyment. Methodologically, it offers replicable framework for affective analysis; practically, it offers exploratory insights for game design and content moderation in digital environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Regionalized life cycle assessment of NMC and LFP batteries across China-EU supply chain configurations under the EU Battery Regulation
abstract: The EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 introduces stringent life cycle carbon footprint requirements that are expected to influence the regional organization of battery production. However, the carbon footprint implications of alternative China-EU supply chain configurations remain insufficiently understood. This study develops a regionalized life cycle assessment framework to evaluate the life cycle carbon footprints of lithium nickel‑manganese‑cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries under alternative regional supply chain configurations between China and the EU. The analysis follows the latest EU methodological guidance and combines proprietary industrial data from leading Chinese electric vehicle (EV) battery manufacturers. The boundary analysis showed that the calculated carbon footprints were sensitive to the life cycle stages included. Under the EU baseline, the carbon footprints of NMC and LFP batteries were 96.2 and 51.6 gCO2e/kWh under the Directive 91/157/EEC-informed reference boundary, 95.9 and 81.3 gCO2e/kWh under the Directive 2006/66/EC-informed reference boundary, and 142.9 and 128.3 gCO2e/kWh under the Regulation (EU) 2023/1542-aligned full life cycle boundary, respectively. Scenario analysis further indicated that regional supply chain reconfiguration can substantially narrow carbon footprint differences relative to Baseline-EU. For NMC batteries, the difference decreased from 59.3 gCO2e/kWh under the export (EX) scenario to 49.3 and 47.7 gCO2e/kWh under the overseas battery production (TB) scenario and partial material pre-processing in the EU (TBM) scenario, respectively. For LFP batteries, the corresponding values decreased from 74.1 to 49.4 and 47.1 gCO2e/kWh. These findings suggest that the regulatory context may encourage supply chain configurations with lower life cycle carbon footprints by altering the regional allocation of production stages. The findings highlight the importance of aligning regional production characteristics with decarbonization potential and provide policy-relevant evidence for coordinated China-EU battery supply chain strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: A Block-Wise Updating Strategy for Approximate Duplicate Detection
abstract: Approximate duplicate detection in data streams aims to determine whether an item is present within a small subsequence of the data stream. It is a fundamental query problem needed in several network applications, such as web crawling and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tag management. Most of the existing algorithms are not space-efficient as they overlook the distributional information of query frequency and membership likelihood. In this paper, we propose CEll Bloom Filter (CEBF) algorithm, a space-efficient data structure designed by adopting a block-wise updating strategy, to solve this problem, and two typical distributions are considered: two typical distributions: (1) uniform query frequency of items, and (2) uniform membership likelihood of items. For an arbitrary sliding window size n and an arbitrary average false positive rate ε ∈ (0, 1), the proposed algorithm needs approximately O(nlog2(1/ε)) bits, which is significantly less than the number of bits used in existing methods. Space lower bound is also derived for these two typical distributions, which demonstrates that the proposed algorithm is near-optimal in terms of space consumption. Experiments are conducted on both synthetic and real datasets, and the experimental results clearly demonstrate that the proposed method is clearly and significantly more effective and promising compared to existing other methods. © The author(s) 2027.

title: A survey charting trust models and systems in self-sovereign identity
abstract: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is widely positioned as the decentralized future of digital identity. However, although traditional SSI literature emphasizes architecture and privacy, it largely overlooks a systematic analysis of how trust is formed, propagated, and managed. Trust is fundamental because, without it, the actions performed by key actors, including credential issuers, lose much of their practical value. In this landscape, trust is the ground on which SSI systems stand; when that ground is absent or unstable, any structure built on it crumbles. Against this backdrop, we chart the landscape of trust through a comprehensive survey of Trust Models (TMs) and Trust Management Systems (TMSs) in SSI. At the abstract level, we analyze TMs by examining the types of trust relationships among SSI actors and how trust is defined and represented. At the implementation level, we discuss TMSs in terms of how trust is represented, stored, and protected in the systems proposed in the literature. We analyzed 26 sources (24 peer-reviewed papers plus the Sovrin whitepaper and governance framework document), consolidated into 24 approaches, benchmarking 16 features across these dimensions. Based on this analysis, we identify five open challenges: enabling cross-chain trust portability; designing a hybrid TM that blends Web of Trust and hierarchies; supporting heterogeneous actors such as IoT devices and humans; implementing privacy-preserving feedback mechanisms; and TM and TMS interoperability in emerging settings, including delegated AI agents. Our analysis offers a compass to guide researchers and developers in selecting trust models and advancing SSI systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Evaluation of cost reduction effects by sector-coupling synergies in timber processing and bioenergy for sustainable forestry in Japan
abstract: The greenhouse gas sequestration capacity of forests is an important pillar in combating global warming; therefore establishing a forest resource circulation system is crucial. Forestry, which includes everything from cultivation to harvesting forests that store carbon dioxide as they grow, and the sawmill industry, which processes this timber, frequently face significant economic challenges. Consequently, proposals are needed to establish systems that improve these industries’ economic competitiveness while also ensuring the forest resources circulation. This study developed a model to evaluate the economic relationship between timber processing and energy consumption from a sector-coupling perspective using a prospective techno-economic analysis. It specifically defines wood utilization as a comprehensive forest resource circulation that includes production, planting, processing, energy utilization, and reforestation. It evaluates the economic interdependence between timber processing and energy utilization when all wood is harvested from forests and both uses are combined. The evaluation results show that combining energy utilization in sawmills processing over 36,000 m3 annually allows for full harvesting from forests, reducing forest residues, and lowering site preparation costs for reforestation. Additionally, using inexpensive electricity from biomass power generation for sawmilling lowers sawmill costs. It has become clear that, at sawmills of a certain size or larger, combining material utilization with energy utilization results in a slight decrease in sawmilling costs, while reducing forestry management costs; overall, this is an effective approach for wood utilization. © 2026 The Authors. title: The viral deviation: a quantitative analysis of social media engagement metrics on non-compliant flight deck behaviors
abstract: Background Normalization of Deviance (NoD) is a well-documented organizational failure mode in aviation, yet its propagation through digital ecosystems remains unexplored. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) highlights a critical mentorship vacuum due to pilot retirements, and social media platforms increasingly serve as informal training environments. This study introduces the concept of Algorithmic Normalization of Deviance- ANoD, hypothesizing that recommendation algorithms systematically reward and amplify “gray-zone” cockpit behaviors that erode sterile flight deck protocols. Method We conducted a stratified netnographic analysis of 150 high-visibility aviation videos (N = 150) across Instagram Reels, split between algorithmically recommended content (n = 100) and curated influencer content (n = 50). A novel coding framework operationalized compliance (Compliant vs. Gray Zone vs. Deviant) and incentive structures. Engagement metrics were analyzed to quantify the algorithmic advantage of non-compliant behavior. Results The analysis reveals a directionally consistent “Viral Deviation” pattern rather than a statistically decisive one. Gray-zone recordings (i.e., technically legal but procedurally borderline) comprised 57% of the sample and attracted higher engagement than compliant content, although this difference was small and did not reach conventional significance (d = 0.24, p = 0.11). The clearest signal emerged between content sources: algorithmically surfaced posts showed significantly higher interaction rates than curated influencer posts (d = 0.31, p = 0.029), a small but statistically significant per-view advantage for content promoted directly by the recommendation system. Structural incentive analysis further indicates that monetization pressures co-occur with increased gray-zone production, structurally analogous to a parallel, shadow curriculum associated with conditions that may facilitate drift. Conclusion The study identifies statistical associations, not causal relationships, and the downstream behavioural impact on pilots is hypothesised from the algorithmic-pattern evidence rather than directly measured. Within those bounds, social media algorithms constitute a structurally unmonitored distribution channel whose observed associations with gray-zone content amplification are consistent with a normalisation-of-deviance feedback mechanism operating beyond current regulatory oversight — an association that warrants urgent empirical validation and proactive governance. We propose a shift from prohibition to risk-stratified governance, recommending that regulators distinguish between handheld (high-risk) and mounted (managed-risk) devices, and integrate digital algorithmic literacy into ab-initio pilot training to counter this new systemic threat. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Automatic behavior tree generation for enhanced human–robot collaborative task planning in industry 5.0: A systematic review
abstract: In the context of Industry 5.0, scheduling heterogeneous resources, such as humans and robots, has become increasingly critical. Task allocation must balance human comfort, ergonomics, and trust with productivity and responsiveness to customer demands. This review explores recent advances and prospects in the automatic generation of schedules and action plans, particularly Behavior Trees (BTs), to improve human–robot collaboration. We examine the application of artificial intelligence techniques to classical production management problems, such as Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP) and Assembly Line Balancing Problems (ALBP), for autonomous task scheduling and robotic behavior design. This includes highlighting innovative scheduling approaches and the advantages of Behavior Trees over traditional models such as Hierarchical Task Networks (HTN) and Finite-State Machines (FSM). Behavior Trees offer a modular and reactive programming structure essential for executing complex tasks assigned to robots. The review also discusses human operators’ perception of robotic actions and identifies best practices for implementing collaborative solutions that prioritize both efficiency and safety. © 2026 The Authors. title: Understanding conflict in protected areas: integrating justice considerations with economic perspectives
abstract: Despite broad agreement on the urgency of sustainability transitions that protect biodiversity, conservation conflicts continue to rise. This paper examines environmental conflicts in protected areas (PAs), highlighting the overlooked link between conflict and justice. Existing frameworks often fail to distinguish between conflict manifestations and determinants, or to integrate justice theories with economic perspectives. This study provides a comprehensive review of the literature to support the analysis of PA conflicts and develops a robust framework that integrates justice considerations with the economic perspective. Conflicts are viewed as inherent to complex social–ecological systems, shaped by social relations and rights over ecosystem services. The framework is structured around three analytical axes: substance (what the conflict is about), process (how it unfolds), and relation (who is involved with-whom). It differentiates between how conflicts appear (i.e., manifestation) and what causes them (i.e., determinants), framed through distributive, procedural, and recognition justice. This perspective challenges linear assumptions that conflicts always stem from injustices, emphasizing their potential to drive institutional change. The framework offers a novel approach to assessing justice-conflict dynamics in PAs governance, providing comprehensive toolkit for promoting equitable conservation strategies. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

title: What drives happiness in 15 European Union countries? The role of income inequality, democracy, and environmental quality
abstract: This study examines happiness as a key dimension of sustainable development by focusing on its socio-economic, political, and environmental correlates. In recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that happiness cannot be explained solely by economic prosperity but is strongly influenced by structural factors such as income distribution, democratic institutions, and environmental conditions. Despite growing interest, empirical studies examining the simultaneous effects of these three fundamental factors on happiness are scarce. This creates a noteworthy gap in the literature. This study aims to fill this gap by empirically examining the effects of income inequality, democracy, and environmental degradation on happiness in 15 European Union countries, including the United Kingdom for comparability, between 2011 and 2022. Per capita income and health expenditure are included as control variables. Methodologically, the study employs MMQR and assesses the robustness of the findings using FGLS, PCSE, and HPJ approaches. The findings suggest that income inequality and environmental degradation are negatively associated with happiness, whereas democracy is positively associated with individuals' happiness. Furthermore, it is found that per capita income and health expenditure are found to be positively related to happiness. The results point to the need for sustainable development goals to be addressed within a holistic framework rather than independently, offering important implications for policymakers. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. title: Investigation of uncertainties associated with human judgment during the inspection and condition assessment of civil infrastructures
abstract: Inspection of civil infrastructure components is a critical task to assess their condition states and plan for appropriate maintenance actions. The process of inspection, however, involves several sources of uncertainty that can influence how a component is rated by an inspector. Despite potential consequences, such uncertainties have remained largely unexplored. This motivated the current study to develop a holistic framework to first measure the agreement and consistency of condition state predictions provided by various inspectors through the inter-rater reliability and intra-class correlation methods. The study then advanced to understand how the provided condition ratings can be analyzed, updated, and aggregated, taking into consideration possible interactions among inspectors during an inspection task. The outcome was quantified based on the inclination of participating inspectors to make more conservative, realistic, or less conservative assessments. The cumulative prospect theory was then utilized to quantify how the risk tolerance of individual inspectors can influence the decision making process, both at the time of inspection and during the service life of civil infrastructure components subjected to inspection. In the absence of similar studies, this investigation’s findings helped improve how condition state ratings received from inspectors can be processed and incorporated into a decision making framework. While the exploration of the psychological roots of why various inspectors rate the same component differently remained outside the scope of this study, the quantification of contributing uncertainties is expected to guide future training programs to further enhance the quality of condition assessment and management decisions made based on inspection reports. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Target item identification for injection attacks in recommender systems via graph-enhanced user representations
abstract: Recommender systems are increasingly threatened by profile injection attacks. However, most existing defenses focus on detecting fake users, which becomes unreliable as modern attacks generate highly concealed profiles and operational platforms often lack attacker labels or attack priors. To address this limitation, we propose TIGER (Target Item Identification via Graph-Enhanced Representations), a hybrid auditing-oriented framework that reframes the final defensive output from user-level fake user labels to item-level suspicious target item candidates. Importantly, TIGER does not eliminate user-side analysis; instead, it uses unsupervised suspicious user discovery as an intermediate support step for downstream auditing. Specifically, TIGER first leverages a small trusted reference set to learn stable item embeddings and aligns unknown data into a shared semantic space. It then constructs graph-enhanced user representations by integrating rating statistics, preference patterns, and item semantics, enabling the extraction of informative suspicious user candidates for target item auditing. Finally, suspicious target item candidates are flagged through a rank-shift auditing strategy that compares recommendation outcomes before and after reintroducing suspicious users. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets under ten representative attack scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TIGER. Across ten attacks, TIGER achieves average DR@5/DR@10 values of 0.4430/0.6120, 0.5550/0.7500, and 0.2670/0.3400 on ML-100K, ML-1M, and Automotive, outperforming the average results of the best baseline selected for each attack by 106.20%/28.25%, 72.36%/64.84%, and 154.29%/111.18%, respectively. These results indicate that TIGER provides a reliable auditing tool for identifying high-risk target item candidates in adversarial recommender systems. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Bridging Transparency Gaps in Construction Claims through Blockchain Integration
abstract: The construction industry plays a vital role in Pakistan's economy, yet it continues to face persistent challenges in claim administration that hinder project performance, transparency, and trust among stakeholders. This study addresses these challenges by identifying the principal shortcomings of conventional claim management systems and developing a blockchain-based claims management application to improve security, traceability, and procedural efficiency. A three-stage research design was adopted. First, a systematic literature review was conducted to identify deficiencies in traditional claim management practices. This was followed by semistructured interviews with fifteen contract specialists involved in extension of time (EOT) claims to validate and refine the identified issues. Second, a decentralized application (DApp) was developed using React.js front-end and Solidity-based smart contracts and deployed on the Polygon test network to enable faster and more cost-effective transactions. Third, the developed system was evaluated through expert review involving 32 participants drawn from contracting, consulting, client organizations, and academia, followed by statistical analysis. The findings indicate that the proposed blockchain-based claims management system (B-CMS) improves data integrity, transparency, traceability, and timeliness in claim administration compared with traditional approaches. However, the system is not intended to replace professional judgment in highly subjective claim situations and is not suitable for capturing oral instructions or unstructured design and work-pattern changes. Despite these limitations, the study demonstrates the feasibility of B-CMS for construction claim administration in Pakistan and offers insights that may be relevant to comparable project environments internationally. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: A bibliometric review of farmer livelihood resilience in Indonesia: A two-decade study
abstract: Farmer livelihood resilience is crucial given the sector's contribution to the national economic resilience, particularly in Indonesia. Despite its importance, a comprehensive synthesis of how this field has evolved over the past two decades remains limited. The objectives of this study are to provide an overview of the circumstances and challenges related to farmer resilience by examining research on farmer livelihood resilience in Indonesia. Employing a hybrid methodology that combines bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review (SLR) guided by PRISMA protocols, this research analyzed 184 articles, 94 conference papers, and 2 review papers indexed in the Scopus database from 2005 to 2025. VOSviewer software was utilized to visualize co-occurrence networks and publication patterns. The results demonstrate a substantial increase in academic interest over the last decade, with a significant peak in publications after 2015. The analysis identified five dominant thematic clusters: (1) Smallholder Farmers’ Climate Change Adaptation in Indonesia; (2) Sustainable Agriculture and Land Conversion Policy; (3) Social Capital and Collective Action for Sustainable Agriculture; (4) Livelihood Strategies of Oil Palm and Agroforestry Farmers; (5) Sustainability of Palm Oil Smallholders. This study fills a critical research gap by bridging quantitative mapping with qualitative insights, offering a strategic roadmap for future scholarly inquiry. The findings emphasize that strengthening farmer resilience in Indonesia requires integrated policy frameworks that prioritize institutional support and optimized social capital. Ultimately, these results provide vital evidence for policymakers to design more inclusive and sustainable agricultural development strategies. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate. © 2026 The Author. Published by Elsevier B.V. title: Educational legacies of christian missions: Evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
abstract: This paper investigates the educational legacies of Christian missions established before independence, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, focusing on contemporary disparities in educational content, quality, access, and outcomes. Using georeferenced data from over 20,000 schools and two million students participating in the Examen National d’État (Exetat) between 2016 and 2019, as well as primary data from a phone survey of 624 school directors, we explore how proximity to Catholic and Protestant missions during the colonial period influences educational opportunities today. We find that schools near historical Christian missions offer a broader and higher-quality curriculum, with increased access to study tracks outside the basic Pedagogy section. Students attending these schools are more likely to pass the Exetat and achieve grades qualifying for university admission, although the magnitude of the effect is modest. Observable school-environment and quality characteristics attenuate the Catholic missionary-proximity coefficient by about half, while demand-side patterns point to additional differences in student composition. Our findings reveal that the strong partnership between missions and the colonial state entrenched spatial inequalities in educational access and quality, inequalities that persist to this day. © 2026

title: LLM-driven paradigm for agent-based modeling and simulation: A review and organizing framework
abstract: Agent-based modeling and simulation (ABMS) serves as a pivotal bottom up paradigm for revealing macro level emergent behaviors through micro level interactions. Classic ABMS remains foundational to the field, while they typically necessitate manual development and labor intensive construction of agent logics. Based on a synthesis of recent advancements, this article synthesizes the literature through a lifecycle-oriented organizing framework that supports the ABMS lifecycle, including (1) a generative workflow leveraging prior knowledge for conceptual abstraction; (2) a simulation modeling framework comprising an agent decision-making architecture integrating multimodal perception, retrieval augmented generation enhanced memory, and chain of thought reasoning alongside communication design and LLM-based code generation; and (3) a simulation data analysis framework that synthesizes micro level quantitative analysis with macro level qualitative analysis. This study aims to provide a methodological perspective for the integration of LLMs into ABMS. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Audiovisual aesthetic matching enhances food evaluation by amplifying pleasure and perceived tastiness
abstract: Aesthetic experiences can shape the evaluations of consumers, including in the case of food. While matching multisensory cues can enhance perception, such interventions have not always been shown to promote consumption as effectively as predicted. The present study examined whether and how the multisensory aesthetic match of food plating and background music can enhance consumers' hedonic evaluations and purchase intentions. In two studies, participants viewed or tasted foods with varying plating aesthetics, either with music matched or mismatched in aesthetic value (e.g., ugly vs. beautiful). The participants provided food evaluations before or after tasting. The results revealed that matched audiovisual aesthetics produced enhancement effects on expected evaluations across different aesthetic levels among female participants, whereas men's ratings were enhanced only for the less-aesthetic plating. In contrast, actual evaluations were amplified only for healthy food with less-aesthetic and unhealthy food with relatively high-aesthetic plating. The multisensory enhancement of aesthetic value occurred through distinct pathways, influencing pre- and post-tasting evaluations through pleasure and perceived tastiness. These findings reveal that the mechanisms of audiovisual aesthetic matching in enhancing food consumption depend on the type of food and the gender of the participant. Aesthetic cues can be applied to nudge emotional engagement and enrich sensory experiences in daily routines, and to promote health-oriented consumption across different goal orientations (e.g., encouraging or curbing consumption). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Coastal residents’ support for marine spatial planning: The role of values, place attachment, and community impacts
abstract: Coastal environments worldwide are subject to rapid transformations, including to mitigate against climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. The potentially significant impacts of these transformations on coastal communities makes it imperative to understand their response to Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) decisions. Our research applied a value-based approach to understand how place attachment and the perceived community impacts of policy interventions influence coastal residents’ support for different MSP options that vary in emphasis between economic exploitation and nature protection. We engaged with residents around Dundalk Bay, Ireland, using a survey which presented two evidence-based MSP options (describing the status quo implying a moderate Marine Protected Area [MPA] co-existing with economic activities, versus a highly protected MPA) in randomised order. We captured participants’ personal values, economic and natural place attachment (EPA; NPA), and the perceived community impacts of each MSP option. We conducted regression analyses and a parallel-serial mediation analysis to determine each factor’s direct and indirect effects on MSP support. Most respondents preferred a shift towards stronger nature protection in the bay. Our analysis supports a multidimensional approach to place attachment and indicates that the alignment of biospheric values, NPA, and perceived community impacts is important for MSP option choice. This is less the case for EPA and its associated perceived community impacts. Overall, perceived community impacts most strongly predicted which MSP option people will support. Considering the drivers behind residents’ support for different policy options can help policymakers improve the design and communication of future MSP proposals. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Effects of China's Community Gridding on Coproduced Reporting of Rainstorm-Induced Emergencies: A Community-Wide Analysis
abstract: Presently, the involvement of citizens in emergency management is inevitable and indispensable, but how to facilitate the participation of citizens remains unclear. Utilizing panel data from 174 communities in China between 2013 and 2023, this study investigated the effects of the community gridding policy (an important policy for facilitating citizen participation in public services in China) on citizens' coproduced reporting of rainstorm-induced emergencies (e.g., small-scale debris flow, water inundation, and trapped citizens) by integrating propensity score matching (PSM) and difference-in-differences (DID) methods. Statistical results showed that the community gridding significantly enhanced both citizens' reporting engagement (represented by the number of citizen reports) and reporting quality (represented by the ratio of the reports that have been accepted by communities to the total received reports). Mediating effect analysis showed that community gridding policy enhanced citizen reporting by increasing the capability of citizen training, reporting rule completeness, and technological maturity. In addition, the effects of community gridding on enhancing citizen reporting strengthened with the increase of the community scale. Furthermore, high risk perception increased the impact of community gridding on citizen reporting. The findings contribute to both the literature on and practice of emergency service coproduction and rainstorm disaster risk reduction. Moreover, those findings provide guidance of improving citizen participation for the jurisdictions that have similar rainstorm risk situations as China. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: Too personal to be accepted? How personalization visibility drives perceived surveillance and advertising intrusiveness
abstract: A central challenge in digital advertising is that firms seek to increase relevance through personalization, yet visibly signaling the use of personal data may provoke consumer discomfort and resistance. Guided by privacy calculus theory and communication privacy management theory, this research develops and tests a model in which personalization visibility shapes perceived intrusiveness through perceived surveillance, with data sensitivity and prior brand trust as boundary conditions. Across five studies, including four controlled online experiments and one real-world field experiment using personalized watch advertisements, we examine how explicit versus implicit personalization cues affect consumers’ privacy-related responses. Study 1 shows that explicit personalized visuals, relative to implicit personalized visuals, increase perceived intrusiveness. Study 2 validates this main effect in a live platform-based advertising environment, showing that explicit personalized visuals increase self-reported intrusiveness and produce directionally consistent behavioral ad-dismissal responses under naturally occurring exposure conditions. Study 3 replicates the effect and demonstrates that perceived surveillance partially mediates it, whereas perceived ad relevance does not account for the effect. Study 4 shows that the positive effect of explicit personalization visibility on perceived intrusiveness is stronger when the advertisement is based on sensitive rather than general consumer data. Study 5 further demonstrates that prior brand trust weakens both the direct effect of explicit personalized visuals on perceived intrusiveness and the indirect effect through perceived surveillance. These findings contribute to consumer behavior theory by identifying personalization visibility as a distinct antecedent of advertising intrusiveness and by clarifying the surveillance-based process through which visible targeting cues trigger privacy-related reactions. By combining controlled experimental evidence with field-based validation, the research also strengthens the ecological validity of the personalization visibility account. Managerially, the results suggest that firms should avoid overly conspicuous personalization cues, especially when sensitive data are involved or brand trust is weak. © 2026

title: Flexible ambition: How to make bold first offers without backlash
abstract: One of the most vexing dilemmas negotiators experience is whether to make the first offer—and how ambitiously to do so. Although research finds that ambitious first offers lead to better outcomes on average, they can also incite extreme boomerang counteroffers, impasses, and resentment. We call these countervailing effects the first-offer double bind: Modest first offers produce poor economic outcomes, but ambitious first offers risk economic and relational backlash. To overcome the first-offer double bind, negotiators need to present their ambitious first offer in ways that invite conciliatory rather than competitive reactions. In this article, we introduce a generalizable solution to the first-offer double-bind: present ambitious first offers that signal flexibility. We highlight several strategies for producing flexible ambition: (a) frame ambitious proposals as offers vs. requests, (b) highlight how one's ambitious offer benefits the other side vs. oneself, (c) propose an ambitious range vs. point value, and (d) present ambitious multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs) vs. a single package offer. Each strategy preserves or strengthens the first-offer anchor, tethering counteroffers to the first offer, while guiding receivers to see ambitious offerers as less aggressive and more cooperative. We close by considering two research frontiers. First, we propose that the flexible ambition approach can mitigate other double binds more broadly, including the gender, social class, and low-power double binds; preliminary evidence suggests that MESOs work equally well for high and low power negotiators and for men and women. Second, we explore how ambitious and flexible first offers should be. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Platform abandonment through push–pull–mooring: Trust, commitment, and generational patterns in U.S. social media
abstract: Generational frameworks frequently explain platform adoption, but rarely platform abandonment. Through a stratified survey of 990 U.S. adults, this study examines how age cohorts (digital natives vs. digital immigrants) respond to platform change and what predicts abandonment across Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, and TikTok. Using the push-pull-mooring (PPM) framework, we found that cohort labels did not predict exit in pooled models. Distrust was the strongest pooled push predictor. Affective and normative commitment reduced abandonment odds, whereas need-based commitment increased them. Generation did, however, structure post-exit destinations: among Twitter/X leavers, digital natives were more likely to name Instagram and TikTok, and older cohorts were more likely to name Facebook. Abandonment is better explained by institutional distrust and multidimensional attachment than by cohort labels, but generation remains consequential for where users go next. Platforms seeking retention should repair credibility and cultivate wanted attachment rather than relying on lock-in or age targeting alone. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Talking to the screen: Influencer nonverbal cues and observed platform engagement in Douyin travel short-form videos
abstract: Short-form travel videos have become important digital service touchpoints, yet little is known about how influencers' auditory and visual nonverbal cues jointly relate to cumulative observed likes. Drawing on processing fluency and cognitive load theory, we computationally extracted acoustic and gestural features from 495 Douyin travel videos posted by 60 influencers and estimated Poisson fixed-effects models of within-creator variation. Harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR)-based acoustic signal quality exhibited a U-shaped association with observed likes, with the fitted minimum occurring at an intermediate HNR level. Faster speaking was associated with fewer likes. Illustrator gestures had no uniform main association, but their association with likes became less favorable at higher vocal pitch and faster speaking rates, with the latter pattern showing greater sensitivity across robustness checks. Highlighter gestures were more favorably associated with likes at higher vocal intensity, although this evidence was comparatively limited. Overall, audiovisual moderation was selective across cue combinations rather than uniform. These observational findings identify bounded associations between nonverbal cues and cumulative observed likes and provide empirically grounded hypotheses for controlled experiments on audio-gesture combinations. © 2026

title: Artificial intelligence in negotiation research: From computational negotiators to psychological evidence
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence are reshaping how negotiation is conducted and studied. AI systems increasingly enter negotiation research in two broad roles: as part of the negotiation process, either as negotiators or as support for human negotiators, and as research instruments that annotate, standardize, and simulate negotiation at scale. As negotiators, these systems range from theory-driven agents to data-driven and hybrid agents, each embedding different assumptions about negotiation. As instruments, they promise scale, consistency, and control, but also raise risks of circular inference, in which AI appears to reveal patterns in human negotiation while actually reproducing patterns learned from its own training data. This review organizes emerging work on AI and negotiation around these two roles and argues that their scientific value depends on psychological grounding. Used naively, AI becomes a mirror of its own assumptions. Used carefully, with grounding in theory and calibration against human evidence, AI can become a transformative tool for advancing negotiation science. © 2026 The Authors

title: The role of masculinity in understanding gender gaps in negotiation
abstract: We review empirical research on masculinity processes in negotiations. Studies to date are typically based on the precarious manhood thesis, which suggests that men seek to demonstrate their manhood to others, or on evolutionary psychology, which suggests that men are susceptible to evolutionary pressures to compete for mates. The current empirical literature on masculinity and negotiation suggests that men negotiate assertively, or even unethically, when they perceive their manhood to be threatened. Moreover, research repeatedly has shown that men's negotiation behavior is influenced by counterpart attributes, particularly the gender of the counterpart. Future research on the role of culture, the propensity to initiate negotiations as a criterion, power, and countermeasures for unethical negotiation behavior is needed. © 2026 The Authors

title: Does retirement reduce household carbon emissions in China? Evidence from fuzzy regression discontinuity design
abstract: This study examines the causal effect of household-head retirement on household carbon emissions (HCEs) in China. Combining multi-wave data from the China Family Panel Studies with household carbon accounting, we construct household-level total carbon emissions (TCEs), distinguishing between direct carbon emissions (DCEs) from household energy use and indirect carbon emissions (ICEs) embodied in the goods and services purchased by households. We estimate the local causal effect of retirement using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design based on China's statutory retirement age of 60 for urban male household heads. The results show that retirement significantly reduces TCEs by approximately 7.4–9.0 tCO₂ per household. This reduction is driven primarily by lower ICEs, while the estimated effect on DCEs is statistically insignificant. Point estimates are larger for households headed by individuals without tertiary education and for low-asset households, but formal bootstrap tests do not reject equality across education or asset groups. The mechanism results suggest that the decline in ICEs is mainly associated with a contraction in overall household consumption, particularly reductions in non-subsistence and work-related expenditure, with limited evidence of a broad shift in consumption composition. Disaggregated results further show that the emission reductions are concentrated in clothing, household facilities and services, and transportation and communication. These findings provide local causal evidence that retirement reshapes HCEs mainly through reductions in consumption-based indirect emissions rather than through changes in direct household energy use, highlighting the importance of life-course transitions for understanding demand-side emission dynamics in aging societies. © 2026

title: Disruption-induced spatial inequality in resilience loss of urban rail transit: A multi-agent simulation analysis
abstract: With the rapid expansion of urban rail transit networks in large cities, operational disruptions occur more frequently, causing varying degrees of accessibility loss and shaping station-level resilience. From the network and spatial perspective, these differences manifest as inequalities in the distribution of transport capacity. To investigate these relationships, this study proposes a scenario-based dynamic simulation analysis framework and applies it to the Beijing urban rail transit system as a case study. High-resolution passenger travel processes are first generated using multi-agent simulation. Then, within a dynamic accessibility and resilience evaluation framework, a multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) model is applied to examine accessibility, resilience, and equity under zero-load, normal operation, and disruption scenarios. The results show that variations in accessibility and resilience are highly sensitive to the location and characteristics of disruptions. Under severe disruptions, suburban corridors and key transfer segments form concentrated clusters of low resilience. MGWR analysis further reveals distinct spatial heterogeneity in the effects of structural attributes, passenger demand pressure, and spatial environmental factors, with different drivers operating at different spatial scales. Overall, this study provides quantitative evidence to inform planning, operational optimization, and equity-oriented governance of urban rail transit systems under complex disruption conditions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Balancing novelty and familiarity: Nonlinear effects of semantic progression on audience engagement
abstract: Research on information diffusion suggests that audience engagement often depends on a balance between novelty and familiarity, but it remains unclear whether narratives follow a similar principle when organizing information for audiences. To examine this possibility, this study analyses 2578 TED talks and models narrative semantic progression along three dimensions: speed, breadth, and circuitousness. The results reveal that semantic breadth and circuitousness are associated with viewership in a nonlinear manner, with moderate levels linked to higher engagement, while both low and high extremes are less effective. In contrast, semantic speed is predominantly negatively associated with viewership. The interaction between semantic speed and semantic breadth further indicates that breadth influences the level of speed at which predicted viewership reaches its maximum. These findings indicate that narratives associated with higher engagement tend to be characterized not by maximum novelty or familiarity, but by a balance between the two. Analyses of podcast data reveal broadly consistent patterns, extending the findings beyond the highly curated context of TED Talks. This study advances a nonlinear perspective on narrative effectiveness and demonstrates the value of Transformer-based embeddings, including large language model embeddings and widely used sentence embedding models, for capturing how meaning unfolds across narrative sequences. title: Nature- versus non-nature-based recreation: A comparative assessment of self-reported anxiety alleviation
abstract: Nature-based recreation delivers vital ecosystem services that shape human physical and psychological well-being, representing a core category of nature's contributions to people within urban and peri-urban social-ecological landscapes. While non-nature-based recreational activities can also improve people's quality of life by mitigating anxiety, the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based recreation to people's mental health, and the factors that influence them, remain largely unknown. Here, we conducted a survey of 15,522 respondents across China and applied structural equation modeling to show that nature-based recreation is associated with significantly stronger self-reported anxiety alleviation than non-nature-based recreation. A longer time allocation to nature-based recreational activities during holidays and weekends was also associated with greater self-reported alleviation of anxiety from nature-based recreation. Furthermore, predictors including environmental pressure, anxiety-related attributes, and socioeconomic status were associated with the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based anxiety alleviation, with these associations partly mediated via recreation engagement. This empirical evidence improves integrated landscape and urban planning frameworks by providing context-specific guidance for sustainable urban recreational space design and cross-regional governance focused on public health. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Is Europe a laggard? Comparing the EU and the US using an interdisciplinary well-being framework
abstract: Well-being is increasingly recognized as a more meaningful measure of societal progress than economic output, yet most international comparisons continue to emphasize economic indicators. This focus has reinforced the perception that Europe is lagging behind the United States, with the productivity gap shaping the European Commission’s recent competitiveness agenda. Here, we compare European and American development from 1990–2023 using an interdisciplinary well-being framework that integrates five scientific schools of thought. We find that while the US increasingly outperformed the EU on productivity and income, the EU caught up in terms of various well-being indicators, including life satisfaction and education, while increasingly outperforming the US in life expectancy and safety. Europe also exhibits more equitable well-being outcomes and achieves them at lower environmental cost. However, in both regions, the conditions underpinning future well-being are under increasing pressure. These results challenge the dominance of economic metrics in evaluating progress and emphasize the need for inclusive development strategies that place sustainable well-being at their core. © 2026 The Authors. title: Women Empowerment and Environmental Sustainability in Africa: The Critical Roles of Electronic Government Services
abstract: Recent literature acknowledges the significance of women’s empowerment in the global agenda for environmental sustainability. While the role of information and communication technology has been acknowledged, only a few studies have examined the relevance and peculiarities of electronic government (e-government) in combating environmental degradation in developing economies. In addition, the role of e-government in the women empowerment-environmental sustainability nexus has not been explored. This study examines the role of electronic government (e-government) in the relationship between women’s empowerment and a sustainable environment across a panel of 31 African countries from 2003 to 2022. Environmental sustainability is proxied by ecological footprint, while women’s empowerment is proxied by women’s political empowerment and the female labour participation rate. The results, based on the system generalised method of moments, pooled ordinary least squares based on Driscoll and Kraay, and panel quantile regression via moments, show that women’s empowerment reduces ecological footprints, while e-government strengthens and complements women’s empowerment to sustain environmental quality in Africa. This result underscores the significance of women’s empowerment in protecting the environment. Hence, policies to enhance the empowerment and participation of women in all spheres of life should be vigorously pursued in the region, while e-government applications serve as an important policy instrument to transition to a safer and more conducive environment. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Forecasting Approaches to Pharmaceutical Supply Management Across Healthcare Settings: A Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Drug shortages remain a persistent global issue affecting essential medicines across healthcare settings. In healthcare settings, inadequate pharmaceutical forecasting and inventory management may lead to suboptimal medicine availability, treatment disruption, and patient harm. Despite advances in automated inventory systems, forecasting practices remain fragmented across healthcare contexts with varying demand conditions and implementation requirements. Objectives: This scoping review aimed to map forecasting methods used in pharmaceutical supply management and examine their application across operational contexts. Methods: Studies reporting forecasting or prediction models in pharmaceutical healthcare settings were included. Studies unrelated to pharmaceutical forecasting, non-healthcare logistics, qualitative designs, editorials, and inaccessible full texts were excluded. Searches were conducted in Ovid MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. Extracted data on forecasting methods, implementation contexts, and operational outcomes were synthesised narratively. A proposed conceptual framework integrating forecasting approaches and contextual triggers was developed through interpretive synthesis. Results: Twenty-four studies (2007–2026) were included, representing 13 identified countries. Four forecasting approaches were identified: rule-based, traditional/statistical, machine learning/artificial intelligence (ML/AI), and hybrid approaches. Traditional/statistical methods were most frequently reported (n = 8), followed by ML/AI approaches (n = 7), hybrid approaches (n = 5), and rule-based approaches (n = 4). Forecasting approaches were reported across operational contexts with differing demand patterns, data availability, and implementation requirements. Conclusions: ML/AI and hybrid approaches were also reported in studies involving uncertainty and demand variability. However, comparative superiority cannot be established, and the proposed conceptual framework remains an interpretive evidence synthesis structure requiring empirical validation. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

title: Staff interactions and individual influences on complaint behaviour in restaurants
abstract: This study examines the influence of early staff interactions and individual characteristics on customer complaint behaviour during restaurant dining. A two-stage mixed-methods design was employed: Study 1 surveyed 790 diners, measuring sociodemographic and personality variables alongside self-reported propensity to complain. Study 2 applied these findings in a longitudinal design tracking 98 customers across 994 restaurant visits over one year, capturing individual and situational factors, including staff interactions. Drawing on voice/exit theory and cognitive appraisal frameworks, findings identify redress orientation as a consistent predictor of complaint propensity, whilst empathy reduces both the likelihood of perceived dissatisfaction and willingness to raise issues verbally. Early staff interactions, particularly making customers feel special upon arrival, significantly reduced complaint propensity, as did service quality and friendliness. These findings contribute to the understanding of the individual and situational determinants of complaint behaviour in the UK hospitality industry. © 2026

title: Towards ethical, co-produced and justice-oriented research with small-scale fishing communities: a multi-scalar call to action
abstract: Small-scale fisheries underpin food security, livelihoods and cultural identity for hundreds of millions of people worldwide, yet remain marginalised within dominant ocean governance and research agendas. Recent shifts toward justice-, equity- and rights-based approaches in ocean governance and policy signal important progress, but their rapid uptake risks remaining largely rhetorical if not grounded in meaningful changes to research practice. This paper draws on the experiential knowledge of researchers working across diverse geographical and institutional contexts to critically examine the structural conditions that shape research with small-scale fishing communities. We identify seven tensions that are recurring and cross-cutting within funding architectures, institutional incentive systems, and global policy agendas that constrain the ability of researchers to conduct ethical, co-produced and justice-oriented work. These include misalignments between global priorities and local realities, knowledge hierarchies, rigid funding models, and academic metrics that undervalue relational and collaborative processes. In response, we propose six principles to enable and guide more equitable research practices with small-scale fishing communities. We emphasise the need for the recognition of diverse knowledge systems and creative outputs, institutional reforms that value long-term partnerships and local impact, and strengthened training in reflexive and ethical research approaches. Framed as a multi-scalar call to action, this paper highlights the shared responsibilities of research funders, academic institutions, policy agencies, NGOs, and researchers in reshaping the systems that govern knowledge production that inform ocean governance. Advancing ocean sustainability requires not only new ideas but structural transformation to ensure that research with small-scale fishing communities is inclusive, accountable and just. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Urban forest cooling efficiency and heat exposure inequity under extreme heat: Evidence from 550 global cities
abstract: Extreme heat has become a key factor affecting urban residents’ quality of life, existing studies on urban forest have focused on their average cooling effects, overlooking whether and how variations in cooling efficiency affect heat exposure inequity. To address these gaps, this study selected 550 cities worldwide with a main urban area exceeding 100 km2 to analyze the relationship between urban forest cooling efficiency and heat exposure inequity over the past 24 years. We found that although tree coverage increased in most cities, the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) deteriorated in nearly half of them, revealing a polarizing pattern: “High coverage turning green, low coverage turning brown.” Notably, tree coverage and EVI were particularly fragile in tropical climates and low Human Development Index (HDI) cities. We found that each 1 % increase in tree coverage reduces the average land surface temperature during extreme heat by 0.31 °C. However, this cooling efficiency is distributed extremely unevenly. The study utilized the population-weighted temperature Gini coefficient to represent the inequity of urban heat exposure. About 25.2 % of cities experienced increased heat exposure inequity, particularly in developed cities, as increasing tree coverage unintentionally exacerbated spatial inequity. At the same time, about 5.6 % of cities even exhibit a forest warming effect, especially in the desert climate zones and low HDI areas. About 66 % of the cities showed that as the cooling efficiency of urban forest increased, there was a corresponding increase in heat exposure equity. The study proposed the concept of the equity potential index and compared the possibility of achieving equity potential for the cooling efficiency of urban forest under the three scenarios: SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP3-7.0. The study showed that SSP1-2.6 is more favorable for temperate climate zones and low-HDI cities, whereas SSP2-4.5 is more beneficial for tropical, continental climates, and very high HDI cities. This study provides a scientific, equity-oriented framework for designing place-specific urban forest strategies that enhance thermal resilience and social sustainability. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Quantifying the prestige of scientific awards: A network-bibliometric framework
abstract: Scientific awards play a central role in recognizing excellence and shaping research trajectories, funding priorities, and disciplinary visibility. Yet despite their importance, scalable and reproducible quantitative frameworks for assessing award prestige remain limited, with prior efforts relying largely on small-scale or perception-based evaluations. This study introduces a data-driven framework for quantifying the prestige of scientific awards by integrating network centrality measures derived from inter-award linkages with bibliometric indicators of prize-winners’ research profiles. Using a dataset of 1352 research-related award records across seven disciplines, we treat award prestige as a latent construct approximated by two external reference dimensions: public attention (crowd-sourced engagement) and professional reputation (expert survey responses). Across three complementary modeling approaches and repeated cross-validation, the framework recovers rankings that are broadly consistent with conventional perceptions of scientific prestige, with awards such as the Nobel Prize, Abel Prize, and Turing Award consistently appearing near the top across external reference dimensions. Among the examined features, network prominence, as measured by eigenvector centrality, emerges as the most consistently important signal, followed by recent bibliometric activity and authorship leadership. The proposed framework offers a scalable and transparent approach to quantifying scientific recognition, providing empirical insights into the structure of academic prestige and informing future evaluations of emerging or underrecognized awards. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Designing the future of consciousness: A components framework and speculative implications
abstract: As technologies increasingly converge with users’ psychophysiology and mental states, perception and mind-altering are emerging as plausibly designable components of user experience. This gives rise to emergent phenomena of digitally induced altered states of consciousness (DIAL) that find application not only in therapeutic and mental health contexts but also in communication and leisure. Modern consciousness-altering technologies primarily exist as early prototypes, and their empirical research tends to constrain the context of use to instrumental functionality. Fictional narrative analysis proposes to push these limitations by considering concepts of technology in imaginary contexts, thereby examining the experiences, social rituals, and ethical issues associated with their use far beyond traditional technical scenarios. This article employs a reflexive thematic analysis of popular science fiction narratives to expand our understanding of how ASCs are integrated into HCI, considering broader sociocultural and sociotechnical contexts. As a result, we identify key aspects of interaction (purpose and context) and combine their subcategories into a framework that facilitates rethinking traditional HCI, revealing potentials that remain inaccessible within clear consciousness. This framework was used to construct five themes, highlighting that the benefits of mitigating cognitive load and deepening technology-mediated communication with DIAL might entail sacrificing identity and autonomy and increasing the pressures of the modern, overcompetitive, hyper-individualistic lifestyle. Thus, the article contributes to the HCI agenda by expanding existing paradigms of interaction with mind-altering technologies and by demonstrating the use of science fiction as a powerful avenue for exploring the design space and critical inquiries about these types of interactions. © 2026 The Author(s). title: The long-term effects of teachers’ gender stereotypes on labor outcomes
abstract: This paper links a teacher-level measure of gender-stereotyped grading — validated against their Implicit Association Test (IAT) scores — to the later schooling and labor-market outcomes of 1.6 million Peruvian students. Exposure to a more stereotyped teacher widens the gender gaps in high-school completion, formal-sector employment, and earnings, driven by boys’ lasting gains rather than by girls’ smaller, short-lived losses. A single year with a math teacher one standard deviation more stereotyped than average raises boys’ on-time graduation by 0.9 percentage points and lowers girls’ by 0.6. Over the five years after high school (ages 17–22), it raises boys’ formal employment by 4%–12% of the mean employment rate and widens the gender pay gap by about 11% in the first two years, while girls’ losses fade thereafter. These effects run through high-school completion, not test scores or college enrollment. The widening gap in male-dominated industries mainly reflects men's entry rather than women's exit, and students show little sign of adopting the stereotypes themselves. Where structural barriers already constrain access to higher education, teachers’ stereotypes shape who finishes school and their early labor-market outcomes, rather than who reaches college. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Bibliometric study of environmental education: Scientific architecture and the transition toward micro-educational and behavioral approaches
abstract: Although scientific production in environmental education has grown steadily, fragmented approaches and limited interdisciplinary integration persist. Moreover, the transition from macronormative frameworks to microeducational approaches oriented toward behavioral change remains insufficiently characterized. The objective of this study was to comprehensively analyze the scientific architecture of environmental education, identifying its structural evolution, key actors, predominant sources, funding dynamics, thematic trends, and scientific production cycle, with particular attention to the shift toward microeducational and behavioral approaches. The study followed a rigorous and consolidated four-stage bibliometric method. A total of 4,952 documents indexed in Scopus were analyzed using the Bibliometrix software, examining six main indicators: (1) authors, (2) sponsors, (3) thematic evolution and conceptual structure, (4) sources, (5) documents, and (6) scientific production. The findings reveal sustained expansion in environmental education, with a productivity peak in 2025 and a projected stabilization toward 2032, confirming its advanced consolidation phase. An editorial structure concentrated in historical core journals—Environmental Education Research and Journal of Environmental Education—was identified, alongside growing interdisciplinary expansion toward sustainability, higher education, and technological innovation. Scientific leadership is concentrated in the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom, although emerging economies such as Brazil and China are gaining prominence. Thematically, macrostructural cores linked to sustainability and sustainable development persist; however, microeducational approaches such as pro-environmental behavior, outdoor environmental education, and environmental knowledge are emerging more strongly, indicating a shift toward the analysis of situated learning processes and behavioral change. Bibliometric findings were contrasted with evidence from other bibliometric studies and systematic reviews. It is concluded that environmental education has evolved from a paradigm centered on global normative frameworks toward a multidimensional model integrating experience, behavior, technological innovation, and community action. The study provides insights for educational policy and teaching practice. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: A survey on fake review detection: From pre-trained language models to large language models
abstract: Online reviews shape consumer decisions, platform governance, and corporate reputation. Fake reviews compromise this information channel by injecting deceptive evidence into rating systems, recommendation pipelines, and public trust mechanisms. The rise of large language models, or LLMs, has changed the problem in two directions. LLMs can generate fluent and context-aware deceptive reviews, while pre-trained language models, or PLMs, and LLMs also provide stronger semantic representations for detection. This survey reviews fake review detection from an information fusion perspective, covering 211 studies published from 2018 to early 2026. We organize existing work by evidence source and fusion level, covering review text, sentiment, rating behavior, temporal metadata, user-product graphs, multimodal content, external knowledge, and LLM-generated signals. We trace the development from traditional machine learning and deep learning to PLM-based and LLM-based methods, and examine how different approaches combine textual, behavioral, structural, and multimodal evidence. We also analyze reported performance trends on widely used Amazon, Yelp, and OpSpam benchmark families, while noting the limitations caused by different label construction procedures, data splits, and evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems in adversarial generation, cross-domain transfer, uncertainty-aware fusion, missing-source robustness, interpretability, and trustworthy evaluation for AI-generated deceptive content. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: A survey of information retrieval and recommender systems in the era of large language models: Two sides of the same task
abstract: The fields of information retrieval and recommender systems have long evolved as distinct disciplines, each with its own methodologies and theoretical foundations. This survey provides a perspective on the convergence of these fields, a transformation catalyzed by the advent of large language models. We maintain that this convergence is far from a trivial overlap of tools, but it embodies a substantial conceptual and architectural unification. Our central contribution is a novel three-part taxonomy that explains the mechanisms of this merger leveraging large language models as (1) an embedded engine, (2) a semantic re-ranker, and (3) a response generator. We show how this trajectory culminates in a paradigm inversion, from weak to strong inversion, where the information-seeking task itself is reshaped. The unification is structurally consolidated through joint search and recommendation architectures and contextually curated by retrieval-augmented generation frameworks. This hypothesis is substantiated by a rigorous, quantitative analysis of scholarly publication trends, which provides empirical evidence of this rapid evolution. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a convergence operating at different velocities dictated by domain-specific latency constraints, while acknowledging critical operational vulnerabilities regarding hallucination and bias. A companion GitHub repository is publicly available and offers the complete data collection methodology, dynamic trend analyses, and a comprehensive, categorized list of the surveyed papers, which will be actively maintained as a living resource for the research community. We conclude that the distinction between retrieval and recommendation is becoming a historical artifact and call for the formal recognition of a new, integrated science of information discovery. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Suppressed inquiry: The hidden toll of working with satisfaction-optimized AI
abstract: LLMs have become thinking companions for hundreds of millions worldwide, and they often do remarkable work. But their satisfaction-optimized design produces suppressed inquiry: the tendency for LLMs to inhibit rather than facilitate users' questioning process. LLMs appear fluent, confident, and seemingly all-knowing, their near-instant and polished output making non-LLM work feel unacceptably tedious and less eloquent. They affirm rather than interrogate users' assumptions, producing output that is deceptively adequate—shallower, less original, and less carefully reasoned than it appears. Seemingly competent systems also reduce vigilance and the monitoring impulse that independent judgment requires. Their responses also confine users within the frame they establish, narrowing what users think to ask. These costs are self-concealing: detecting them requires the very engagement that they suppress. And repeated delegation gradually atrophies users' capacity to reason independently. Three converging pressures make correction difficult: commercial incentives that reward satisfaction over substance, LLMs’ tendency to revert to satisfaction-optimized defaults even when users push back, and a societal drift toward less-effortful engagement. We propose a research agenda to deepen the understanding of suppressed inquiry and how to counter it, to move closer to the remarkable thinking partners LLMs promised to be. © 2026 The Authors
