title: Artificial intelligence systems distort upstream selection in human social learning
abstract: Humans are social learners who depend on observing others to acquire knowledge, norms, and behaviors, a capacity that underlies cumulative cultural evolution. Social learning unfolds in two stages: upstream selection determines what information becomes visible, and downstream selection determines what learners copy from that visible sample. Downstream selection occurs through biases such as conformity bias (copying what appears common) and prestige bias (copying those who appear highly respected). These downstream biases can be adaptive when upstream selection yields a sample that reflects the population's true distribution, so that what appears common is actually common and those who appear respected are actually competent. We argue that digital technologies disrupt this condition, creating an upstream selection problem. Engagement-based algorithms amplify the tails of the distribution, surfacing rare and extreme content, whereas generative AI collapses it toward the mode (of the population or the user), erasing the surrounding diversity. Crucially, in each system the optimization signal shapes both visibility and prestige. For engagement-based algorithms, the signal is engagement: creators who post extreme content become more visible and, through the likes, shares, and followers, appear more prestigious. For generative AI, the signal is statistical typicality: it makes a modal answer dominant and, with no alternatives shown, makes the model that produced it appear more prestigious. These distortions can give rise to emergent group-level phenomena, including pluralistic ignorance and illusory consensus. Synthesizing evidence across psychology, cultural evolution, and computational social science, we provide a framework for how digital technologies disrupt social learning and outline interventions for restoring functional cultural transmission. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: More alike than unalike: Contextually aligned authority arguments amplify sustainable choices across cultures
abstract: Most research is conducted in Western societies, with few studies from Latin America. This oversight has led to a narrow understanding of the effectiveness that various sustainability-oriented interventions have in countries with different cultural values. As consumers play a vital role in mitigating climate change issues, this behavioral field experiment investigates whether reliance on the authority and commitment-consistency principles from social influence increases individuals' inclination to choose sustainably, and whether the effectiveness of these principles is culturally contingent. Participants from Ecuador and Norway (N = 346) were randomized to one of three conditions (control vs. authority vs. commitment-consistency), with the latter two conditions containing a message tailored to its associated social influence principle. After replying to some survey items, participants made a choice between a more (vs. less) sustainable option. A chi-square test revealed that both social influence conditions jointly boosted choice likelihood of the more sustainable option relative to the control condition, supporting our initial preregistered hypothesis. However, contrary to our second preregistered hypothesis, a regression-based simple moderation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 1) showed no country moderation in the effectiveness of these social influence principles; instead, the results were largely attributable to the authority condition alone, which was considerably more effective than both other conditions across countries, regardless of participants' trust in authorities and their need for consistency. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of contextually aligned authority arguments as a viable way to foster pro-environmental behaviors. © 2026 The Authors

title: Trustworthy artificial intelligence in advanced manufacturing
abstract: Additive manufacturing is relying more and more on artificial intelligence for prediction, control, and real-time decisions. Deployment, however, is still difficult. The main reason is that the underlying thermal, flow, and microstructural behavior can shift as the process changes, which makes reliable model performance hard to maintain. This review examines how trustworthy artificial intelligence (TAI) can be used to close that gap in digital twins for additive manufacturing across both metallic and ceramic systems. It frames trustworthiness as a technical condition for deployment and translates it into an AM-specific operational framework. From that point onward, it examines how current workflows handle reliability, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, explainability, robustness, generalizability, fairness, and transparency. A structured evaluation of sixty studies in metallic and ceramic additive manufacturing systems reveals a distinct trend. Robustness and generalizability receive much more attention than transparency, explainability, and fairness. The coverage is also stronger in metallic systems than in ceramic ones. To move beyond binary classification, the review further applies a structured evidence-depth rubric that distinguishes absent coverage, limited or implicit evidence, method-level evidence, and operational evidence for each TAI attribute. We further show that trustworthy deployment depends on more than predictive accuracy. It also depends on physically consistent models as well as updates that account for uncertainty. Decision support has to remain interpretable as well. Model transfer across machines and materials should be treated as controlled adaptation, where reusable physics, sensing, and validation elements are separated from material-specific features that require recalibration. The validation path must also support qualification and industrial deployment, leading to a more cohesive digital twin framework. It brings together physics-based models, reduced-order models, learning-based surrogates, multimodal sensing, and trust-aware evaluation. The main finding is that trustworthiness is the missing technical link between digital twins that can be confidently used in advanced manufacturing and promising AI-enabled demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors

title: Evolution and lifecycle mapping of research methods based on the Boston Matrix in library and information science from 1995 to 2025
abstract: Developing an evolution framework for research methods is essential for advancing Library and Information Science (LIS), but existing research method schemas remain fragmented and limited. This study proposes an automated framework combining AI-driven methods to mine, classify, and a temporal analysis based on the Boston Matrix to map the lifecycles of research methods. Using a comprehensive dataset of 31,913 articles from 21 LIS journals (1995–2025) as a validation corpus, the framework integrates semantic clustering for bottom-up entity extraction with generative top-down ontology mapping. This approach dynamically maps methods into a four-stage lifecycle schema: mainstream, emerging, marginalized, and mature, revealing distinct evolutionary trajectories and the broader computational turn within LIS. Validated through quantitative threshold testing and qualitative evaluation, the proposed framework significantly reduces manual coding subjectivity and enhances replicability. By empirically comparing the subfields of librarianship and information science, this study accounts for inherent thematic variations and uncovers their distinct paces of methodological adoption. Ultimately, this study offers a robust automated framework for longitudinal methodological tracking, theoretically demonstrating how diverse AI-driven and traditional methods synergistically coevolve and assume distinct scholarly roles within the emerging AI4Science paradigm. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: The security unlock: How rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial?
abstract: Previous literature on the determinants of entrepreneurship has not explored the role of social pension. Leveraging variation in the roll-out timing of a universal rural pension program across Chinese counties, our analysis, at both the individual and aggregate levels, reveals that pension provision led to an increase in entrepreneurship among the younger generation. We show that this effect operates through two primary channels: an intergenerational transfer channel and a local demand channel. Specifically, the pension program mitigates upward transfers from adult children to elderly parents, while boosting local consumer demand, which exerts a demand-side “pull” effect on enterprise establishment. Our findings may shed new light on the interplay between pension, intergenerational resource allocation, and entrepreneurial activity. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Algorithmic fairness as a human–technology interaction problem
abstract: Algorithms shape high-stakes decisions across society. While promising efficiency, algorithms also raise fairness concerns. This article proposes that algorithmic fairness is best understood as a human–technology interaction problem rather than a purely technical challenge. Algorithms can reproduce human biases, amplify them through feedback loops, or create new forms of unfairness through objectives, proxies, and seemingly neutral variables. Yet they can make decision processes more explicit, disparities more visible, and actively mitigate discrimination. Fairness depends not only on statistical properties but also on how algorithms are designed, used and experienced by those affected by their decisions. This article therefore offers an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates insights from social justice, psychology, computer science, judgment and decision-making, and management. © 2026 The Author

title: From smart cities to smart villages: Evolution, domains, and policy implications for smart rural development
abstract: Smart villages have evolved from early parallels with urban smart city models into a comprehensive, multidimensional framework that integrates digital infrastructure, agriculture, local enterprises, tourism, and sustainability. This expanded framework recognizes the unique characteristics and potentials of rural areas, moving beyond the urban-centric logic of technology adoption. This review aims to examine the conceptual evolution of smart village research, track emerging methodological trends, and analyze global implementation trajectories. In the early stages, many studies concentrated on definitional debates and approaches that were primarily centered on technology. However, more recent perspectives have begun to emphasize the importance of integrating technological innovation with social innovation, community empowerment, participatory governance, and environmental stewardship. Methodological approaches have also advanced significantly, shifting from conceptual reflections and single-case studies toward more diverse methods including comparative studies, bibliometric mapping, and participatory action research. These evolving methods enable a deeper and more nuanced understanding of smart village dynamics. Regional approaches demonstrate distinct emphases: European initiatives focus on service revitalization and smart specialization; Asian and African strategies prioritize connectivity, renewable energy access, and digital inclusion; while Latin American programs increasingly integrate climate-smart agricultural practices. Despite regional differences, common challenges remain, including the persistent rural digital divide, fragmented coordination among multiple stakeholders, issues of financial sustainability, and the emergence of new forms of inequality. Policy directions increasingly stress the importance of place-based strategies, building local capacities, establishing supportive governance structures, and fostering inclusive participation. The review concludes by identifying critical areas for future research, such as the creation of unified evaluation metrics, conducting longitudinal impact assessments, and embedding smart village initiatives within broader rural development and climate resilience agendas. Overall, smart villages represent dynamic and promising pathways for driving innovation-led, inclusive, and sustainable rural transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: From design attributes to social life: Modelling conviviality in urban underground spaces
abstract: From being infrastructure utilities, urban underground spaces (UUS) have developed into multipurpose public spaces that combine commercial, cultural, and transit functions. While their technical and spatial contributions to compact urbanism are evident, their capacity to foster conviviality, the experiential quality of inclusiveness, sociability, and shared belonging, is less understood. This study develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework that operationalizes conviviality in UUS by linking seven spatial-perceptual dimensions (safety and security, identity and meaning, accessibility, functionality, environmental comfort, aesthetics, and structure and form) to behavioral mediators of willingness to use and social interaction, culminating in perceived conviviality. Using the Theatre-Shahr underground complex in Tehran as a case study, data were collected through structured surveys and analyzed via Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that although environmental factors generally have a positive indirect effect on perceived conviviality, social interaction emerges as the primary mechanism shaping conviviality in urban underground spaces, while willingness to use plays only a complementary and limited mediating role in this process. Among the environmental factors, accessibility, environmental comfort, and safety and security show the strongest effects. In contrast, some variables, particularly identity and meaning and structure and form, do not demonstrate statistically significant effects in certain pathways. These findings suggest that planning and design strategies for urban underground spaces should prioritize environmental qualities that support social interaction, to enhance perceived conviviality. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Facilitator or hallucination trap? A social-cognitive account of AI-generated misinformation handling in GenAI-assisted L2 writing
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has demonstrated remarkable potential in second language (L2) learning, yet it is prone to hallucinations. Empirical research on how GenAI-generated misinformation is handled in educational contexts remains scarce. Accordingly, little is known about how these practices shape learning processes and outcomes. Guided by social cognitive theory, the current study frames students' GenAI-assisted L2 writing (using a tailored GenAI writing agent) in a hallucination-prone context in which misinformation was implanted. We examine AI literacy, higher-order thinking resources (i.e., critical thinking and creativity), L2 writing resources (i.e., L2 writing grit and self-regulatory writing strategies), English writing self-efficacy (EWSE), AI-generated misinformation detection (AI-MD), and L2 writing performance within this framework. Using a multi-method approach, combining a qualitative interview study (N = 35), two lab experiments (N = 140), and a large-scale questionnaire survey (N = 406), we find that critical thinking positively predicts GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance via AI-MD, and that negative priming on AI hallucinations significantly improves students’ AI-MD and their GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance, relative to neutral or positive priming. Furthermore, the cross-sectional survey focuses on personal factors and shows that AI literacy significantly predicts EWSE both directly and indirectly through a cognitive–generative pathway involving higher-order thinking resources and a motivational–regulatory pathway involving L2 writing resources. These findings extend social-cognitive accounts of GenAI-assisted L2 writing and inform instruction that helps learners evaluate AI outputs, manage misinformation risks, and sustain their own writing processes. © 2026

title: Self-disclosure to intelligent virtual agents: A scoping review and the disclosure affordance–actualization–governance framework
abstract: Intelligent virtual agents (IVAs) have become digital social objects to which people disclose personal, emotional, health-related, and other sensitive information. Yet similar cues—including anthropomorphism, social presence, empathy, gaze, anonymity, and structured questioning—are associated across studies with greater disclosure, refusal, impression management, socially desirable responding, or discomfort. Searches covered four bibliographic databases without publication-year restrictions through March 17, 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar searching on May 20, 2026. This review, reported with reference to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), maps 88 empirical studies and introduces the Disclosure Affordance–Actualization–Governance (DAAG) framework as a middle-range account linking specific empirical findings with broader explanations of IVA-mediated disclosure. DAAG distinguishes sociotechnical interaction ecology; perceived safety from judgment, relational receptivity, expressive latitude, and boundary agency; disclosure actualization; affective, relational, and functional consequences; governance; and evidential reach—the extent to which studies observe perception, behavior, consequences, time, and governance. The literature is most developed for disclosure onset, sensitive reporting, emotional expression, and immediate system acceptance, but remains thin on persistence, reciprocity, subjective–behavioral divergence, correction, revocation, and downstream data use. Recurrent patterns are consistent with IVA cues being interpreted through evaluation risk, partner responsiveness, observability, topic sensitivity, competence, privacy, and control. DAAG is not presented as a validated causal model, but as a framework for explaining when digital social interaction supports, redirects, or appropriately constrains self-disclosure. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Autonomy-supportive mediation and scam susceptibility: The role of literacy among middle-aged and older adults
abstract: Although online scams increasingly threaten middle-aged and older adults, existing research has largely focused on individual literacy and short-term interventions, leaving the development and application of scam literacy in everyday contexts less understood. Drawing on parental mediation theory and self-determination theory, this study conceptualizes autonomy-supportive mediation (ASM) as a family-based socialization context for developing aging parents' scam-related literacy. It also considers face concern, a personal orientation reflecting individuals’ motivation to protect their social image from potential social judgment. This study tested two complementary models that distinguish between the foundation of scam literacy (scam knowledge) and its activation (cyber-risk beliefs). Data were collected through a cross-sectional vignette-based survey of 404 middle-aged and older adults in China between February 13 and February 27, 2025, using a volunteer-assisted convenience sampling strategy. The results indicated that higher levels of ASM were linked to lower scam loss, with this association mediated by scam knowledge and moderated by face concern. Moreover, ASM was positively related to cyber-risk beliefs, which were subsequently linked to greater systematic information processing and suspicion toward potential scams. These findings suggest that effective scam prevention depends not only on what individuals know, but also on whether they recognize and respond to risks in real-world situations. This study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive family communication in combating online scams. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Management: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
abstract: This study presents an examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in the disaster management (DM) cycle to support human decision-making systems. There is an urgent need for holistic application strategies that support disaster risk reduction given the increasing frequency and severity of disaster events. This stems from the growing adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and natural language processing in transforming disaster management. This is to enable the development of high-performance tools for assessing disaster impacts and addressing un-met human needs. This study reviewed journals and conference proceedings articles from three different academic databases: Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Article selection and query refinement were conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to support methodological approach. The review explored scholarly perspectives on AI application in DM phases to support human-centered decision-making processes in reducing disaster impacts on human lives. Findings from the review indicate that most existing studies focus primarily on the AI application in the response phase. Despite its potential, integrating AI into disaster management remains challenging, particularly due to widespread misconceptions about adoption of AI, as well as ongoing ethical, trust, and security concerns. This study emphasizes the comprehensive application of AI to enhance planning, encourage proactive measures, and improve response and recovery efforts during disaster events. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: “The Right to Repair”: A systematic literature review and research agenda for an emerging interdisciplinary field
abstract: The Right to Repair (R2R) is an important arena in which restrictive repair practices, including limits on access to spare parts, manuals, software, and specialised tools, as well as product designs that inhibit repair, are being contested. Although scholarly interest in R2R is growing rapidly, research remains fragmented across disciplinary and empirical domains, limiting the development of a coherent understanding of its implications for technology-society relations. In response, this paper presents a systematic literature review that maps and synthesises existing research on R2R. Specifically, it (1) consolidates empirical evidence on the implications of R2R; (2) examines how the concept has been theorised across disciplines; and (3) identifies key conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. By organising this literature into coherent thematic domains and tracing the relationships between them, the review argues that the effective realisation of R2R depends on a socio-technical capacity: the practically exercisable ability to repair produced through the interaction between legal entitlements, technological architectures, economic arrangements, and social capabilities. It also reveals disciplinary and geographical imbalances and identifies four tensions structuring future research: formal ownership versus effective control, legal entitlement versus practical repair capacity, universal frameworks versus situated repair practices, and systemic transformation versus continuity. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Dependent development at the energy transition: placing lithium imaginaries in Neoliberal and Contentious Peru
abstract: We examine lithium and development imaginaries in mining-dependent Peru, asking: What are these imaginaries? What narratives underpin them? Who articulates and shares them, and from where? What forms of state (in)action are envisioned in relation to them? The case study elucidates how alternative “imagined futures” coexist within a natural resource–dependent economy. The ruling national elites in Lima have a neoliberal imagination, treating lithium like any other mineral resource in the country. In contrast, professional elites in the mineral-rich but peripheral region of Puno adopt a resource nationalist view, advocating for direct state involvement in lithium industrialization and the transformation of the domestic energy system, shaped by beliefs on Bolivia's developmental pathway. Among rural community leaders as well as political and social leaders in the districts near lithium and uranium deposits, however, the prevailing idea is that of a social license. In this view, each community has the capacity to negotiate development terms with mining companies independently. In the broader imagination at the resource periphery of a peripheral national economy, the state is perceived primarily as a minimalist governmental actor, necessary only to oversee and ensure the enforcement of mine-community agreements and to provide basic infrastructure. Thus, elites at the political center and communities near expected resource developments converge in their immediate pursuit of rents promised by resource commodification. In the dominant discourses, environmental concerns are often subordinated to economic development goals. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Online direct-to-consumer channel introducing and ordering strategies of fresh supply chain considering disruption risks and yield constraints
abstract: The rise of online direct-to-consumer (DTC) channels expands fresh producers’ distribution networks while intensifying competition with traditional retail channels. Meteorological disasters threaten the DTC channel's reliability, dynamically reshaping the coopetition between fresh producers and retailers. This study develops a theoretical framework to examine strategic interactions within a fresh supply chain, comparing a traditional monopoly model with an integrated distribution system that incorporates both DTC and traditional retail channels. Disruption risks and yield constraints faced by producers are considered. The findings suggest producers should introduce DTC channels during yield contraction but exercise caution in surplus periods. Despite disruption risks, DTC channels pressure retailers to accept higher wholesale prices and increase orders, enhancing the sales revenue of fresh produce with limited yield. However, rising disruption probabilities incentivize retailers to reduce order quantities strategically, leading to a higher risk of stagnation for fresh produce. © 2026 International Federation of Operational Research Societies.

title: Events under fire: Developing an urgent anthropology for events during armed conflicts
abstract: This conceptual and methodological research note addresses event industry dynamics during armed conflicts, proposing an urgent anthropology approach to document transformations in real time. Using Ukraine as an example, we illustrate how event organizations have adapted to existential threats since the 2022 Russian invasion, demonstrating resilience through cultural initiatives, charitable events, and creative repurposing of resources. We argue that these practices have the potential to sustain cultural identity and to contribute to economic development, social cohesion and morale in conflict settings. To overcome the methodological and ethical challenges of traditional ethnography in war zones, we propose a novel citizen science framework within the urgent anthropology paradigm, leveraging digital technologies, social media, and participatory methods. This approach can decentralize knowledge production, mitigate researcher risk, and create longitudinal archives of industry adaptations. Our proposal supports SDG 16 by suggesting ways to link events and tourism research to peace, justice, and institutional resilience. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Carbon trading in community-based forest management: A bibliometric mapping of scientific publications from 2000 to 2025
abstract: Carbon trading in community-based forest management (CBFM) has emerged as a promising mechanism for simultaneously addressing climate change mitigation and improving the welfare of rural communities. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 203 scientific publications obtained from Scopus, covering the period 2000 to 2025, with an analytical focus on the period 2010-2024. Using VOSviewer v.1.6.20 and Scopus's built-in analysis, this study analyzes publication trends, author participation patterns, geographic distribution, journal sources, and thematic structure through author collaboration, co-occurrence of keywords, and bibliographic linking networks. Results show a sharp acceleration in publication growth following key climate policy milestones, including the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (2013), the Paris Agreement (2015), and COP26 (2021), with a record 21 articles published in 2024. Nepal and Indonesia emerged as dominant knowledge producers, collectively contributing 42.4% of total publications. Thematic mapping identified three main research clusters: carbon governance in CBFM, carbon measurement and quantification, and multifunctional forest landscape ecology. A critical knowledge gap was identified: while the supply side of carbon measurement of forest carbon stocks and biomass has been well documented, the demand side of how communities access, negotiate, and fairly obtain benefits from carbon markets remains largely unexplored. These findings underscore the urgent need for interdisciplinary research that links technical carbon measurement with institutional, economic, and social dimensions of equity to promote fair and scalable carbon trading within the framework of community forest governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Does artificial intelligence improve social stability risk performance in China?
abstract: This paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to improving the social stability risk level in China. Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation and increasingly complex governance challenges, AI has been widely adopted in areas such as public security, social management, and risk monitoring. However, its actual effectiveness in mitigating social stability risks remains underexplored. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions in China, this study constructs an empirical framework to evaluate the impact of AI policy on social stability risk levels. The analysis integrates indicators of technological capacity, governance performance, and socio-economic conditions, and applies quantitative methods to identify both direct and indirect effects. The findings suggest that AI policy significantly reduces social stability risks by promoting digital economy development, increasing wage levels and investment in education. At the same time, the results reveal notable regional heterogeneity. The AI policy significantly reduces social stability risk in the central and western regions, and areas with moderate digital economy development, but has no statistically significant effect in economically developed and digitally advanced areas. The study also highlights potential challenges, including data governance concerns and uneven technological access, which may offset some of AI's benefits. This research contributes to the literature by linking technological innovation with social governance outcomes and provides policy implications for leveraging AI to promote social stability. It suggests that policymakers should not only invest in AI infrastructure but also address institutional and regional disparities to ensure inclusive and effective risk management. © 2026 The Authors

title: Tourism's temporal pathways: A deceleration framework
abstract: This research introduces Tourism Deceleration as a theoretically grounded framework for understanding temporal recalibration in tourism. Building on social acceleration theory and consumer deceleration framework, we conceptualize tourism deceleration as a situated temporal negotiation through which travelers recalibrate pace, attention, mobility, digital connectivity, and presence. Using hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis supported by LLM-assisted coding and human validation, we analyze 367 unique Reddit posts and 21,554 comments related to slow travel and long-term travel. The findings show that decelerated travel is often negotiated through practical, social, and personal constraints rather than simply chosen as a preferred travel style. Episodic deceleration remains the most explicit form of decelerated travel, while extended duration often intersects with embodied practices, reduced mobility pressure, and selective negotiation of digital technologies. The research note contributes by distinguishing tourism deceleration from slow tourism and explaining how travelers manage time under conditions of choice, context, and constraint. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The evolving science of negotiation alternatives: New contexts, new perspectives
abstract: We review the past decade (2016 – present) of empirical research on negotiation alternatives across multiple disciplines, including dyadic bargaining, international trade, and civil conflict interventions. Three themes emerged in our analysis: First, research has focused on how the effects of a negotiator's BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) are not person-invariant but are instead moderated by the characteristics of the party who “holds” the BATNA. Second, studies are establishing the conditions under which negotiation alternatives can backfire and hurt a negotiator's performance. Third, an emerging stream of research challenges our conventional understanding of BATNA by highlighting its perceptual nature and the possibility that it may exist on multiple levels within a given negotiation. We close by outlining future directions for each of these emerging themes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Nodding of virtual humans does not necessarily increase customer trust: a temporal analysis
abstract: Virtual humans can potentially facilitate engaging customer interactions, but remain rarely used in customer service. Their embodiment enables virtual humans to use non-verbal listening cues like nodding. Nodding is theorized to increase trust in virtual humans, but literature on this effect is scarce, inconsistent, and only uses measurements after interactions. This study therefore aims to research how nodding of virtual humans influences customer trust, by (1) studying the following hypothesized mediation: nodding (social cue) triggers perceived responsiveness (social signal), which subsequently increases trust (social response); and (2) studying temporal trust dynamics within a customer interaction using exploratory analyses. An online experiment (N = 429) was performed, using a between-subjects design with two conditions: a virtual human either nodded during listening or did not. To isolate nodding optimally, participants watched a video of a customer interaction: a virtual human advised a customer on a wardrobe. While watching, participants used a slider scale to keep updating their temporal trust in the virtual human. Afterwards, participants answered questionnaires on trust and perceived responsiveness. Results showed that nodding did not increase trust or perceived responsiveness, nor did nodding build temporal trust. Temporal trust was built throughout the customer interaction, mostly when the virtual human was speaking. Exploratory analysis found that nodding increased anthropomorphism. Possibly, nodding did not influence trust because other social cues already caused trust-building. Virtual human developers should therefore be aware that nodding does not necessarily build customer trust. The temporal trust scale was useful for visualizing trust-building throughout customer interaction videos. © 2026 The Authors

title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy
abstract: Influencer marketing has become an integral part of retail branding strategies. As the creator economy continues to expand, influencer collaborations are now viewed as strategic partnerships rather than promotional activities. Despite this transition, sustaining authentic and long-term brand-influencer partnerships remains a significant yet underexplored challenge. Combining Social Exchange Theory (SET) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT) into a unified motivational-exchange framework, this research focuses on how brand practices operate simultaneously as relational exchange resources and as psychological need-satisfying inputs within influencer–brand partnerships. With a mixed-methods two-phase approach, this study exmains how brand ethical–purpose alignment, autonomy support, and AI co-creation are linked to influencers' sense of ownership and thriving, as well as citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity. In Study 1, 22 semi-structured interviews were conducted with professional influencers across four regions, intended to understand their lived partnership experiences. In Study 2, responses from 422 influencers were analysed using structural equation modelling and moderation analysis. The study also examines serial indirect pathways through which brand practices are associated with voluntary citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity via Collaboration Ownership and Influencer Thriving. The findings suggest that autonomy support, purpose alignment, and AI co-creation enablement are positively associated with influencers' ownership and thriving. These again are associated with higher levels of voluntary advocacy and intentions to continue partnerships. Therefore, the research positions influencer collaboration as relational rather than transactional and highlights the significance of autonomy, ethical-purpose congruence, and relational fairness in understanding sustainable relationships between influencers and brands. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Why skilled migrants stay or leave host countries: A belongingness theory perspective
abstract: While skilled migrants have a high propensity to quit their jobs and leave host countries, little is known about why some skilled migrants leave while others stay. This paper draws on belongingness theory to examine the mediated effects of work and non-work sense of belonging between skilled migrants’ local language proficiency and host country exit, and the moderated effects of work and non-work social support from locals between local language proficiency and both belonging types. Regression analyses of time-lagged, multisource data collected from 159 foreign academics in Japan suggest that local language proficiency was positively related to work sense of belonging, which was subsequently negatively related to host country exit. Furthermore, the positive relationship between local language proficiency and work sense of belonging was stronger when work and non-work social support were high. This paper contributes to the literature by providing a novel perspective on skilled migrants’ host country experiences, shifting the focus from withdrawal cognitions to belongingness and host country exit, and integrating language proficiency into the theory of belongingness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: When imperfect food meets joint consumption: a social influence perspective
abstract: Drawing on social influence theory, this research examines the interaction effect of food appearance (imperfect vs. perfect) and consumption context (solo vs. joint) on consumers' preferences. Across five experiments, we show that a joint (vs. solo) consumption context exacerbates the reduction in consumers' purchase intention toward imperfect food. In addition, perceived risk and purchase embarrassment mediate this interaction effect on both purchase intention and willingness to pay (WTP). We further identify self-construal and discount information as boundary conditions. Regarding self-construal, for consumers with an interdependent self-construal, joint consumption amplifies the effect of imperfect appearance on perceived risk, purchase embarrassment, and purchase intention. In contrast, for those with an independent self-construal, these amplifying effects are not significant. In terms of discount information, when it is displayed, joint consumption amplifies the effect of imperfect appearance on perceived risk, purchase embarrassment, and purchase intention. When it is absent, however, only the effect on purchase intention remains, albeit attenuated. Finally, the presence of discount information shifts the underlying mechanisms of the interaction toward greater reliance on indirect pathways. This research offers practical guidance for promoting suboptimal food in joint consumption contexts. © 2026

title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered. © 2026 The Author(s).

title: Seeing through the mind: Explainable multimodal AI for depression detection—A review
abstract: Depression detection using multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving, transitioning from traditional machine learning techniques to deep learning architectures built on pre-trained transformer encoders. These systems integrate textual, acoustic, visual, and physiological signal streams through early, intermediate, late, and hybrid fusion strategies to improve predictive performance. However, a significant gap persists in model interpretability: post-hoc attribution frameworks (such as SHAP and LIME) dominate recent work, accounting for over 70% of studies published in 2024–2025, while clinician-centered validation is reported in only about 18% of the full reviewed corpus. Consequently, existing explanations are rarely validated for explainability quality dimensions; for example, SHAP attributions are known to degrade under inter-modality collinearity, and reported systems frequently lack alignment with established diagnostic criteria (e.g., DSM-based or PHQ-9 symptom structures). To close the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical utility, this review jointly synthesizes multimodal datasets, feature extraction strategies, machine learning and deep learning taxonomies, fusion strategies, and explainability techniques across 72 included studies. Finally, we outline critical future directions, emphasizing standardized XAI benchmarks, clinician-in-the-loop validation studies, and knowledge-driven neuro-symbolic reasoning. © 2026

title: The persuasive power of video in hospitality: How guest-generated video reviews influence customer engagement
abstract: Guest-generated video reviews are increasingly prevalent on online travel platforms, yet their effects and mechanisms remain underexplored. Drawing on media richness theory, this study is among the first to examine whether and how such reviews enhance customer engagement, measured by subsequent review volume. We adopt a multimethod approach that combines econometric analysis with a controlled experiment to establish causal inference and uncover underlying mechanisms. Using a 24-month panel of 4471 hotels on Ctrip.com, difference-in-differences results show that guest-generated video reviews significantly increase customer engagement, with stronger effects for higher-tier or large hotels. Experimental evidence further demonstrates that these effects operate through increased information diagnosticity and social presence. Additional video content analysis reveals that human presence, higher informational richness, better visual quality, and longer duration further amplify the positive effects. These findings extend media richness theory to consumer-generated video reviews and offer insights into how richer review media stimulate engagement in hospitality settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How to move you? The persuasive effects of influencer narrative styles in recommending tourism activities
abstract: Influencers exert significant promotional effects in tourism marketing; however, few empirical studies have examined how different types of tourism activities can strategically leverage these effects through influencer narrative style. To address this gap, this study draws on Heuristic-Analytic Theory to investigate how personal and professional narrative styles align with relaxing and challenging tourism activities to maximize influencers’ persuasiveness. The study analyzes secondary data from 1187 social media posts and conducts three scenario-based experiments with 1438 participants. Results show that personal narrative style is more persuasive for relaxing activities, whereas professional narrative style works better for challenging activities. Moreover, experience resonance and knowledge acquisition are identified as key underlying mechanisms. Notably, the study introduces temporal distance in travel decision as a moderator, highlighting the importance of dynamic temporal cues in influencer recommendations. The findings provide valuable theoretical contributions and practical implications for optimizing influencer marketing strategies in the tourism context. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Gendering conversational AI in human–AI interaction: The role of interaction context and sexist ideology in shaping user evaluations
abstract: As human–AI interaction becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, users often infer social identities from AI systems, including gender. Moving beyond the conventional view of AI gender as a static, designer-assigned attribute, this study conceptualizes AI gender as a user-constructed perception shaped by contextual cues. Integrating social role theory, the stereotype content model, and ambivalent sexism theory, we conducted a 2 (AI gender cues: male vs. female) × 3 (interaction context: service-oriented, warm-authoritative, vs. serious-authoritative) between-subjects experiment with Chinese participants (N = 833) to examine how interaction context, perceived AI gender, and sexist ideology jointly shape evaluations of AI competence, warmth, and trustworthiness. The results showed that interaction context significantly influenced gender attribution, with the serious-authoritative condition eliciting stronger gender categorization and a masculinization bias regardless of assigned gender cues. The evaluative consequences of perceived AI gender were also context-dependent: perceived femininity consistently linked with warmth, but was associated with competence and trustworthiness primarily in the serious-authoritative condition. Hostile and benevolent sexism further moderated these relationships in distinct ways. By shifting attention from designed gender to perceived gender, this study offers a more process-oriented account of AI anthropomorphism and demonstrates the value of integrating the stereotype content model with ambivalent sexism theory to explain bias in human–AI evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Sensing the path forward: AI as amplifier in sensory and consumer science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how sensory and consumer data are collected, analyzed, and used. A common fear is that algorithms will displace trained panels and that predictive models will replace expert judgment. We argue the opposite: as AI automates what is easy to formalize, the value of what only humans can do (embodied sensing, cultural interpretation, ethical judgment, and meaning-making) rises. This paper is not a systematic review. It advocates a particular perspective (AI as amplifier of sensory expertise), informed by on-the-ground experience through the recent rise of large language models, including what has worked and what has not in practice. Three industry case studies from PepsiCo, Danone, and Kenvue support that perspective. The principles (knowledge management, automation, predictive modeling, people-centered adoption; humans in the loop; culture before algorithms) are meant to apply beyond large companies, including academia and smaller groups. That perspective also guided a selective literature reading focused on Food Quality and Preference and related journals, mainly from 2022 to early 2026. We clarify what AI is and is not, trace the path from chemometrics to neuromorphic sensing, and describe a four-pillar framework from a Pangborn 2025 industry workshop. Self-reported case outcomes include up to 50% faster analysis and a 75% reduction in reporting time; calculation details were not disclosed to us and the figures are not independently validated. The three organizations built the same capabilities in different orders and met the same barriers (culture, talent, IT collaboration). We also propose narrative-driven analysis with large language models and a near-term research agenda. Central message: when machines predict, humans must decide. © 2026

title: An integrated analytical framework for natural gas pricing: combining multi-source drivers, forecast enhancement, and model interpretability
abstract: With the global pursuit of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), accurate forecasting and mechanistic interpretation of natural gas pricing have become increasingly important. As a transition fuel in the shift toward a low-carbon energy system, natural gas plays a vital role in balancing energy accessibility and environmental sustainability. However, rising economic uncertainty and geopolitical risks present significant challenges to effective price forecasting and policy formulation. In response, we develop a data-driven analytical framework for natural gas pricing that integrates feature engineering and forecast enhancement to achieve accurate point-interval forecasts and investment timing. Leveraging advanced explainability techniques, the framework systematically uncovers the spatiotemporal heterogeneity in global gas market drivers. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional models in predictive accuracy and reveals important lag effects and interaction mechanisms among influencing factors. These findings validate the framework's ability to support pricing decisions and risk hedging for energy enterprises, and to provide scientific evidence for regional energy policymaking through quantification of heterogeneity. Ultimately, it offers key support for improving resource allocation efficiency and advancing the achievement of SDG targets. © 2026

title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions
abstract: The dialectic relationship between the production of post-growth knowledge and ongoing construction of social reality is a complex one, but one that warrants attention. In this scoping review, we respond to the emergent interest in post-growth politics and theories of change. We aim to complement existing reviews of post-growth policy proposals and recommendations with an analysis of peer-reviewed studies on interventions – deliberate attempts by one state, market or civil society actor to influence another. Drawing on a socio-ecological systems leverage points perspective embedded within a political economy inspired mapping of social forces, we develop a conceptual framework for explaining strategic trade-offs made by actors to achieve various forms of depth.Our findings point to asymmetrical relationships between actors-executor pairs and a pattern of neoliberal subjectification in both intervention design and analytical focus. We also find that whilst post-growth interventions can readily achieve discursive depth, it is often accompanied by institutional shallowness and temporal fragility. We conclude with reflections on strategic implications for post-growth researchers and movements. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life. title: Modality effects in human–technology interaction
abstract: This paper reviews emerging research on how different interaction modalities influence information processing and behavior when using new technological devices. A conceptual framework of modality effects is proposed which argues that different input (vocal, haptic) and output modalities (audial, visual) can trigger both cognitive and affective processes that alter users' downstream behaviors. For example, information consumed audially from voice technology rather than visually on a screen can enhance both cognitive load (i.e., cognitive process) and one's sense of social presence (i.e., affective process), which ultimately shape the types of choices made through the technology. The work concludes with a discussion of future research directions in this domain. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Masculine honor, social visibility, and safety non-compliance: intentions and approval judgments in high-risk sectors in Turkey
abstract: Unsafe work in high-risk sectors cannot be explained only by knowledge deficits or weak safety management; workers may also attach reputational meaning to visible compliance. Drawing on honor theory and occupational-safety research on risk perception and social context, this study examined whether masculine honor values (hereafter honor values)—the belief that a man’s worth depends partly on a publicly defensible reputation—were associated with unsafe work intentions, lower perceived risk, and greater approval of safety-rule non-compliance among male workers in Turkish construction and shipbuilding. A worker survey (N = 244) was combined with a within-person vignette experiment in which the focal hazard was held constant while visibility was manipulated and audience identity and prior social comment varied orthogonally. Honor values were positively associated with unsafe work intentions (H1a) and approval of others’ violations (H1b), and negatively associated with perceived risk (H2). Perceived risk partially accounted for the honor–intention association (H3). The association between honor values and approval of non-compliance was stronger when the violation was public rather than private (H4), consistent with a reputational, visibility-contingent account. These findings identify a micro-level sociocultural pathway that complements knowledge- and risk-based accounts of safety decisions. They also suggest that safety communication and supervisory practice should address the social meaning of compliance, while the cross-sectional mediation and judgment-based vignette outcome limit causal and behavioral inference. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Negotiation across the social sciences: An interdisciplinary review
abstract: Psychological investigations have generated numerous insights into how two parties bargain. To build on this literature, we review recent research across multiple disciplines, focusing on aspects of negotiation that have received relatively little attention, namely individual differences, multiparty negotiations, and contextual factors. Insights into individual differences are observed in the developmental psychology, artificial intelligence, and social psychology literature. Investigations in these domains show that young children can think strategically about exchange, that individual differences shape the information negotiators obtain and how they utilize information, and that situational factors can constrain or facilitate the expression of individual differences. Insights into multiparty negotiations emerge from the social networks and political science literature. Investigations in these domains explore novel multiparty dynamics, highlighting the importance of structural position in bargaining, and demonstrating that relationship history can shape coalition formation. Insights into contextual factors emerge from the economic and public health literature. Investigations in these domains challenge assumptions about core negotiation concepts such as power and alternatives. Overall, an interdisciplinary perspective on negotiation complements and enriches psychological understanding, and provides implications for interventions, future theoretical development, and empirical research. © 2026 The Authors

title: Folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy: A bibliometric study and systematic literature review
abstract: The forces of globalization and digital transformation have intensified attention toward the need to strengthen cultural identity through education, including the use of folklore as a meaningful learning resource. However, existing studies on folklore in learning remain fragmented. While much of the literature focuses on either cultural preservation or specific educational applications, the gap lies in a systematic exploration of folklore's pedagogical role across different contexts and educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the development of research on folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy through a bibliometric approach combined with a systematic literature review. For the bibliometric analysis, metadata records of articles published between 2015 and 2025 were processed from the Google Scholar database. Data for the systematic literature review were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and the article selection process followed PRISMA procedures. A total of 41 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer, while article identification and screening were supported by Publish or Perish. The bibliometric findings indicate a significant increase in publications over the past decade, accompanied by a thematic shift from cultural heritage preservation toward the integration of cultural values within educational contexts. The SLR findings show that the research is predominantly qualitative in nature, with folktales and legends as the most frequently used forms of folklore, and books and e-modules as the main learning media employed to strengthen cultural literacy. The findings suggest that folklore-based learning fosters students’ cultural awareness, internalizes values, strengthens identity formation, and deepens the understanding of local culture. This study contributes by providing a more integrated understanding of folklore as a pedagogical tool for cultural literacy, emphasizing its role in curriculum design. Future research should focus on expanding methodological diversity and exploring broader applications of folklore-based learning across various educational contexts. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: How social media content shapes enrollment intention: Distinguishing firm-generated and user-generated effects through TPB and self-identity
abstract: The increasing reliance on social media has transformed how prospective students gather and evaluate information when selecting universities. This study examines how firm-generated content (FGC) and user-generated content (UGC) influence students' behavioral intention to enroll in private universities through psychological mechanisms grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and self-identity. Specifically, the study investigates both direct and indirect effects of FGC and UGC on behavioral intention, mediated by attitude toward behavior, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and self-identity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed, with data collected from 295 final-year high school students in Banten, Indonesia. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that FGC has a significant direct and indirect effect on behavioral intention, whereas UGC does not have a significant direct effect but appears to operate primarily through indirect pathways. Among the mediators, subjective norms emerge as the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude toward behavior and self-identity. In contrast, perceived behavioral control does not significantly influence behavioral intention. The findings suggest that FGC and UGC function through distinct mechanisms. While institutional content can directly shape behavioral intention, user-generated content primarily influences intention through social and psychological processes. These results highlight that the effectiveness of social media communication depends not only on information exposure but also on how information is cognitively evaluated, socially validated, and integrated into individuals' self-concept. This study contributes to the literature by distinguishing between different types of social media content and extending the TPB framework with self-identity in the context of higher education decision-making. The findings provide insights for understanding how digital communication influences complex behavioral decisions in contemporary educational environments. © 2027 Malque Publishing, .

title: Cross cultural patterns of linguistic aggression and aggressive combat content enjoyment: A computational study of PUBG reviews across six continents
abstract: This study explores global patterns of linguistic aggression and appreciation for aggressive combat content as expressed in reviews of PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds (PUBG), analyzing over 18.7 million Google Play Store English language reviews from over 80 countries. Grounded in the General Aggression Model (GAM), it integrates media psychology, cross cultural communication, and computational social science to assess emotional expression in user generated content. Two indices, Aggression Score and Appreciation of Aggressive Content (AAC), were constructed using NLP, sentiment analysis, and lexicon-based tagging to capture hostile sentiment (anger) and positive reinforcement (joy, ratings, likes) in aggression-related reviews. Results reveal a significant increase in the average intensity of both scores over time, with reviews grouped under South America exhibiting higher average aggression and AAC scores within the dataset, while reviews grouped under Australia show comparatively lower levels of these measures. The study uses GAM as a conceptual lens to interpret large-scale, naturalistic expressions of aggression and enjoyment. Methodologically, it offers replicable framework for affective analysis; practically, it offers exploratory insights for game design and content moderation in digital environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: How do sustainability capabilities create retail performance over time? dynamic evidence from U.S. and Chinese retailers
abstract: This study examines how sustainability-oriented technological innovation, sustainable supply chain management, and corporate social responsibility relate to environmental and manager-reported organisational performance in retail firms over time. Drawing on the natural resource-based view, institutional theory, and stakeholder theory, the study analyses a 12-wave monthly panel of 2410 retailers in the United States and China, comprising 26,998 firm-month observations. A multi-group hierarchical Bayesian continuous-time dynamic structural equation model estimates within-firm relationships, effects over one-, three-, and six-month intervals, time-varying mediation, and country differences. Technological innovation predicts environmental performance in both countries, but it strengthens sustainable supply chain management only in China. Sustainable supply chain management predicts organisational performance in both countries. Corporate social responsibility predicts environmental performance in both countries, while its direct short-run organisational effect is positive in the United States and negative in China. Environmental performance converts into organisational performance, and all three proposed indirect effects emerge, only in China during the focal six-month window. Exploratory analysis identifies integration-driven accelerators, evidence-driven pragmatists, and weakly-coupled drifters. The findings characterise retail sustainability as a dynamic conversion system with country-specific pathways to environmental and organisational outcomes; implications for individual customer responses require separate empirical testing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: ThreatNet: A multi-class dataset and LLM-based framework with class-imbalanced fine-tuning for life threat detection
abstract: Detecting life-threatening intent in online text is an increasing challenge as social media increasingly influence public conversation. Current models often face challenges related to insufficient data, class imbalance, and domain variability between platforms. This study proposes ThreatNet, a manually annotated multi-class dataset that contains a variety of linguistic indicators and different intensities of threats sourced from multiple online sources. Using this benchmark, we perform a comprehensive empirical evaluation of seven instruction-tuned LLMs (Flan-T5, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-4B-IT, Mistral-Instruct-7B, Falcon-Instruct-7B, Zephyr-7B-Alpha, Phi-3-Mini-3.8B) and four transformer baselines (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, DeBERTa). We analyze the impact of class imbalance mitigation strategies, few-shot prompting (0, 4, 8, 16 shots), and model scale. Experimental results, reported with standard deviations over five runs, show that Flan-T5 achieves 85.67% ± 0.81% macro-average F1 on ThreatNet, while LLaMA-3.1-8B attains 97.12% ± 0.38% accuracy on the YouTube-Threat-Corpus. These results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its usefulness for life-threatening intent detection. The code is available at https://github.com/AIPMLab/ThreatNet. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: THE VALUE OF RECOMMENDATIONS FROM SOCIAL MEDIA ANALYSTS IN ONLINE INVESTMENT COMMUNITIES
abstract: This study examines the informational value of stock recommendations issued by social media analysts through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using comprehensive data from Seeking Alpha, we demonstrate that these recommendations significantly predict abnormal stock returns over a two-month horizon, with no subsequent reversal, suggesting that they convey incremental information not captured by sell-side analysts or textual sentiment. Guided by SDT, we further show that predictive accuracy varies systematically with analysts’ motivational contexts. Recommendations are more informative when issued by analysts identified as traders, whose direct financial stakes deepen the internalization of extrinsic incentives, and by analysts with high comment-section engagement, where interactive feedback supports needs for competence and relatedness. Conversely, predictive ability declines with longer platform tenure, consistent with motivational saturation as psychological needs become satisfied, and with higher posting frequency, where cognitive overload undermines need satisfaction. Finally, we find that both editorial selection and user-driven engagement effectively identify recommendations with greater ex-post informativeness. In an era of information abundance in online investment communities, our SDT-grounded analysis offers investors guidance for signal extraction and provides platform designers with principled insights for fostering higher-quality content ecosystems. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. Therefore, this study constructs a multi-source heterogeneous hypergraph with higher-order semantics, spanning the “Science-Technology-Industry” dimensions. By mapping the structural phase transitions of weak signals across an “Outlier-Mutation-Key Node” trajectory, we devise a quantifiable indicator system to shift the analytical paradigm from static retrospective detection to dynamic evolutionary tracking. Using a dataset of 145,316 papers, 79,050 patents, and 5941 project records from the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) fuel cell domain (2015–2024), we identify 226 candidate nodes exhibiting this trajectory. A two-round Delphi expert evaluation confirms 193 of these nodes as expert-confirmed weak signals, establishing Delphi-validated reference labels for subsequent model evaluation. We then employ Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Dynamic Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN), and Large Language Models (ZS-LLM and ICL-LLM) to prospectively predict weak signals with disruptive potential. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). This synergy between higher-order topology and semantic intelligence effectively filters stochastic noise and enables meaningful predictive capability of emerging technologies, providing an exploratory decision-support framework for technology foresight. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Smart and green solutions in the catering and hospitality: A review of the existing literature
abstract: The integration of digital technologies and sustainability practices is reshaping the catering and hospitality industry, yet research on smart and green solutions remains fragmented. This study maps the intellectual and thematic development of this field through a bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed publications using VOSviewer, Biblioshiny, and Microsoft Excel. The findings reveal substantial growth in research interest and increasing interdisciplinary contributions across countries, institutions, and authors. Keyword analysis identifies artificial intelligence, sustainability, digital transformation, and social media as dominant themes, while circular economy, Internet of Things (IoT), and customer behavior represent emerging areas. The analysis also highlights a relatively underexplored intersection of AI, IoT, and circular economy, suggesting important opportunities for future research. By consolidating the intellectual structure and emerging themes, this study provides a research agenda for advancing smart and sustainable solutions that enhance operational efficiency, customer experience, environmental performance, and competitiveness in the hospitality sector. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE COIN: CLICKBAIT’S INFLUENCE ON CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION IN SOCIAL MEDIA
abstract: As social media increasingly operates within algorithm-driven attention economies, clickbait has become a pervasive engagement tactic. However, prior research has not fully explained the psychological mechanisms linking clickbait to downstream consumer behavior. Existing studies have also largely treated clickbait as an isolated persuasive cue, overlooking its dynamic interactions with other elements in social media ecosystems. Drawing on psychological reactance theory (PRT) and uses-and-gratifications theory (UGT), this study develops an integrated framework to examine when clickbait harms versus facilitates consumer responses. Across four experiments, we test a sequential mediation model in which perceived intrusiveness and advertising avoidance transmit the effects of clickbait on purchase intention. We further introduce message appeal congruence as a key boundary condition. The results indicate that clickbait does not uniformly produce negative outcomes. When headline-induced motivations align with the gratifications delivered by the content, perceived intrusiveness and reactance are attenuated. When they are misaligned, advertising avoidance increases and purchase intention declines. This research advances the clickbait literature by shifting attention from static credibility judgments to dynamic goal-directed processing and by identifying gratification fulfillment as an upstream regulator of psychological reactance in social media contexts. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: When service environments signal ideology: Customer responses to ideological cues
abstract: Service environments increasingly contain visible cues that communicate political engagement, religious identities, LGBTQ + affiliation, environmental advocacy, and other collective values. Although servicescape research has traditionally emphasized atmospheric, aesthetic, and functional cues, less is known about how customers interpret ideological cues embedded within routine service encounters. Drawing on servicescape research and social identity theory, this research examines how ideological servicescape cues are associated with customer discomfort, avoidance intentions, and stated store-choice decisions. Three preregistered, scenario-based experiments in a coffee shop context examine ideological cues displayed through employees and the physical service environment. Study 1 shows that political cues generate greater discomfort than environmental and lifestyle cues, although they do not differ significantly from religious or LGBTQ + cues. Study 2 shows that matching political cues displayed across employee and environmental touchpoints generate greater discomfort than political cues displayed through a single source, while perceived authenticity does not account for this association. Study 3 shows that political cues are associated with lower stated store choice than environmental cues, particularly when matching political cues appear across employee and environmental touchpoints. Across studies, customer discomfort statistically accounts for part of the association between ideological cue conditions and avoidance intentions or stated store-choice decisions. The findings extend servicescape scholarship by showing that politically charged symbolism may shape customer responses through both cue content and cue-source configuration. Because the studies rely on scenario-based experiments and stated responses, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of observed marketplace behavior or realized financial outcomes. © 2026 The Authors
