title: A dynamic graph query-based data pricing method via multi-armed bandits
abstract: Graph query-based data pricing is promising for pricing answer subgraphs in graph databases according to diverse buyer queries. However, existing methods provide limited support for adaptive price updates when the broker must balance transaction revenue with transaction success rate under incomplete buyer-valuation information. To bridge this gap, we propose GQPRM, which includes: (1) a vertex-edge pricing mechanism that prices a first-time queried answer graph through non-negative atomic prices; (2) a multi-armed bandit (MAB)-based strategy that discretizes repeated-query prices into candidate actions and uses historical acceptance/rejection records for exploration and exploitation; (3) an entropy-weighted feedback update that allocates the observed subgraph-level price variation to vertices and edges in a demand-sensitive manner, rather than assuming that binary feedback uniquely identifies a single overpriced element; and (4) a smart contract-based incentive allocation mechanism that records ownership and supports auditable reward allocation between the data broker and data owners. Experiments on three typical datasets demonstrate that GQPRM improves cumulative transaction value and transaction success rate over the static baseline under the evaluated settings. © 2026

title: EXPLORING THE HEALTH KNOWLEDGE CO-CONSTRUCTION ON SHORT VIDEO PLATFORMS
abstract: Short video platforms have become an important channel for doctors to conduct health science popularization. This study aims to explore the factors influencing health knowledge co-construction on short video platforms. Based on arousal theory, we develop an empirical model to examine the effects of video vividness, video complexity, emotional attitudes, and doctor popularity on health knowledge co-construction. We collected data from the largest short video platform in China, comprising a total of 4,009 videos and 1,040,230 comments for empirical analysis. This study combined machine learning, large language models, and econometric models to test the theoretical model. The results show that: (1) video vividness has a significant positive effect on health knowledge co-construction; (2) video complexity has a negative effect on health knowledge co-construction; (3) there is an inverted U-shaped relationship between emotional attitude and health knowledge co-construction; (4) doctor popularity positively moderates this curvilinear relationship. This study contributes to the literature on knowledge co-construction, expands the understanding of health knowledge co-construction on short video platforms, and provides practical guidance for platform managers and doctors. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: An adaptive-problem structure framework for survival relevance in temporal processing
abstract: Research on survival-relevant cues and subjective time often groups stimuli into immediate-survival, reproductive, and social categories. These labels do not explain why cues within one category recruit different temporal processes across contexts and perceivers. The Adaptive-Problem Structure (APS) Framework characterizes the adaptive problem indicated by a cue through two separable appraisals: ecological urgency, the time sensitivity and cost of delaying a response, and interpretive indeterminacy, the extent to which adaptive meaning and the appropriate response remain unresolved. APS predicts when these appraisals recruit established arousal, attention, information-sampling, and memory processes, how diagnostic context changes those links, and which personality differences strengthen them. Temporal consequences depend on the timing paradigm, interval, and response format. We outline independent ratings, selective within-domain manipulations, process measures, and staged construct validation. Five predictions specify task conditions, personality mappings, comparison baselines, and non-supporting outcomes. APS offers testable constraints on mechanism recruitment and prediction for new stimuli; the framework itself remains to be empirically validated. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: The role of citizen science in engaging older adults with age-friendly green spaces
abstract: This project addresses the global challenges of an ageing population and rapid urbanisation by exploring how citizen science can support the engagement of older adults in shaping age-friendly green spaces. Conducted in the City of Unley, South Australia, the study engaged 30 older residents (aged 60+) as citizen scientists to trial a multi-format audit tool and co-reflect on its use in practice for creating age-friendly environments, generating practical insights for future research and design practice. Integrating audits into participants’ daily routines and everyday life spaces ensured that findings reflected lived experiences. Citizen science was not merely a data collection tool but a sustained dialogue, with regular workshops and informal café sessions supporting motivation, peer learning, and collaborative analysis. Participants reported challenges such as sustaining long-term motivation, but also highlighted opportunities for empowerment, confidence-building, and strengthened community ties. Importantly, many older adults described shifts in how they experienced their environments—becoming more observant, extending their walking habits, and growing more confident in voicing ideas. Several participants continued their civic engagement beyond the project, illustrating the lasting impact of participation. The study contributes methodological insights into designing inclusive citizen science initiatives, offering guidance on recruitment, tool development, and engagement strategies tailored to older populations. Overall, this study demonstrates the power of citizen science not only to generate grounded data but also to empower older adults and co-produce inclusive urban knowledge. Findings provide process-focused insights into age-friendly engagement and illustrate the broader potential of citizen science in shaping equitable, community led public spaces. Overall, this research demonstrates how citizen science can move beyond data collection to become a co-creative process that empowers older adults and informs age-friendly urban transformation. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Rethinking institutional support for migrant businesses in Sweden: A strategic management– oriented scoping review
abstract: Migrant entrepreneurship has become an increasingly important contributor to Sweden’s economic and social landscape; however, the institutional environment supporting migrant-owned businesses remains fragmented and difficult to navigate. This study conducts a scoping review to map existing knowledge on the opportunities, barriers, and systemic gaps affecting migrant entrepreneurs in Sweden. The review draws on peer-reviewed journal articles, policy reports, and grey literature published between 2020 and 2026, identified primarily through the Scopus database and complementary manual searches. A total of 18 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using a thematic synthesis approach. The findings reveal that migrant entrepreneurs contribute significantly to job creation, innovation, and regional development, particularly in sectors such as retail, hospitality, and services. However, they face persistent barriers including limited access to finance, bureaucratic complexity, language constraints, and weak integration into institutional support networks. The analysis further shows that although Sweden possesses a wide range of support mechanisms, these are often poorly coordinated, resulting in duplication, inefficiencies, and limited accessibility for migrant entrepreneurs. Guided by the resource-based view (RBV) and contingency theory, this study develops a strategic pathways model consisting of three interrelated pillars: resource mobilization, adaptive strategy, and collaborative alignment. The model provides a conceptual framework for enhancing institutional effectiveness and improving the inclusiveness of entrepreneurial support systems. The study highlights the need for a more integrated, flexible, and strategically coordinated support ecosystem. It also identifies critical gaps in empirical research and calls for future studies to test the proposed model in real-world institutional settings. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Anchoring sustainability: A new paradigm for maritime clusters
abstract: The environmental footprint of maritime transport, combined with growing social and regulatory pressure to tackle pollution, has brought the shipping industry to the forefront of the sustainability agenda. The role of industry clusters is becoming increasingly relevant to this discourse, given their influence across all dimensions of sustainability. Surprisingly, although this profound relationship is well documented, it has not received sufficient scholarly attention. This study analyses the highly fragmented literature on maritime clusters and sustainability using a novel combination of bibliometrics and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven thematic analysis. On this basis, a framework is developed that captures the interaction between clusters and the key components of sustainability. The findings suggest that sustainability should not be treated as an isolated strategic initiative or the outcome of regulatory pressure, but as a key dimension of cluster competitiveness. Additionally, it emerges that digital innovation acts as a cross-cutting enabler of sustainability in maritime clusters, linking the economic, social/governance, and environmental pillars of the proposed framework. Overall, this study provides actionable insights for maritime practitioners and policy makers alike. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Perceived placeness in creative tourism: Conceptualization, scale development and implications for transformative experiences
abstract: Creative place-making combines cultural heritage, spatial design, creative symbolism, and experiential affordances to cultivate distinctive destinations, yet what tourists holistically perceive in these places remains underexplored. Drawing on atmospheric aesthetics theory, this study conceptualizes perceived placeness in creative tourism as tourists' holistic perception of the environmental and atmospheric qualities that make creative tourism destinations experientially distinctive. To operationalize this construct, content analysis was used to identify its dimensions and initial items. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses refined these items into a 20-item, five-dimensional scale comprising environmental qualities, historical-cultural embeddedness, creative-symbolic ambiance, restorative affordance, and emotional affordance. The nomological relevance of the scale was further established by examining its implications for transformative experiences via authenticity. Theoretically, this study positions perceived placeness as an integrative perceptual field between place-making and tourists’ psychological responses, and contextually elaborates atmospheric aesthetics theory in creative tourism. Practically, the scale provides a timely tool for evaluating and planning creative place-making efforts and curating meaningful tourist experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Greenhouse gas emission under a dual-disposability approach: Assessing environmental technical efficiency in the airline industry
abstract: This study provides a robust analysis of environment-adjusted airline efficiency under a dual-disposability assumption for undesirable output. It employs also a two-stage methodology to investigate the complex and heterogeneous relationships between airline operational profiles and their environmental efficiency. Technical efficiency is estimated in the first step using a Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) based on the Directional Distance Function (DDF) under both assumptions of the technological characterization of gas emissions, contractible versus non-contractible. In the second step, to analyze the factors influencing the estimated efficiency scores, a Tobit second-stage regression is employed. Results show that efficiency scores under strong disposability are systematically and significantly higher than those obtained under weak disposability, with an average difference of 11.9 percentage points. The findings also indicate a positive and statistically significant relationship between the LCC variable and technical efficiency, implying that airline groups with LCC subsidiaries achieve higher efficiency levels. Based on their specific trade-off between operational and environmental inputs, the analysis of technical efficiency elasticities classifies airlines into five groups. These range from “Strong Proactive Environmental Performers” to “Low Efficiency High-Cost” groups, whose efficiency improvements are structurally linked to either an optimization or a deterioration of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions performance. The technical efficiency elasticity with respect to revenue share and to fuel efficiency are parallel across all airlines, while the elasticity for GHG consistently exhibits the opposite sign. We provide one of the few systematic comparisons of efficiency scores under weak versus strong disposability. This comparison allows us to quantify the systematic contraction in measured efficiency that occurs when greenhouse gas emissions are modeled as a technologically costly output rather than a costless byproduct. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Going green to compete: Male-biased operational sex ratio, status motivation, and men's relative green product preference
abstract: Motivating men to choose environmentally preferable products remains an important challenge. Across six studies, this research examines how operational sex ratio (OSR), defined as the ratio of reproductively available men to women, is associated with men's relative preference for green products over conventional alternatives. OSR can characterize a broader demographic environment or serve as a population cue in a local social setting. A cross-level analysis in China showed that men living in provinces with more male-biased OSRs assigned greater priority to environmental protection, whereas women showed no corresponding association. Randomized experiments showed that perceived male-biased OSR increased men's relative green product preference; perceiving a female-biased OSR did not produce a corresponding increase among women. title: Digitalising waqf for sustainable development growth: Investigating user intentions through technology readiness and ethical commitment
abstract: The digitalisation of cash waqf represents a promising avenue within Islamic social finance, offering substantial potential to enhance the welfare and socio-economic development of Muslim communities. Through digital platforms, cash waqf can be collected, managed and distributed more efficiently, transparently and widely compared to traditional methods. Despite these advantages, the level of public participation and contributions to digital cash waqf platforms remains significantly below expectations. This gap highlights the need to better understand the factors that influence individuals’ willingness to adopt digital channels for charitable giving. This study aims to explore the determinants that influence individuals’ intentions to contribute to cash waqf via digital platforms by employing the Technology Readiness framework. Specifically, the study examines the roles of optimism, innovativeness, insecurity, discomfort, and moral obligation in shaping users’ behavioural intentions toward online waqf contributions. Data were collected through an online survey involving 211 Muslim respondents in Malaysia who have experience with digital financial services. The data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The findings reveal that optimism, insecurity, and moral obligation have a positive and significant influence on individuals’ intentions to donate cash waqf through digital platforms. In contrast, discomfort demonstrates a significant negative effect, indicating that feelings of technological anxiety and lack of confidence in using digital systems may discourage adoption. Given the limited empirical research on digital cash waqf, this study contributes valuable insights into the psychological and behavioural factors influencing online donation behaviour. The findings provide practical implications for waqf institutions and policymakers to design strategies that reduce technological barriers while strengthening moral and religious motivations, thereby encouraging wider adoption of digital cash waqf platforms, particularly in developing countries with similar socio-economic environments. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Experiential and symbolic pathways to luxury fashion brand equity: The contingent role of brand attachment and subjective norm
abstract: The study develops and tests an integrated moderated mediation model to explain how emotional attachment, shaped by experiential and symbolic brand stimuli, is associated with consumer-based brand equity (CBBE) in the luxury fashion context, and the role of consumers’ social environment, drawing on Attachment Theory, the Lovemarks framework, and the Theory of Planned Behaviour. Data were collected from 544 luxury fashion consumers and were analysed using Hayes' PROCESS Model 15. Both brand experience and brand mystery were positively associated with brand attachment. Brand attachment was also positively associated with CBBE and significantly mediated the indirect associations between experiential and symbolic brand resources and CBBE. Furthermore, subjective norm moderately weakens the positive relationship between brand attachment and CBBE, indicating that while subjective norm weakens the relationship between emotional attachment and consumers' evaluations of luxury fashion brands, it does not replace it. This study advances luxury branding research by showing how an identity-based relational mechanism is associated with broader CBBE, with experiential encounters and symbolic meanings relating to brand equity through emotional attachment. By integrating Attachment Theory, the Lovemarks framework, and the Theory of Planned Behaviour within a unified framework, the study shows that experiential and symbolic brand resources are associated with luxury brand equity through complementary relational pathways. © 2026

title: ResGAT: A residual graph attention network for technology transfer prediction in Chinese universities
abstract: University patent transfer in China remains sparse, and only a small fraction of university patents are licensed or assigned. Technology-transfer offices must still judge which patents are worth promoting and which enterprises are plausible recipients. Existing matching methods rely on content similarity, collaborative filtering, or shallow heterogeneous graphs. They rarely model patent–patent, patent–entity, and entity–entity relations together with patent attributes when positive transfer labels are extremely scarce. This study proposes a residual graph attention network (ResGAT) for technology-transfer object recognition. Built on three meta-paths, ResGAT uses relation-specific attention together with a shared feature transformation. It stacks residual graph-attention layers on the homogeneous branches to limit over-smoothing, and it uses a shallow cross-type branch to pass entity information to patents. A two-stage procedure then estimates transfer probability and ranks candidate transferees by dot-product similarity. On a civil-engineering patent graph from a Chinese university, and on seven strategic-emerging-industry subsets, ResGAT outperforms heuristic, linear, and multi-relational graph baselines under the same 10-fold protocol. The model also returns ranked enterprise lists for high-potential patents, so transfer offices receive a concrete shortlist rather than only a transfer score. © 2026

title: Meaning in the age of AI: Experiencing less, needing more
abstract: What does it mean to be human when artificial intelligence (AI) can simulate human thought and creative labor with increasing fidelity? Unlike AI, humans experience meaning in life. Yet AI may create a paradox for meaningfulness. AI may reduce people's ability to experience meaning by disrupting selfhood (loss of effort and self-efficacy), social relationships (reduced mattering and connection), and culture (erosion of value and stability). At the same time, it may heighten people's need for meaning by challenging human exceptionalism and increasing the need for coherence amidst upheaval. This paradox—experiencing less while needing more—is what we term the AI Meaning Gap. Yet meaninglessness is not inevitable. If developed and used intentionally, AI could become a tool for reflection, understanding, and self-growth, thereby enhancing meaning. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: When ads look worth keeping: Screenshotable design increases ad saving and Facebook ad liking
abstract: As social media advertising increasingly competes in fast-scrolling feed environments, an important but understudied question is whether some ads succeed by functioning less as transient persuasive messages and more as saveable information objects. Drawing on affordance theory and uses and gratifications reasoning, this research examines whether screenshotable ad design increases preservation-oriented engagement by making ads seem useful for later use. Across five studies, including controlled online experiments and a naturalistic simulated-feed experiment, screenshotable ads were associated with higher ad saving intention and Facebook ad liking relative to non-screenshotable ads. The results are consistent with perceived future utility as a mediating mechanism: screenshotable design increased perceived future utility, which in turn was associated with higher saving-related responses and Facebook ad liking intention. The process was stronger when consumers anticipated a future rather than immediate need, such that perceived future utility translated more strongly into ad saving and liking under future-need conditions. In addition, screenshotable design more strongly increased perceived future utility when information density was high rather than low, indicating that saveable structure is most effective when the ad contains enough substantive content to justify preservation. The findings contribute to consumer research on digital advertising response by identifying screenshotable ad design as a distinct visual structure that can shape consumers’ interpretation of an ad as a later-use resource, and they offer guidance for managers designing social media ads intended to be kept, revisited, and positively engaged with over time. © 2026

title: Corporate environmental credit rating and social stability: Evidence from capital-labor conflicts in China's polluting industries
abstract: Mitigating capital-labor conflicts is essential for maintaining social stability. Using China's Enterprise Environmental Credit Evaluation System (EECES) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines the impact of corporate environmental credit rating on capital-labor conflicts. The results indicate that EECES reduces capital-labor conflicts in polluting industries by approximately 17.63%, although its effect weakens over time. Channel tests show that EECES mitigates capital-labor conflicts by reducing workers' pollution exposure risk, improving corporate environmental information transparency, and enhancing social trust in corporations. Moreover, in cities with weaker social governance capacity, EECES exerts a stronger restraining effect on capital-labor conflicts, suggesting that it effectively compensates for deficiencies in social governance. Further analysis reveals that although EECES reduces industrial output, it significantly promotes economic transformation. Overall, these findings highlight EECES as an effective policy tool for safeguarding social stability. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Beyond the accession event: Joint regional membership duration and completion of cross-border acquisitions
abstract: Cross-border acquisition (CBA) completion is often hindered by institutional barriers, imposing substantial costs on deal participants. While regional integration aims to reduce such barriers, prior research predominantly treats regional integration as a discrete accession event, leaving post-accession adaptation dynamics and their underlying mechanisms underexplored. Drawing on new institutional economics and social learning theory, we argue that joint regional membership duration increases CBA completion likelihood, with country-dyadic M&A stock serving as the mediating carrier via the sequential pathways of institutional alignment and social learning. We further examine how initial regulatory distance and cultural distance condition this mechanism. Using a sample of 8009 announced CBAs across the European Union (2010–2022), we find support for the mediation pathway and show that both regulatory and cultural distance weaken this indirect effect. This study advances the literature by moving beyond discrete event-based integration framing and refines the understanding of cross-national distance within integrated regional blocs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Community participation intensity on asynchronous biodiversity and human well-being responses to ecological restoration in global drylands
abstract: Ecological restoration serves as a key strategy for addressing desertification and ecosystem degradation in global drylands. However, achieving synergistic benefits for both biodiversity and human well-being remains a significant challenge for sustainability. Although community participation is increasingly promoted, quantitative evidence remains limited on how participation intensity is associated with measured ecological and social outcomes in dryland restoration. A dataset encompassing 744 effect sizes from 41 independent studies across global drylands was constructed to conduct a meta-analysis. The synthesis indicated positive benefits relative to degraded baselines, while composite biodiversity and composite human well-being showed asynchronous responses across community participation intensity. For composite biodiversity, the pooled mean estimate corresponded to an average increase of 122.11% relative to degraded baselines. Limited community participation was associated with long-term positive patterns in the composite biodiversity (159.35%) and composite human well-being (130.71%), whereas extensive community participation showed an evidence-limited and marginally supported positive tendency in composite human well-being in the short term. Eventually, we propose an adaptive framework in which livelihood-support components may be emphasized during early restoration, followed by lower-disturbance stewardship considerations as biodiversity recovery stabilizes. Overall, our findings provide exploratory quantitative evidence for discussing how community participation may affect asynchronous ecological and social outcomes in dryland restoration. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Unveiling research trends in artificial intelligence adoption based on the UTAUT: A bibliometric analysis supporting SDGs and future outlook
abstract: The development of AI adoption across disciplines has become a major global concern, especially with the UTAUT model that runs concurrently. This study aims to map research trends on AI adoption within the UTAUT model in conceptual, intellectual, and social structures. The research utilises a bibliometric approach from the Scopus database for the period 2018-2025 on related topics. Data analysis was conducted descriptively using Biblioshiny (Rstudio). The study found a very positive and significant development in research on AI adoption within the UTAUT model across various disciplines, aligning with the SDGs, particularly points four, nine, and seventeen. The countries that contributed most were China and the USA. Interesting themes for studying the development of UTAUT model implications include social influence, performance expectancy, behaviour, perceived risk, digital literacy, and AI anxiety. In SDG 4, the adoption of AI in higher education is crucial by incorporating perceived risk and digital literacy to achieve effective personalised learning. In SDG 9, organisational and corporate levels within managerial structures are important for combining structural and psychological factors that influence AI adoption. AIMDSS in the healthcare sector is essential for supporting health innovation and infrastructure. Meanwhile, for SDG 17, discovering best practices for AI adoption across various fields needs to be accelerated, particularly in Africa, South America, and most of Eastern Europe. The implications of this research point to the development of institutional guidelines for AI adoption and the exploration of the UTAUT model. By highlighting the evolving role of contextual, ethical, and governance-related factors, this study provides a foundation for aligning AI adoption strategies with sustainable development objectives and informs future empirical and policy-oriented research. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Mapping the evolution of communication research in aquatic conservation: A systematic literature review of emerging patterns and research opportunities (2015–2025)
abstract: This review examines the development of communication research in aquatic conservation through a systematic literature review. Although communication is increasingly recognized as crucial for environmental governance, promoting aquatic conservation remains underexplored and often treated instrumentally. Using the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this review analyzed eleven articles (n = 11) published between 2015 and 2025, drawn from Scopus and Web of Science databases. Findings indicate that existing studies are predominantly presented in the Global North and tend to emphasize media representation, message framing, and individual behavioral change. These patterns suggest that communication is often conceptualized as a tool for disseminating information rather than as a broader social process. Most of the research described is qualitative, further strengthening the exploratory nature of the evidence. This review identifies limited engagement with systemic perspectives in understanding how communication shapes environmental responses. To address this, this study introduces Niklas Luhmann's social systems theory as an analytical lens for reinterpreting communication in aquatic conservation. From this perspective, communication is understood as a process of systemic resonance in which environmental issues are selectively interpreted across different social systems. This study contributes to the field by providing an exploratory synthesis of existing research and highlighting the need for more methodologically robust, geographically diverse, and theoretically grounded studies. The findings also underscore the importance of shifting from instrumental approaches to a more systemic understanding of environmental communication. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Expand or carve up? Evaluating market dynamics of premium airline entry with extended synthetic control methods: Evidence from STARLUX airlines
abstract: This study examines the effects of STARLUX Airlines' entry as a newly established premium full-service carrier on Taiwan's international air transport market. Using the synthetic control method (SCM) and an extended SCM framework, the analysis evaluates changes in passenger demand following the airline's entry, encompassing both single and multiple treated units, including individual routes and interconnected markets. A conditional growth model was subsequently employed to distinguish market expansion from demand redistribution. Results indicate that although only 9 out of 24 treated markets showed statistically significant expansion, STARLUX's entry still revealed latent demand and contributed meaningfully to overall market growth despite the relatively small size of STARLUX as compared to its primary competitors, China Airlines and EVA Airways. This effect was particularly evident in business-oriented and transfer-focused segments, while some tourism-driven and politically sensitive markets saw limited or negative responses. This study contributes to the literature by highlighting the demand-side influence of premium airline entry, extending SCM to multi-unit and network-based applications, and providing a replicable framework for evaluating airline market interventions in liberalized environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Mobile internet connectivity and climate change literacy in Africa
abstract: Addressing climate change requires individual behavioral shifts and a deep understanding of its impacts, yet the role of information and communication technologies (ICT), a powerful driver of social movements and cultural shifts, in shaping climate change literacy remains underexplored. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how ICT, particularly mobile Internet connectivity, influences climate change literacy in Africa. I provide the first systematic evidence on the impact of mobile Internet connectivity on climate change literacy by exploiting variations in peer-based Internet connectivity in an instrumental variable strategy. Using newly georeferenced individual-level data on climate change literacy from over 42,000 respondents across 31 African countries, I show that mobile Internet connectivity has a modest yet robust effect on climate literacy, raising it by approximately 0.57 points for a typical adopter. Heterogeneity analysis shows that mobile Internet access primarily enhances the knowledge-based dimensions of climate literacy, particularly climate awareness and understanding, while also improving risk perceptions to a lesser extent. This suggests that mobile Internet contributes to climate literacy mainly by expanding access to factual information and knowledge about climate change. Suggestive evidence reveals that Internet connectivity can help close climate-related information gaps, among socio-economically disadvantaged groups, such as women, farmers, and those without formal education. Although Internet connectivity increases the frequency of using Internet and social media for news, there is no strong evidence that these platforms serve as channels linking Internet connectivity to climate literacy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Should generative AI be responsible to users? Developing and validating the user-generative AI psychological contract scale
abstract: As GenAI becomes increasingly embedded in AI-enabled service interactions, users' evaluations of AI are extending from functional performance to expectations regarding responsibility and obligation. Drawing on Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) theory and psychological contract theory, this study defines the user–generative AI psychological contract (AIPC) as users' beliefs about the responsibilities and obligations GenAI should fulfill toward them during ongoing interaction and develops a corresponding scale. Study 1 used purposively recruited interviews (N = 26) to identify the construct content domain. Study 2 used two nonprobability online-panel samples of active GenAI users (N = 507 and N = 506) to develop the items and examine the factor structure, reliability, and construct validity. Study 3 used the same 506-case sample employed for structural validation in Study 2 to provide an initial test of the nomological network among AIPC, AI anthropomorphism, and co-creation intention. Results indicate that AIPC consists of three dimensions—the functional support contract, relational collaboration contract, and ethical safety contract—and forms a 16-item scale. Users reported the strongest expectations regarding ethical safety. Anthropomorphism was indirectly associated with co-creation intention through functional support and relational collaboration, but not through ethical safety. The findings extend psychological contract theory to user–AI relationships and provide a measurement tool for studying responsibility expectations toward GenAI. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Factors affecting public transport adoption in Riyadh- case study
abstract: Riyadh's greenhouse gas emissions and urban climate risks are likely heightened by accelerated urbanization and profound dependence on private cars. Despite the government's investment in public transportation, societal resistance to giving up private cars and using public transit persists due to cultural and traditional factors. Within the Gulf context, this study is the first to investigate the unique socio-cultural and urban context of Riyadh to understand university students' mobility behavior, identify four factors that significantly are associated with their travel choices, and quantitatively rank the relative influence of these factors. Surveys (n = 710) were used to assess four key factors, analyzed via multiple regression, chi-square, and t-tests. Results indicate that, in descending order of influence, psychological factors (explaining 23% of the variance) have the most significant association with students' willingness to switch to public transport in Riyadh, followed by trip characteristics (13%), urban factors (12%), and socioeconomic and demographic factors (12%). The result suggests that, alongside infrastructure improvements, coordinated strategies are required to change social norms, enhance environmental awareness, and create culturally responsive incentives. The findings support the implementation of place-based policies for sustainable mobility. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Digital influences on green economic participation: The role of eWOM in shaping circular consumption among young vietnamese consumers
abstract: Circular business models (CBMs) are increasingly recognized as a strategic mechanism for advancing sustainable consumption and supporting green economic growth, particularly in emerging economies where rising consumption intensifies pressures on natural resources and waste management systems. Concurrently, the rapid expansion of social media and digital commerce has elevated electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) to a central role in shaping how young consumers interpret, evaluate, and normalize sustainability-oriented business practices. Despite this growing intersection, limited empirical evidence explains how specific attributes of eWOM translate into consumers’ intentions to participate in CBMs, especially in developing-market contexts such as Vietnam. Addressing this gap, the present study adopts a quantitative approach using survey data from 1,142 young Vietnamese consumers to examine how core dimensions of eWOM influence information acceptance and, subsequently, participation intentions in CBMs within the retail sector. A rigorous multi-stage analytical procedure was employed, including reliability testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate the measurement model, and structural equation modeling (SEM) to assess the structural relationships among latent constructs. The results indicate that all four eWOM attributes positively influence information acceptance, which in turn significantly drives participation intention. Among these factors, relevance emerges as the most influential attribute, suggesting that sustainability-related messages are most effective when aligned with consumers’ personal needs, values, and decision contexts. The findings also confirm the mediating role of information acceptance in translating eWOM quality into behavioral intention. By validating both the measurement and structural models, this study enhances the robustness of IAM-based explanations in the context of circular consumption and extends the literature on digital influence in emerging markets. Practically, the study highlights the importance of designing relevant, credible, and comprehensive sustainability communication strategies. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted with caution due to the cross-sectional design and non-probability sampling approach. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: When loyalty points become donations: The effects of redeemability, point expiration, and descriptive norm information
abstract: Although loyalty programs and checkout charity are widely implemented across retail industries, the integration of reward point donations into online checkout charity remains rare, and consumer behavior in this context is not yet fully understood. While a few studies have explored reward point donations and generally reported positive consumer responses, to the best of our knowledge, little research has examined how reward point characteristics and situational factors influence consumers' willingness to donate. To address this gap, the present research examines, across three studies, the effect of point redeemability on consumers’ donation intention through online checkout charity, as well as the moderating roles of point expiration and descriptive norm information. Study 1 shows that consumers exhibit higher donation intention when their reward points are non-redeemable than when they are redeemable. Study 2 demonstrates that the interaction between point redeemability and point expiration significantly influences donation intention, while Study 3 shows that the interaction between point redeemability and descriptive norm information also significantly affects donation intention. The findings provide actionable insights for retailers seeking to design more effective reward point donation programs and enhance social impact through online checkout charity. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Epistemic justice and deep-sea mining: UNCLOS’s facilitation of epistemic diversity the International Seabed Authority’s decision-making process
abstract: The paper discusses epistemic justice as a central justice framework to be considered in the regulatory process of exploitative deep sea mining, with the aim of bringing attention to the relevance of epistemic justice and diversity to deep sea mining scholarship. Epistemic justice is here understood as deeply connected to a broader social equity, and entails the fair treatment of different ’knowers’ and a creation, sharing, and validation of knowledge that is fundamentally diverse rather than based on one dominant knowledge-tradition. The paper reflects on epistemic justice in energy- and ocean governance, and asks whether and how United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) facilitates that such justice is sought in the regulatory process of deep sea mining by focusing on procedural rules for the International Seabed Authority (ISA) and the representation of different knowers in the decision-making process, including its Council's structure, authority, and composition. It concludes that a very small number of individuals has the power to bring about a very large change in deep sea mining regulations, currently without legal requirements to include experiential, traditional or other forms of knowledges beyond the scientific method in the decision-making process. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Technostress in the age of digital transformation and AI: A bibliometric–systematic literature review for HRM research
abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are reshaping human resource management through algorithmic recruitment, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and generative tools. While these systems improve efficiency, they also intensify technostress through opacity, surveillance, reduced control, and digitally intensified work arrangements. Responding to a fragmented literature spanning both AI-enabled and broader digital work systems, this study provides a B-SLR that maps technostress in digital transformation while identifying AI-specific stressors as a key emerging stream for HRM research. Drawing on 194 Scopus-indexed articles, we combine performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, dominant themes, and intellectual structures. The review shows how AI-specific stressors extend established technostress mechanisms and shift attention toward transparency, control, fairness, and responsible HRM design. We conclude with actionable implications for researchers and practitioners aiming to design more transparent, responsible, and sustainable digital and AI-enabled HRM systems. © 2026 The Authors

title: The allure of imperfection: How ugly-cute aesthetics drive purchase intentions
abstract: The rise of social media has increased both aesthetic diversity and consumer attention to product appearance and emotional appeal. This research examines the commercially successful yet under-researched “ugly-cute” aesthetic, exemplified by products like Pop Mart's LABUBU. Moving beyond traditional approaches that treat beauty (or ugliness) and cuteness as separate dimensions, we investigate their interactive effects through four studies: one field experiment and three online experiments, involving participants from both China and the United States. Our findings show that the combination of ugly-cute configurations can attenuate the purchase-intention disadvantage associated with ugliness-related aesthetic deviation, with this effect explained by perceived social value and moderated by consumption setting (public vs. private). Specifically, this effect is more pronounced in public consumption settings, where consumers are more likely to seek social approval and positive evaluation from others, thereby amplifying perceived social value in purchase decisions. These results advance the literature on product design and consumer aesthetics by identifying a psychological explanation underlying consumer responses to atypical aesthetics, and provide practical insights for designing products that generate perceived social value (e.g., feeling accepted, gaining approval, or being positively regarded by others). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Divergent relationships between moral disengagement and cyberbullying bystander response behaviors: Examining the amplifying roles of humor and anonymity
abstract: While bystander response behaviors are pivotal for cyberbullying (CB) intervention, prior research has yielded inconsistent findings regarding their correlates, partly because it has often treated diverse bystander responses as a monolithic construct and failed to distinguish constructive defense from aggressive defense. Furthermore, few empirical studies have examined how digital affordances interact with individual factors in relation to diverse bystander responses within a Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) framework. To address these gaps, this study examined the main and interactive associations of individual moral disengagement (MD), perceived anonymity, and humor of CB with four distinct online bystander responses (constructive defense, aggressive defense, inaction, and reinforcement). A final analytic sample of 1201 Chinese secondary school students, selected via multi-stage random sampling, completed a survey assessing MD, CB contexts, and real online bystander responses. Multilevel analysis indicated that MD, perceived anonymity and humor were consistently and negatively associated with constructive defense but positively associated with inaction. Conversely, MD and anonymity were positively associated with aggressive defense, whereas humor showed no significant link. Regarding reinforcement behaviors, perceived anonymity and humor were positive predictors, whereas MD exerted a non-significant association. Moderation analyses revealed that anonymity strengthened MD's positive associations with inaction and reinforcement, whereas humor amplified MD's association solely with reinforcement. These findings underscore the necessity of distinguishing constructive from aggressive defense and integrating individual moral cognition with contextual cues for both exploring correlates of online bystander response and designing CB interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Enhancing situational awareness in health systems: A scoping review of technologies and cross-industry insights
abstract: Background: Situational awareness technologies are increasingly utilised in healthcare systems to facilitate timely and coordinated decision-making. Reported implementation considerations include data quality, governance, and integration into everyday workflows. Objective: This scoping review aimed to map technologies, systems, and methods used to enhance situational awareness in health service delivery and to identify approaches used in other industries that could be adapted for healthcare, particularly in regional and remote settings. Methods: We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidance for scoping reviews. Electronic databases (PubMed and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between January 2000 and October 2025. Reference lists and citation searches in Google Scholar were also examined. Records meeting the inclusion criteria were screened and reviewed, with key data extracted using a structured charting form and synthesised into seven application domains. Results: Searches identified 744 records, of which 23 studies were included. These covered diverse technologies such as dashboards, forecasting models, alert systems, and geospatial decision environments. Most studies were from high-income countries (n = 19). Studies reported potential benefits for visibility, coordination, and decision-making. However, most evidence was descriptive, with limited evidence of whether these systems improve service delivery. Recurrent implementation challenges included data fragmentation, limited interoperability, and misalignment between governance and workflow. Conclusions: This review highlights the need for more rigorous and context-sensitive evaluations of technologies used to enhance situational awareness in healthcare, especially in regional and resource-limited settings. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

title: Conflict expression: A decade of group conflict research
abstract: The conflict expression framework was developed to generate new practical and theoretical insights into how conflict communication affects group processes and negotiated outcomes. The framework proposes that conflict expressions vary along two dimensions: directness and oppositional intensity. The framework suggested that the effects of different types of conflict on group processes and outcomes likely depend on how the conflict is expressed, that conflict within groups is likely perceived differently by different members of the same social unit, and that conflict affects negotiation processes dynamically through reciprocated statements and responses. We review research building on the framework – including empirical tests of the main propositions, methodological advances, and as a theoretical foundation for conflict communication research more broadly – and identify directions for the future. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Encountering the “familiar stranger”: Activating latent cultural identification among Vietnamese tourists in China
abstract: Tourism studies have largely examined cultural identification through encounters with difference, while paying less attention to culturally proximate travel contexts. Drawing on schema theory, this study examines how latent cultural identification (LCI) emerges when sedimented cultural meanings become perceptible and interpretable during travel. Based on interviews with 41 Vietnamese tourists traveling in China, the findings indicate that material, social, and mediated cues make routinized meanings noticeable, while internalized cultural schemata help tourists interpret them in relation to their cultural self-understanding. Affective resonance amplifies this process by intensifying the salience and self-relevance of interpreted meanings. Behavioural responses vary across compliance, inquiry, reinterpretation, and co-creation, reflecting different degrees of self-reflection and social embeddedness. By highlighting the role of cultural schemata in LCI, this study extends tourism identity research and shows how LCI can help tourists locate their own culture within the wider world-cultural landscape, enrich personal meaning-making, and foster intercultural exchange. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: A study analyzing factors retarding digital transformation and configuration pathways: Based on the perspective of digital transformation acceptors
abstract: The high-touch service nature of the hospitality industry highlights that the success of digital transformation depends primarily on human factors rather than technology itself. Existing research indicates that approximately 80% of strategic initiatives fail due to employee resistance to change or capability deficits. Furthermore, nearly three-quarters of middle managers and staff exhibit resistance toward such transformations. This alarming trend raises a fundamental question: how can the hospitality industry navigate the inherent tension between high-touch emotional labor and digital depersonalization to transform employee resistance into proactive adoption? While traditional research frequently focuses on hotel management as change promoters, this study shifts the analytical focus to hotel employees as change recipients. Guided by cognitive appraisal and social information processing theories, within the context of hotel service scenarios, this research constructs models of resistance mitigation and antecedent condition linkages across individual, organizational, and managerial levels. Through an empirical analysis of 545 survey responses from various hotel categories and the application of fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), this study systematically explores the mechanisms of resistance alleviation and the synergistic effects of the identified influencing factors. Regression results indicate that digital literacy, digital strategy consensus, and perceptions of digital technology warmth and capability are negatively associated with hotel employee resistance to digital transformation. Additionally, organizational strategic flexibility and digital leadership positively moderate the relationships between these individual factors and resistance. The fsQCA results further identify two primary equifinal patterns sufficient for fostering a state of low resistance, demonstrating how strong digital leadership serves as a social cue that effectively compensates for the absence of organizational strategic flexibility. Ultimately, this research deepens the understanding of human-centered digital transformation in the hospitality sector and offers theoretical frameworks for managers to mitigate employee resistance to digital initiatives, thereby facilitating successful strategic implementation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: From perceived attractiveness to visitation: Multi-scale measurement and influencing factors across 143 Chinese historic cities
abstract: Effective tourism management requires understanding how attraction attributes and supporting factors shape tourists’ perceived attractiveness, and how these in turn translate into visitation. We develop a tourist-centered framework using 610,136 reviews across 2128 heritage attractions in 143 cities, measuring multi-scale perceived attractiveness with a large language model pipeline and visitation with review volume, then identifying the factors that influence both metrics using XGBoost and SHAP. Results show that (1) perceived attractiveness and visitation share a multi-core spatial structure, while visitation displays a polarized long-tail distribution; (2) attraction attributes, especially official designation, visual quality, and ticket pricing, dominate both metrics but shape them differently; (3) positively perceived social, economic, scientific, historic and aesthetical values increase visitation, whereas political value is negatively associated; and (4) accessibility and spatial agglomeration also contribute positively. Practically, multi-scale benchmarking identifies underperforming attractions, while attraction-scale value profiles and the identified influencing factors guide targeted strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Mapping the global landscape of mentorship in women’s entrepreneurship: A bibliometric review (2000–2025)
abstract: Mentorship is increasingly recognised as a critical enabler of women’s entrepreneurial participation and success. However, existing scholarship remains fragmented, conceptually inconsistent, and unevenly distributed across global contexts. This study conducts a bibliometric analysis of mentorship in women’s entrepreneurship, examining peer-reviewed literature published between 2000 and 2025 globally. To enhance methodological robustness and address limitations associated with narrow keyword selection, a multi-stage search strategy was employed using the Scopus database. A total of 878 records were identified through the Scopus database. The final dataset includes 621 articles, allowing for a detailed analysis of publication trends, geographic distribution, authorship patterns, and thematic development within the field. The findings reveal a significant concentration of research output in the Global North, particularly in the United States and the United Kingdom, with comparatively limited representation from developing regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa. Thematic analysis indicates strong clustering around mentorship, coaching, entrepreneurial ecosystems, and capacity building, highlighting both conceptual convergence and fragmentation. Furthermore, the results show that mentorship is frequently embedded within broader entrepreneurial support frameworks rather than examined as a standalone construct. In response, this study advances a Gendered Social Capital and Learning framework to provide a more integrated understanding of mentorship processes in women’s entrepreneurship. The study contributes to the literature by offering a robust, data-driven overview of the field, identifying key gaps in geographic and theoretical coverage, and highlighting the methodological implications of keyword selection in bibliometric research. The findings provide valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners seeking to design more inclusive and contextually relevant mentorship interventions for women entrepreneurs. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Shared value vs plural values. Contesting renewable energy projects of the Enel Group
abstract: The energy transition triggers urgent questions about what values are important, who controls transitional processes, and who has the power to define the answers to the climate crisis. Energy companies claim their central role in the development of renewable energy as the ultimate solution. However, communities affected by large-scale renewable energy projects have extensively raised environmental and social justice concerns and denounced the industry's poor practices and abuses.In this article, we analyse 15 socio-environmental conflicts around renewable energy projects owned by the Enel Group, one of the world's largest energy utilities, through the values and valuation languages of the affected communities. We map them onto five dimensions: environmental, health-related, socio-economic, ontological, and political. We build on environmental justice and ecological economics literature on valuation languages and employ counter-accounting to gather bottom-up evidence of grievances.We argue that, while the company claims that RE is the ultimate solution and the ‘Creating Shared Value’ approach is beneficial to all parties, those impacted by Enel's projects question the corporate model of energy transition and defend a plurality of values embedded in relational worldviews that are systematically misrecognised. We eventually criticise the corporate self-attributed moral and value-centred mandate in the energy transition and call for inclusive research about desirable energy futures rooted in plural and relational value systems. title: Beyond technological determinism: A multidimensional framework and research agenda for consumer trust in blockchain applications
abstract: Blockchain technology is increasingly integral to domains such as finance, supply chain, commerce and tourism, yet consumer trust remains a pivotal barrier to its widespread adoption. Studies on trust in blockchain contexts have significant conceptual and contextual limitations that inhibit a holistic understanding of trust formation. In this study, we draw on the antecedents, decisions, outcomes and theory, context, methods (ADO-TCM) framework to systematically review 53 high-quality multidisciplinary studies. We identify three critical issues: (1) technological determinism that conflates technical capability with consumer trust, marginalising psychological, social and institutional factors; (2) theoretical convergence around acceptance models that obscures blockchain-specific trust phenomena; and (3) a narrow geographic and domain scope that creates self-reinforcing knowledge hierarchies limiting generalisability across applications and cultures. To address these gaps, we propose a multidimensional trust framework integrating three dimensions: technological architecture trust, information source trust and social actor trust, reflecting blockchain's sociotechnical structure. Central to this framework is a four-paradigm typology that classifies trust into interpersonal, technology, institutional, and sociotechnical perspectives, revealing that the prevalence of technological determinism reflects theoretical inertia rather than genuine consensus. We complement this with three research themes: multi-level theoretical integration, innovative methodologies and contextual expansion. This study contributes to the information systems discourse by providing a theoretical foundation for understanding trust in complex sociotechnical systems beyond acceptance models. By conceptualising consumer trust as a dynamic, multidimensional construct shaped by interactions between users, technology, and institutions, we offer a research agenda with actionable directions for advancing blockchain trust theory and practice. © 2026 The Authors

title: The dark side of disrespect: How workplace incivility breeds service sabotage and turnover
abstract: This study examines how different sources of workplace incivility affect frontline hotel employees. Drawing on Conservation of Resources Theory and Social Identity Theory, Study 1 compares the effects of employee incivility (originating internally) and customer incivility (originating externally) on emotional exhaustion. Based on a scenario-based experiment with 263 participants, the results show that employee incivility causes greater emotional exhaustion than customer incivility. Study 2 further differentiates in-group sources by their hierarchical level—supervisor, same-level colleague, and subordinate—and examines their specific impacts on emotional exhaustion, which, in turn, affects sabotage and turnover intentions. Using survey data from 302 respondents, the findings reveal that same-level colleague incivility has the strongest negative impact, followed by supervisor, subordinate, and customer incivility. Perceived organizational support buffers these effects. The study contributes to workplace incivility research in collectivist and high power-distance cultures and offers practical implications for hotel management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Registered Report Stage I: Signaling green, securing greenbacks: Sustainability claims and venture funding in hospitality & tourism start-ups
abstract: Tourism's sustainable transition increasingly depends on startups capable of scaling credible innovations. Yet to lead this transformation, they must convince investors that sustainability claims reflect genuine commitment rather than symbolism. This study tests whether, and under what conditions, startups' sustainability communication on X (Twitter) attracts external funding. Integrating signaling and legitimacy theory, we argue that costly, externally validated messages (e.g., stakeholder collaborations or investment-backed actions) enhance pragmatic legitimacy and capital inflow. Analyzing 3869 startups across 94 countries, we link few-shot-classified social-media posts with Crunchbase funding data using a multilevel hurdle model. The study positions startups as the vanguard of tourism's sustainable future, introduces investor funding as an outcome of sustainability communication, and demonstrates a scalable machine-learning approach for field-wide analysis. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Inside and out: Exploring how internal and external CSR perceptions influence hospitality employees’ service sabotage
abstract: Although corporate social responsibility (CSR) has been shown to exert positive effects on hospitality organizations and their stakeholders, the interactive effect of internal CSR (ICSR) and external CSR (ECSR) perceptions on employees’ subsequent service behaviors remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and cue consistency theory, this study aims to explore how the interaction between ICSR and ECSR perceptions influences employees’ service sabotage. Time-lagged data were collected from 366 hotel employees at two time points and analyzed using hierarchical regression. The results indicate that the ICSR × ECSR interaction has a significant effect on employee service sabotage. Specifically, ECSR perceptions suppress service sabotage only when ICSR perceptions are high. This relationship is mediated by perspective taking. Furthermore, corporate reputational identification strengthens the negative effect of perspective taking on service sabotage. This study offers valuable insights for CSR practices in the hospitality industry and points to promising directions for future research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Structural Determinants of Household Resilience in Earthquake-Affected Communities: A Case Study from Bawean Island
abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic impacts of the March 2024 earthquake on household resilience in Bawean Island, East Java, Indonesia. Data for this study were collected through a survey with a snowball sampling technique, with a total of 221 valid respondents from affected regions. Using a household survey across 12 affected villages and partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), the study identifies critical factors contributing to household resilience, namely social, economic, human, and physical capital assets. The findings can be explained in two ways. First, the result confirms social, economic, human, and physical capital as critical resilience determinants. Second, higher household resilience could reduce the impact of natural disasters. This study can be an input for policymakers to strengthen household resilience in disaster-prone areas to support sustainable development goals (SDGs). © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: Participatory short film production and student well-being: A narrative review from media literacy and sociocultural perspectives
abstract: In an AI-driven media ecology, short-form video platforms have intensified interest in participatory filmmaking (PFM) as a learner-centered practice in higher education. However, the relationship between student-led short-film production and holistic well-being remains conceptually scattered and methodologically uneven. This narrative review examines how PFM may support student well-being through media literacy and sociocultural learning processes, with particular attention given to the transferability of these mechanisms to Chinese higher education. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2025 were searched in Scopus, Web of Science, and CNKI using combinations of “participatory video,” “filmmaking,” “higher education,” and “well-being.” A total of 238 records were screened. Studies were excluded if they focused on non-higher-education settings, addressed media consumption rather than student production, contained no interpretable well-being-related outcomes, or lacked peer-reviewed empirical content. Fifteen studies were retained for full analysis. Data were extracted on context, modality, participants, methods, well-being domains, and pedagogical mechanisms and then coded through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke and sensitized by media literacy and sociocultural theory. Three recurring mechanisms emerged: reflective authorship, which supports meaning making, critical judgment, and psychological resilience; collaborative scaffolding, which strengthens belonging, shared regulation, and social confidence; and embodied practice, which connects tool-mediated action to attention, physical vitality, and situated learning. However, the evidence base remains small, course bound, and dominated by short-term qualitative designs, with limited work in non-Western settings. This review therefore proposes the participatory filmmaking well-being framework (PFWF) as an empirically anchored synthesis and outlines implications for curriculum design, student support, and future mechanism-testing research in Chinese universities. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Exemption or backfire? The double-edged effect of AI attribution strategy on brand trust in digital content moral crises
abstract: Human-AI collaboration has become central to brand content production, but AI's black-box nature obscures responsibility in digital content moral crises. When such content is perceived as violating widely shared social values, brands increasingly attribute such incidents to AI errors. Prior research has mainly emphasized the responsibility-exemption role of AI attribution strategy, offering limited insight into its moral risks, mixed consequences, and underlying mechanisms. Drawing on the fact-value model, this study conducts five scenario-based experiments to examine how AI attribution strategy affects brand trust in this crisis context. The findings reveal a double-edged effect. At the factual level, this strategy increases consumers' perceived responsibility reduction, thereby producing an exemption effect that supports trust repair. At the value level, it also triggers perceived moral indifference, thereby producing a backfire effect that damages trust. This double-edged effect is moderated by public opinion and consumer traits. High negative electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) dispersion strengthens the perceived responsibility reduction path, whereas low negative eWOM dispersion strengthens the perceived moral indifference path. AI literacy strengthens the exemption effect by helping consumers understand AI-related technical limitations, whereas hostile attribution bias strengthens the backfire effect by leading consumers to question the moral motives behind the brand's technical explanation. This study advances crisis attribution research by examining AI attribution as a proactive brand communication strategy under attribution ambiguity and shows how it can reduce factual blame while raising value-based moral concerns. The findings offer guidance for using AI attribution carefully and reducing ethical communication risks. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Renewable electricity penetration and retail price dynamics: Global evidence on transitional costs of the energy transition
abstract: The global expansion of renewable energy represents a structural transformation with profound macroeconomic and financial implications. This study investigates the impact of renewable electricity penetration on retail electricity prices using a multi-country panel. The study employs a comprehensive multi-layered empirical framework to address endogeneity, dynamic adjustment, and cross-country structural heterogeneity. The results reveal that renewable penetration is associated with statistically significant short-to medium-term increases in residential electricity prices. However, this effect is nonlinear and conditional on fossil fuel dependence. Once fossil reliance falls below a critical threshold, the marginal price impact weakens substantially. Distributional evidence shows that renewable price effects are amplified in high-price electricity markets. These findings suggest that renewable expansion generates transitional system costs rather than permanent inefficiencies, highlighting the importance of structural conditions in shaping energy transition outcomes and broader economic stability. © 2026 The Authors. title: Hemisphere-aware Graph Convolution and 3D Structural Fusion for multi-modal fMRI brain-disorder classification
abstract: Multimodal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a valuable source of information for precisely classifying neurological disorders, which is why it is widely used in the diagnosis of these diseases. However, traditional methods struggle to capture the spatiotemporal dynamics of the brain and single-modality approaches overlook voxel-level structural information. This limits the accuracy of imaging diagnoses of neurological diseases. This study therefore selected resting-state fMRI samples from the Autism Spectrum Disorder (ABIDE) and Parkinson's Disease (PPMI) datasets, proposing the multi-modal half-brain perception framework MSHAGL. This comprises a shared-weight half-brain–whole-brain graph convolutional network (CHW-GCN) and a three-dimensional structure encoder (GBConvNet3D). These are combined with multi-head gated fusion and redundancy suppression loss for joint optimization. Specifically, dynamic maps of the left and right hemispheres and the whole brain are constructed, cross-scale functional connectivity features are extracted, and 3D fMRI volumes are utilized to capture spatial structural patterns. Gating mechanisms achieve dynamic alignment and weighted fusion of temporal-structural features. In classification experiments on the ABIDE and PPMI datasets for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), the results demonstrate that hemispheric perception modelling and multimodal fusion effectively enhance diagnostic sensitivity and robustness while revealing abnormal connectivity and spatial activation patterns related to disease. This provides new tools for supporting clinical decisions about brain diseases and discovering imaging biomarkers. Our code at https://github.com/Aurora-s-02/MSHAGL. © 2026

title: Text-driven causal mapping of PET/rPET circularity in Australia: A dynamic factor–network analysis
abstract: PET circularity is often evaluated by recovery volumes, although performance ultimately depends on whether recovered material can be converted into quality-assured outputs and absorbed by viable end markets. Yet the mechanisms connecting policy, markets, technology, and stakeholder behavior remain dispersed across heterogeneous evidence. We developed a source-attributed, time-stamped causal-network approach using 750 Australian government, industry and NGO, corporate, and media documents published during 2010–2025. Causal extraction, semantic normalization, sentiment assignment, and graph construction yielded 2794 factor nodes and 1588 unique causal edges. The network was strongly externalized: policy, market, and social factors were more numerous and highly connected than internal technical and operational factors. Persistent barriers combined cost and price volatility, inconsistent recyclate quality, infrastructure gaps, and weak policy implementation. Positive mechanisms clustered around standards and measurement, design for recyclability, operational capacity, and end-market development; their circular value depended on retained material quality and the end use reached. Source attribution revealed systematic framing differences, with media coverage concentrating negative implementation narratives. Temporal and regional analyses indicated a shift from limited attention to rapid expansion and subsequent consolidation, alongside national structural hubs and differentiated state pathways. A full-text academic shadow corpus preserved the broad problem domains but changed their hierarchy: academic evidence foregrounded material and processing mechanisms, whereas the primary corpus foregrounded institutional coordination and market implementation. The contribution is therefore not a universal ranking of Australian interventions, but an auditable framework for identifying how technical feasibility becomes, or fails to become, operational circularity under different institutional conditions. © 2026 The Authors

title: Analysis of retail resilience in Seoul's neighborhood commercial districts Amidst the COVID-19 shock
abstract: This study examines the economic resilience of neighborhood commercial districts in Seoul in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Moving beyond static before–after comparisons, we employ a Panel Interrupted Time Series (Panel ITS) design to separately identify (i) the immediate level shift at the onset of the shock, conceptualized as resistance, and (ii) the subsequent change in the growth trajectory as conditions transitioned toward the endemic phase, conceptualized as recoverability. The results show that structural diversity, operationalized via Shannon's entropy, functions as a key buffering mechanism: it attenuates initial revenue losses and is associated with a steeper post-shock recovery trend. Importantly, we also document pronounced spatial heterogeneity across Seoul's five major sub-markets. Central business districts exhibit heightened exposure and larger initial downturns, while recovery trajectories vary across sub-markets. Taken together, these findings imply that urban management should complement place-based physical upgrading with ecosystem-oriented strategies—specifically, “portfolio diversification” approaches that strengthen sectoral complexity and reduce systemic vulnerability within local commercial ecosystems. © 2026 The Authors.
