title: From smart cities to smart villages: Evolution, domains, and policy implications for smart rural development
abstract: Smart villages have evolved from early parallels with urban smart city models into a comprehensive, multidimensional framework that integrates digital infrastructure, agriculture, local enterprises, tourism, and sustainability. This expanded framework recognizes the unique characteristics and potentials of rural areas, moving beyond the urban-centric logic of technology adoption. This review aims to examine the conceptual evolution of smart village research, track emerging methodological trends, and analyze global implementation trajectories. In the early stages, many studies concentrated on definitional debates and approaches that were primarily centered on technology. However, more recent perspectives have begun to emphasize the importance of integrating technological innovation with social innovation, community empowerment, participatory governance, and environmental stewardship. Methodological approaches have also advanced significantly, shifting from conceptual reflections and single-case studies toward more diverse methods including comparative studies, bibliometric mapping, and participatory action research. These evolving methods enable a deeper and more nuanced understanding of smart village dynamics. Regional approaches demonstrate distinct emphases: European initiatives focus on service revitalization and smart specialization; Asian and African strategies prioritize connectivity, renewable energy access, and digital inclusion; while Latin American programs increasingly integrate climate-smart agricultural practices. Despite regional differences, common challenges remain, including the persistent rural digital divide, fragmented coordination among multiple stakeholders, issues of financial sustainability, and the emergence of new forms of inequality. Policy directions increasingly stress the importance of place-based strategies, building local capacities, establishing supportive governance structures, and fostering inclusive participation. The review concludes by identifying critical areas for future research, such as the creation of unified evaluation metrics, conducting longitudinal impact assessments, and embedding smart village initiatives within broader rural development and climate resilience agendas. Overall, smart villages represent dynamic and promising pathways for driving innovation-led, inclusive, and sustainable rural transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Psychological vulnerability in conversational AI: How incentive and urgency manipulations alter trust formation and privacy behaviour across healthcare, financial, commercial, and security contexts
abstract: Users increasingly interact with conversational AI systems in sensitive domains, yet little is known about how psychological manipulation techniques systematically alter privacy decision-making and trust formation across different contexts. We examined how two manipulation mechanisms, incentive-based (Need & Greed) and urgency-based (Time), influence user behaviour in healthcare, financial, commercial, and home security interactions.In a within-subjects experimental study (N=30[jls-end-space/]) using an interactive, scenario-based methodology, we investigated how context shapes vulnerability to manipulation. Participants engaged with control, Need & Greed, and Time conditions across four domains whilst we measured trust, comfort levels, willingness to disclose information, and perception of privacy and security.Both manipulation techniques significantly reduced comfort (p<0.001[jls-end-space/]) and increased information disclosure (p<0.05[jls-end-space/]), but context moderated these effects substantially. Time pressure increased trust in healthcare contexts whilst decreasing it in financial domains, revealing domain-specific vulnerability patterns. Qualitative analysis identified psychological mechanisms underlying these effects: prior digital experiences, agent characteristics, urgency sensitivity, and context-dependent risk assessment.These findings demonstrate that psychological vulnerability to manipulation operates through context-specific pathways, challenging one-size-fits-all protection approaches. The research provides empirical evidence for developing domain-aware security frameworks that address psychological dimensions alongside technical protections, advancing both human-computer interaction theory and practical system design. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Reputation and value signals as moderators of advertising spend efficiency in E commerce search advertising
abstract: China hosts the world's largest e‑commerce search advertising market, yet merchants persistently misallocate advertising budgets by treating ad spend as a monotonic driver of sales efficiency. Drawing on the Resource‑Based View (RBV) and Information Overload Theory, this study investigates how advertising spend intensity (ASI) affects two core efficiency metrics—the Ad‑to‑Sales Ratio (ASR) and Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), as well as the moderating roles of two structural market factors. Keyword Specificity (KS) reflects the semantic breadth of keywords ranging from generic terms to long‑tail queries, whereas Category Competition Intensity (CCI) captures the density of competing products within each keyword market. Based on keyword‑level panel advertising data from a home appliances and household goods retailer operating on China's leading business‑to‑consumer platform, alongside supplementary observational data on competing products, this study identifies an inverted‑U‑shaped relationship between ASI and both ASR and ROAS: advertising efficiency improves with greater spending initially but declines after crossing a category‑specific threshold. KS shifts the efficiency peak toward higher spend levels, meaning long‑tail keywords can maintain efficiency under greater advertising investment. By contrast, CCI compresses this optimal spending range and triggers earlier efficiency deterioration in highly competitive categories. These findings extend the RBV and Information Overload Theory to sponsored‑search research and provide keyword‑type and competition‑dependent spending benchmarks for practitioners in Chinese e‑commerce. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. The findings of this study will help academics and policy makers to design institutional arrangements which are fit-for-purpose for bringing accountability for nature. © 2026 The Authors. title: Audit fees under accounting and auditing standards: A communicative action perspective
abstract: This study investigates audit fee determination under accounting and auditing standards by moving beyond dominant economic and agency-based explanations toward a critical, normative perspective. The study conceptualizes audit fees as a social construct shaped by the interaction between professional judgment, regulatory systems, and market forces by using Theory of Communicative Action developed by Jürgen Habermas. Using a semisystematic literature review (SsLR), this research synthesizes empirical audit fee studies published between 2010 and 2024 and analyzes them through a Habermasian lens to explore the tension between the auditors’ professional lifeworld and the systemic logic embedded in accounting and auditing standards. A comprehensive search of the Scopus database resulted in a final sample of 33 empirical studies. These studies were then used as the basis for an analysis examining how accounting and auditing regulations contribute to the colonisation of audit fee-setting practices. The findings indicate that standards such as IFRS, auditing standards, and regulatory oversight regimes function as steering mechanisms. These standards orient audit fee determination toward instrumental rationality, compliance, and risk mitigation. While these standards enhance transparency and comparability, they also increase audit complexity, documentation requirements, and litigation risk. The limitation of this study is that it depends on empirical literature with quantitative data. Nevertheless, this study contributes by expanding audit fee research into a normative-communicative framework, highlighting audit fees as a guiding medium in modern audit systems. This study offers a novel critical perspective by positioning audit fees as outcomes of communicative and power relations rather than purely economic transactions. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and fear of missing out: Evidence from network analysis and a daily diary study
abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and fear of missing out (FoMO) are common psychological vulnerabilities during emerging adulthood, yet their item-level organization and daily temporal associations remain underexplored. Study 1 ( N = 875) used item-level network analysis in an undergraduate sample to examine the conditional association structure of IU and FoMO. Study 2 ( N = 235) used a 14-day diary design and dynamic structural equation modeling to examine their within-person temporal associations at the construct level. In Study 1, IU and FoMO formed two communities with stronger within-community than cross-community connections. In Study 2, both constructs showed autoregressive continuity and positive bidirectional cross-lagged associations. Higher daily IU was associated with higher next-day FoMO, while higher daily FoMO was associated with higher next-day IU. Together, the findings describe complementary aspects of the IU-FoMO relationship: Study 1 identifies candidate item-level interface domains, whereas Study 2 independently shows temporal coupling between daily IU and daily FoMO at the construct level. These findings may inform future research and the development of interventions for uncertainty-related distress and socially specific missing-out concerns among college students. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Mechanisms for digital business model innovation in international new ventures from developing economies
abstract: Digital international new ventures (DINVs) increasingly leverage ecosystem partnerships to drive digital business model innovation (DBMI) and navigate global markets. However, research to examine how such partnerships contribute to DBMI is limited, particularly in resource-constrained firms from developing economies. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, organizational learning theory and an ecosystem-based digital learning perspective, we investigate the role of ecosystem partnerships in enabling DBMI through the development of digital learning capabilities. Based on survey data from 147 DINVs in a developing economy, findings suggest that ecosystem partnerships enhance digital learning, which in turn facilitates DBMI. Moreover, foreign market turbulence tends to positively moderate the relationship between ecosystem partnerships and digital learning capability. In addition to demonstrating how DINVs build innovation capacity under volatile conditions, findings help to extend perspectives on capabilities, learning, and ecosystems. Leveraging ecosystem partnerships, digital learning, and digital business model innovation appears to enhance the performance of DINVs. Ecosystem partnerships appear to be especially valuable to DINVs when market turbulence is high. The study offers theoretical and practical insights into the mechanism through which DINVs from developing economies can achieve digital innovation, and provides policy implications for supporting their international growth. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Journey to the bargaining table: Signaling, seeking, and screening
abstract: Negotiation scholarship has focused extensively on what happens at the bargaining table—how parties make offers, manage conflict, and reach agreements. Far less attention has been paid to how parties get to the table in the first place. In this article, we argue that the journey to the table deserves greater scrutiny. We organize pre-table dynamics around three behaviors: signaling (communicating whether and how negotiation might proceed), seeking (approaching a counterpart to propose bargaining), and screening (deciding whether to engage with or withdraw from a seeker). We review recent and foundational work bearing on each, identifying where the field has made progress and where significant gaps remain. These pre-table processes have important implications for negotiated outcomes, for negotiations that never occur, and for understanding how opportunity and bias operate before parties ever sit down together. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How does responsible governance affect firms’ Innovation resilience? A matching perspective on responsible leadership and responsible AI
abstract: Innovation resilience has become a critical capability for firms to withstand risks and achieve sustainable growth. However, how responsible governance shapes firms’ innovation resilience remains underexplored. Drawing on signaling theory and conservation of resources theory, this study examines the effects of responsible leadership, responsible AI, and their congruence on firms’ innovation resilience. Using survey data from 480 firms in China’s manufacturing and strategic emerging industries, we conduct empirical analyses with nonlinear regression and response surface analysis. The results show that: (1) responsible leadership has an inverted U-shaped relationship with firms’ innovation resilience; (2) responsible AI has a negative effect on firms’ innovation resilience; (3) congruence between responsible leadership and responsible AI is conducive to firms’ innovation resilience; (4) firms exhibit higher innovation resilience under the high responsible leadership-high responsible AI configuration than under the low responsible leadership-low responsible AI configuration; (5) compared with the low responsible leadership-high responsible AI configuration, firms achieve higher levels of innovation resilience under the high responsible leadership-low responsible AI configuration; and (6) organizational unlearning and organizational innovation climate positively moderate the effect of responsible leadership-responsible AI congruence on firms’ innovation resilience. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Management: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
abstract: This study presents an examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in the disaster management (DM) cycle to support human decision-making systems. There is an urgent need for holistic application strategies that support disaster risk reduction given the increasing frequency and severity of disaster events. This stems from the growing adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and natural language processing in transforming disaster management. This is to enable the development of high-performance tools for assessing disaster impacts and addressing un-met human needs. This study reviewed journals and conference proceedings articles from three different academic databases: Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Article selection and query refinement were conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to support methodological approach. The review explored scholarly perspectives on AI application in DM phases to support human-centered decision-making processes in reducing disaster impacts on human lives. Findings from the review indicate that most existing studies focus primarily on the AI application in the response phase. Despite its potential, integrating AI into disaster management remains challenging, particularly due to widespread misconceptions about adoption of AI, as well as ongoing ethical, trust, and security concerns. This study emphasizes the comprehensive application of AI to enhance planning, encourage proactive measures, and improve response and recovery efforts during disaster events. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: “The Right to Repair”: A systematic literature review and research agenda for an emerging interdisciplinary field
abstract: The Right to Repair (R2R) is an important arena in which restrictive repair practices, including limits on access to spare parts, manuals, software, and specialised tools, as well as product designs that inhibit repair, are being contested. Although scholarly interest in R2R is growing rapidly, research remains fragmented across disciplinary and empirical domains, limiting the development of a coherent understanding of its implications for technology-society relations. In response, this paper presents a systematic literature review that maps and synthesises existing research on R2R. Specifically, it (1) consolidates empirical evidence on the implications of R2R; (2) examines how the concept has been theorised across disciplines; and (3) identifies key conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. By organising this literature into coherent thematic domains and tracing the relationships between them, the review argues that the effective realisation of R2R depends on a socio-technical capacity: the practically exercisable ability to repair produced through the interaction between legal entitlements, technological architectures, economic arrangements, and social capabilities. It also reveals disciplinary and geographical imbalances and identifies four tensions structuring future research: formal ownership versus effective control, legal entitlement versus practical repair capacity, universal frameworks versus situated repair practices, and systemic transformation versus continuity. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: The Olympic effect revisited: 1950–2019
abstract: Rose and Spiegel (2011) identified a positive trade-promoting effect of hosting the Olympic Games, yet they did not account for multilateral resistance terms in their analysis, which are emphasized in the structural gravity model by Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). This paper revisits the trade effects of the Olympics using a nonparametric matching method developed by Chang and Lee (2011), analyzing a comprehensive gravity dataset encompassing 187 economies from 1950 to 2019. Our findings suggest that hosting the Olympics is positively associated with bilateral trade. For pairs in which both countries have hosted, the matching estimate corresponds to a long-run trade difference with an implied increase of approximately 15 times relative to matched nonhost pairs. Under an assumed trade elasticity of 4, this estimate corresponds to an illustrative trade-cost equivalent of approximately 50%. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Artificial intelligence is not enough to enhance organizational performance
abstract: This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI), supply chain visibility, supplier integration, and organizational performance through the lens of Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT). Drawing on empirical data from UK-based organizations that have adopted AI technologies, we employ structural equation modeling along with mediation and moderation analyses to test our hypotheses. The findings indicate that AI does not have a significant direct effect on performance; instead, its impact is fully mediated through supply chain visibility and supplier integration. This supports the view that AI-driven supply chain visibility acts as an information-processing mechanism that enhances firms' ability to coordinate, collaborate, and integrate with supply chain partners, thereby improving organizational performance. Furthermore, supply uncertainty positively moderates the relationship between supplier integration and performance, amplifying the benefits under conditions of higher uncertainty. This study contributes to the literature by clarifying AI's indirect role in driving performance and highlighting the importance of embedding AI within broader organizational capabilities. It also offers practical insights for managers seeking to leverage AI to enhance supply chain integration and organizational effectiveness. © 2026

title: Your recommendation and my choice: The impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion
abstract: Personalized recommendation features launched by integrated online shopping platforms with multi-brand competition trap consumers in the dilemma of product choice constrained by algorithmic recommendation convergence, and induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. Against this backdrop, this article systematically examines the existence, antecedents, and boundaries of consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. The results show that algorithmic recommendation convergence significantly triggers consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion and suppresses their purchase intentions. Specifically, in addition to perceived lack of self-control affecting algorithmic recommendation aversion, consumers' state of choice overload caused by homogeneous recommendation convergence is the key reason for perceived lack of self-control and the emergence of algorithmic recommendation aversion. Meanwhile, the results further demonstrate that in multi-brand markets with multi-oligopolistic brand coexistence, brand agglomeration further narrows consumers' brand and product choice scope, making it more likely to induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. In contrast, in a single-brand-dominated market structure, the core brand effect can leverage its dominant market position and market recognition to mitigate the impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. These findings expand the research perspective on consumer algorithmic bias, emphasize the importance of brand strategies, and provide timely and critical insights for understanding and alleviating consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Phygital pop-up stores: Measuring immersion, novelty, and post-visit purchase behavior using eye-tracking and biometrics
abstract: Phygital pop-up stores hybrid retail environments fusing physical spaces with digital layers represent an accelerating frontier in contemporary retailing. However, the precise cognitive mechanisms through which these sensor-driven environments translate immediate sensory engagement into durable long-term consumer choices remain under-theorized. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model, Expectation Confirmation Theory, and Trust Theory, this study develops an integrated model positioning consumer trust as a critical mediator between phygital experiential antecedents and downstream purchasing commitments. Primary data were collected from 612 adult consumers across the United Kingdom and Australia via a stratified intercept sampling protocol. Objective measures of consumer immersion were captured using eye-tracking metrics and galvanic skin response indices embedded within a structured self-report survey. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) reveals that while immersive experiences, novelty, interactivity, and enjoyment associate positively with retrospective post-visit purchase behavior within a 30-day window (R2 = 0.482), consumer trust functions as the dominant direct predictor (β = 0.274, p < 0.001) and an essential gatekeeper mediating the immersion–purchase pathway. Multi-group analysis indicates that tech experience significantly moderates immersion and interactivity tracks, whereas gender exhibits structural invariance. This biometrically validated framework offers strategic resource-allocation priorities for experiential retail developers. © 2026

title: Carbon trading in community-based forest management: A bibliometric mapping of scientific publications from 2000 to 2025
abstract: Carbon trading in community-based forest management (CBFM) has emerged as a promising mechanism for simultaneously addressing climate change mitigation and improving the welfare of rural communities. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 203 scientific publications obtained from Scopus, covering the period 2000 to 2025, with an analytical focus on the period 2010-2024. Using VOSviewer v.1.6.20 and Scopus's built-in analysis, this study analyzes publication trends, author participation patterns, geographic distribution, journal sources, and thematic structure through author collaboration, co-occurrence of keywords, and bibliographic linking networks. Results show a sharp acceleration in publication growth following key climate policy milestones, including the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (2013), the Paris Agreement (2015), and COP26 (2021), with a record 21 articles published in 2024. Nepal and Indonesia emerged as dominant knowledge producers, collectively contributing 42.4% of total publications. Thematic mapping identified three main research clusters: carbon governance in CBFM, carbon measurement and quantification, and multifunctional forest landscape ecology. A critical knowledge gap was identified: while the supply side of carbon measurement of forest carbon stocks and biomass has been well documented, the demand side of how communities access, negotiate, and fairly obtain benefits from carbon markets remains largely unexplored. These findings underscore the urgent need for interdisciplinary research that links technical carbon measurement with institutional, economic, and social dimensions of equity to promote fair and scalable carbon trading within the framework of community forest governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: The effects of adolescents' digital and environmental literacy on parents’ green consumption: A reverse intergenerational socialization perspective
abstract: Drawing on reverse socialization theory, this study examines how adolescents' digital and environmental literacy influence parents' green consumption behavior (GCB). Using matched adolescent–parent survey data, we employ PLS-SEM to test net and mediating effects and fsQCA to identify configurational pathways leading to high levels of parents' GCB. The results show that adolescents' digital literacy and environmental literacy are both positively associated with parents' GCB. Parents' decision-making confidence mediates the relationship between adolescents' digital literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a capability empowerment pathway, whereas parents' personal norms mediate the relationship between adolescents' environmental literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a norm activation pathway. The fsQCA results further identify nine configurational pathways, indicating that parents’ GCB is characterized by equifinality and conditional substitution. This study extends reverse socialization theory to the context of family green consumption and offers practical implications for promoting green consumption within families. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Don't promise me, prove it: Leveraging blockchain affordances to reduce uncertainty and build consumer purchase confidence in sustainable fashion
abstract: While the role of blockchain technology in shaping sustainable consumer behaviors is increasingly examined, empirical understanding of its capability to reduce uncertainty and enhance consumers' purchase confidence remains limited, particularly within the sustainable fashion context. In addressing this gap, the current study examines how blockchain affordances, including transparency, traceability, and immutability, contribute to sustainable product uncertainty reduction (SPUR) and strengthen consumers’ purchase confidence. It further examines the mediating roles of perceived information diagnosticity (PID), perceived sustainable product quality (PSPQ), and the moderating role of information literacy (IL). A hybrid PLS-SEM and fsQCA approach was applied to analyze the data from 437 Vietnamese Gen Z sustainable fashion consumers. PLS-SEM results reveal that blockchain affordances indirectly affect purchase confidence, primarily through PID and PSPQ rather than SPUR, with IL exhibiting mixed moderated mediation effects. Complementarily, fsQCA identifies ten solution configurations leading to high purchase confidence and seven associated with its absence. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Negotiation and relationships: Insights from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature
abstract: Negotiations often unfold within ongoing relationships, making relationships integral to negotiation processes and outcomes. Yet, despite repeated calls for greater attention to relational dynamics, behavioral negotiation research has largely relied on paradigms that minimize the role of relationships. We review research from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature (e.g., on close relationships, marketing, strategy, and operations) that conceptualize negotiation as embedded within ongoing relationships. We show that negotiations in relationships unfold under distinct starting conditions that shape negotiators’ interpretations, judgments of appropriateness and risk, and the interplay between negotiation processes, outcomes, and the longer-term relationship. As a result, negotiations in relationships often involve managing both objective and relational interests simultaneously, producing beliefs, behaviors, and outcomes that differ from dominant findings in behavioral negotiation research. We conclude by encouraging more dynamic, relationally embedded perspectives and methods that capture how negotiation unfolds across ongoing relationships and repeated interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Registered Report - Stage II: Do good, feel luckier: How cause-related marketing in unpredictable tourism products boosts tourists’ purchase intention?
abstract: Marketing unpredictable tourism experiences like aurora or wildlife viewing poses distinct challenges due to their inherent uncertainty, yet research on effective strategies remains limited. In Stage I of this Registered Report, we proposed that cause-related marketing (CRM) would boost purchase intention for unpredictable tourism products more effectively than traditional discounts by activating a karmic investment mechanism (i.e., self-luck expectancy), especially under consumer-focused framing. Through an eye-tracking experiment, a quasi-experimental field study, and three scenario-based experiments, we found no conclusive evidence that CRM outperforms discounts in increasing purchase intention, nor support for the mediating role of self-luck expectancy. Although a moderating influence of protagonist focus was observed, its effect contradicted our hypothesis. However, an unexpected finding emerged: luck primes significantly elevate self-luck expectancy and enhance purchase intention. These results suggest that practitioners should either exercise caution in deploying standard CRM from a cost-benefit perspective or enhance its utility by fostering deeper consumer moral engagement. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Political elites and access to economic opportunities in China's rural market transition
abstract: Understanding whether political elites maintain advantages in accessing economic opportunities during market transitions is crucial for assessing the distributional consequences of market-oriented reforms. This study examines whether political status provides rural households with advantages in accessing production resources and income opportunities during China's recent wave of marketization, and how these advantages vary with the degree of market development. Using three waves of the China Family Database spanning 2015–2019 and employing an instrumental variable approach, we find that political elites maintain persistent advantages in accessing economic opportunities. Relative to non-elites, cadre households exhibit 20.1 percentage points higher rates of receiving agricultural subsidies, 38.8 percentage points higher rates of owning agricultural machinery, and 9.7 percentage points greater likelihood of operating nonfarm businesses. As marketization advances, the sources of elite advantage shift from agriculture to commercial activities. While advantages in agricultural production weaken, reflecting reduced state-controlled resource allocation channels, advantages in business operations strengthen consistent with elites converting political capital into entrepreneurial opportunities. Our findings suggest that rural marketization in China reallocates rather than reduces opportunity gaps. This pattern indicates that even as market reforms diminish traditional avenues for political privilege, they simultaneously open new market-based opportunities that preserve elite advantage. These findings have broader implications for understanding how political power influences access to opportunities during market transitions in developing economies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Using emojis to uplift emotion: Effects on mental health chatbots’ performance
abstract: As AI-based chatbots increasingly expand access to mental health support, understanding how text-based systems convey emotional attentiveness without face-to-face nonverbal cues is important. Emojis may serve as lightweight paralinguistic cues, yet their effects in mental health support remain unclear. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and psychological ownership theory, this study examines associations between emoji use and users’ emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Two scenario-based online experiments were conducted in China using random sampling through Credamo, yielding 459 valid responses (59 in the pretest and 400 in the main study). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and the PROCESS macro. Across the experiments, emoji use was associated with more favorable emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Mediation analyses supported an indirect pathway through perceived warmth and psychological ownership, whereas the corresponding competence-based pathway was not supported. AI literacy strengthened the perceived warmth–psychological ownership association but, contrary to predictions, weakened the perceived competence–psychological ownership association. Moderated mediation analyses provided preliminary support for AI literacy strengthening the warmth-based indirect effects of emoji use on emotional well-being and continuance usage intention. The corresponding effect on satisfaction was not supported. These findings extend research on AI-mediated mental health support by identifying a warmth–psychological ownership pathway and the differentiated role of AI literacy. The study also offers preliminary, context-bounded guidance for the strategic and context-sensitive use of emojis in supportive, non-clinical chatbot interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees
abstract: Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings. © 2026

title: Spatial optimization of land use for synergizing economic development and carbon neutrality based on an efficiency-driven PLUS model
abstract: Optimizing land-use allocation is important for achieving regional carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality targets. Existing land-use simulation studies generally incorporate carbon objectives through ex-post assessment or macro-level land-demand optimization, leaving historical grid-level carbon–economic performance disconnected from future spatial allocation. To further address this limitation, we developed LUCE-PLUS, a framework that links grid-scale land-transition accounting and efficiency evaluation with PLUS-based spatial simulation. Using Jiujiang City, China, as a case study, we quantified conversion costs, economic-output changes, and carbon emissions induced by observed land-use transitions from 2010 to 2020 at a 30-m resolution. A single-stage mixed-integer linear programming super-efficiency range-adjusted measure (Sup-RAM) model treated carbon emissions as a weakly disposable undesirable output and enabled discrimination among efficient grid-level transition units while ensuring Pareto-efficient projections. The resulting surfaces of economic efficiency and carbon–economic synergy efficiency were incorporated into PLUS as scenario-specific predictors of land-use expansion probabilities. Land-use patterns in 2030 were simulated under natural-development, economic-dominant, and carbon–economic dual-objective scenarios while aggregate land demand and planning constraints were held constant. Mean carbon–economic synergy efficiency was 20.5% lower than mean economic efficiency, indicating that economic efficiency alone may understate the carbon-related environmental costs of land-use transitions. Compared with the dual-objective scenario, the economic-dominant scenario increased the projected GDP increment by only 0.04% but raised land-use-change-induced carbon emissions by 7.3%. Impervious-land expansion under the dual-objective scenario also showed a stronger tendency toward locations associated with lower carbon-stock losses. LUCE-PLUS therefore provides a performance-informed approach to low-carbon spatial allocation under fixed land-demand targets. From an environmental impact assessment perspective, the framework could support alternatives analysis in strategic environmental assessment of territorial spatial plans by enabling ex ante comparison of projected land-use patterns, carbon-stock changes, and economic outcomes under consistent planning constraints. © 2026

title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy
abstract: Influencer marketing has become an integral part of retail branding strategies. As the creator economy continues to expand, influencer collaborations are now viewed as strategic partnerships rather than promotional activities. Despite this transition, sustaining authentic and long-term brand-influencer partnerships remains a significant yet underexplored challenge. Combining Social Exchange Theory (SET) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT) into a unified motivational-exchange framework, this research focuses on how brand practices operate simultaneously as relational exchange resources and as psychological need-satisfying inputs within influencer–brand partnerships. With a mixed-methods two-phase approach, this study exmains how brand ethical–purpose alignment, autonomy support, and AI co-creation are linked to influencers' sense of ownership and thriving, as well as citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity. In Study 1, 22 semi-structured interviews were conducted with professional influencers across four regions, intended to understand their lived partnership experiences. In Study 2, responses from 422 influencers were analysed using structural equation modelling and moderation analysis. The study also examines serial indirect pathways through which brand practices are associated with voluntary citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity via Collaboration Ownership and Influencer Thriving. The findings suggest that autonomy support, purpose alignment, and AI co-creation enablement are positively associated with influencers' ownership and thriving. These again are associated with higher levels of voluntary advocacy and intentions to continue partnerships. Therefore, the research positions influencer collaboration as relational rather than transactional and highlights the significance of autonomy, ethical-purpose congruence, and relational fairness in understanding sustainable relationships between influencers and brands. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How local–global identity shapes physical-digital preferences through convenience preference
abstract: Despite the functional advantages of digital products, consumers’ preferences between digital and physical formats remain highly heterogeneous in a marketplace where globalization and renewed localism coexist. Drawing on identity-based motivation theory, this research examines how local versus global identity influences consumers' preferences for physical versus digital products through convenience preference. Across three studies (five sub-studies), we demonstrate that a relatively stronger local-over-global identity is associated with greater preference for physical over digital consumption formats. Further analyses reveal an asymmetric effect that local identity drives stronger preferences for physical products, whereas global identity does not produce a corresponding increase in preference for digital formats. We further identify convenience preference as the underlying mechanism, showing that stronger local identity reduces convenience preference, thereby increasing preference for physical products. These findings reconceptualize physical versus digital preferences as identity-consistent choices rather than purely functional evaluations. By identifying convenience as an identity-contingent motivational preference, this research advances identity-based motivation theory and provides timely insights into how identity orientations shape consumer preferences amid ongoing digital transformation and heightened societal attention to globalization–localism dynamics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Natural Hazards, Critical Infrastructure Systems, and Resilience Enhancement: A Structured State-of-the-Art Review and a Synthesis-Based Rapid Assessment Framework
abstract: Critical infrastructure systems (CISs) are increasingly exposed to natural hazards whose impacts are amplified by infrastructure interdependence, urban complexity, and the growing prevalence of compound and cascading events. Existing research provides valuable insights into individual hazards, infrastructure components, modeling methods, and resilience metrics, but these insights remain difficult to translate into preliminary decision support because they are organized across different hazard types, sectors, analytical scales, and decision contexts. This article presents a structured state-of-the-art review of natural hazards, CIS impacts, and resilience enhancement. A two-pathway review strategy was adopted. A Web of Science (WoS) core search was used to characterize the bibliometric landscape and identify WoS-sourced core synthesis studies, while a targeted anchor-search pathway was used to verify foundational concepts, hazard mechanisms, methodological approaches, resilience frameworks, and authoritative institutional sources. The review clarifies the conceptual distinction among dependencies, interdependencies, compound hazards, cascading failures, service disruption, and resilience; synthesizes cross-hazard infrastructure impact mechanisms; compares major method families for hazard-impact and resilience assessment; and develops a synthesis-derived rapid resilience assessment framework for preliminary screening and prioritization under constrained data and time conditions. The synthesis indicates that future CIS resilience assessment would benefit from moving beyond isolated asset-damage analysis toward integrated workflows that link hazard loading, component vulnerability, network functionality, service consequences, recovery capacity, uncertainty, and feasible intervention choices. The article contributes a more transparent evidence-source structure, an evidence-to-decision bridge, and a bounded decision-oriented framework for organizing future research and practical resilience screening. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

title: Imperfection in motion: Implied motion reduces negative associations of imperfect produce
abstract: Food waste remains a major sustainability challenge, with imperfect fruits and vegetables often rejected due to their appearance. Prior studies suggest that food choices are mostly automatic, implicit, and habitual, rather than made through deliberated choice. Such insights suggest why explicit messaging to increase consumers' imperfect food purchasing has shown limited effectiveness and highlight opportunities for behaviour change via less mindful means. This study investigates the extent to which negative implicit associations for “imperfect” (vs. “perfect”) exist, and whether implied motion (e.g., fruit splashing into water) can mitigate these evaluations. In a pre-registered study, participants (N = 145) completed an in-person multi-dimensional Implicit Association Test (IAT) to examine their implicit attitudes in static and motion contexts. Results showed that participants' implicit associations were positive for perfect produce and negative for imperfect produce, suggesting an “Ugly = Bad” association. However, exposure to implied motion imagery significantly reduced this negativity effect toward imperfect fresh produce, while having no significant effect on perfect produce. Our findings link implicit attitudes to sustainable food acceptance and demonstrate the potential of visually-based interventions, such as implied motion, to reduce negative aesthetic biases and support behaviour change aimed at increasing acceptance of imperfect produce and reducing food waste. © 2026 The Authors

title: Examining the layered veil of pay transparency: Implications for perceived ambiguity, sensemaking, and negotiation
abstract: In the last decade, pay transparency—making pay information more accessible and understandable—has become a defining workplace reform. We examine the common assumption that pay transparency reduces pay disparities by improving negotiation outcomes. Our cross-disciplinary review suggests that pay transparency's effects on negotiation hinge on three factors: (1) how transparency is operationalized (i.e., what type of pay information is shared); (2) how people interpret the information provided; and (3) whether transparency alone can motivate and equip individuals to leverage that information to negotiate effectively. We distinguish three interrelated negotiation-relevant layers of pay transparency—job offer, peer, and market—and then assess how these reduce ambiguity, shape negotiator sensemaking, and influence negotiation processes and outcomes. We conclude by outlining implications for future negotiation research and practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Teaching by example? Teacher ICT use and middle school students’ computer and information literacy across China and the United States
abstract: Background: In the digital era, Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) has become a crucial educational outcome. While teacher Information and Communication Technology (ICT) use is widely promoted to enhance student digital skills, its effectiveness may vary significantly across different national education systems. Aims: This study investigates the impact of teacher ICT use on middle school students' CIL in China and the United States. It aims to compare these cross-national effects and examine the mediating roles of school ICT resources and institutional support in shaping these relationships. Methods: Using nationally representative data from the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) 2023, this research employs regression models and instrumental variable (2SLS) methods to address potential endogeneity. Mediation analyses further explore how school-level factors transmit teacher ICT effects. Results: The analysis reveals striking cross-country differences: in China, all dimensions of teacher ICT use significantly improved students' CIL, whereas these effects were statistically insignificant in the United States. School ICT resources and support fully mediated teacher ICT effects in China but only partially mediated ability effects in the U.S. Additionally, student background factors consistently influenced CIL across both countries. Conclusion: While teacher ICT experience demonstrates universal importance, the broader impact of instructional ICT practices depends critically on national context and institutional support systems. The findings highlight the complex interplay between teacher practices, school resources, and national educational environments in shaping digital literacy outcomes. © 2026

title: Disclosing AI without losing consumers: When and how AI disclosure works in advertising
abstract: Extant research on AI disclosure examines its negative impact across various domains, but limited attention has been paid to why these effects occur and how they can be mitigated in advertising. To address this gap, we examine why consumers react negatively to AI disclosures in advertising, identify the boundary of this effect, and propose strategies to mitigate it. Across three studies, we show that AI disclosure reduces consumers’ attitudes toward the advertisement and purchase intentions through decreased perceived creativity. More importantly, we find that product type serves as a boundary condition for this effect, and that the negative influence of AI disclosure (vs. human designer disclosure) is attenuated when AI is identified as an employee. Implications for both theories and practices are discussed. © 2026

title: Models for risk management in the procurement process within organizational contexts: A systematic literature review
abstract: Over the past decade, supply chain management has faced extreme volatility, culminating in the unprecedented disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, resilience in procurement has transitioned from a secondary attribute to an indispensable requirement for operational continuity. This study classifies the state of the art in procurement risk management within the post-pandemic landscape (2021–2025). It analyzes the transition from reactive approaches toward predictive and prescriptive perspectives to address supply chain volatility. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Based on a structured search in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, an initial pool of 1,109 records was screened. This resulted in a final sample of 107 high-impact peer-reviewed articles. These studies were evaluated using thematic content analysis and classified into ten technical categories based on their functional orientation. The evidence reveals a fragmented methodological ecosystem where Hybrid Models (21.5%) and Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM, 16.8%) techniques predominate. A shift is observed from static approaches toward the integration of robust optimization, tail risk metrics like Conditional Value at Risk, and Machine Learning. However, a gap is identified between algorithmic complexity and corporate adoption. The study establishes that Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Blockchain are indispensable governance requirements to overcome the black box problem in strategic decision-making. This research contributes a functional classification of tools based on their diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive orientation. Furthermore, it provides managers with a tiered roadmap to achieve analytical maturity. This guides organizations from foundational visibility using synthetic indices, through fuzzy multi-criteria evaluations, toward the responsible implementation of stochastic programming and AI. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Perceived control and stress reactivity in algorithm-supported hiring decisions
abstract: Algorithms increasingly determine who gets interviewed, flagged, or passed over in hiring, often without explanation, consistency, or any mechanism for response. Yet the psychological mechanisms through which algorithm-supported decision-making shapes stress responses remain insufficiently specified. This article develops a theoretically grounded framework linking diminished perceived control to stress reactivity in algorithm-mediated decision-making contexts. Drawing on self-determination theory, decision-making process frameworks, and psychological safety, the manuscript integrates empirical evidence from research on AI hiring practices, including findings on Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) individuals navigating applicant tracking systems. The framework identifies three primary mechanisms through which AI-supported decision-making may influence stress reactivity: limited transparency, inconsistent decision processes, and constrained opportunities for feedback. This work offers a foundation for empirical work on how technologically mediated environments shape cognitive appraisal, perceived control, and stress. These dynamics extend beyond hiring to any structured assessment context in applied behavioral and clinical settings. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. title: The persuasive power of video in hospitality: How guest-generated video reviews influence customer engagement
abstract: Guest-generated video reviews are increasingly prevalent on online travel platforms, yet their effects and mechanisms remain underexplored. Drawing on media richness theory, this study is among the first to examine whether and how such reviews enhance customer engagement, measured by subsequent review volume. We adopt a multimethod approach that combines econometric analysis with a controlled experiment to establish causal inference and uncover underlying mechanisms. Using a 24-month panel of 4471 hotels on Ctrip.com, difference-in-differences results show that guest-generated video reviews significantly increase customer engagement, with stronger effects for higher-tier or large hotels. Experimental evidence further demonstrates that these effects operate through increased information diagnosticity and social presence. Additional video content analysis reveals that human presence, higher informational richness, better visual quality, and longer duration further amplify the positive effects. These findings extend media richness theory to consumer-generated video reviews and offer insights into how richer review media stimulate engagement in hospitality settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The road to hell is paved with good intentions: How does the construction of low-carbon cities affect corporate low-carbon technological innovation in manufacturing?
abstract: Low-carbon technological innovation (LCTI) is crucial for decarbonization and global climate change mitigation. Taking China's Low-carbon City Pilot (LCCP)—a pioneering exploration for low-carbon development through policy innovation—as an exogenous policy shock, this study utilizes a staggered difference-in-difference-in-differences model and the data of China's manufacturing firms to examine the causality between the voluntary carbon regulation and LCTI. For the first time, the results indicate that the LCCP enactment significantly hinders corporate LCTI, contradicting the predictions of the Porter hypothesis. Mechanism analysis reveals that under the LCCP framework, local governments are authorized to design innovative policies tailored to their specific conditions and are responsible for their own assessment. Using a two-stage LLM-based approach to construct a climate policy uncertainty perception index, we confirm that this “bottom-up” approach introduces significant policy uncertainty faced by firms and weakens their motivation for LCTI involvement. Furthermore, the compliance costs associated with the policy crowd out the funds for LCTI, further hindering firms from engaging in LCTI. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the adverse impact is more evident among firms exhibiting high risk aversion, ones with high artificial intelligence (AI) technology exposure, ones situated in non-resource-based cities, and state-owned ones, and that the adverse impact is significant for emission reduction technologies and zero-carbon technologies, but not for negative-carbon technologies. Additionally, all three pilot batches negatively impact corporate LCTI, suggesting that institutional modifications have not led to intended positive outcomes. This empirical research offers novel evidence regarding the efficacy of the LCCP and yields valuable policy insights—stable policy expectations and robust supervision mechanisms are crucial for achieving policy goals. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Exploring Italian consumer perceptions and acceptance of innovative foods and food technologies: insights from a national survey
abstract: Innovative foods and food technologies face barriers to adoption in Italy, where food plays a central role in identity and social life. This study investigates Italian consumer responses to seven innovative food products and technologies using a consumer survey (N = 2000), stratified by age, gender, and geographical region. The survey included psychometric scales assessing food neophobia, food technology neophobia, disgust sensitivity, trust, sensation seeking, and health interest. It measured perceptions of risk, benefit, familiarity, and emotions associated with each product. Findings indicate that Italian consumers show high levels of food and technological neophobia, coupled with low trust and strong health concerns. Acceptability varied significantly across sociodemographic groups: higher education and income were associated with higher trust and sensation seeking and lower neophobia, whereas female and older respondents exhibited higher disgust sensitivity and greater resistance to innovation. Exploratory clustering identified two broad clusters of aggregated consumer profiles. One cluster was associated with younger age, higher educational attainment and household income, together with greater trust and sensation seeking, whereas the other was associated with older age, lower educational attainment and household income, together with greater food and food technology neophobia and disgust sensitivity. Emotional responses emerged as correlates of acceptability, with curiosity most positively and disgust most negatively. Products most aligned with product ideals were plant-based proteins, algae, and unusual fruits, while insect-based proteins and cultured meat faced the greatest barriers. These findings highlight the importance of reinforcing trust and curiosity while addressing disgust to promote sustainable Italian food innovation. © 2026 The Authors

title: Not naive, just gullible: psycho-cognitive vulnerability and fraud victimization in Italy
abstract: Fraud represents a growing and complex threat in contemporary societies, with consequences that extend beyond economic losses. Despite increasing international evidence, limited research has examined the psychological and cognitive factors associated with fraud victimization in the Italian context, particularly in relation to online scams. This study examines individual differences and fraud experiences among 600 Italian adults through an online survey assessing sociodemographic characteristics, fraud experiences, personality traits, gullibility, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy. Results revealed that more than half of the sample (n = 416) reported exposure to scam attempts, most of which occurred through remote channels (either exclusively online or in combination with offline channels). A smaller subset (n = 115) reported actual fraud victimization. A binomial logistic regression was conducted to identify individual factors associated with fraud victimization among exposed individuals. Gullibility emerged as the only statistically significant predictor, indicating that higher gullibility was associated with a greater likelihood of victimization, whereas sociodemographic characteristics, personality traits, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy were not significantly associated with victimization. These findings highlight that fraud prevention strategies may benefit from considering psycho-cognitive vulnerability factors alongside traditional financial and digital literacy initiatives. © 2026

title: Sensing the path forward: AI as amplifier in sensory and consumer science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how sensory and consumer data are collected, analyzed, and used. A common fear is that algorithms will displace trained panels and that predictive models will replace expert judgment. We argue the opposite: as AI automates what is easy to formalize, the value of what only humans can do (embodied sensing, cultural interpretation, ethical judgment, and meaning-making) rises. This paper is not a systematic review. It advocates a particular perspective (AI as amplifier of sensory expertise), informed by on-the-ground experience through the recent rise of large language models, including what has worked and what has not in practice. Three industry case studies from PepsiCo, Danone, and Kenvue support that perspective. The principles (knowledge management, automation, predictive modeling, people-centered adoption; humans in the loop; culture before algorithms) are meant to apply beyond large companies, including academia and smaller groups. That perspective also guided a selective literature reading focused on Food Quality and Preference and related journals, mainly from 2022 to early 2026. We clarify what AI is and is not, trace the path from chemometrics to neuromorphic sensing, and describe a four-pillar framework from a Pangborn 2025 industry workshop. Self-reported case outcomes include up to 50% faster analysis and a 75% reduction in reporting time; calculation details were not disclosed to us and the figures are not independently validated. The three organizations built the same capabilities in different orders and met the same barriers (culture, talent, IT collaboration). We also propose narrative-driven analysis with large language models and a near-term research agenda. Central message: when machines predict, humans must decide. © 2026

title: Empowering leadership in educational contexts: A bibliometric analysis to guide management in the framework of SDG 4
abstract: Empowering leadership (EL) has emerged as a critical leadership approach in educational contexts, particularly in response to increasing demands for innovation, teacher autonomy, and sustainable institutional development. However, despite the rapid growth of studies in this field, the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, thematic evolution, and contribution to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) remain fragmented and insufficiently synthesized. Therefore, this study aims to provide a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of EL research in educational settings indexed in the Scopus database from 1999 to 2026. A total of 84 publications were analyzed using bibliometric performance indicators and science mapping techniques, including co-authorship analysis, keyword co-occurrence, three-field plot visualization, citation analysis, and thematic clustering, supported by Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. The results reveal a strong upward publication trend with a coefficient of determination of R² = 77.54%, particularly accelerating after 2018 and reaching the highest output in 2025. Citation influence remains concentrated in foundational studies published in high-impact journals such as Journal of Applied Psychology, Journal of Knowledge Management, and Leadership Quarterly. China and Indonesia emerge as major international collaboration hubs, while Indonesia shows the strongest author–keyword linkage. Keyword analysis identifies dominant themes related to psychological empowerment, teacher autonomy, innovative work behavior, job satisfaction, and distributed leadership. Notably, 74 out of 84 publications (88.1%) are aligned with SDG 4, highlighting the strong integration of EL research with global educational sustainability agendas. This study offers the first structured intellectual map of EL in education, identifies influential contributors and emerging research directions, and provides evidence-based guidance for educational leadership development aligned with quality education and sustainable transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Prioritizing configuration relevance via compiler-based refined feature ranking
abstract: Modern programming languages, most notably Rust, offer advanced linguistic constructs for building highly configurable software systems as aggregations of features—identified by a configuration. However, they pose substantial challenges for program analysis, optimization, and testing, as the combinatorial explosion of configurations often makes exhaustive exploration infeasible. In this manuscript, we present the first compiler-based method for prioritizing configurations. Our approach consists of four main steps: (1) extracting a tailored intermediate representation from the Rust compiler, (2) constructing two complementary graph-based data structures—a feature dependency graph capturing inter-feature code-level dependencies weighted by predicate structure, and an atom dependency tree encoding the extent of code governed by each feature—, (3) using centrality measures to rank features, and (4) refining the ranking by considering the extent of code they impact. A fixed number of most relevant configurations are generated based on the achieved feature ranking. The validity of the generated configurations is guaranteed by using a SAT solver that takes a representation of feature dependencies in conjunctive normal form. We formalized this approach and implemented it in a prototype, RUSTYEX, by instrumenting the Rust compiler. An empirical evaluation on higher-ranked open-source Rust projects shows that RUSTYEX efficiently generates user-specified sets of configurations within bounded resources, while ensuring soundness by construction. The results demonstrate that centrality-guided configuration prioritization enables practical exploration of large configuration spaces, and we discuss the implications and open challenges for future configuration-aware analysis and optimization. © 2026 The Authors

title: The neglected dimension: Arousal, emotions and product choices
abstract: This article presents an overview of the ways in which arousal may be an important influence on consumer product choices. It is recognised that the recent emphasis on measures of emotions in consumer studies has its origins in the limitations of measures of liking to predict choices, and that there is evidence that such measures have added value to traditional hedonic ratings. The possibility that this improvement derives from the fact arousal is implicitly included in emotion measures is considered. In addition, measuring arousal may avoid some of the uncontrolled aspects of measuring emotions, including those related to individual variability in language use. The research evidence for arousal being directly involved in consumer decision making is discussed. Finally, there is an overview of the ways in which arousal can be assessed in consumer studies. © 2026 The Author

title: Hero products and the value of position in live streaming commerce evidence from Douyin
abstract: Every livestream sales session has one product that sells best, and the minutes in which it is shown are when the broadcast's audience peaks. This paper asks what that moment is worth to the products around it: can the items that follow the hero, or those shown just before it, turn the traffic it attracts into sales of their own? Using 260,252 product–session observations from 8123 Douyin sessions and an event-study design with session fixed effects, we find conversion highest in the slot immediately after the hero, exceeding products more than five positions away by 0.0177. The advantage is not borrowed traffic. It appears before the hero as much as after it, and only the adjacent slot breaks that symmetry; when the same product is compared with itself across sessions in which it sat at different distances, most of the advantage disappears except beside the hero. The running order therefore reveals mainly which products a streamer places near the featured item, and we report a positional association rather than an attention spillover. What survives is conditional. Scoring each product's own listing title with a large language model, we find that credibility signals attenuate the advantage while informativeness moves it in both directions, and the advantage exists only where the hero appears in the first third of the running order, vanishing when it is held until the end. For managers, the slots flanking an early-placed hero are worth allocating deliberately; positions further down the lineup are not. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: How they collaborate matters: collaboration modes and task fit in human-AI recommendations
abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly used in online product recommendation, yet it remains unclear how consumers interpret different role configurations and when such configurations facilitate adoption. Drawing on mind perception theory, we argue that collaboration mode signals the collaborative system's task-relevant capability profile, and that its effectiveness depends on whether this profile fits the judgment-support requirements of search versus experience goods. Evidence from one field experiment and two scenario-based experiments indicates that AI-dominant collaboration is more effective for search-good recommendations, whereas human-dominant collaboration is more effective for experience-good recommendations, and that this fit effect is mediated by perceived diagnosticity. In addition, AI empathy functions as a compensatory interaction cue, improving consumers' evaluations of AI-dominant collaboration in experience-good contexts by enhancing perceived diagnosticity and recommendation adoption intention. Overall, this research moves product recommendation research beyond simple comparisons between human and AI sources toward a consumer-centered understanding of visible collaboration modes, while also offering implications for the design of more effective human-AI collaborative recommendation strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The dual impact of cap-and-trade policies on innovations and the moderating role of accumulated resources
abstract: While the cap-and-trade policy is a widely adopted mechanism for addressing climate change, its impact on firms' innovation portfolio remains underexplored. To balance regulatory compliance with profitability, firms must strategically allocate limited resources across different technology innovations based on their existing resource endowments. This study examines how the cap-and-trade policy alters firms' innovation resource allocation across different types of technologies with a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical validation. Our theoretical model suggests that while the policy encourages firms to invest more in green technology, it may crowd out resources from more profitable conventional innovation. This effect is less pronounced for firms with substantial stocks of green innovation resources, but stronger for those with extensive conventional innovation stocks. Using a difference-in-differences approach and firm-level patent data covering enterprises affected by China's regional cap-and-trade pilots, we find that the policy reduces the share of conventional patents by 5.951 percentage points on average, confirming the crowding-out effect. Our moderating analysis further reveals that each additional accumulated green patent mitigates this negative impact by 0.018 percentage points, whereas each additional accumulated conventional patent amplifies it by 0.002 percentage points. Additional significant heterogeneity is also observed, conditional on industry characteristics (pollution intensity, competition intensity, and SOE dominance) and firm-level attributes (R&D intensity, profitability, and governance structure). These findings underscore the importance of guiding highly regulation-sensitive firms toward a balanced innovation transition while encouraging less regulation-sensitive firms to engage more actively via well-targeted and supportive policies that foster both green and conventional innovation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy: A bibliometric study and systematic literature review
abstract: The forces of globalization and digital transformation have intensified attention toward the need to strengthen cultural identity through education, including the use of folklore as a meaningful learning resource. However, existing studies on folklore in learning remain fragmented. While much of the literature focuses on either cultural preservation or specific educational applications, the gap lies in a systematic exploration of folklore's pedagogical role across different contexts and educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the development of research on folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy through a bibliometric approach combined with a systematic literature review. For the bibliometric analysis, metadata records of articles published between 2015 and 2025 were processed from the Google Scholar database. Data for the systematic literature review were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and the article selection process followed PRISMA procedures. A total of 41 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer, while article identification and screening were supported by Publish or Perish. The bibliometric findings indicate a significant increase in publications over the past decade, accompanied by a thematic shift from cultural heritage preservation toward the integration of cultural values within educational contexts. The SLR findings show that the research is predominantly qualitative in nature, with folktales and legends as the most frequently used forms of folklore, and books and e-modules as the main learning media employed to strengthen cultural literacy. The findings suggest that folklore-based learning fosters students’ cultural awareness, internalizes values, strengthens identity formation, and deepens the understanding of local culture. This study contributes by providing a more integrated understanding of folklore as a pedagogical tool for cultural literacy, emphasizing its role in curriculum design. Future research should focus on expanding methodological diversity and exploring broader applications of folklore-based learning across various educational contexts. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .
