title: Brand stereotypes, information processing, and consumer acceptance of Chinese automobiles: The moderating roles of perceived brand globalness and brand credibility in an emerging market
abstract: Stereotypes about Chinese products persist in many developing economies, even as Chinese manufacturers have substantially upgraded their technological capabilities and product quality. However, the cognitive pathways linking systematic and heuristic information processing to consumers’ stereotype-based perceptions of brand warmth and competence remain underexplored in the evaluation of high-involvement foreign products. Drawing on the heuristic-systematic model, stereotype content model, and signaling theory, this study develops and tests a process-based framework explaining how information processing routes shape stereotype-based brand perceptions, which in turn influence product evaluations and purchase intentions toward Chinese automobiles in Vietnam. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed. A qualitative phase with 20 in-depth interviews was conducted to explore consumers' cognitive processes and refine the theoretical framework. Subsequently, survey data from 638 Vietnamese consumers were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings demonstrate that systematic information processing strengthens perceived brand competence and warmth, whereas heuristic processing weakens both dimensions, thereby reinforcing brand stereotypes. Perceived brand competence and warmth enhance product receptivity, judgment, and quality, which collectively drive purchase intention. Perceived brand globalness weakens the negative effects of heuristic information processing and amplifies the positive effects of systematic information processing on stereotype-related perceptions. Brand credibility strengthens the conversion of product-level evaluations into purchase intention. Theoretically, this study integrates HSM, SCM, and ST to clarify the sequential relationships linking information processing, stereotype-based brand perception, product evaluation, and purchase intention. Practically, the findings offer actionable guidance for Chinese automobile brands seeking to attenuate legacy stereotypes and build consumer acceptance in culturally resistant emerging markets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Beyond data disclosure: A health system transparency framework informed by evidence and Iranian insights
abstract: Objectives: Although transparency is widely recognized as a cornerstone of good health governance, existing studies have often addressed individual dimensions of transparency, with limited integration of these dimensions into a comprehensive conceptual framework for health systems. This study aimed to develop a conceptual framework for health system transparency by integrating evidence from Iran. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in six sequential phases between 2021 and 2024. Three systematic scoping reviews synthesized existing transparency frameworks, implementation principles, and the applications, benefits, risks, barriers, and opportunities of transparency in health systems. Findings were complemented by in-depth interviews with 35 Iranian experts, refined through three expert panels involving 16 participants, and finalized using a three-round modified Delphi study with 23 participants in the final round. Results: The resulting framework conceptualizes transparency as a multi-level governance system comprising strategic contexts and infrastructures, stakeholder interactions, implementation drivers and constraints, transparency application domains, and tactical and technical implementation principles. Rather than viewing transparency as information disclosure alone, the framework emphasizes dynamic interactions between governance conditions, data users, feedback mechanisms, and potential contributions to organizational learning and system improvement. Conclusion: The proposed framework provides an integrated conceptual foundation for designing, implementing, and evaluating transparency reforms in health systems. Although informed by evidence from Iran, its governance-oriented architecture may be transferable to other health systems, provided that context-dependent components are adapted to local institutional, political, legal, and socio-cultural conditions. Public interest summary: Health system transparency is more than making information publicly available. This study developed a framework showing how transparency can become part of everyday health system governance. It identifies the political, administrative, economic, and social conditions needed to support transparency, the role of citizens, researchers, media, and other data users in creating demand for information, and the factors that can either support or hinder implementation. The framework also identifies key areas where transparency is needed, including governance, finances, medicines, workforce, research, and healthcare services, and provides practical and technical principles for implementation. Although developed using evidence from Iran, the framework addresses transparency challenges that may also arise in other health systems and may help policymakers design more coordinated and sustainable transparency reforms. Its broader structure may also be relevant to other public sectors, although contextual adaptation would be required. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

title: Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: How certification credibility and benefit framing shape heterogeneous consumer responses to sustainable products in e-commerce
abstract: On e-commerce platforms, sustainable products succeed or fail on a compressed product page where certification logos, benefit descriptions, and platform trust cues compete for attention. Retailers treat these cues as interchangeable signals, yet they address two different questions: can the product be trusted, and is it right for me? Signalling theory answers the first through costly, verifiable certification; goal-framing theory answers the second through benefit claims activating competing motivations. Whether they operate as one mechanism or two remains unresolved in retailing research. Using a discrete choice experiment with 477 Chinese consumers analysed through aggregate conditional logit, latent class analysis, and trust-stratified models, we show they are separable strategic levers. The certification credibility hierarchy (dual and international premiums above the domestic schemes) holds broadly across all three motivational segments, whereas benefit-framing valuation differs sharply between them, and this segment-level dissociation is the evidence for their separability. Platform trust does not significantly moderate certification premiums. Latent class analysis reveals a dual-motivated majority (53.5 per cent) that stated self-classification systematically understates, making choice-derived rather than self-reported segmentation essential for targeting. Extending goal-framing theory, the study's central contribution shows certification quality as a novel external cue: superior certification shifts dual-motivated consumers' default health preference toward environmental framing, narrowing it to near-parity, with a ¥16.68 break-even threshold at which the two framings reach indifference. These findings show heterogeneous consumer response is structured by the interaction between signal architecture and motivational composition, with implications for certification investment, benefit communication, and segmentation in sustainable retailing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: XAI in the human-agent-environment loop: how do task, explanation strategy, and AI literacy shape user engagement?
abstract: This study explored how tasks, explanation strategies, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy levels collectively influenced human interaction with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in a single-target prediction task. Using a within-subjects experiment with 70 participants, the study examined combinations of four AI-assisted prediction tasks—varying in prediction target (human-related vs. human-unrelated) and stakes (high vs. low)—and six explanation strategies (model-based, comparison-based, input influence-based, sensitivity-based, demographic-based, and case-based), across participants with varying AI literacy (AIL). Results showed that explanation strategies had the most significant impact on human-XAI interaction in most aspects, especially on prediction change with XAI assistance. Additionally, explanation strategies significantly affected all perception and experience indicators, except for curiosity. Compared to the scope of explanations, the content provided by strategies had a greater influence on user predictions. Strategies with trends and ratios, such as case-based (CA) and demographic-based (DE), were more effective. Conversely, strategies lacking trends and ratios, such as model-based (MO) and comparison-based (CO), were generally the least effective. For users, AI literacy influenced all performance metrics, especially re-prediction time. Higher AI literacy was significantly associated with longer re-prediction time. Tasks had moderate impacts on the XAI interaction process, especially experience measures. In the human-related tasks (recidivism and shipwreck survival prediction), participants reported lower subjective experience ratings among the tasks examined, particularly regarding perceived justice. In the high-stakes, human-unrelated task (wine quality prediction), participants gave the most favorable experiential ratings among the tasks in the study. Furthermore, second-order effects related to explanation strategies had significant impacts on various metrics. On the one hand, the interaction between explanation strategies and task characteristics influenced prediction changes. Global explanations, such as the input-influence-based (IN) and MO strategies, performed better on human-related tasks than on human-unrelated tasks. In contrast, local explanations, such as the sensitivity-based (SE) and CO strategies, showed the opposite pattern. On the other hand, the impact of explanation strategies on user perception and experience was moderated by AI literacy. Users with lower literacy tended to prefer local explanations, while users with higher literacy preferred global explanations. The content of the XAI explanation significantly affected the quality, while the scope had subtle interactive effects with different tasks and users. These effects with XAI, majorly interpreted through the Elaboration Likelihood model (ELM), provide evidence supporting adaptive XAI within the human-agent-environment loop. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: From brand hate to behavioral response: A recourse-contingent exit-voice-loyalty-neglect framework for digital consumer markets
abstract: Three decades of brand hate research have mapped what triggers consumer hate and catalogued how hateful consumers respond, avoiding, switching, complaining, retaliating, subverting, without connecting these two halves through one behavioral logic. This paper closes that gap by importing the Exit-Voice-Loyalty-Neglect (EVLN) framework into the brand hate domain and extending it with a boundary condition the literature has ignored: structural recourse availability. Brand hate's dimensional profile, whether anger, contempt, aversion, or fear dominates, depends on whether its trigger is relational (betrayal, transgression, ideological incompatibility) or structural (algorithmic, platform-based, institutional unfairness), and this profile sets a default EVLN response tendency. Whether that tendency is realized depends on structural recourse, the inverse of switching costs, platform dependence, and powerlessness. When recourse is blocked, Exit tendencies redirect toward Voice where a channel exists, and toward Neglect, termed informed helplessness, where none does. We develop eight propositions specifying this redirection process, including a measurement-validity proposition showing informed helplessness is indistinguishable from loyalty in standard satisfaction measures, and a release proposition explaining how dormant hate resurfaces when conditions change. The framework helps managers and policymakers identify trapped haters and sets an agenda for measuring them. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Determinants of visit intention to Lake Toba geopark: The roles of publicity, destination awareness, destination image, and word of mouth
abstract: Tourism research has increasingly emphasized the importance of communication and perception factors in shaping tourists’ behavioral intentions, particularly in sustainable tourism destinations such as geoparks. However, limited studies have comprehensively examined the interplay between destination publicity, word of mouth (WOM), destination awareness, destination image, and visit intention within the context of UNESCO Global Geoparks. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the relationships among these variables in the context of Lake Toba Geopark, Indonesia, by applying the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) framework. A quantitative approach was employed using a structured online survey distributed to 425 respondents who had previously visited Lake Toba Geopark. The collected data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with AMOS. The findings reveal that destination publicity does not significantly influence destination awareness or destination image. Similarly, destination awareness does not directly affect tourists’ visit intention. In contrast, WOM significantly influences destination awareness, while destination awareness significantly enhances destination image. Furthermore, destination image emerges as the strongest determinant of visit intention. These findings indicate that tourists’ behavioral intentions are shaped more strongly by interpersonal communication and psychological perceptions than by conventional publicity exposure. This study contributes theoretically by extending the application of the SOR framework in geopark tourism through the integration of publicity, WOM, awareness, and image variables into a single model. Practically, the findings suggest that tourism stakeholders and destination managers should prioritize strategies that encourage positive WOM, strengthen destination awareness, and enhance destination image through authentic tourist experiences and digital engagement. Ultimately, destination image plays a central role in encouraging tourists’ intention to visit Lake Toba Geopark. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: THE POWER OF FACIAL EXPRESSIONS IN SALES AVATARS: ELEVATING CONSUMER INTERACTION IN METAVERSE COMMERCE
abstract: Metaverse commerce is reshaping e-commerce by offering immersive and interactive shopping experiences. Sales avatars, defined as digital representations of firm frontline employees in metaverse commerce, play critical roles in delivering real-time and interactive experiences. Drawing on the theory of affordances and the needs-affordances-features framework, this study investigates how the facial expressions of sales avatars (smiling vs. crying) influence consumer avatars’ interaction outcomes and the underlying mechanisms through subcultural appeal. Further, we test when the mechanism by which sales avatars’ facial expression leads to consumer interaction outcomes via subcultural appeal is amplified or weakened depending on sales avatar’s anthropomorphism. We conducted four experiments in which consumers were exposed to virtual commerce contexts that we built on the VRChat metaverse platform. The results reveal that unlike real-world interactions, crying sales avatars compared to smiling sales avatars elicit higher intentions to interact with the sales avatar, purchase a virtual item from the sales avatar, and spread positive WOM about the experience. This counterintuitive effect is driven by consumers’ heightened perceptions of subcultural appeal in the crying sales avatar context. However, when sales avatars exhibited high anthropomorphism (human-like vs. cartoon-like), the positive effect of the crying expression weakened. These findings provide actionable insights into how to strategically leverage sales avatars’ facial expressions in highly immersive metaverse commerce, where consumers’ desire for subcultural values is relatively high. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. .

title: Green by association? Restaurant presence on food-waste reduction platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal for brand equity
abstract: Food-waste reduction platforms allow restaurants to redistribute surplus food, but their branding implications remain unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we conceptualize restaurant presence on these platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal that embeds sustainability and commercial meanings within the same marketplace cue. Across three experiments, we examine whether this hybrid signal enhances restaurant brand equity through green brand image and whether consumer residence and restaurant type condition its effects. Study 1 shows that platform presence enhances brand equity, partially through green brand image. Study 2 replicates the main effect and provides directional evidence that the premium of platform presence may be stronger among urban than rural consumers. Study 3 shows that this effect depends jointly on consumer residence and restaurant type, and that mediation through green brand image is evident primarily for full-service restaurants. These findings identify platform presence as a hybrid, context-dependent sustainability signal with branding implications. © 2026 The Authors

title: Choice set expansion and dual-domain loss aversion in food delivery platforms: Evidence from price-time trade-offs
abstract: This study examines how delivery-tier expansion shapes online food delivery choices when price-time trade-offs are held constant. Drawing on context-dependent choice theory and prospect theory, we conducted a between-subjects discrete-choice experiment with 438 South Korean consumers assigned to either a two-tier menu (Free and Economy) or a three-tier menu (Free, Economy, and Single-order). Paid options offered the same price per minute saved, isolating choice-set structure from economic efficiency. Adding single-order delivery significantly reduced free delivery selection and captured 30.49% of choices. Economy delivery's incumbent-relative share increased slightly but not significantly, indicating no reliable canonical compromise effect. Across logit and cross-nested logit models, price loss aversion was associated with free delivery selection, whereas time loss aversion was associated with faster paid tiers, especially single-order delivery. The findings position delivery portfolios as behavioral segmentation devices in platform-mediated hospitality services. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The paradox of withdrawal: How managerial turnover intention and attitudes shape performance appraisal quality in high-contact service
abstract: Purpose: Performance appraisal quality depends on the discretionary effort of the rater. This study examines rater-side psychological antecedents of appraisal rigor among hospitality managers, focusing on how managers’ positive attitudes toward the job and the organization drive appraisal quality and whether that relationship is disrupted by the managers’ own turnover intention. Design/methodology/approach: Data were collected from 318 U.S. hospitality managers through a multi-stage screening protocol on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Because job satisfaction and organizational commitment were empirically indistinguishable in the sample (r = .976), a higher-order Managerial Attitudes factor was specified to test the two attitudinal hypotheses jointly. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to estimate direct and moderating effects. Common method variance was addressed procedurally and through a marker-variable technique combined with an unmeasured latent method construct. Findings: Managerial Attitudes had a strong positive relationship with self-reported appraisal quality (β =.71 in the method-adjusted model). Contrary to the “withdrawal–negligence” prediction of Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, turnover intention showed a small but significant positive direct association with appraisal rigor, and its interaction with attitudes was not statistically significant. The pattern is consistent with a “Lame Duck Objectivity” account in which anticipated exit releases managers from certain political constraints on evaluative candor, but reverse causality, statistical power, and measurement limitations remain plausible alternatives that the design cannot rule out. Originality/value: The study reframes managerial withdrawal as a scope condition of COR rather than a uniform trigger of task disengagement, and it demonstrates the utility of a higher-order attitudinal factor for handling discriminant-validity breakdown in hospitality data. Boundary conditions on generalizability — including racial and gender homogeneity of the sample, single-source measurement, and cross-sectional design — are discussed in detail, and a program of multi-source, longitudinal, and gender- and race-balanced replications is proposed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Exploring the role of green human resource management in enhancing employee well-being and job satisfaction in the it sector
abstract: Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) has received a growing academic interest with organizations starting to incorporate the sustainability of the environment into their strategic human resource management. The present paper offers a synthesis and systematic review of the existing body of literature to identify the impacts of GHRM practices on employee well being, job satisfaction as well as environmental performance, especially in the IT industry. A systematic literature review was conducted. The sources of records were Google Scholar (n = 317) and Scopus (n = 312), which returned 629 preliminary studies. After applying inclusion criteria based on peer-review, relevance and timeframe criteria, 156 articles were selected for detailed analysis. Literature was grouped based on the Ability-Motivation-Opportunity (AMO) framework to assess the performance of GHRM practices in the main HR functions. The results show that green training and development (80% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) and reward management (85% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) have the greatest correlation with the employee engagement and sustainability outcomes. The other contribution made towards the development of a psychological green climate and the encouragement of organizational citizenship behaviour towards the environment (OCBE) is recruitment, job design, and performance appraisal. Nevertheless, there are gaps of measurement structures and multi-level empirical validation of sectors. The research finds out that holistic integration of GHRM between HR functions boosts employee motivation, job satisfaction, and performance on organizational sustainability. Organizations can attain long-term competitive advantage by integrating environmental values into the HR systems, especially those operating in the knowledge-intensive sectors like the IT sector, in addition to promoting the sustainability of the larger society. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: Transforming hospitality and tourism services through artificial intelligence: The influence of experiential dimensions on user satisfaction, continuance intentions, and word-of-mouth
abstract: This study investigated how five key experiential dimensions (i.e., embodiment, human-oriented perception, feeling of security, emotions, and co-experience) shaped user satisfaction with AI-enabled services in hospitality and tourism settings and how satisfaction subsequently influenced continuance intention and word-of-mouth. Data was collected through an online survey of 380 participants who had previously used AI-enabled hospitality or tourism services, and structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed hypotheses. The results revealed that embodiment, human-oriented perception, feeling of security, and emotions had a significant impact on user satisfaction. In addition, satisfaction was positively associated with continuance intentions and positive word-of-mouth, underscoring the importance of experiential dimensions in sustaining user engagement. The findings extend theoretical understanding by identifying user experience as a determinant of post-adoption behavior in AI-enabled service contexts. The study further provided practical insights for designing emotionally attuned, secure, and human-oriented AI systems that foster satisfaction and customer loyalty. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Hard-work orientation as an individual difference: Passion and subjective vitality as sequential mechanisms of student engagement
abstract: Effort has a well-documented dark side: excessive work has been linked to burnout, and persistence after failure to hopelessness. Effort is also an individual difference, in that people vary in how strongly they believe effort is valuable and necessary for achievement. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study asks why an effort-oriented disposition might generate psychological resources rather than deplete them. Passion and subjective vitality were tested as a sequential motivational and energetic process linking hard-work orientation to student engagement, using three-wave time-lagged data from 524 students in northern India. Hard-work orientation was positively associated with passion, subjective vitality, and engagement. Both mediators carried significant indirect associations, and the serial indirect pathway through passion and subjective vitality was also significant. The findings locate the bright side of effort in how effort is regulated rather than in how much of it is expended. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Environmental qualities in green and natural spaces: Fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature as pathways to perceived visit-related health benefits
abstract: Rising levels of stress and mental ill-health have intensified interest in nature-based public health approaches, including green social prescribing and nature as medicine. However, it remains unclear whether different environmental qualities are associated with different aspects of visit experience, and how these experiences relate to perceived visit-related health benefits. This study examined direct associations of biodiversity, safety, accessibility and cleanliness problems with perceived visit-related health benefits, and indirect associations involving fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature. Cross-sectional data from 19,814 adults in England who reported a recent visit to a green or natural space in the People and Nature Survey (PaNS) were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In the direct-effects model, biodiversity, safety and accessibility were positively associated with perceived visit-related health benefits, whereas cleanliness problems showed a negative association. Most of these direct associations were substantially attenuated when the two visit experiences were included, and both experiences were positively associated with perceived benefits. The pathway model also revealed differentiated associations across experiences, with safety most closely associated with fresh air / peace and tranquillity, biodiversity with feeling closer to nature, and cleanliness problems showing a negative indirect association through fresh air / peace and tranquillity. By considering qualities of the setting alongside experiences during the visit, the findings highlight the value of a quality-experience-benefit perspective in which different environmental qualities may show different patterns of association with perceived visit-related health benefits through particular visit experiences. This perspective may help inform the selection and management of natural settings used in nature-based public-health approaches, particularly where specific visit experiences are intended to be supported. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior
abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. While existing GenAI literature has largely focused on the scale, frequency, and operational patterns of its application, it has largely overlooked the inherent imbalances within these P-R cycles. Building on control theory, this study investigates how and when GenAI usage is related to employees’ corner-cutting behavior (CCB). Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. By conceptualizing GenAI usage through the dual lenses of expectation induction and cognitive friction operating within P-R cycles, our findings extend and refine traditional perspectives on human-AI interaction in the workplace. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: A survey charting trust models and systems in self-sovereign identity
abstract: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is widely positioned as the decentralized future of digital identity. However, although traditional SSI literature emphasizes architecture and privacy, it largely overlooks a systematic analysis of how trust is formed, propagated, and managed. Trust is fundamental because, without it, the actions performed by key actors, including credential issuers, lose much of their practical value. In this landscape, trust is the ground on which SSI systems stand; when that ground is absent or unstable, any structure built on it crumbles. Against this backdrop, we chart the landscape of trust through a comprehensive survey of Trust Models (TMs) and Trust Management Systems (TMSs) in SSI. At the abstract level, we analyze TMs by examining the types of trust relationships among SSI actors and how trust is defined and represented. At the implementation level, we discuss TMSs in terms of how trust is represented, stored, and protected in the systems proposed in the literature. We analyzed 26 sources (24 peer-reviewed papers plus the Sovrin whitepaper and governance framework document), consolidated into 24 approaches, benchmarking 16 features across these dimensions. Based on this analysis, we identify five open challenges: enabling cross-chain trust portability; designing a hybrid TM that blends Web of Trust and hierarchies; supporting heterogeneous actors such as IoT devices and humans; implementing privacy-preserving feedback mechanisms; and TM and TMS interoperability in emerging settings, including delegated AI agents. Our analysis offers a compass to guide researchers and developers in selecting trust models and advancing SSI systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. Therefore, this study constructs a multi-source heterogeneous hypergraph with higher-order semantics, spanning the “Science-Technology-Industry” dimensions. By mapping the structural phase transitions of weak signals across an “Outlier-Mutation-Key Node” trajectory, we devise a quantifiable indicator system to shift the analytical paradigm from static retrospective detection to dynamic evolutionary tracking. Using a dataset of 145,316 papers, 79,050 patents, and 5941 project records from the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) fuel cell domain (2015–2024), we identify 226 candidate nodes exhibiting this trajectory. A two-round Delphi expert evaluation confirms 193 of these nodes as expert-confirmed weak signals, establishing Delphi-validated reference labels for subsequent model evaluation. We then employ Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Dynamic Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN), and Large Language Models (ZS-LLM and ICL-LLM) to prospectively predict weak signals with disruptive potential. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). This synergy between higher-order topology and semantic intelligence effectively filters stochastic noise and enables meaningful predictive capability of emerging technologies, providing an exploratory decision-support framework for technology foresight. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: Smart and green solutions in the catering and hospitality: A review of the existing literature
abstract: The integration of digital technologies and sustainability practices is reshaping the catering and hospitality industry, yet research on smart and green solutions remains fragmented. This study maps the intellectual and thematic development of this field through a bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed publications using VOSviewer, Biblioshiny, and Microsoft Excel. The findings reveal substantial growth in research interest and increasing interdisciplinary contributions across countries, institutions, and authors. Keyword analysis identifies artificial intelligence, sustainability, digital transformation, and social media as dominant themes, while circular economy, Internet of Things (IoT), and customer behavior represent emerging areas. The analysis also highlights a relatively underexplored intersection of AI, IoT, and circular economy, suggesting important opportunities for future research. By consolidating the intellectual structure and emerging themes, this study provides a research agenda for advancing smart and sustainable solutions that enhance operational efficiency, customer experience, environmental performance, and competitiveness in the hospitality sector. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use. © 2026 The Authors

title: Negotiating your way to the top: Conflict management by women leaders in family businesses
abstract: Family businesses are a fertile ground for women to take up different leader roles. The way up as well as functioning at the nexus of the business family and family business offer unique negotiation challenges. Women leaders play a central role in preserving family harmony while safeguarding business performance, acting as mediators in cases of intra-family conflict and developing their career as leaders. Traditionally oriented succession dynamics, inequality, and lack of legitimacy as business leaders and family leaders require specific and high-level negotiation competencies. This review explores the structural and cultural challenges that women face in their family businesses as family members as well as the negotiating and conflict management competencies needed in both family and business. © 2026

title: Policy-driven electrification in rural areas: Integrating carbon pricing and activity-based costing in strategic decision models
abstract: Rural electrification is essential for sustainable development; however, balancing upfront infrastructure investment, carbon reduction, and long-term economic performance remains a significant decision problem. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework that combines Activity-Based Costing (ABC), carbon taxation, and optimization modeling to compare Progressive Replacement, Hybrid Carbon Market Electrification, and One-Time Replacement. The analysis uses a 10-year planning horizon, a 5% benchmark discount rate, and a USD 30/tCO2 carbon tax in a normalized planning-scale scenario. Recalculation from the annual scenario tables gives cumulative direct operational emissions of 41,800 tCO2 for Progressive Replacement, 28,100 tCO2 for the Hybrid Carbon Market strategy, and 10,000 tCO2 for One-Time Replacement. Using the 5% benchmark discount rate, corresponding total-system NPVs are approximately USD 2.863 million, USD 1.527 million, and USD 1.313 million, respectively. Sensitivity analysis further indicates that One-Time Replacement remains the lower-cost strategy across the reported carbon-tax and discount-rate scenarios. The framework clarifies how electrification timing, activity-level costs, and carbon-price exposure jointly shape rural electrification decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Unpacking the pathways from green intellectual capital to green recovery performance: The power of employee voice and intrinsic motivation
abstract: Our paper proposes and tests a moderated mediation model that examines how green intellectual capital relates to green recovery performance, highlighting green promotive and prohibitive voice behaviors as mediators and intrinsic motivation to share knowledge as a moderator. Results based on time-lagged data gathered from FLEs in environmentally certified Spanish hotels revealed that the association between green intellectual capital and green recovery performance operated through green voice behaviors. Both green promotive and green prohibitive voice behaviors mediated the green intellectual capital-green recovery performance link. However, intrinsic motivation to share knowledge strengthened only the promotive pathway. This finding underscores an asymmetry in how motivational states condition the translation of intangible resources into recovery behaviors. Our research positions voice behavior as a proximal mechanism through which green intellectual capital translates into sustainable outcomes and shows that the amplifying role of intrinsic motivation depends on the form of voice at stake. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When service environments signal ideology: Customer responses to ideological cues
abstract: Service environments increasingly contain visible cues that communicate political engagement, religious identities, LGBTQ + affiliation, environmental advocacy, and other collective values. Although servicescape research has traditionally emphasized atmospheric, aesthetic, and functional cues, less is known about how customers interpret ideological cues embedded within routine service encounters. Drawing on servicescape research and social identity theory, this research examines how ideological servicescape cues are associated with customer discomfort, avoidance intentions, and stated store-choice decisions. Three preregistered, scenario-based experiments in a coffee shop context examine ideological cues displayed through employees and the physical service environment. Study 1 shows that political cues generate greater discomfort than environmental and lifestyle cues, although they do not differ significantly from religious or LGBTQ + cues. Study 2 shows that matching political cues displayed across employee and environmental touchpoints generate greater discomfort than political cues displayed through a single source, while perceived authenticity does not account for this association. Study 3 shows that political cues are associated with lower stated store choice than environmental cues, particularly when matching political cues appear across employee and environmental touchpoints. Across studies, customer discomfort statistically accounts for part of the association between ideological cue conditions and avoidance intentions or stated store-choice decisions. The findings extend servicescape scholarship by showing that politically charged symbolism may shape customer responses through both cue content and cue-source configuration. Because the studies rely on scenario-based experiments and stated responses, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of observed marketplace behavior or realized financial outcomes. © 2026 The Authors

title: Employee-led disclosure of anthropomorphism in tourism GAI failure recovery: A mind perception model from tourists and employees
abstract: Generative AI (GAI) is increasingly mediating tourism service encounters, reshaping GAI failure recovery within a broader tourist–employee–GAI service configuration, in which GAI serves as the failure source, employees act as recovery agents, and tourists are the end recipients. Drawing on Mind Perception Theory, we theorize and test a post-failure recovery tactic in which employees intentionally foreground anthropomorphic aspects of the failing GAI during recovery interactions. Across six scenario-based experiments and two on-site simulation studies ( N = 2061), results provide convergent evidence that employee-led disclosure of GAI anthropomorphism (vs. control) improves recovery outcomes for both tourists and employees through mirrored mechanisms. Specifically, it increases tourist forgiveness by elevating perceived GAI experience and increases state employee satisfaction by elevating perceived GAI agency. These benefits weaken under high tourist anger or employees' perceptions of tourist anger and are further contingent on tourists' AI expertise and employees’ competitive versus collaborative mindset. The findings advance tourism research by offering parallel dyadic evidence on GAI failure recovery beyond a tourist-centric lens, extending Mind Perception Theory through stakeholder-contingent effects of perceived experience and perceived agency, and repositioning anthropomorphism in recovery as a co-produced mechanism jointly enacted through employee framing and available GAI interface affordances. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Invisible data infrastructure and cross-domain digital innovation: Evidence from data groups in China
abstract: This study examines whether and how formalized data governance reshapes firms’ digital innovation by exploiting the staggered establishment of municipal data groups in China. Using a difference-in-differences design and Chinese A-share listed firms from 2008 to 2024, we find that municipal data group establishment significantly expands firms’ cross-domain digital innovation. This effect is stronger among state-owned enterprises, regulated industries, firms in cities with lower technological complexity, and regions with more developed market and factor environments. Additional analyses provide evidence consistent with several potential pathways: municipal data groups are associated with changes in R&D uncertainty, managerial innovation expectations, interregional collaboration, and innovation activities. Further analysis reveals a quantity–quality divergence: data group establishment increases patent output but is associated with lower average measured patent quality, particularly among firms receiving stronger innovation incentives. This pattern is consistent with multiple explanations, including incentive responses and innovation composition changes. By conceptualizing municipal data groups as Invisible Data Infrastructure, this study advances research on digital governance and corporate innovation by showing how institutionalized data access and coordination mechanisms expand firms’ innovation boundaries. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Decoding entrepreneurial intention: A systematic review, theoretical framework synthesis, and research trajectories
abstract: Entrepreneurial intention (EI) is a critical psychological construct for understanding the precursors of entrepreneurial behavior. Despite a surge in empirical research over the past decade, the literature on EI remains fragmented across theoretical frameworks, methodological approaches, and contextual applications. This study systematically reviews 53 peer-reviewed articles on entrepreneurial intention published between 2018 and 2025 to synthesize theoretical frameworks, methodological patterns, key findings, and future research directions. Guided by the PRISMA approach, the review reveals the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) as the predominant model, frequently integrated with constructs from Social Cognitive Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, and moral or contextual frameworks. Quantitative cross-sectional designs dominate the methodological landscape, often involving university student samples and the use of structural equation modelling techniques for hypothesis testing. Findings consistently confirm the central role of attitude, perceived behavioral control, and self-efficacy in predicting EI, while more recent studies highlight the growing significance of emotional intelligence, cultural influences, institutional support, and entrepreneurship education. However, the review identifies key limitations, including the overreliance on student-based samples, a lack of longitudinal and experimental designs, and limited generalizability to actual entrepreneurial behavior in real-world settings. Additionally, contextual diversity across emerging and developed economies remains underexplored. In response, the study proposes five future research trajectories: theoretical expansion beyond dominant models, increased adoption of behavioral and longitudinal approaches, broader contextual and demographic inclusion, pedagogical innovation in entrepreneurship education, and stronger interdisciplinary collaboration. By mapping evolving trends and gaps in EI research, this review provides a foundation for more dynamic, inclusive, and practically relevant scholarship in entrepreneurship studies. © 2027, Malque Publishing. .

title: How should conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products? Matching recommendation set granularity with time pressure
abstract: With the widespread application of conversational recommendation agents (CRA) on e-commerce platforms, an increasing number of consumers use a CRA to support product choices. Existing research has mainly focused on the accuracy of CRA recommendations, with limited attention paid to how candidate products should be organized and whether this organization should be adapted to consumers' current decision contexts. Drawing on the product set granularity perspective and the heuristic–systematic model, this study examines the matching effect between recommendation set granularity (coarse vs. fine) and time pressure (high vs. low) on consumers' intention to adopt CRA recommendations and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms. The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure. The two matching effects operate through perceived fluency and perceived attractiveness, respectively. Furthermore, consumer knowledge affects the relative effectiveness of the two matching strategies: the match between coarse recommendation set granularity and high time pressure is more effective for consumers with low product knowledge, whereas the match between fine recommendation set granularity and low time pressure is more effective for consumers with high product knowledge. These findings extend CRA research from recommendation content to the organization of candidate products and provide guidance for retail platforms to adjust recommendation set granularity according to consumers’ time pressure and product knowledge. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: The automation paradox: Efficiency gains vs. workforce concerns in human-AI collaboration
abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security. © 2026

title: Municipal utilities and SDG adoption: Evidence from Austria and Germany
abstract: This paper explores how municipal utilities (MUs) in Austria and Germany adopt and integrate the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into their strategies, strategic projects and management controls (MCs). MUs have a long tradition of delivering public infrastructure services, such as energy, water, and public transport, in the two focus countries. As important municipal enterprises, MUs must position themselves on a continuum between their public mission and their business orientation, and therefore act in a financially sustainable manner. Taking SDG adoption seriously is in line with the public mission orientation. Drawing on legitimacy theory, the study investigates whether MUs engage with the SDGs symbolically or substantively. The research is based on nineteen semi-structured interviews conducted with representatives from sixteen MUs, allowing for an in-depth qualitative analysis of strategic alignment, project implementation, and related MCs. The findings reveal considerable variation in SDG integration, showing that most MUs are still in an early, emerging stage of adoption, which is still at a symbolic level. By providing empirical insights from two countries with long-standing traditions of municipal service provision by local government-owned public utilities, the study contributes to the limited literature on SDG adoption in municipal enterprises and enhances understanding of the legitimacy dynamics shaping SDG practices in local state-owned entities. © 2026 The Authors. title: Good listening as a wise negotiation tactic
abstract: Listening is a foundational interpersonal skill. Effective listening is central to managing the dual demands of negotiation: competing over limited resources while sustaining cooperation and trust. Nevertheless, limited research has shed light on how to listen effectively in negotiation. Integrating research from psychology, communication, and negotiation, we identify three common listening traps that undermine negotiation effectiveness: negotiators tend to focus too much on: (1) the self (and too little on others); (2) resolving disagreement (and too little on exploring it); and (3) what is said (and too little on what remains unspoken). We propose three approaches for effective listening in negotiations: (1) listening to understand rather than persuade; (2) listening for movement and change; and (3) making listening observable through concrete verbal and nonverbal behaviors. We argue that high-quality listening improves both informational and relational outcomes by facilitating deeper information exchange, increasing trust, and supporting integrative agreements. By highlighting high-quality listening as a wise negotiation tactic, this article illustrates how negotiators can better navigate the tension between cooperation and competition in mixed-motive interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: AI guest personalization as driver of hotel performance and hotel guest behavior: A dual-model analysis
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven personalization is reshaping hotel operations, yet evidence on its financial effects and guest acceptance mechanisms remains limited. This study adopts a dual-perspective design combining hotel-level performance modeling with guest-level behavioral analysis. Study 1 examines revenue dynamics using Interrupted Time Series (ITS), SARIMA forecasting, and TOPSIS, comparing AI-driven and non-AI-driven hotels based on publicly documented implementations of AI personalization. Findings indicate heterogeneous short-term responses but more consistent differences in long-term revenue stability and predictability. Study 2 develops a Diffusion of Innovation–based structural model extended with trust in AI as a mediator, using survey data from 1396 hotel guests. Relative advantage and compatibility increase trust and adoption intention, whereas complexity reduces them; trust partially mediates these effects. Multi-group analysis reveals model differences between business and leisure guests. Overall, the study provides complementary evidence on revenue dynamics and adoption mechanisms of AI personalization in hospitality. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Unveiling the effects of multidimensional urban shrinkage on urban flood resilience: A case study of the Yangtze River Basin, China
abstract: Climate change poses growing flood-management challenges for cities undergoing economic, demographic, and spatial decline. Using 1921 city-year observations for 113 prefecture-level cities in China’s Yangtze River Basin (YRB) from 2007 to 2023, this study develops a six-subsystem urban flood resilience (UFR) framework encompassing socioeconomic conditions, ecological environment, infrastructure, institutional support, spatial structure, and climate stress. The analysis integrates CRITIC-TOPSIS, coupling coordination analysis, GeoShapley, mechanism tests, and probabilistic scenario simulation. The results reveal four main findings. (1) Both UFR and subsystem coordination improved significantly, with Sen slopes of 0.0023 and 0.0059 per year, respectively. (2) Drainage infrastructure, economic activity, and fiscal capacity made the largest predictive contributions, whereas the associations of population and spatial shrinkage were smaller, more heterogeneous, and more dependent on local context. (3) The mechanism tests further indicate partial pathways through population density and impervious surface. (4) The expansion scenario produces the highest projected coordination level, followed closely by SSP1, whereas SSP3 yields the lowest trajectory. Economic shrinkage remains below the baseline, whereas population- and spatial-shrinkage trajectories are not clearly separated from it in several comparisons. These findings identify robust associations and scenario-dependent pathways rather than causal effects. The analysis is subject to data constraints relating to event-level inundation, damage, and infrastructure condition, suggesting that future research should incorporate finer-scale hazard and asset-condition information and extend validation to other river basins. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Capability, opportunity, and motivation for healthy eating: Exploring gender-specific pathways
abstract: Women generally consume a healthier diet than men; however, both fall short of dietary guidelines. Health behaviour theories are often applied in a gender-neutral manner, implicitly assuming that explanatory models operate similarly across groups. This conceptual replication tested the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model for dietary behaviour, originally evaluated in a female-dominant sample, in a male-dominant sample (N = 1358; 67% male). Using the same measurement battery and a closely aligned analytic approach, structural equation modelling indicated acceptable overall fit, with the COM-B model explaining 22% of the variance in diet quality. As in the original study, capability and opportunity were associated with behaviour indirectly through motivation, which was the strongest predictor of diet quality. At the indicator level, the male-dominant model retained action control and habits (capability), descriptive norms and the home food environment (opportunity), and self-efficacy, intentions, affective attitudes and perceived behavioural control (motivation), whereas identity, decision-making barriers, instrumental attitudes and the shopping environment indicator were not retained during trimming. These differences, relative to the female-dominant model, suggest potential variation in how COM-B constructs are operationalised across gender-dominant samples and should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Discriminant validity concerns (habits–action control; self-efficacy–intention) further indicated overlap between conceptually distinct constructs in the male-dominant sample. Overall, findings support the stability of the higher-order COM-B pathway while highlighting potential group differences in indicator contributions, with implications for measurement and population-sensitive intervention design. © 2026 The Authors. title: Affordances and paradoxical engagement in virtual immersive learning platforms: A configurational analysis across demographic groups
abstract: Virtual immersive learning platforms (VILPs), integrating immersive technologies, gamified design, and learning tools, enable meaningful engagement in learning while also creating possibilities for compulsive engagement. Drawing on a sociotechnical affordance perspective, this study examines how configurations of affordances are associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and how these pathways vary across demographic conditions. Using a mixed-methods design, we first uncover the core affordances of VILPs and organize them within a sociotechnical perspective. We then employ a two-stage fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine affordance configurations associated with different engagement outcomes and the role of demographic conditions. The findings show that meaningful and compulsive engagement are associated with distinct combinations of affordances and these configurational patterns vary across demographic conditions. These findings advance understanding of VILP engagement by revealing the configurational pathways associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and offering practical insights into designing more inclusive and responsible learning platforms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

label: Social Sciences
title: Synergy or backfire? Adding virtual influencers to advertisements featuring human influencers: The roles of sensory cues and temporal framing
abstract: In recent years, virtual influencers (VIs) have emerged as a salient presence in brand communication. Firms are increasingly featuring them alongside human influencers (HIs) in advertising campaigns. Yet whether such HI–VI co-endorsement creates synergy or instead backfires remains unclear. Drawing on cue utilization theory and the elaboration likelihood model, this research examines how endorsement format, defined as advertisements featuring only HI(s) versus HI–VI co-endorsement, and advertising sensory cue type (distal vs. proximal) jointly shape consumers’ purchase intentions, and how this relationship varies across temporal frames (past vs. future). Results from four experiments (total N = 1293) show that advertisements featuring both an HI and a VI are more effective than advertisements featuring only HIs when distal sensory cues are emphasized, but less effective when proximal sensory cues are highlighted. These effects operate through two distinct mechanisms: perceived novelty explains the synergy associated with HI–VI co-endorsement under distal sensory cues, whereas perceived authenticity explains the advantage of advertisements featuring only HIs under proximal sensory cues. Moreover, future-oriented framing strengthens the novelty-based effectiveness of HI–VI co-endorsement, whereas past-oriented framing favors advertisements featuring only HIs through authenticity-based evaluations, particularly when proximal sensory cues are emphasized. By identifying when HI–VI co-endorsement succeeds or fails, this research extends endorsement theory from a source-substitution perspective to a hybrid co-endorsement perspective and provides practical implications for advertising strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Why travelers prefer humans over artificial intelligence (AI): Developing and testing an AI aversion model in tourism
abstract: As tourism businesses increasingly adopt artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance traveler decision-making, a persistent reluctance to rely on AI-generated recommendations has emerged as a critical barrier. This research addresses this gap by developing and validating an AI aversion model that identifies the factors driving traveler resistance to AI-generated recommendations. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research uncovered five core drivers rooted in the perceived absence of human nature attributes: lived experience, emotional engagement, contextual understanding, domain specific knowledge, and proactive engagement in communication. Twenty-three items were developed and validated in a multicultural context. Additionally, we revealed that individual differences (i.e., rational vs. emotional personalities) play a moderating role, which can offer a way to mitigate the negative impacts of AI. The findings offer theoretical contributions by enriching the understanding of AI aversion and repositioning technology resistance through a human lens and extending practical implications for firms aiming to integrate AI effectively. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

title: Circular economy approaches to sustainable food waste management in the hospitality and food services sector
abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) as a model has become a widespread approach to promoting sustainability through the restoration and regeneration of products and materials within production and consumption. Despite the plethora of work done, research on the application of CE principles for food waste management in the hospitality and food services (HaFS) sector remains scarce. This study adopts a conceptual review approach and follows the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to address this gap through exploring the role of CE in reducing and managing food waste in the HaFS sector through a review of papers between 2015 and 2026. The findings indicate that collective efforts of both actor-internal (hospitality managers and staff) and actor-external (customers, local authorities and government) stakeholders are essential to achieve sustainable and circular practices. Additionally, a framework that supports managerial decision-making by aligning with external stakeholders to enable circular food waste management is proposed for adoption in the HaFS sector. This research also calls for further research on CE implementation in the HaFS sector, both in terms of policy and practical approaches. © 2026 The Authors

title: What drives happiness in 15 European Union countries? The role of income inequality, democracy, and environmental quality
abstract: This study examines happiness as a key dimension of sustainable development by focusing on its socio-economic, political, and environmental correlates. In recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that happiness cannot be explained solely by economic prosperity but is strongly influenced by structural factors such as income distribution, democratic institutions, and environmental conditions. Despite growing interest, empirical studies examining the simultaneous effects of these three fundamental factors on happiness are scarce. This creates a noteworthy gap in the literature. This study aims to fill this gap by empirically examining the effects of income inequality, democracy, and environmental degradation on happiness in 15 European Union countries, including the United Kingdom for comparability, between 2011 and 2022. Per capita income and health expenditure are included as control variables. Methodologically, the study employs MMQR and assesses the robustness of the findings using FGLS, PCSE, and HPJ approaches. The findings suggest that income inequality and environmental degradation are negatively associated with happiness, whereas democracy is positively associated with individuals' happiness. Furthermore, it is found that per capita income and health expenditure are found to be positively related to happiness. The results point to the need for sustainable development goals to be addressed within a holistic framework rather than independently, offering important implications for policymakers. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. title: When products speak: The effects of product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication on consumer responses to carted products
abstract: Shopping cart abandonment is a pervasive challenge in e-commerce, with more than 70% of online shopping carts failing to convert into purchases. In this context, this research examines whether and how anthropomorphic communication directed at carted products influences consumers' responses to shopping cart reminders. Across five experiments, we find converging evidence that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication enhances consumers' purchase-related responses to carted products. Study 1 shows that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication generates stronger responses than both non-anthropomorphic and brand-as-subject anthropomorphic communication, while Study 2 demonstrates that these effects are robust across different levels of pity conveyed in the message. Study 3 identifies state empathy and perceived interestingness as parallel mediators. Study 4 further demonstrates that these indirect effects are stronger among consumers with an emotional (vs. rational) decision-making style. Finally, Study 5 extends the findings to behavioral responses, showing that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication increases behavioral cart re-engagement and reduces consumers’ reported likelihood of cart abandonment. This research advances understanding of anthropomorphic communication in shopping cart contexts and offers actionable guidance for the design of shopping cart reminders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Organizational responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI versus human failures in government services
abstract: Existing research provides only limited insights into whether, compared to traditional human service failures, artificial intelligence (AI) failures in government services lead the public to attribute more responsibility to the service organization, and whether outsourcing necessarily alleviates organizational responsibility attribution. To advance this debate, this study conducted three pre-registered survey experiments. Study 1 (N = 1112) reveals that citizens attributed more responsibility to the service organization for AI service failures than to human service agents. The effect was mediated by the perceived service provider's controllability, rather than by counterfactual thinking. Study 2 proposed and tested two distinct pathways, namely the responsibility-transfer and controllability-transfer pathways. The objective was to explain how diminished controllability perceived at the individual service provider level increases the attribution of responsibility to the organization. Empirical evidence (N = 1084) supports the responsibility-transfer pathway. When citizens perceive that AI agents have less control over services than humans, they assign less responsibility to the AI agent and transfer more responsibility to the service organization. Study 3 (N = 1007) examines whether disclosing that the AI agent was externally developed mitigates the attribution of organizational responsibility. Compared to in-house AI systems, outsourcing to either a state-owned enterprise or a private enterprise, rather than to other government organizations, reduced organizational responsibility. In this study, this reduction was substantial enough to eliminate the disparity between AI and human service failures. This study advances theories of responsibility attribution in the digital era, highlighting the nuanced role of outsourcing transparency and the responsibility-transfer mechanism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Influencer beware: The buffering role of sponsor–influencer fit in the commercialization-authenticity trade-off
abstract: As social media influencers (SMIs) increasingly commercialize their online presence through sponsored content, understanding how sponsorship intensity shapes consumer responses has become important. Drawing on attribution and congruence theories and the entity-referent correspondence (ERC) framework, this study examines how sponsorship levels influence audience engagement and purchase intentions through perceived personal authenticity (PPA) and whether these effects depend on sponsor–SMI fit. Three experimental studies were conducted to test the proposed relationships. The results show that higher sponsorship levels reduce consumers’ intention to follow influencers and share their content. Sponsor–SMI fit attenuates the negative effect of sponsorship intensity on PPA. Thereby mitigating its adverse effects on consumer engagement and purchase intentions. We further demonstrate that sponsorship level affects consumer responses indirectly through PPA and that this indirect effect is contingent on sponsor–SMI fit. These findings advance the influencer marketing literature by applying the ERC framework to distinguish the different authenticity types and their impact on consumer behavior. The study also extends attribution and congruence theories by explaining how and when commercialization influences consumer responses and offers practical guidance for balancing monetization and authenticity in influencer marketing. © 2026 The Authors

label: Social Sciences
title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms
abstract: Amidst the crowded media environment and growing consumer disconnection from nature, leveraging biophilia - the innate human tendency to connect with nature - offers a compelling way for service firms to attract and engage consumers. Although biophilia in service environments has been studied, its comprehensive application in service-firm promotions - both direct and indirect - remains underexplored. This research advances service literature by examining the effects of direct and indirect biophilia in service advertising using schema congruity theory. Across two studies, we show that indirect biophilia led to more favorable ad evaluations compared to direct biophilia and no biophilia (control). Although direct biophilia is known for restorative effects, we show that indirect biophilia in service advertising (i.e., abstract depictions of natural scenes, nature-like materials, and color schemes) outperforms direct biophilia by eliciting perceived novelty and mystery, which in turn enhance ad evaluations and behavioral intentions. Furthermore, our findings indicate biophilia yields the greatest benefits when the service is conceptually aligned with nature.
